pages.abstract: The page discusses the economic profit power curve for 2024, showing that top-performing companies are expected to create most of the industry's value. It highlights the contributions of the top 1, 10, 20, and 50 companies, with the top 20 companies (Super Winners) contributing 89% of the economic profit. The data is based on H1 actuals and H2 analyst consensus from the McKinsey Global Fashion Index.
pages.title: However, top-performing companies are still expected to create most of the industry’s value

pages.abstract: The 2023 Super Winners list highlights luxury brands' dominance in economic profit, with LVMH leading significantly. Sportswear and department stores experienced shifts, with new entrants like Moncler and El Puerto de Liverpool, while others like JD Sports and Macy's fell off the list. The luxury segment saw record profits, while sportswear brands faced challenges. Further reshuffling is anticipated in 2024.
pages.title: Luxury tops the Super Winners list, while sportswear and department stores shift places

pages.abstract: Nikhil Thukral discusses L Catterton's strategies in identifying valuable companies amidst market challenges, emphasizing long-term value, brand identity, and pricing power. The firm tracks consumer behavior and leverages data to navigate economic shifts, focusing on brands like Birkenstock and Ganni. In 2025, these qualities will be crucial for separating leaders from laggards, especially in the luxury sector.
pages.title: L Catterton: Finding Value in a Tough Market

pages.abstract: The document discusses the evolving priorities of investors in fashion companies, emphasizing profitability and gross margin. It highlights the importance of understanding consumer behavior and brand DNA. The text also explores the changing dynamics of luxury and the rise of challenger brands, particularly in sportswear, and how consumer spending patterns are shifting towards experiences.
pages.title: For millennia, people have thought about their place in society based on what high-badge products do in terms of conferring that. The basic need we don’t think goes away.

pages.abstract: The document discusses how technology enables brands to activate consumer tribes cost-effectively, exemplified by What On's success against Nike. It also explores the impact of interest rate changes on investor strategies and the shift in business valuation focus towards sustainable profitability.
pages.title: The State of Fashion 2025

pages.abstract: The document discusses market dynamics, exit strategies, consumer behavior, and investment themes in the fashion industry. It highlights the importance of understanding consumer segments, the rise of the middle class in Asia, and the shift towards valuing experiences over traditional asset accumulation. It also emphasizes the need for omnichannel growth and the role of wholesalers in brand distribution.
pages.title: All cohorts of consumers, both older and younger, are increasingly valuing experiences over traditional asset accumulation.
Glossary

pages.abstract: This page provides definitions and explanations for various key terms and concepts in the fashion industry, covering topics such as artificial intelligence, sustainability, economic models, consumer behavior, and trade agreements. It aims to offer a comprehensive understanding of the industry's terminology and practices.
pages.title: Key Terms and Definitions in Fashion Industry
References
Contact Information for The Business of Fashion
Contact Information for McKinsey's Global Consumer Leadership Team

24.file_desc:
The authors express gratitude to various contributors from McKinsey and The Business of Fashion for their roles in creating the State of Fashion 2025 report, including survey participants, interviewees, and team members.
This page introduces key contributors to The State of Fashion 2025, detailing their roles, expertise, and contributions to the fashion industry. It highlights their backgrounds, professional experiences, and specific areas of focus within the industry.
The fashion industry faces significant challenges in 2025, including consumer price sensitivity, economic uncertainty, and regional disparities. Growth opportunities exist but require adaptability. Sluggish revenue growth is expected, with non-luxury driving economic profit. Geographic shifts in revenue drivers are also occurring, with Europe, the US, and Asia playing key roles.
The fashion industry is adapting to changing consumer priorities by localising go-to-market models, broadening price ranges, and focusing on brand positioning. Brands are also reevaluating consumer cohorts, with the 'Silver Generation' of over-50 customers becoming more significant. Improving the in-store shopping experience and leveraging AI for product discovery are key strategies. Supply chain agility, sustainability, and embracing new technologies are essential for future success.
This page introduces the industry outlook, focusing on the market share dynamics and how the game is leveling up. It highlights the evolving landscape and competitive shifts in the fashion industry.
The BoF-McKinsey State of Fashion 2025 Executive Survey reveals that uncertainty remains the dominant sentiment among fashion leaders. Only 20% expect conditions to improve in 2025, while 39% anticipate worsening conditions. Key concerns include consumer confidence, geopolitical instability, and economic volatility, with inflation becoming less of a concern as central banks lower interest rates.
The fashion industry is expected to experience low single-digit growth in 2025, with a structural deceleration following the post-pandemic boom. Brands will focus on capturing market share due to muted consumer confidence. Retail sales growth forecasts by geography and segment are provided for Europe, US, and China, showing varying growth rates for non-luxury and luxury segments.
The document outlines the macroeconomic challenges facing Europe, the US, and China, with projections for GDP growth and market growth in the luxury and non-luxury sectors. Europe faces economic uncertainty, while the US sees rising consumer power. China experiences a structural slowdown. Luxury demand varies by region, influenced by factors like consumer confidence and UHNWI population growth.
Fashion executives anticipate modest growth in 2025, driven by volume rather than price increases. A shift from price to volume growth is expected, with nearly two-thirds of executives predicting volume growth in the low single digits. Consumers' sensitivity to price hikes, especially among middle- and lower-income shoppers, is influencing this trend.
Fashion executives are prioritizing differentiation through localization, assortment variety, and AI innovation while reducing focus on cost improvements. Sustainability is less emphasized as executives seek growth opportunities. The biggest opportunities in 2024 and 2025 include sustainability objectives, AI leverage, and differentiation strategies.
The page discusses global economic shifts and consumer trends impacting the fashion industry, including trade reconfiguration, emerging growth in Asia, AI-driven product discovery, the rise of older consumers, and cost-conscious shopping behaviors.
This page discusses key trends in the fashion industry for 2025, including enhancing in-store experiences, challenges faced by online marketplaces, the rise of challenger sportswear brands, inventory management issues, and the need for collective sustainability efforts.
This page introduces the reconfiguration of trade, featuring an image of container ships at a port, symbolizing the evolving dynamics of global trade logistics.
Global trade is shifting due to political alignment, rising costs, and sustainability targets. Fashion brands will diversify sourcing in Asia and focus on nearshoring. Key insights include increased trade barriers, diversification of US imports away from China, and growth in nearshoring investments. Executive priorities involve assessing sourcing, collaborating with suppliers, and partnering with stakeholders for sustainability.
The page discusses the diversification of global trade sourcing and reduction in geopolitical distance of trade flows. It highlights the shift from a US-China-centric trade relationship to a multi-polar structure due to geopolitical tensions and market changes. Key points include the decrease in US imports from China, EU's efforts to diversify supply chains, and major economies reducing trade risks by aligning with geopolitically similar countries.
The document discusses the diversification of apparel and textile sourcing, highlighting a shift away from China towards other Asian markets and nearshoring. It details the percentage changes in imports for the US and Europe from 2019 to 2030E, emphasizing the decline in China's share and the rise of other regions. The text also explains the reasons behind this trend, including supply chain resilience, cost competitiveness, and nearshoring strategies.
The page discusses the impact of rising sourcing costs, tariffs, and sustainability targets on sourcing diversification. It highlights a 165% increase in Asia-to-US shipping costs, a 5x increase in trade restrictions, and 63% of fashion brands needing to accelerate emission reduction efforts. The text also mentions labor cost shifts, EU import duties, and investments in decarbonization.
Fashion brands are increasingly looking to Asian countries like India and Bangladesh for manufacturing due to their growing capabilities and incentives. India is expected to play a prominent role, with government investments and reforms. However, challenges in production and quality control persist. Bangladesh faces disruptions, leading to order shifts. The trend is expected to continue as Asia becomes a top sourcing hotspot.
Nearshoring interest has surged, with investments increasing in the US and Europe. Despite challenges like limited capacity and higher costs, nearshoring offers benefits such as improved productivity, faster lead times, and reduced environmental impact. Government incentives and strategic initiatives further support this trend.
Latin America is becoming a key nearshoring hub for US fashion companies due to advantageous trade agreements and cost-effective shipping routes. Turkey is emerging as a crucial sourcing location for European brands, offering reduced order-to-fulfilment times and increased supply chain traceability.
This page outlines executive priorities for flexible supply chains and close supplier relationships, emphasizing footprint assessment, strategic partnerships, and industry collaboration for efficiency, resilience, and sustainability.
A fashion show in Mumbai, featuring models in yellow floral outfits walking along a decorated runway, set against the backdrop of the Gateway of India, symbolizing Asia's growing influence in fashion.
This page discusses Asia's new growth engines in the fashion industry, highlighting India's strong growth and Japan's luxury market boom. It provides key insights and executive priorities for fashion executives to adapt to changing consumer preferences and market dynamics in Asia.
China's economy, now worth $18 trillion, is projected to grow by 4.5% in 2025, but this reflects a slowdown from previous years. The IMF forecasts a further decline to 3.3% by 2029. This economic deceleration impacts the fashion market, with apparel sales growth halving compared to 2019 levels. Consumer confidence and property transactions are at all-time lows, and the debt-to-GDP ratio has reached a historic high.
The non-luxury segment sees domestic brands gaining share, while the luxury segment faces a slowdown due to changing consumer preferences and government policies. Domestic brands in non-luxury grew by 6 percentage points from 2013 to 2023, while international brands declined. In the luxury market, despite some brands' growth, overall luxury spending in China slowed, with consumers shifting towards more affordable products and spending abroad projected to increase.
Fashion executives are optimistic about growth prospects in Asia, particularly India and Japan. The sentiment is especially high for mature APAC regions like Japan and Korea, and emerging markets like Indonesia and Thailand are also gaining prominence. The BoF-McKinsey survey shows a positive outlook for these regions in 2025.
India's fashion market is set to grow significantly, driven by a strong middle class and digitisation in non-luxury, and demographic and structural factors in luxury. The middle class is expected to reach 1 billion by 2050, while the UHNWI population is projected to grow 50% by 2028. Aspirational luxury consumers are also increasing, and new luxury malls are emerging in tier-one cities.
The document discusses the challenges and considerations for fashion brands entering the Indian market, including infrastructure limitations, the importance of local partners, unique consumer preferences, and regulatory requirements. It highlights the growth plans of brands like Mango, Decathlon, and Bulgari, and the need to adapt to regional nuances and cultural influences.
Japan's luxury market surged in 2024 due to yen depreciation, attracting global shoppers and boosting duty-free sales. Tourism also recovered, with a significant increase in visitors from various countries, contributing to the growth in tax-free shopping spend compared to 2019.
The Japanese luxury market is projected to grow between 8-12% by 2025, driven by both international and domestic demand. Brands are expanding their presence, and tourism spending is expected to reach $100 billion by 2030. Domestic sales are robust, supported by a growing number of ultra-high-net-worth individuals.
This page discusses the importance of a localised go-to-market strategy for fashion brands in Asia, highlighting the need to tailor product portfolios, supply chains, and marketing to local preferences. It also emphasizes the development of strong omnichannel propositions, leveraging both owned and third-party channels, with specific examples from China, India, and Japan.
Myntra, led by CEO Nandita Sinha, is a key player in India's fashion e-commerce market, targeting young, aspirational consumers. It leverages influencer content, premium offerings, and global sourcing to attract over 60 million monthly active users. The platform uses AI for styling services and collaborates with Bollywood celebrities, catering to Gen-Z trends and global fashion awareness.
India's unique combination of sourcing and consumption capacity makes it an attractive market for international fashion brands. E-commerce platforms like Myntra play a crucial role, with traditional and western wear both growing. Luxury and bridge-to-luxury brands are finding a place, with accessories and watches leading the luxury market. Gen-Z customers drive growth in affordable, trend-forward merchandise.
This page discusses the shopping behaviors of India's Gen-Z consumers, highlighting their increased purchase frequency and preference for digital and social media-driven shopping experiences. It also covers Myntra's strategies, including the use of influencers, short videos, and collaborations, to engage this demographic effectively.
India faces challenges in retail infrastructure and brand building, but technological innovations like AI-led product discovery and assistance tools are improving consumer engagement and business performance.
This page introduces the concept of 'Discovery Reinvented,' featuring a woman actively searching on a laptop, symbolizing modern methods of information discovery and innovation in digital exploration.
This page discusses the challenges faced by fashion shoppers due to overwhelming choices and introduces AI-powered solutions for brand and product discovery. It highlights key insights from fashion executives and customer preferences, emphasizing the role of AI in enhancing engagement and conversion rates. Executive priorities include building AI foundations, prioritizing high-value use cases, and implementing guidelines for AI use.
The page discusses how choice paralysis and search dissatisfaction negatively impact customer experience in online shopping. Retailers are addressing this by reducing product offerings and utilizing AI for better search results, though challenges remain.
The page discusses the potential of generative AI in fashion, highlighting product discovery as the top use case. It covers growing customer demand for AI-powered shopping, increased competitiveness in AI quality and cost, greater accuracy of AI tools, and emerging commercial success stories.
This page discusses industry shifts expected in 2025, focusing on AI-driven personalization in fashion search and content. It highlights the transition from non-personalized to highly personalized experiences, emphasizing contextual searches, real-time recommendations, and integrated social commerce journeys.
The page discusses how emerging AI challengers are redefining product search in the fashion industry. It highlights AI-powered shopping platforms like Daydream, which has onboarded over 2,000 brands and retailers, and AI-powered discovery partners like Capsule, which achieved a 99% match rate of user images with shoppable links. It also mentions Constructor’s AI product search, which has seen a 20x increase in return on investment for some brands. The page emphasizes the use of natural language, image recognition, and machine learning to enhance the online shopping experience.
Multi-brand retailers like Alibaba and Zalando are leveraging vast product data and AI technologies to enhance content curation. Alibaba's Wenwen chatbot improves click-through rates with personalized recommendations, while Zalando's AI assistant and generative AI tools enhance user experience and content relevance.
Social media is transforming fashion discovery and purchase, with social commerce markets in the US and UK expected to double by 2027. Predictive algorithms, content tools, and integrated shopping journeys are key drivers, with TikTok and Pinterest leading the way through AI and shoppable content.
Fashion players should adopt a value-focused approach to AI-enabled discovery by building AI foundations, prioritising value and accuracy, and managing risks and ethics. This involves embedding AI literacy, establishing a technology backbone, identifying tech partners, and optimising product data. It also requires applying a prioritisation framework, employing a test-and-learn approach, and consistently monitoring AI models to ensure customer trust and authenticity.
This page features an image of Jane Fonda on the L'Oréal Paris runway, highlighting the concept of 'Silver Spenders' and their influence in the fashion industry.
The page discusses the growing importance of the 'Silver Generation' in fashion sales, highlighting their significant contribution to global spending and wealth. It advises brands to rethink marketing strategies, assess product appeal, and establish KPIs to engage this demographic effectively.
The page discusses the challenges fashion brands face in targeting younger generations, highlighting Gen-Z's financial pressures, brand exploration tendencies, and feeling overwhelmed by brand exposure. Despite these challenges, Gen-Z remains a key focus for fashion brands.
The global population aged over 50 is growing faster than any other cohort due to longer life expectancies and declining birth rates. By 2050, this age group will represent more than a third of the global population. This trend is particularly strong in advanced economies like the US, China, and the EU5, where the share of the population aged over 50 will exceed 40% by 2050. Even in emerging markets like India, the older cohorts are expected to grow significantly.
The Silver Generation, with greater wealth and resilience, is driving significant global spending growth, particularly in fashion. Their higher disposable income and changing attitudes towards age stereotypes contribute to increased fashion expenditure compared to younger generations.
The Silver Generation prioritizes functionality, comfort, and value over trends and style. They are brand loyal, prefer timeless designs, and seek versatile products. Brands should focus on creating out-of-home experiences to capture their attention.
The Silver Generation prefers multi-brand retail stores for fashion shopping, is less likely to embrace omnichannel shopping, and is less inclined towards resale and sustainability-focused brands. They are more likely to seek inspiration in physical stores and use social media for fashion discovery in China.
This page discusses how brands like New Balance, J.Crew, and Uniqlo achieve inter-generational appeal through strategic branding, marketing, and product assortment. New Balance revives retro styles and collaborates with icons, J.Crew focuses on timeless designs and digital marketing, and Uniqlo emphasizes functional, high-quality pieces with technical features.
This page outlines executive priorities for brands targeting the Silver Generation, emphasizing the need to rethink customer segmentation, diversify product portfolios, and define data-driven channel strategies. It highlights the importance of leveraging data, offering innovative products, and adapting KPIs to ensure long-term ROI and customer loyalty.
J.Crew, an American retailer, is projected to hit record sales in 2024 under CEO Libby Wadle's leadership. Wadle and her team reversed the brand's decline by balancing product strategy and adapting to post-pandemic consumer behavior, without losing its core customer base.
J.Crew's turnaround strategy focuses on creative leadership, design excellence, and customer experience. The brand aims to balance heritage with modernity, appealing to multi-generational customers while inspiring new ones. Key actions included bringing in new design leaders and relaunching the catalogue. The core customer is style-focused and ageless, and the brand strives for timeless, ageless products.
J.Crew maintains a balance in design through customer data and product insights, offering heritage items in modern iterations. They adapt their supply chain for creative processes, using Italian fabrics with long lead times, and establish a dynamic cycle to react to business and world trends while preserving product integrity.
The document discusses the evolving role of distribution channels in reaching diverse customer segments, emphasizing the importance of store experiences and online convenience. It highlights the resurgence of catalogues as a storytelling tool and the significance of connecting with customers through meaningful brand experiences.
This page introduces the concept of a value shift, likely related to the changing value of secondhand clothes. It features an image of a person browsing through a rack of various secondhand clothing items, highlighting the shift in consumer preferences towards sustainable and affordable fashion options.
Macroeconomic pressures lead to cost-conscious shopping behaviors, with 64% of US shoppers trading down. Over 70% plan to buy from off-price retailers. Brands must emphasize value in communications and product strategy to capture customer wallets.
Fashion customers are increasingly looking to spend less and smarter, driven by low consumer confidence and economic uncertainty. Over 60% of consumers in the US and UK are trying to save money on fashion, with varying strategies across income levels, including trading down and seeking better value.
The page discusses how value-oriented consumer behaviors are likely to persist even as economies improve, with shoppers planning to spend the same or less on fashion. It highlights the prioritization of experiences and travel over fashion and the stickiness of value-seeking behavior. The survey data shows various behaviors consumers would continue even with more money, emphasizing cost-saving strategies.
Off-price retailers, including TJX and Ross, are experiencing significant revenue growth and profitability improvements, outpacing the broader market. This trend is driven by consumer demand for value and affordability. Traditional off-price retailers and e-commerce brands are both benefiting from this dynamic, with Zalando's B2C channel and BestSecret showing notable growth.
The resale market is rapidly growing, driven by consumers seeking value in secondhand apparel. By 2025, it is expected to account for 10% of the global apparel market. Brands like Sandro and Shein are capitalizing on this trend by offering resale programs and platforms, enhancing customer loyalty and attracting new users.
The pursuit of affordable alternatives, known as 'dupe mania,' has gained popularity among Gen-Z and nearly one third of US adults. Brands like Shein, Lululemon, and Quince have capitalized on this trend by promoting dupes through influencers, hosting pop-ups, and offering high-quality replicas at affordable prices. The #dupe hashtag on TikTok has nearly 6 billion views, and UK shoppers frequently buy dupes for savings or as great alternatives.
Brands must identify customer value drivers, communicate value effectively through campaigns and channels, and integrate value into their channel and product strategies to attract and retain value-conscious shoppers while maintaining brand equity.
Ralph Lauren has successfully pitched the idea of 'Ralph's World,' a preppy wonderland, to consumers at various price points. Despite higher prices, the brand remains popular, with busy stores and rising stock prices. However, it now faces challenges due to global economic factors, and is focusing on storytelling and core products for longevity.
The document discusses the strategy of brand elevation through storytelling, product quality, and shopping experience, aiming to connect with diverse consumer groups from the ultra-rich to aspirational buyers. It emphasizes the importance of value, timeless style, and a unique brand experience across all touchpoints.
The document discusses the evolution of stores and consumer engagement strategies, emphasizing brand-cultural moments, direct-to-consumer focus, and the integration of technology and lifestyle experiences in retail.
This page discusses Ralph Lauren's strategy in China's luxury market, emphasizing core products, brand recognition, and long-term growth potential. It highlights the company's focus on iconic items, consumer trust, and strategic category expansion, while addressing market challenges and opportunities.
This page highlights the human side of sales, focusing on the interaction between a sales assistant and a customer in a clothing store. It emphasizes the personal and relational aspects of sales, showcasing a collaborative moment where the assistant assists the customer in selecting an item.
This page discusses the importance of enhancing the in-store experience through empowering store associates, highlighting key insights and executive priorities for improving customer and employee satisfaction.
The page discusses the importance of maximizing customer engagement in stores as in-store sales growth slows in 2025. It highlights the need for high-quality service and staff engagement to prevent missed sales and emphasizes the evolving role of stores in the digital age.
Store associates significantly influence shopper satisfaction and loyalty. Human interactions, like styling advice and assistance, are key differentiators, boosting conversion and delight. Non-human elements, such as store atmosphere and checkout efficiency, are essential but do not differentiate experiences. Younger and aspirational shoppers value human interactions more.
This page highlights the critical challenges of human capital in the retail sector, emphasizing the high turnover rate, rising costs, and customer dissatisfaction due to poorly trained staff. It discusses the labor shortage, wage growth, and the financial impact of losing employees, urging retailers to address these issues to retain associates and improve store experiences.
This page discusses the importance of upskilling store staff and investing in tech support tools to enhance customer interactions. It highlights the need for efficient training methods like AI-powered learning and micro-learning. The page also emphasizes the role of digital tools in facilitating omnichannel sales and improving customer engagement through CRM technologies. Case studies from Reiss, Aritzia, Kering, and Target illustrate successful implementations of these strategies.
Employee incentives should focus on customer lifetime value and modern shopping habits. Examples include Frasers Group's employee festivals and awards, Dior's performance-based points for tailored experiences, and Nordstrom's Style Board emails for digital sales commissions. These incentives enhance employee satisfaction and align with meaningful work aspects.
Retailers are adopting data-driven staff deployment and leveraging technology like RFID to streamline manual tasks, enhancing customer satisfaction and operational efficiency. Examples include Aritzia's data-informed scheduling, Faherty's gig staffing, BJ’s Wholesale's automated inventory tasks, and Uniqlo's RFID self-checkout.
Retailers should prioritize career development and compensation to improve employee retention. Employees value career growth, inspiring leadership, and meaningful work. High employee satisfaction leads to better customer experience and reduced turnover costs.
This page outlines executive priorities for retailers to develop an end-to-end employee value proposition, including enabling staff with training and tools, motivating store associates with broader incentive structures, optimising processes for high-value activities, and retaining employees through coaching and one-to-one interactions.
Aritzia, a Canadian retailer, experienced hypergrowth post-pandemic due to its minimalist wardrobe staples and CEO Jennifer Wong's strategic retail and employee development programs. With 124 locations, Aritzia emphasizes customer service, premium real estate, and a tight product strategy.
This page discusses Aritzia's retail strategy, emphasizing personalized customer service, store format evolution, and the importance of location and in-store experience. It highlights the role of style advisors in building relationships and the impact of visual merchandising on customer engagement.
The page discusses the sales associate recruitment and retention process at Aritzia, highlighting the opportunities for growth, the rewarding work environment, and the company's commitment to promoting from within.
The page discusses Aritzia's employee retention strategies during Covid-19, retail expansion plans in the US, and the factors contributing to its growth, including product innovation, store experience, technology, and infrastructure investment.
This page illustrates the disruption in marketplaces, specifically focusing on the shift towards mobile shopping. A woman is depicted browsing and purchasing clothes through a mobile app, highlighting the convenience and accessibility of online marketplaces.
Non-luxury marketplaces face significant challenges post-Covid-19, with share prices plummeting. Europe's online fashion marketplaces suffered substantial economic losses. Despite Amazon's resilience in the US value segment, department stores and fashion pure-players are adapting. China's social commerce and low-cost players are thriving. Executive priorities include enhancing assortment, customer lifetime value, profitability, tech modernisation, and cost efficiency.
Online fashion marketplaces face challenges due to increased customer acquisition costs, high return rates, and production complexity. Consumers demand flexible experiences and tech upgrades, impacting growth expectations and requiring strategic investments.
The first wave of online marketplaces experienced a surge in stock prices due to inflated valuations during the Covid-19 pandemic but have since faced sharp declines. Specialised fashion players are particularly vulnerable, while diversified companies like Zalando have managed better. Investors now prioritize profitability over sales growth, impacting unprofitable businesses like Asos and Boohoo.
European online fashion marketplaces face challenges from low-cost competitors and traditional retailers. McKinsey data shows significant value destruction in 2023. To adapt, marketplaces are focusing on profitable orders, exploring new value pools, building scale, and leveraging generative AI. These strategies aim to enhance profitability and competitive positioning in the evolving fashion landscape.
Amazon Fashion dominates the US online fashion market with over 40% of total revenue in 2023, while Shein and Temu face challenges. Mid-market and premium segments remain fragmented, with department stores and fashion pure-players expanding their reach.
The page discusses the importance of social and live commerce in China's online fashion market, highlighting the competition between traditional platforms and social platforms. It emphasizes the need for brands to manage profitability with livestreamers and balance branded and value items. The growth of monthly active users for major platforms is also presented.
This page outlines five key actions for first-wave marketplaces to ensure longevity: making assortment competitive, maximising customer lifetime value, creating new profitability avenues, modernising tech and talent, and leveraging AI for cost reduction. Each action includes specific strategies to enhance competitiveness, customer engagement, and operational efficiency.
Mytheresa, under CEO Michael Klider, has become a leader in online luxury retail by focusing on top-spending customers and innovating. Despite a sector-wide slowdown, the company remains profitable and is acquiring Yoox-Net-a-Porter to strengthen its position. Klider anticipates a slow but steady recovery in 2025 and emphasizes the importance of customer loyalty and strategic expansion.
The document discusses the challenges faced by luxury e-commerce, particularly in China, and the expectation of continued stabilization in the sector. It highlights the importance of economic growth, women's participation in the workforce, and regulatory permits for emerging growth opportunities. It also emphasizes the need to understand customer desires and redefine luxury in the digital age.
Mytheresa employs a mix of in-person events, digital marketing, and strategic advertising to acquire and retain high-value customers. They focus on building customer loyalty through personalized experiences and product recommendations, emphasizing the importance of customer satisfaction in driving repeat business.
The document discusses strategies for luxury e-tailers like Mytheresa to maintain dominance in a competitive market. It emphasizes the importance of operational excellence, full-price selling, excellent customer service, and strategic marketing to ensure profitability and customer loyalty. The text also addresses the challenges of managing costs and maintaining brand partnerships in an evolving retail landscape.
This page showcases a tennis player in a sportswear showdown, highlighting the player's attire and action during a match. The sportswear includes a white headband, a white long-sleeve shirt under a white short-sleeve shirt, and a white short. The player is captured mid-swing, hitting a tennis ball with a racket against a green background.
The sportswear market is witnessing a significant shift with challenger brands expected to dominate economic profits by 2024. Key insights highlight the rapid growth of sportswear compared to the broader fashion market, with specific regional data. Executive priorities emphasize innovation, marketing, partnerships, and strategic distribution to enhance brand presence and profitability.
Challenger sportswear brands are projected to surpass incumbent brands in economic profit by 2024, driven by faster revenue growth and improved profitability. This trend is supported by data showing challengers' increasing market share and economic profit compared to incumbents from 2018 to 2024.
Challenger brands have successfully expanded market share by delivering visible innovations, targeting specialised categories, tapping into cultural marketing, and filling wholesale whitespace. They have reimagined running footwear, tailored offerings for niche sports, leveraged celebrity culture, and capitalised on the shift in distribution channels.
Sportswear is projected to grow faster than the overall fashion market in 2025, driven by health and wellness trends, increased sports content access, and generational shifts. Key regions like China, the US, and Europe will see significant growth, with China leading at 5-6 percentage points. The global sports tourism sector is also expected to grow by 18% by 2030.
The document discusses the competitive landscape in the sportswear market, highlighting significant stock performance gains by challengers like Asics, On, and Deckers. Incumbents, except for Adidas, have faced challenges. The need for incumbents to innovate in product, marketing, and channel strategies is emphasized.
Brands diversify their offerings to balance customer reach and cultural credibility. Performance and athleisure brands expand into new categories, while material and product innovations are crucial for building credibility. Fewer breakthrough innovations have emerged, but Nike leads in patents. The global fanbase for racket sports has grown significantly.
The sports sponsorship market is growing, with athletes partnering with smaller brands for more control. Brands are focusing on credible spokespeople and incorporating cultural elements into marketing. Examples include Zendaya with On, Rosé with Puma, and Adidas' local initiatives in China.
Sportswear brands are balancing DTC and wholesale strategies. DTC focuses on customer experience and community building, while wholesale aims to increase reach and brand presence. Retailers are expanding stores and diversifying brand offerings to attract more customers.
Brands should focus on product innovation, effective marketing strategies, and authentic partnerships to gain market share. They should invest in breakthrough innovations, diversify product offerings, and reintroduce styles. Marketing should convey innovation benefits clearly and target credible channels. Partnerships should be built with emerging athletes, celebrities, and local communities. A distribution strategy with distinct channel roles is crucial for customer engagement and profitability.
New Balance, aiming for $10 billion in sales, discusses its unique brand and athlete partnership strategies, focusing on innovation and maintaining strong relationships with partners to stay ahead in the sneaker market.
New Balance emphasizes controlling its destiny by staying close to consumers, understanding shopping trends, and delivering products at the intersection of sport and fashion. As a private company, it focuses on long-term strategies, domestic manufacturing for quality control, and innovation through investments in manufacturing and product innovation centers. It leverages its archive for authentic retro designs, ensuring innovation and performance.
This page discusses the importance of authenticity in brand DNA, the competitive sneaker market, and the strategic balance between product quantity and sales maximization. It highlights the role of analytical teams and market understanding in managing the dynamic retail landscape.
New Balance discusses its strategy of balancing direct-to-consumer sales with wholesale partnerships, emphasizing shared values and bespoke approaches in collaborations. The brand aims to be a premium sports brand by aligning with partners who share its vision.
The page illustrates inventory excellence through a woman working in a warehouse, emphasizing the importance of efficient inventory management and handling.
The page discusses the challenges of inventory management in the fashion industry, emphasizing the need for end-to-end planning excellence, tech adoption, and agile supply chains. It highlights key insights on excess stock and discount trends and outlines executive priorities for breaking down silos, incentivizing inventory excellence, and leveraging technology.
The fashion industry faces unique inventory challenges due to rapid trend cycles, unpredictable seasonality, lengthy supply chains, and product/channel complexity, making it increasingly difficult for brands to manage seasonal stock and meet consumer demands.
Fashion brands face significant challenges with excess stock and stock-outs, leading to financial losses and missed revenue opportunities. In 2023, the industry produced 2.5-5 billion excess garments, with excess stock valued between $70 billion and $140 billion. In 2024, despite stable inventory levels, many brands struggled with inventory management. Luxury brands saw inventory increases, and major companies like LVMH and Kering reported substantial excess inventory. Brands resorted to discounting, affecting profitability. Stock-outs due to inaccurate purchasing and forecasting resulted in up to 20% monthly profit loss.
Brands are prioritising profitability by optimising inventories due to flat sales and increased markdowns. Sustainability regulations, such as the EU's Ecodesign for Sustainable Products and California's Extended Producer Responsibility, are adding pressure to reduce over-production and waste. Managing inventory effectively can help brands achieve sustainability targets and maintain profitability.
Fashion brands are adopting proactive tactics like data-driven planning, dynamic open-to-buy adjustments, and network optimisation using tech tools to improve inventory management. These strategies aim to reduce inventory levels, enhance forecasting accuracy, and control stock risk, with significant investments in digital intelligence expected by 2025.
This page discusses the need for end-to-end collaboration across the value chain to achieve sustained impact in inventory management. It highlights the inefficiencies of isolated solutions and emphasizes the importance of breaking down silos, setting up cross-functional teams, establishing clear review cadences, aligning incentive structures, and connecting systems for better inventory performance.
This page outlines executive priorities for brands to adapt to change through an updated operating model and mindset shift. It emphasizes embedding collaborative processes, widening accountability for inventory levels, and leveraging technology-enabled tools for better decision-making and data transparency.
This page introduces 'The Sustainability Collective,' featuring an image of wind turbines, symbolizing sustainable energy solutions and collective efforts towards environmental conservation.
The fashion industry faces significant sustainability challenges, with many brands lagging on decarbonisation goals and low prioritisation of sustainability risks. Collective action is essential to address these issues, focusing on dual mission commitments, supplier consolidation, and data-driven traceability.
The page discusses barriers to sustainability in the fashion industry, including high investment costs, fragmented supply chains, and consumer behavior inconsistencies. It highlights the economic and operational challenges, the complexity of supplier and brand fragmentation, and the disconnect between consumer actions and values regarding sustainable fashion.
The page discusses the challenges faced by brands, suppliers, and innovators in the fashion industry regarding sustainability. Many brands are scaling back their sustainability commitments, and suppliers are struggling to meet science-based targets due to feasibility and costs. Sustainable innovations face difficulties in scaling due to financing and volume requirements. The graph illustrates the yearly reduction in scope-three emission intensity across fashion brands, showing that many brands need to accelerate their efforts to meet 2030 targets.
The fashion industry must act swiftly to address rising apparel consumption and carbon emissions. Brands can achieve cost-effective decarbonisation through sustainability levers, supplier collaboration, and material innovation, reducing waste and overproduction while sharing costs and risks.
This page discusses the importance of long-term brand-supplier collaboration in reducing industry emissions, highlighting key strategies for brands to consolidate supplier relationships, embrace long-term commitments, and address industry bottlenecks. It also presents case studies of H&M Group, Bestseller, CIP, the Future Supplier Initiative, and PVH Corp. in their efforts to promote sustainability through renewable energy projects and financing initiatives.
Brands can foster sustainable-material innovation by making bold investments, de-risking commercial prospects, and building in-house expertise. Examples include H&M's partnership with Syre for polyester recycling and Inditex's collaboration with Ambercycle for next-gen materials.
Brands can reignite progress by focusing on sustainability initiatives, rethinking supplier contracts, and getting granular on data. This involves adopting a dual mission, shifting to a collective model, committing to commercialisation, embedding new supplier sourcing processes, ensuring decarbonisation adherence, consolidating suppliers, partnering with traceability providers, and mapping the entire value chain.
The fashion industry's economic profit is reaching record levels, but market dynamics are shifting. Luxury players are losing ground to non-luxury brands, with the gap between top and bottom performers at its smallest since 2011. Key insights include a 16% growth in economic profit from 2022 to 2023, with expectations of record-high levels in 2024. However, the luxury segment faces margin pressure, while non-luxury brands, especially sportswear and mall brands, show strong profitability. The top 20% of players are expected to lose value, while the bottom 20% gain, closing the performance gap.
The fashion industry is projected to achieve record economic profit in 2024, driven by margin improvements and revenue growth. The McKinsey Global Fashion Index (MGFI) tracks financial growth and value creation through economic profit (EP), which is expected to stabilize at 2.8x pre-Covid levels. The industry's focus on profitability has led to significant margin gains, resulting in disproportionate value creation.
The fashion industry has seen record-high economic profit (EP) but investor uncertainty about future value creation has led to lower valuations. Companies need compelling strategies and narratives for sustainable growth. Luxury valuations are slightly higher in 2024 compared to 2022, while non-luxury valuations continue to decline.
The non-luxury segment is driving value creation in the fashion industry, with a significant shift from luxury. This trend is expected to continue, with non-luxury contributing more to economic profit than luxury in the coming years.
The document discusses how consumer downtrading is impacting the luxury and non-luxury fashion markets. Luxury brands face challenges due to pricing and demand, while non-luxury brands, especially in the mid-market, are expected to see improved profitability. The data shows economic profit trends across different market segments from 2021 to 2024, highlighting shifts in consumer behavior and market performance.
The document discusses the impact of cost cuts and operational improvements on EBITA margins across different fashion segments. Luxury margins are expected to decline, while non-luxury segments, including premium/bridge and mid-market, have seen record-high margins. Specific examples include Inditex's inventory reduction, Levi Strauss & Co.'s cost savings, and Zalando's margin growth. The affordable luxury and value/discount segments are expected to see margin growth but remain below historical peaks.
In 2024, the luxury segment faces challenges with 77% of companies expecting negative EP growth due to plateauing revenues and reduced margins. The remaining 23% anticipate modest positive EP growth driven by revenue increases, though overall EP growth remains limited.
In 2024, non-luxury segments will focus on profitability, leading to more evenly distributed value creation. Super Winners like Inditex and Fast Retailing will continue driving EP growth, while Mall Brands and Sportswear challengers improve performance. Pure online marketplaces face disruptions but show early signs of improvement.
Mall brands are undergoing transformations to boost profitability and investor confidence. Gap is enhancing its image, American Eagle Outfitters is regaining momentum with operational improvements, and Abercrombie & Fitch is targeting a broader audience. These efforts are expected to drive economic profit growth in the non-luxury segment.
The gap between top and bottom performers in the fashion industry is narrowing, with bottom performers improving and top performers, particularly in luxury, declining. The top 20% of companies' contribution to economic profit is expected to decrease by 13 percentage points from 2022 to 2024, while the bottom 20% is expected to increase by 13 points.
The page discusses the economic profit power curve for 2024, showing that top-performing companies are expected to create most of the industry's value. It highlights the contributions of the top 1, 10, 20, and 50 companies, with the top 20 companies (Super Winners) contributing 89% of the economic profit. The data is based on H1 actuals and H2 analyst consensus from the McKinsey Global Fashion Index.
The 2023 Super Winners list highlights luxury brands' dominance in economic profit, with LVMH leading significantly. Sportswear and department stores experienced shifts, with new entrants like Moncler and El Puerto de Liverpool, while others like JD Sports and Macy's fell off the list. The luxury segment saw record profits, while sportswear brands faced challenges. Further reshuffling is anticipated in 2024.
Nikhil Thukral discusses L Catterton's strategies in identifying valuable companies amidst market challenges, emphasizing long-term value, brand identity, and pricing power. The firm tracks consumer behavior and leverages data to navigate economic shifts, focusing on brands like Birkenstock and Ganni. In 2025, these qualities will be crucial for separating leaders from laggards, especially in the luxury sector.
The document discusses the evolving priorities of investors in fashion companies, emphasizing profitability and gross margin. It highlights the importance of understanding consumer behavior and brand DNA. The text also explores the changing dynamics of luxury and the rise of challenger brands, particularly in sportswear, and how consumer spending patterns are shifting towards experiences.
The document discusses how technology enables brands to activate consumer tribes cost-effectively, exemplified by What On's success against Nike. It also explores the impact of interest rate changes on investor strategies and the shift in business valuation focus towards sustainable profitability.
The document discusses market dynamics, exit strategies, consumer behavior, and investment themes in the fashion industry. It highlights the importance of understanding consumer segments, the rise of the middle class in Asia, and the shift towards valuing experiences over traditional asset accumulation. It also emphasizes the need for omnichannel growth and the role of wholesalers in brand distribution.
This page provides definitions and explanations for various key terms and concepts in the fashion industry, covering topics such as artificial intelligence, sustainability, economic models, consumer behavior, and trade agreements. It aims to offer a comprehensive understanding of the industry's terminology and practices.

pages.title: McKinsey on the Maritime Industry
Contents
Contents (continued)

pages.abstract: This introduction highlights the global shipbuilding industry's significance in trade and its challenges, including technological advancements, geopolitical tensions, and workforce transitions. It discusses opportunities for shipyards to modernize and integrate Industry 4.0 technologies while addressing decarbonization and talent acquisition.
pages.title: Introduction

pages.abstract: The American shipbuilding industry faces challenges like aging infrastructure and talent shortages. By leveraging untapped domestic capacity, the industry can accelerate growth and meet escalating demand.
pages.title: Charting a new course: The untapped potential of American shipyards

pages.abstract: American shipbuilding faces a critical inflection point due to increased demand from the US Navy and AUKUS partnership. Despite challenges like talent gaps and outdated models, the US has latent shipbuilding capacity. To meet demand, shipbuilders should rebuild the workforce, reenergize shipyards, modernize digital systems, align culture around performance, and engage in strategic economic development.
pages.title: American shipbuilding has reached a critical inflection point

pages.abstract: The document projects changes in maritime manufacturing employment across various subindustries from 2022 to 2032. It highlights that key maritime trades will experience job displacement due to increased demand in battery and semiconductor production. While some sectors like electrical equipment and computer products will see job gains, others such as apparel and fabricated metal products will face significant job losses. Overall, there is an expected net loss of 39,000 jobs in key maritime trades but a gain of 33,000 jobs in adjacent industries.
pages.title: Key maritime manufacturing trades will be displaced by higher demand from battery and semiconductor production.

pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of talent acquisition and retention in shipbuilding, emphasizing the use of analytics to improve hiring and reduce attrition. It also highlights the need to reenergize existing shipyard infrastructure by addressing bottlenecks and improving operational efficiency.
pages.title: Shipbuilding Talent and Shipyard Footprint

pages.abstract: This page discusses two key levers for shipbuilders to optimize their existing facilities: lean improvements and targeted capital investments. It emphasizes the importance of reducing complexity, improving operational discipline, and integrating digital systems to enhance transparency and performance. Examples of successful lean initiatives and digital interventions are provided, highlighting the need for cross-functional coordination and data integration to avoid inefficiencies and bottlenecks.
pages.title: Two levers can help shipbuilders get the most out of their existing footprints

pages.abstract: This page discusses digital transformation in shipbuilding, focusing on digital supplier management, performance management, and value stream management. It highlights the importance of aligning organizational culture and metrics with performance goals to enhance efficiency and collaboration.
pages.title: Digital Transformation in Shipbuilding

pages.abstract: This page discusses the organizational health of advanced industrial companies, particularly shipbuilders, showing that 70% have lower health scores than the global median. It highlights the need for shipbuilders to reorganize around value, reset culture, and engage in strategic economic development through collaboration and investment in centers of excellence.
pages.title: Seventy percent of advanced industrial companies, including shipbuilders, have lower organizational health scores than the global median.

pages.abstract: The American shipbuilding industry faces challenges but has opportunities for growth through workforce initiatives, supplier partnerships, and strategic investments. Addressing employee well-being and leveraging existing industrial base capabilities are crucial for sustainable economic outcomes and future success.
pages.title: The American shipbuilding industry's challenges and opportunities

pages.abstract: The aerospace and defense industry faces labor shortages and rising demand. Addressing five talent imperatives can enhance productivity and create value.
pages.title: The talent gap: The value at stake for global aerospace and defense

pages.abstract: The global aerospace and defense sector is experiencing a talent gap due to low unemployment rates, aging workforce, and mismatched skill priorities. Employers face challenges in recruiting, retaining, and reskilling talent, impacting performance. Closing this gap could yield significant cost savings and competitive advantages for A&D companies.
pages.title: The global aerospace and defense (A&D) sector is booming

pages.abstract: This page discusses the mismatch between aerospace and defense employers and employees regarding the most important skills. It highlights geographical differences in employee value propositions and the need for regional strategies to address the talent gap. The page also emphasizes the importance of organizational health and performance management in closing the talent gap and improving productivity.
pages.title: Aerospace and defense employers and employees are not on the same page when it comes to the skills they deem most important.

pages.abstract: This page discusses the top employee experience factors for aerospace and defense employees in the US and Europe, highlighting differences in why they join, stay, and leave. It also identifies skill, will, and time gaps affecting productivity and emphasizes the need for companies to address these issues to reduce attrition and vacancy rates.
pages.title: Aerospace and defense employees in Europe and the United States value different aspects of the employee experience during their careers.

pages.abstract: The talent gap in aerospace and defense companies can cost $300-330 million annually due to lack of skills, engagement, inefficiency, and attrition. Addressing these issues through coordinated talent management involving HR can mitigate productivity losses.
pages.title: The talent gap could cost a median-size aerospace and defense company $300 million to $330 million a year.

pages.abstract: Leading aerospace and defense companies are taking five critical actions to maximize talent return and value capture. These include understanding talent needs, establishing a hiring engine, focusing on high-return learning, managing talent culture, and transforming HR. They address evolving skills pools, forecast labor needs, and build strategic hiring plans. HR is becoming a strategic partner, and companies are creating 'talent win rooms' for streamlined hiring. Reskilling existing employees is prioritized for high ROI, with a focus on outcomes and strategic alignment.
pages.title: Leading aerospace and defense companies follow five critical actions to maximize their return on talent and capture the value at stake.

pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of managing talent and culture in the A&D sector to improve performance and employee experience. It highlights the need for HR to evolve and adopt new strategies, including upskilling employees and leveraging gen AI for administrative tasks. The page also emphasizes the challenges and opportunities in talent management as the sector faces workforce dynamics and aging employees.
pages.title: Managing talent and culture to propel performance and experience

pages.title: Identifying the true constraints underlying production delays helps leaders determine what to address during legacy site redesign.

pages.title: Rigorous site redevelopment strategies

pages.abstract: The evolving global security environment is driving increased defense spending, with NATO aiming for 2% GDP spending and APAC countries like Japan and South Korea boosting their naval budgets. Collaboration between the naval industry and navies is crucial to address evolving needs and challenges like talent shortages.
pages.title: Key developments shaping the global naval market

pages.abstract: The document discusses the significant increase in global conflicts between 2010 and 2022, the changing public perception of security risks, challenges faced by navies in maintaining mission readiness, and the impact of technological advancements on naval operations.
pages.title: Changing global threat perceptions

The naval market is expected to grow, with a shift towards the APAC region.
pages.title: Compared with 2021, the public’s perception of risk is still significantly higher, especially in the G-7.

pages.abstract: The document discusses the projected growth in the naval market, highlighting the Asia-Pacific region's above-average growth, followed by Europe. Frigates and corvettes are identified as the largest submarket in surface vessels. The implications for the naval industry include evolving customer needs and new market dynamics, urging shipbuilders to consider strategic decisions.
pages.title: Asia-Pacific shows above-average market growth, followed by Europe.

pages.abstract: The document discusses the projected growth of the conventional submarine market, reaching €10 billion by 2033. The text also emphasizes the importance of offering affordable solutions to address funding pressures in naval acquisition, balancing various priorities such as fleet modernization and talent attraction.
pages.title: Conventional submarines will reach a market volume of €10 billion in 2033.

pages.abstract: The document discusses the largest sub-segment of the surface vessel market, focusing on frigates and corvettes. The text emphasizes the importance of standardization and economies of scale in the industry.
pages.title: Frigates and corvettes are the largest sub segment within the surface market.

pages.abstract: The document discusses the challenges faced by incumbent shipbuilders in the international naval export market due to new types of competitors. It outlines strategies for incumbents to remain competitive, including leveraging local partnerships, acquiring shipyards in export markets, and focusing on new capabilities in electronics and unmanned technology. The text also highlights the importance of improving shipyard operations through digitalization to address delays and cost overruns.
pages.title: Staying competitive amid new players in the international naval export market

pages.abstract: Vertical integration can enhance shipbuilders' value capture and efficiency by consolidating operations. Deploying digital operating models and digital twins can streamline shipbuilding processes, reduce errors, and predict faults. Digitalizing general and administrative functions can further drive cost savings and efficiency.
pages.title: Vertical integration: An alternative approach to capturing value

pages.abstract: The page discusses strategies for addressing naval asset shortages through collaboration between navies and industry, including innovative maintenance solutions, digital twins, 3D printing at sea, and remote maintenance support. It also highlights the importance of addressing critical skills shortages in the naval industry through digitalization and automation.
pages.title: Collaborating with industry stakeholders to address naval asset shortages

pages.abstract: The naval market is transforming with expanding budgets and demand for advanced vessels. Opportunities for shipbuilders lie in adapting and innovating through digitalization, automation, and partnerships. Cohort-based training and retention efforts can address labor shortages. Successful innovators will thrive in this dynamic market.
pages.title: Naval Industry Transformation and Opportunities

This page serves as an introduction to the executive summary section of the document.
This page discusses the challenges and opportunities in China's retail market, emphasizing the need for digital transformation. It highlights key trends, retailer struggles, and the importance of organizational redesign for successful digitalization.
This white paper discusses China's retail industry's digital transformation, highlighting the challenges and opportunities brought by COVID-19 and omni-channel expansion. It emphasizes the need for a fundamental transformation in digital thinking and technology across business units to achieve significant earnings growth. The paper also presents research on the current state of digitalization among China's retailers and analyzes major trends reshaping Chinese retail, providing digital solutions for various retail formats.
This chapter discusses the current state of digital transformation in China's retail industry, highlighting its progress and challenges. It provides insights into how technology is reshaping retail operations and consumer experiences.
The page details four stages of digital transformation in retail, from IT infrastructure upgrades to platform-based ecosystem building, highlighting the current focus on online operations and digital intelligence among Chinese retailers.
The majority of retailers focus on front-end digital capabilities, with 70% prioritizing online channels and omni-channel membership. Digital marketing and supply chain are also significant areas of focus. However, challenges remain in digitalizing the mid and back-end of the value chain. Retailers are heavily investing in digital transformation, but the return on investment is unclear.
Retailers prioritize digital transformation, with 94% considering it a top strategic initiative. 79% expect it to drive significant growth, and 76% anticipate cost savings. However, 45% face challenges with uncertain ROI, especially in online channels.
Chinese retailers face challenges in digital transformation due to unclear strategies, talent shortages, uncertain ROI, rigid processes, and low employee awareness. The analysis of various retail sectors aims to provide best practices for successful digitalization.
This chapter discusses four significant trends that are reshaping the Chinese retail landscape, focusing on the impact of digitalization and technological advancements.
The page discusses the widening scope of digital transformation in China's retail market as growth slows. It highlights declining profits and the shift towards leaner operations. The 'traffic dividend' era is concluded, with early digital adopters facing challenges. Retailers are now focusing on improving core competitiveness and refining omni-channel operations.
The page discusses the challenges and strategies retailers face in adapting to changing consumer behaviors, emphasizing the need for quality merchandise, detailed assortment and pricing strategies, and embracing multiple roles in retail stores to enhance customer experiences.
This page discusses the evolving roles of retail stores in the digital age, emphasizing the need for digital transformation to enhance consumer experiences, support omni-channel operations, optimize 'last mile' delivery, and deliver value-added services. It highlights the importance of store layout, staff roles, and customer-centric strategies.
This chapter discusses the market challenges faced by the retail industry and the role of digitalization in addressing these challenges. It highlights the importance of adapting to digital trends to remain competitive in the evolving retail landscape.
This section discusses the challenges facing hypermarkets and supermarkets in China, including consumer fragmentation, low profitability, and rising costs. It highlights the need for digital transformation to address these issues and mentions the flat growth of hypermarkets and pressure on revenues and profits for supermarkets. The text also refers to McKinsey surveys revealing the triple challenges of consumer base fragmentation, online profitability issues, and rising operating costs.
The document details the market size and CAGR of China's hypermarket and supermarket sectors from 2018 to 2021, showing a 2.6% annual growth. It highlights consumer fragmentation due to weak value propositions and alternative options, with the market experiencing polarized consumption trends and challenges in supply-side innovation.
The document discusses the challenges faced by traditional hypermarkets and supermarkets due to fragmented grocery formats and channels. It highlights three shifts in consumer preferences: polarized consumption, heightened demand for hyper-convenience, and diversified purchasing occasions. These shifts require hypermarkets and supermarkets to adapt by engaging consumers through omni-channel strategies.
This page discusses the challenges faced by hypermarkets and supermarkets, including issues with convenience, cost performance, product strengths, service, and experience. It highlights the difficulties in competing with new retail enterprises and the concerns regarding omni-channel expansion and rising operating costs.
This page discusses digital transformation strategies for hypermarkets and supermarkets, focusing on differentiating value propositions, improving omni-channel fulfillment, and deploying user operations across channels to maximize customer value. It highlights the importance of flexible delivery options, smaller store formats, and data-driven customer segmentation.
This page discusses strategies for traditional hypermarkets and supermarkets to achieve user operations goals, including attracting new customers, increasing ATV, stimulating repurchases, and improving customer loyalty. It emphasizes the importance of leveraging data, enhancing upstream control, tapping into private-brand value, and adopting data-driven intelligent product selection to elevate the appeal of stores and products.
This page discusses strategies for reducing store operating costs in key business areas for hypermarkets and supermarkets, focusing on refining fresh product operations, sales volume forecasts, digitalized product ratings, sales progress monitoring, promotion optimization, intelligent loss identification, and efficient inventory management. It also touches on reducing fulfillment costs for D2D business.
The page discusses integrated store-warehouse and dark store models, highlighting their advantages and disadvantages. It emphasizes the importance of unified inventory management and reducing labor costs through digitalized labor management. Examples of using algorithmic insights for scheduling labor and increasing order-picking efficiency are provided.
This page discusses strategies for improving supply chain efficiency in hypermarkets and supermarkets, including integrated omni-channel systems, advanced automation technology, and cross-department decision-making mechanisms to reduce costs and enhance customer response.
This section discusses how digitally enabled convenience stores (CVS) can navigate market challenges. Despite strong overall growth, the market is fragmented. Consumer demand and policy support drive steady growth, with a 12% CAGR over five years. CVS maintain sales growth through convenience and timeliness. Lower-tier market expansion is rapid but uneven, with intense competition in tier-one cities and gaps in lower-tier cities.
China's convenience store sector has experienced significant growth, with a double-digit CAGR of 12% since 2017. The number of stores has also grown at a double-digit rate of 18%, although this growth has slowed due to COVID-19. The market expansion is particularly notable in lower-tier cities, where the population covered by a single convenience store is higher compared to Tier-1 cities.
The document discusses the tripartite competitive landscape in the Chinese CVS market, characterized by premium CVS, local community grocery stores, and new digital-enabled stores. It highlights the challenges of slowing customer traffic growth, reliance on manual labor, and operational difficulties in achieving scalable expansion.
Digitalization enhances CVS efficiency by refining site selection, operations, merchandising, and supply chain management. It uses data-driven approaches for precise site selection, customer-centric merchandising, and intelligent demand forecasting to reduce costs and increase sales.
This page discusses how digital store management systems empower staff and operations personnel by optimizing labor arrangements and task plans, reducing work hours without compromising service quality. It highlights the role of algorithmic workloads and automatic task orders in enhancing efficiency and adaptability in store operations.
Shopping malls in China face challenges despite recent growth. Digital transformation is crucial for sustainable performance. Solid growth has created a safe harbor for offline retail. Shopping malls should expand and capture secondary growth opportunities.
The document discusses market size and growth forecasts for China's shopping malls, highlighting challenges such as asset-heavy operating models, ESG requirements, and the need for differentiation in a highly homogenized market. It also notes the '80-20' distribution in the market and the profitability issues faced by many projects.
This section discusses digital initiatives for sustainable shopping mall success, emphasizing IT infrastructure transformation, advanced data analytics, and IoT systems. It highlights intelligent rental pricing, tenant mix management, smart building solutions, and green energy consumption. It also explores differentiated business operations and new consumer businesses to enhance customer-centric positioning and profitability.
This page discusses how multi-channel integration and digital intelligence are transforming the retail experience. Yintai Retail Group exemplifies this by offering value-added services like shoe and bag care, enhancing consumer stickiness. Shopping malls are evolving into mentors, providing digital empowerment and tools for precision marketing and operations diagnostics.
Specialty stores enhance value chains by offering niche products and services, leveraging digitalization for efficiency and customer experience. They focus on high-quality goods, segmented demand, and operational excellence in both front-end and back-end processes.
This page discusses how specialty retail value creation is driven by efficiency and user experience, categorizing stores into efficiency-first, user-experience-first, and user-efficiency-driven types. It provides strategies for 3C electronics, footwear and apparel, retail pharmacies, and beauty and mother and baby stores to improve performance by focusing on specific aspects of the value matrix.
Retail pharmacies must leverage consumer insights and innovation to differentiate from competitors by offering value-added services and strategic product assortments.
This chapter discusses four essential digital enablers crucial for digital transformation in the retail sector. It highlights the importance of these enablers in driving change and innovation within the industry.
The middle office is crucial for enhancing operational efficiency and supporting multi-channel business development in retail. It helps in developing reusable business capabilities, expanding into new markets, and reducing labor costs through standardized operations. A complete digital middle office architecture integrates business, data, and technology components for organizational support.
This page describes the architecture of retail middle offices, including business, data, and technology middle offices. It explains their roles in supporting front and back offices, with a focus on operations, data management, and technology infrastructure. The content includes an exhibit illustrating various components of the middle office architecture.
The business middle office is essential for improving operational efficiency in retail. It centralizes front-end operations, enhancing agility and effectiveness. Types include user operations, store operations, merchandising, and supply chain middle offices, each with specific functions to optimize various aspects of retail operations.
This page discusses key considerations for retailers when building a business middle office, emphasizing its role in supporting and supervising front offices, clarifying responsibilities, and adapting to business needs. It highlights the importance of aligning middle office functions with front office objectives and considering factors like consumer proximity, regional attributes, and scenario complexity. The middle office's development is described as a long-term, phased project.

pages.abstract: This page introduces the importance of MSMEs in global economies, their productivity challenges, and the need for a detailed study to enhance their contribution. It outlines the scope of research by the McKinsey Global Institute, covering 16 countries and various subsectors, aiming to identify opportunities for MSMEs to work with larger companies for mutual growth.

pages.page_path: library_pages\A microscope on small businesses_ McKensey_2024_05_02\page_9.jpg
pages.abstract: This page outlines the definitions, scope, and data limitations for a research study on MSMEs across 16 countries. It details the types of MSMEs studied, size category definitions, scope of data, level of aggregation, and methods for measuring productivity. The data focuses on nonfarm sectors and uses 2019 data to avoid COVID-19 distortions, with some variations in data availability across countries.
pages.title: Definitions, scope, and data limitations

pages.page_path: library_pages\A microscope on small businesses_ McKensey_2024_05_02\page_10.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses limitations in data availability, excluding certain sectors like financial services and agriculture, and notes the exclusion of some emerging economies. The findings are limited to a narrower 'business' economy and may not be globally representative.
pages.title: Definitions, scope, and data limitations (continued)
