pages.title: Industrial worker in Indonesia

pages.page_path: library_pages\A microscope on small businesses_ McKensey_2024_05_02\page_12.jpg
pages.abstract: MSMEs significantly contribute to global GDP and employment, with their impact varying across countries. They account for roughly half of global GDP and 40% of all employment, with higher contributions in emerging economies compared to advanced ones.
pages.title: 1. Small businesses power the economies of today and tomorrow

pages.page_path: library_pages\A microscope on small businesses_ McKensey_2024_05_02\page_13.jpg
pages.abstract: MSMEs are significant job creators and contributors to value added in both advanced and emerging economies, with notable variations across sectors and countries. They play a crucial role in production, particularly in accommodation, food, construction, professional services, and trade sectors.
pages.title: MSMEs generate the majority of jobs and roughly half of total corporate value added.

pages.page_path: library_pages\A microscope on small businesses_ McKensey_2024_05_02\page_14.jpg
pages.abstract: MSMEs contribute significantly to various sectors in both advanced and emerging economies, driving business dynamism and innovation. Their growth into large companies enhances overall economic productivity and competitiveness.
pages.title: MSMEs operate in every sector, with varying economic contributions.

pages.page_path: library_pages\A microscope on small businesses_ McKensey_2024_05_02\page_15.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the scaling up of MSMEs into large companies since 2000, highlighting country-specific variations. It includes a bar chart showing the share of scaled-up companies by country and explains factors contributing to this trend, such as market opportunities, country-level dynamics, and sector-specific characteristics. The text also mentions structural barriers faced by MSMEs in some countries and the role of innovation and investment in certain sectors.
pages.title: About one in five large companies scaled up from being MSMEs since 2000 but there is variation among countries.

pages.page_path: library_pages\A microscope on small businesses_ McKensey_2024_05_02\page_16.jpg
pages.abstract: MSMEs in emerging economies exhibit greater dynamism in core sectors like construction, utilities, and transportation. Investment in physical infrastructure rises faster in earlier stages of development. Microenterprises in India, Kenya, and Nigeria face low productivity challenges. Mining and ICT companies scaled up more overall, while construction, utilities, and transportation MSMEs were more dynamic in emerging economies.
pages.title: MSMEs can boost national productivity while staying small or by fueling larger companies

pages.page_path: library_pages\A microscope on small businesses_ McKensey_2024_05_02\page_17.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the role of MSMEs in different economies, highlighting that in richer economies, employment shifts from microenterprises to larger companies, while in emerging economies, MSMEs, particularly microenterprises, are crucial for sustaining livelihoods.
pages.title: In emerging economies, the MSMEs that are so vital to sustaining livelihoods are heavily skewed toward microenterprises.

pages.page_path: library_pages\A microscope on small businesses_ McKensey_2024_05_02\page_18.jpg
pages.title: Warehouse supervisor in Thailand

pages.page_path: library_pages\A microscope on small businesses_ McKensey_2024_05_02\page_19.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the significant productivity gap between MSMEs and large companies, highlighting variations across countries and sectors. It explains that MSME productivity lags behind large companies and analyzes the factors contributing to these differences, including the size of MSMEs and sector mix.
pages.title: 2. Boosting MSME productivity could yield significant value

pages.page_path: library_pages\A microscope on small businesses_ McKensey_2024_05_02\page_20.jpg
pages.abstract: The exhibit compares MSME productivity with that of large firms across various countries, showing a significant gap, especially in emerging economies. The productivity ratio and gap are visualized for both emerging and advanced economies, with data sourced from various economic and business censuses and surveys.
pages.title: MSME productivity lags behind that of larger firms across countries, with a wider gap in emerging economies.

pages.page_path: library_pages\A microscope on small businesses_ McKensey_2024_05_02\page_21.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the productivity ratios of microenterprises compared to large companies and other MSMEs across various countries. It highlights that microenterprises generally have lower productivity ratios. The page also notes that the lack of scale significantly impacts the productivity gap in certain sectors, with MSMEs in ICT facing the largest gap. Despite the advantages of larger scale, small businesses offer unique opportunities for entrepreneurship.
pages.title: Microenterprises typically have a smaller productivity ratio relative to large companies than other MSMEs.

pages.page_path: library_pages\A microscope on small businesses_ McKensey_2024_05_02\page_22.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the MSME productivity ratio across various sectors and countries, highlighting that MSMEs are as productive as large companies in some sectors like utilities and administrative services. It also explains the role of MSMEs in shaping social fabric, their advantages in innovation, and their contributions to large company productivity through work fissuring and higher-value work.
pages.title: The MSME productivity ratio varies among and within sectors and among countries, but less so in manufacturing and ICT.

pages.page_path: library_pages\A microscope on small businesses_ McKensey_2024_05_02\page_23.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses how intangible capital impacts productivity in various sectors, highlighting that MSMEs face challenges in adopting advanced technologies and accessing financial resources compared to large companies. The productivity gap is wider in sectors like ICT and professional services, where intangibles play a significant role. Large companies benefit from scale, organizational efficiency, and better access to high-skill talent, contributing to their higher productivity and financial performance.
pages.title: Intangible capital

pages.page_path: library_pages\A microscope on small businesses_ McKensey_2024_05_02\page_24.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the productivity gap between MSMEs and large companies, highlighting factors like global connections, financial capital, and access to infrastructure. It explains how MSMEs face challenges in accessing global markets and financing, and how narrowing this gap could significantly boost GDP. The page also notes the potential for MSMEs to improve productivity through various means, including structural shifts and scaling up.
pages.title: Narrowing the productivity gap is equivalent to 5 to 10 percent of GDP

pages.page_path: library_pages\A microscope on small businesses_ McKensey_2024_05_02\page_25.jpg
pages.abstract: The document assesses the value of narrowing the productivity gap between MSMEs and large companies across various subsectors in different countries. It uses benchmarks to estimate the potential economic impact, focusing on first-order effects while acknowledging the complexity of broader multiplier effects. The analysis excludes certain sectors and self-employed individuals for consistency and comparability across countries.
pages.title: Estimating the value of narrowing the productivity gap

pages.page_path: library_pages\A microscope on small businesses_ McKensey_2024_05_02\page_26.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the potential economic impact of narrowing productivity gaps between MSMEs and large companies, with the highest value in emerging economies like Kenya, India, Indonesia, and Nigeria. The sectors with the most economic output from improving MSME productivity are trade, manufacturing, and construction. The ICT sector plays a significant role in narrowing the productivity gap in several countries.
pages.title: Narrowing the subsector productivity gap with large companies is equivalent to 2 to 15 percent of GDP.

pages.page_path: library_pages\A microscope on small businesses_ McKensey_2024_05_02\page_27.jpg
pages.abstract: The document highlights the significant contributions of trade, manufacturing, construction, and ICT sectors in narrowing productivity gaps across advanced and emerging economies. It provides a detailed breakdown of sectoral contributions, emphasizing the varying importance of these sectors in different countries. The analysis excludes certain sectors due to data inconsistencies and includes additional sectors based on country-specific data availability.
pages.title: Trade, manufacturing, construction, and ICT represent the most value from narrowing productivity gaps.

pages.abstract: The document discusses the need for a detailed analysis of MSME productivity across various subsectors to identify specific opportunities for improvement. It highlights the wide variation in productivity ratios within sectors and subsectors, emphasizing the importance of a granular approach to prioritize actions for boosting MSME productivity.
pages.title: 3. Looking through a microscope to fill the gaps

pages.page_path: library_pages\A microscope on small businesses_ McKensey_2024_05_02\page_30.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the significant variation in MSME productivity ratios across subsectors in Germany, using a detailed chart. It highlights that the best-performing MSMEs vary by country and activity type. The trade sector is used as an example, showing that Japanese MSMEs in automotive trade are top performers due to vertical integration, while they lag in retail and wholesale trade.
pages.title: Within sectors, the MSME productivity ratio varies significantly among subsectors: Germany example.

pages.page_path: library_pages\A microscope on small businesses_ McKensey_2024_05_02\page_31.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the significant variation in productivity ratios among countries within trade subsectors, highlighting the importance of focusing on high-value subsectors for MSMEs. The image illustrates the integration of advanced robotics in an industrial setting, showcasing the collaboration between humans and machines. It emphasizes the future of work, focusing on the deployment of AI technologies and the importance of skill development in Europe and beyond.
This section analyzes the impact of automation, AI, and other trends on wholesale and retail trade, financial services, manufacturing, and healthcare sectors in Europe and the United States, assessing changes in labor demand and skills requirements.
Wholesale and retail trade is the most impacted sector by European employment demand changes. By 2030, 2.8 million people may need to switch jobs. Demand for office support and customer service roles is decreasing, while managerial, business, and legal roles are increasing. Automation and AI are transforming routine tasks, and e-commerce is reshaping logistics and consumer interactions. The top 5 growing roles include managers and health technicians, while declining roles include financial clerks and sales workers.
This page details the evolution of skill mix and total work hours in Europe and the US for wholesale and retail trade from 2022 to 2030 under a faster automation scenario. It highlights the most affected skills in various categories, showing a significant shift towards technological and cognitive skills while physical and basic cognitive skills decline.
The adoption of generative AI in Europe's finance sector could lead to a decrease in labor demand by 2030, particularly in office support and customer service roles. The shift to digital platforms will increase demand for STEM professionals and technological skills, while also emphasizing social and emotional skills in managerial roles. Approximately 600,000 individuals in banking may need to change occupations by 2030.
This page details the projected changes in skill demand within the European financial services sector from 2022 to 2030 under a faster automation scenario. It highlights the evolution of work hours by skill category, showing increases in technological and social-emotional skills, while physical/manual and basic cognitive skills decrease. The most affected skills include advanced IT, communication, and basic data processing, with variations between Europe and the US.
The European manufacturing sector is projected to experience a net decline in employment demand by 2030, with significant shifts in labor demand. Production work and office support roles are expected to decline, while demand for STEM, management, and business/legal roles may grow. Technological advancements and automation are driving this shift. Actions towards net zero will foster job creation in expanding industries but reduce demand in contracting industries. Approximately 2.1 million individuals may need to change occupations. Demand for technological, social, and emotional skills is expected to rise, while demand for basic cognitive and physical/manual skills may decline.
This page details the projected evolution of skill demand in European manufacturing from 2022 to 2030 under a faster automation scenario. It highlights significant increases in technological and higher cognitive skills, while physical and basic cognitive skills are expected to decline. The most affected skills include basic IT, leadership, and data processing, reflecting a shift towards advanced technology and communication.
The healthcare sector in Europe is projected to experience significant labor demand growth by 2030, driven by rising demand for health aides and healthcare professionals. The aging population and mental health challenges are key drivers. Around 500,000 workers may need to change occupations, with office support roles declining due to automation. Technological and social skills will see substantial growth.
The document details the projected changes in skill requirements in the European healthcare sector from 2022 to 2030 under a faster automation scenario. It highlights the evolution of work hours by skill category, showing an increase in technological and social skills while physical and basic cognitive skills decrease. The most affected skills include IT, communication, and leadership, with significant shifts in the demand for advanced literacy and project management.
This chapter discusses the potential implications of AI and gen AI deployment on the workforce, highlighting the uncertain consequences for workers in lower-wage jobs. It explores how demand for higher-wage occupations could rise, benefiting workers with above-median incomes, while those below the median may face limited wage increases or even decreasing income. The text emphasizes the importance of understanding the impact on different wage bands and the divergence in outcomes for workers.
The page discusses how labor market disruptions could shift demand towards higher-wage jobs, with varying impacts across European countries. Countries like the Czech Republic and Sweden may benefit most from transitioning workers into higher-wage occupations, while Denmark could see greater demand for middle-wage jobs. The data shows expected changes in employment shares by wage bands for Europe and the US, highlighting potential shifts towards higher-wage occupations.
The page discusses how labor demand in Europe and the US could shift towards higher-wage occupations by 2030. It presents a table showing changes in employment share by wage band for various countries, indicating potential increases in higher-wage roles and decreases in lower-wage roles. The data is based on a 'faster' scenario for Europe and a 'midpoint' scenario for the US, with occupations categorized into quintiles based on average wages.
The page discusses the necessity for low- and middle-wage workers to acquire additional skills to transition to higher-wage jobs. It highlights the potential skills profile of occupations based on wage brackets, emphasizing the importance of technological, social, and emotional skills for higher-wage occupations. The data presented shows the time spent using various types of skills by wage band in Europe, illustrating the shift in skill requirements as wages increase.
This page discusses the potential of generative AI in enhancing and reshaping skills acquisition, emphasizing its role in creating personalized learning experiences, simplifying complex information, and providing real-time feedback. A case study illustrates how a company improved operational efficiency and productivity through AI-assisted training.
This page discusses the likelihood of workers in low- and middle-wage jobs needing to change occupations due to economic transitions. It highlights disparities between Europe and the United States, emphasizing the need for intervention mechanisms and reskilling, particularly for those with lower educational attainment and in roles susceptible to automation.
The document highlights that workers in lower-wage positions are more likely to face occupational transitions by 2030. It provides data on expected changes in employment share across different wage bands and educational levels for Europe and the US, emphasizing the impact on gender distribution in these occupations.
This chapter discusses the role of technological transformation in shaping the future of work, emphasizing the need for organizations and policymakers to adopt AI and automation while focusing on skill upgrades and human capital enhancement for sustained productivity growth.
This page discusses the choices for managing technology and workforce transitions, emphasizing the importance of a proactive stance by companies in anticipating technological changes, establishing worker training structures, and supporting employees. It highlights the role of policymakers in facilitating occupational transitions and the risks of a reactive stance that may hinder economic growth.
This page discusses the potential effects of technology adoption and worker redeployment on European productivity growth, considering scenarios of fast and late technology adoption and varying levels of worker redeployment. It highlights the importance of decisions made today for future economic outcomes.
The page discusses the potential impact of AI adoption and work hour redeployment on labor productivity growth in Europe. It presents a scenario analysis showing that faster AI adoption with higher redeployment of automated workers' hours can lead to higher productivity growth without additional unemployment, while slower adoption with lower redeployment may result in lower productivity growth and potential job losses.
Companies need to transform workforces for new work landscapes. Leaders should understand automation's potential, plan strategic workforce shifts, and address AI's broader impacts on society.
This page discusses the importance of prioritizing people development in AI transformation, including setting up talent win rooms, accelerating AI capabilities, and training nontechnical talent. It also highlights the need for leaders to pursue executive education on automation technologies and engage in comprehensive involvement in gen AI transformation efforts.
The document outlines four key action pillars for leaders to effectively engage with automation technologies, emphasizing workforce planning, talent development, and strategic education. It highlights the need for a full perspective on automation potential, early adoption of relevant technologies, and organizational talent assessment. The text also stresses the importance of aligning workforce skills with automation needs, addressing talent gaps, and facilitating skill reallocation. Additionally, it underscores the role of executive education in driving business and employee value through automation.

This page discusses the impact of automation and net-zero transition on productivity and labor market trends, including GDP calculations, job displacement, and macroeconomic catalysts. It also examines trends accelerated by COVID-19.
The page discusses skills demand and transitions, occupational shifts, and a proprietary skills demand survey methodology. It explains the framework used, the categorization of workforce skills, and the survey of executives from five countries to gauge skill demands and AI impact.
The exhibit details the geographic and sectoral distribution of respondents in a McKinsey survey, highlighting participation from five countries and various industries. pages.abstract: The travel and tourism sector faces unique challenges in addressing climate change, contributing 8-11% of global GHG emissions. Decarbonization is complex due to the sector's scale and variety. Committing to a net-zero pathway is crucial to avoid severe climate outcomes.

pages.title: A Large, Growing Contributor to Global Emissions

The page also notes the expected growth in travel activity, emphasizing the industry's increasing role in global GHG emissions.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Accelerating the transition to net-zero travel_strategies for action_McKinSey_2022_09_01\page_12.jpg

It highlights the importance of stakeholder pressure and the need for companies to act on sustainable actions to avoid being viewed as higher-risk investments. The strategies include identifying and sequencing decarbonization initiatives, partnering for business travel decarbonization, closing the 'say-do' gap among leisure travelers, and building new sustainable travel businesses.

It highlights the growing concern over emissions in travel decisions, the importance of ESG topics for employees, and the focus on sustainability policies by regulators and governments. pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_1.jpg
pages.title: AI for social good: Improving lives and protecting the planet

pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_2.jpg
pages.title: Table of contents

pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_3.jpg
pages.abstract: AI is being used to advance all 17 SDGs, with generative AI opening new possibilities. Progress in AI R&D has expanded its potential applications. However, responsible use and addressing challenges in data quality, governance, and AI talent access are crucial for scaling AI solutions and achieving SDGs.
pages.title: AI is already being used to further all 17 SDGs

pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_4.jpg
pages.abstract: This chapter discusses the potential of AI to accelerate progress toward achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). It explores how AI technologies can be leveraged to improve lives and protect the planet, highlighting various applications and their impact.
pages.title: Chapter 1 How AI can accelerate progress toward reaching all of the SDGs

pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_5.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the broad applicability of AI to various Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), highlighting its potential in areas like drug screening, vaccine design, and supply chain optimization. It emphasizes the democratization of AI capabilities through generative AI, enabling remote users to perform tasks that previously required specific expertise. The page also mentions a growing database of AI use cases and the significant increase in real-life AI deployments over the past six years.
pages.title: Adoption of generative AI could significantly increase and democratize access to new capabilities.

pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_6.jpg
pages.abstract: The document details the number of AI-enabled use cases identified per UN Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) in 2023, showing that about 600 use cases support the SDGs. It highlights that 82% of these cases have at least one deployment. The data is categorized by SDGs, with SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-Being) having the highest number of use cases (165), followed by SDG 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions) with 55. The document also notes that the library of use cases is based on publicly available data and will continue to evolve.
pages.title: About 600 AI-enabled use cases have the potential to support the UN Sustainable Development Goals.

pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_7.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the alignment between AI's perceived potential and its deployment for various Sustainable Development Goals. It highlights that not-for-profit AI deployments are concentrated in specific SDGs like health, education, and climate action, despite the perceived potential being higher in other areas. The analysis excludes certain SDGs due to their broad applicability and focuses on the discrepancy between AI potential and deployment levels.
pages.title: The number of not-for-profit deployments does not necessarily reflect the perceived AI potential for each Sustainable Development Goal.

pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_8.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the untapped AI potential in several SDGs, providing examples of how AI can address No Poverty, Zero Hunger, and Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions. It also outlines the exploration of AI deployments in SDGs with recognized potential and those with less recognized but impactful applications.
pages.title: We explore potential and existing deployments in three of the SDGs with the most widely recognized potential. We also explore two SDGs where AI does not have widely recognized potential but has had an impact in select areas.

pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_9.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the inherent risks of adopting AI, including impaired fairness, malicious use, and privacy concerns. A survey of 60 experts identified these as the top risks, with not-for-profits more concerned about misinformation and economic stability, while for-profits focused on intellectual property infringement. A bar chart illustrates the differences in concerns between not-for-profits and other organizations.
pages.title: Managing the risks of adopting AI

pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_10.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the risks of AI, including impaired fairness, malicious use, data privacy and security threats, and performance and explainability issues. It highlights the need for organizations to understand and prioritize these risks, especially for not-for-profits with limited resources. The page also mentions tools and methodologies to mitigate these risks.
pages.title: AI for social good: Improving lives and protecting the planet

pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_11.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses AI applications in healthcare related to SDG 3, focusing on maternal and newborn health in Kenya and India. It highlights AI solutions like PROMPTS and mMitra, which improve care quality and reduce maternal mortality through personalized messaging and predictive models.
pages.title: Existing deployments related to SDG 3: Good Health and Well-Being

pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_12.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses AI applications in predicting protein structures for drug discovery, enhancing quality education through AI algorithms, and enabling communication for people with disabilities. It highlights challenges in implementing AI in education due to infrastructure limitations in low-income countries and showcases successful use cases like AlphaFold and Livox.
pages.title: AI for social good: Improving lives and protecting the planet

pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_13.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses AI applications in education and climate action, highlighting Educate Girls' use of machine learning to enroll girls in school and various AI-driven initiatives for climate resilience, including forest conservation and flood forecasting.
pages.title: Sample use case: Bolstering girls' enrollment in school

pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_14.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses AI's role in achieving SDG 1 (No Poverty) and SDG 2 (Zero Hunger). It highlights successful AI deployments, such as distributing aid during the COVID-19 pandemic in Togo and improving agricultural practices in India. AI is shown to enhance efficiency, accuracy, and productivity in poverty alleviation and food security initiatives.
pages.title: Existing deployments related to SDG 1: No Poverty and SDG 2: Zero Hunger

pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_15.jpg
pages.abstract: This chapter discusses the role of funding for AI initiatives in supporting Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). It explores how financial resources allocated to AI projects can contribute to achieving global sustainability objectives.
pages.title: Chapter 2 How funding for AI initiatives supports SDGs

pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_16.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the alignment of AI funding with SDGs, highlighting that 40% of private capital investments in AI companies contribute to SDGs. It analyzes funding distribution across different SDGs, noting disparities and potential for private entities to address gaps. It also examines the geographical distribution of AI funding, emphasizing the need for more focus on lower-income countries.
pages.title: About 40 percent of private capital investments into the 20,000 AI companies we analyzed contributed directly or indirectly toward at least one of the 17 SDG thematic areas.

pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_17.jpg
pages.abstract: This page analyzes the flow of grant and private capital funding toward Sustainable Development Goals where AI has the most recognized potential. It highlights the funding distribution across various SDGs, emphasizing SDG 3: Good Health and Well-Being and SDG 4: Quality Education as receiving significant funding. The data is sourced from Foundation Directory, Candid, and PitchBook, covering the period 2018–23.
pages.title: Grant and private capital funding tends to flow toward Sustainable Development Goals where AI has the most recognized potential.

pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_18.jpg
pages.abstract: This chapter discusses the challenges associated with scaling AI for social good, emphasizing the complexities and obstacles that need to be addressed to ensure AI's positive impact on society.
pages.title: Chapter 3 Challenges of scaling AI for social good

pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_19.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the significant presence of AI in social and education sectors, highlighting that 48% of funders and 66% of not-for-profits use AI. It emphasizes the need for larger-scale deployment of AI solutions for social good and notes that 55% of AI research and deployment grants are $250,000 or less, focusing on targeted research rather than large-scale expansion.
pages.title: AI in Social and Education Sectors

pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_20.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the challenges organizations face when deploying AI for social good, focusing on data, talent, and change management. It highlights the top 5 AI risks based on a survey of experts, emphasizing data availability, AI talent, and organizational receptiveness as the most significant hurdles.
pages.title: Experts say the top challenges to scaling AI for social good relate to data, talent, and change management.

pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_21.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses challenges in data availability, AI talent accessibility, and organizational receptiveness to AI applications for social good. It highlights issues like data quality, uneven talent distribution, and the need for training and explainability in AI tools for effective implementation.
pages.title: Data availability, accessibility, and quality

pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_22.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses AI-related risks to vulnerable people and the need for widespread alignment among stakeholders. It highlights the potential of simpler gen AI tools to expand AI use and unlock value from open data. However, it also identifies additional barriers to scaling, such as limited internet access and high compute costs, which require grants and political will to overcome.

pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_23.jpg
pages.abstract: This chapter discusses strategies for stakeholders to expedite the deployment of AI for social good, emphasizing collaboration and ethical considerations.
pages.title: Chapter 4: How stakeholders can accelerate the deployment of AI for social good

pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_24.jpg
pages.abstract: This section outlines six cross-cutting approaches to mitigate challenges in AI for social good, emphasizing the importance of partnerships. These partnerships can enhance reach, data sharing, resource access, and innovation ecosystems, bringing together diverse stakeholders to create impactful AI solutions.
pages.title: Forming partnerships to accelerate impact

pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_25.jpg
pages.abstract: This section discusses the role of digital public goods in supporting sustainable development goals, highlighting initiatives like Google DeepMind's GraphCast and Data4SDGs. It emphasizes the importance of open data and collaboration but notes challenges in coordination and resource duplication.
pages.title: 2. Supporting the development of digital public goods

pages.page_path: library_pages\AI for social good_ Improving lives and protecting the planet_McKinsey_2024_05_01\page_26.jpg
pages.abstract: This section discusses strategies to enhance data quality and usability for AI-driven SDG applications, emphasizing support for data collection in resource-poor contexts and incentives for data sharing. AI is being used to advance all 17 SDGs, with generative AI opening new possibilities. Progress in AI R&D has expanded its potential applications. However, responsible use and addressing challenges in data quality, governance, and AI talent access are crucial for scaling AI solutions and achieving SDGs.
This chapter discusses the potential of AI to accelerate progress toward achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). It explores how AI technologies can be leveraged to improve lives and protect the planet, highlighting various applications and their impact.
This page discusses the broad applicability of AI to various Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), highlighting its potential in areas like drug screening, vaccine design, and supply chain optimization. It emphasizes the democratization of AI capabilities through generative AI, enabling remote users to perform tasks that previously required specific expertise. The page also mentions a growing database of AI use cases and the significant increase in real-life AI deployments over the past six years.
The document details the number of AI-enabled use cases identified per UN Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) in 2023, showing that about 600 use cases support the SDGs. It highlights that 82% of these cases have at least one deployment. The data is categorized by SDGs, with SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-Being) having the highest number of use cases (165), followed by SDG 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions) with 55. The document also notes that the library of use cases is based on publicly available data and will continue to evolve.
The page discusses the alignment between AI's perceived potential and its deployment for various Sustainable Development Goals. It highlights that not-for-profit AI deployments are concentrated in specific SDGs like health, education, and climate action, despite the perceived potential being higher in other areas. The analysis excludes certain SDGs due to their broad applicability and focuses on the discrepancy between AI potential and deployment levels.
This page discusses the untapped AI potential in several SDGs, providing examples of how AI can address No Poverty, Zero Hunger, and Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions. It also outlines the exploration of AI deployments in SDGs with recognized potential and those with less recognized but impactful applications.
The page discusses the inherent risks of adopting AI, including impaired fairness, malicious use, and privacy concerns. A survey of 60 experts identified these as the top risks, with not-for-profits more concerned about misinformation and economic stability, while for-profits focused on intellectual property infringement. A bar chart illustrates the differences in concerns between not-for-profits and other organizations.
This page discusses the risks of AI, including impaired fairness, malicious use, data privacy and security threats, and performance and explainability issues. It highlights the need for organizations to understand and prioritize these risks, especially for not-for-profits with limited resources. The page also mentions tools and methodologies to mitigate these risks.
This page discusses AI applications in healthcare related to SDG 3, focusing on maternal and newborn health in Kenya and India. It highlights AI solutions like PROMPTS and mMitra, which improve care quality and reduce maternal mortality through personalized messaging and predictive models.
This page discusses AI applications in predicting protein structures for drug discovery, enhancing quality education through AI algorithms, and enabling communication for people with disabilities. It highlights challenges in implementing AI in education due to infrastructure limitations in low-income countries and showcases successful use cases like AlphaFold and Livox.
This page discusses AI applications in education and climate action, highlighting Educate Girls' use of machine learning to enroll girls in school and various AI-driven initiatives for climate resilience, including forest conservation and flood forecasting.
This page discusses AI's role in achieving SDG 1 (No Poverty) and SDG 2 (Zero Hunger). It highlights successful AI deployments, such as distributing aid during the COVID-19 pandemic in Togo and improving agricultural practices in India. AI is shown to enhance efficiency, accuracy, and productivity in poverty alleviation and food security initiatives.
This chapter discusses the role of funding for AI initiatives in supporting Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). It explores how financial resources allocated to AI projects can contribute to achieving global sustainability objectives.
This page discusses the alignment of AI funding with SDGs, highlighting that 40% of private capital investments in AI companies contribute to SDGs. It analyzes funding distribution across different SDGs, noting disparities and potential for private entities to address gaps. It also examines the geographical distribution of AI funding, emphasizing the need for more focus on lower-income countries.
This page analyzes the flow of grant and private capital funding toward Sustainable Development Goals where AI has the most recognized potential. It highlights the funding distribution across various SDGs, emphasizing SDG 3: Good Health and Well-Being and SDG 4: Quality Education as receiving significant funding. The data is sourced from Foundation Directory, Candid, and PitchBook, covering the period 2018–23.
This chapter discusses the challenges associated with scaling AI for social good, emphasizing the complexities and obstacles that need to be addressed to ensure AI's positive impact on society.
The page discusses the significant presence of AI in social and education sectors, highlighting that 48% of funders and 66% of not-for-profits use AI. It emphasizes the need for larger-scale deployment of AI solutions for social good and notes that 55% of AI research and deployment grants are $250,000 or less, focusing on targeted research rather than large-scale expansion.
The page discusses the challenges organizations face when deploying AI for social good, focusing on data, talent, and change management. It highlights the top 5 AI risks based on a survey of experts, emphasizing data availability, AI talent, and organizational receptiveness as the most significant hurdles.
This page discusses challenges in data availability, AI talent accessibility, and organizational receptiveness to AI applications for social good. It highlights issues like data quality, uneven talent distribution, and the need for training and explainability in AI tools for effective implementation.
This page discusses AI-related risks to vulnerable people and the need for widespread alignment among stakeholders. It highlights the potential of simpler gen AI tools to expand AI use and unlock value from open data. However, it also identifies additional barriers to scaling, such as limited internet access and high compute costs, which require grants and political will to overcome.
This chapter discusses strategies for stakeholders to expedite the deployment of AI for social good, emphasizing collaboration and ethical considerations.
This section outlines six cross-cutting approaches to mitigate challenges in AI for social good, emphasizing the importance of partnerships. These partnerships can enhance reach, data sharing, resource access, and innovation ecosystems, bringing together diverse stakeholders to create impactful AI solutions.
This section discusses the role of digital public goods in supporting sustainable development goals, highlighting initiatives like Google DeepMind's GraphCast and Data4SDGs. It emphasizes the importance of open data and collaboration but notes challenges in coordination and resource duplication.
This section discusses strategies to enhance data quality and usability for AI-driven SDG applications, emphasizing support for data collection in resource-poor contexts and incentives for data sharing. It also highlights the importance of expanding AI talent pools through near-term initiatives like talent loans and long-term investments in training and education, particularly in underrepresented regions.
This page discusses the importance of an inclusive, user-centric approach in AI development and the creation of business models for scaling AI solutions. It highlights Rainforest Connection's use of autonomous listening devices to monitor logging activity and Thorn's business model for combating child sexual abuse. The text emphasizes the need for collaboration among stakeholders to address challenges in scaling AI for social good.
This page outlines the methodology used to assess AI's impact on UN SDGs, including data collection from use cases, surveys, interviews, foundation grants, and private capital investment analysis. It also acknowledges contributors and collaborators in the research.

It discusses the potential for carbon capture and storage (CCS) in aluminum smelters and the challenges associated with on-site anode production. The document also introduces the concept of carbochlorination with CO₂ regeneration as an alternative to the traditional Hall-Héroult process, emphasizing its potential for reducing energy consumption and integrating with CCS.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Aluminum decarbonization at a cost that makes sense_McKinsey_2022_01_01\page_26.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the implementation of carbon capture and storage (CCS) technology in aluminum smelters, which could reduce CO2 emissions by over 60%. It covers the cost implications, technological challenges, and potential benefits of retrofitting existing smelters with CCS. The page also explores the capital and operating expenditures associated with decarbonization efforts, including the use of inert-anode technology.
pages.title: Implementation of carbon capture and storage technology could reduce smelter CO2 emissions by more than 60 percent.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Aluminum decarbonization at a cost that makes sense_McKinsey_2022_01_01\page_27.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the costs and benefits of various technologies for decarbonizing aluminum production, focusing on the Bayer process and comparing different energy sources and technologies like CCS, inert anodes, MVR, and green hydrogen. It highlights the trade-offs between capital and operating costs and the potential for cost reduction through technology improvements and learning curves.
pages.title: Refining: The Bayer process

pages.page_path: library_pages\Aluminum decarbonization at a cost that makes sense_McKinsey_2022_01_01\page_28.jpg
pages.abstract: This page compares the capital expenditure for Hall-Héroult (HH), HH with carbon capture and storage, and inert anode technologies. The inert anode technology demands a significant retrofit cost, primarily due to the need for new potrooms and vertical cell configuration. However, some costs like anode rodding and chlorination plant are eliminated. The retrofit cell cost for inert anode is notably higher than HH.
pages.title: Inert-anode technology can be retrofitted, but it still demands a significant retrofit cost.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Aluminum decarbonization at a cost that makes sense_McKinsey_2022_01_01\page_29.jpg
pages.abstract: This page compares the operating expenses of different smelting technologies, focusing on raw materials, electricity, anodes, labor, and other costs. It highlights the impact of carbon capture and storage and inert anodes on expenses, showing potential savings and increased costs. The inert anode technology offers longer anode life and reduced labor costs but has higher initial anode costs. Overall, the inert anode technology can reduce total operating expenses by 3% to 10% compared to the Hall-Héroult process.
pages.title: The operating expenses of smelting technologies depend on electricity prices.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Aluminum decarbonization at a cost that makes sense_McKinsey_2022_01_01\page_30.jpg
pages.abstract: This page compares various boiler types for CO2 emissions reduction in aluminum production, detailing their efficiency, costs, and technology readiness levels. Electric and hydrogen-fired boilers show potential for significant emissions reduction compared to natural gas boilers.
pages.title: Electric or hydrogen-fired boilers may eliminate CO2e emissions associated with digestion.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Aluminum decarbonization at a cost that makes sense_McKinsey_2022_01_01\page_31.jpg
pages.abstract: This page compares the decarbonization potential of calcination technologies using natural gas, a hydrogen-based calciner with electrolysis, and natural gas with carbon capture and storage. It highlights the thermal input, fuel requirements, CO₂ emissions, and costs associated with each method, emphasizing the lower CO₂ production and higher costs of the hydrogen-based calciner.
pages.title: Decarbonization of calcination technologies may be achieved through a hydrogen-based calciner.

pages.title: Model key inputs.

It details emerging examples, emissions, logic or limitations, and maturity levels. The text also explores how CCS can be applied to aluminum smelting, petcoke calcination, and anode baking furnaces to reduce CO2 emissions, with a focus on economic viability and technological advancements.
The document compares CO₂ concentrations in the aluminum value chain with other industries, highlighting that typical CO₂ concentrations in aluminum production are relatively low. It discusses the potential for carbon capture and storage (CCS) in aluminum smelters and the challenges associated with on-site anode production. The document also introduces the concept of carbochlorination with CO₂ regeneration as an alternative to the traditional Hall-Héroult process, emphasizing its potential for reducing energy consumption and integrating with CCS.
The page discusses the implementation of carbon capture and storage (CCS) technology in aluminum smelters, which could reduce CO2 emissions by over 60%. It covers the cost implications, technological challenges, and potential benefits of retrofitting existing smelters with CCS. The page also explores the capital and operating expenditures associated with decarbonization efforts, including the use of inert-anode technology.
The page discusses the costs and benefits of various technologies for decarbonizing aluminum production, focusing on the Bayer process and comparing different energy sources and technologies like CCS, inert anodes, MVR, and green hydrogen. It highlights the trade-offs between capital and operating costs and the potential for cost reduction through technology improvements and learning curves.
This page compares the capital expenditure for Hall-Héroult (HH), HH with carbon capture and storage, and inert anode technologies. The inert anode technology demands a significant retrofit cost, primarily due to the need for new potrooms and vertical cell configuration. However, some costs like anode rodding and chlorination plant are eliminated. The retrofit cell cost for inert anode is notably higher than HH.
This page compares the operating expenses of different smelting technologies, focusing on raw materials, electricity, anodes, labor, and other costs. It highlights the impact of carbon capture and storage and inert anodes on expenses, showing potential savings and increased costs. The inert anode technology offers longer anode life and reduced labor costs but has higher initial anode costs. Overall, the inert anode technology can reduce total operating expenses by 3% to 10% compared to the Hall-Héroult process.
This page compares various boiler types for CO2 emissions reduction in aluminum production, detailing their efficiency, costs, and technology readiness levels. Electric and hydrogen-fired boilers show potential for significant emissions reduction compared to natural gas boilers.
This page compares the decarbonization potential of calcination technologies using natural gas, a hydrogen-based calciner with electrolysis, and natural gas with carbon capture and storage. It highlights the thermal input, fuel requirements, CO₂ emissions, and costs associated with each method, emphasizing the lower CO₂ production and higher costs of the hydrogen-based calciner.
This page outlines the key inputs for a model related to aluminum decarbonization, covering refinery, smelter, and financial aspects. It details specific inputs for each category, including capacity, utilization rates, investment scenarios, energy sources, and financial parameters.

Generative AI offers significant economic opportunities and challenges for organizations.
