The page also mentions key milestones like AlphaGo and the broad utility of tools like ChatGPT, emphasizing their ability to perform routine tasks.
This page discusses the evolution and impact of generative AI, highlighting its capabilities in writing, composing music, and creating digital art. It explains the role of foundation models and deep learning in powering generative AI applications, their ability to process large datasets, and the challenges in computational power and responsibility. The page also covers the rapid growth in funding for generative AI, the advancements in LLMs like GPT-4 and Claude, and the concentration of investments in North America. It concludes by emphasizing the potential of generative AI to transform various business functions and unlock significant economic value.
This section introduces the potential of generative AI to create value for companies and transform the workforce, sharing initial findings across various functions and industries.
This page discusses the potential impact of generative AI through two lenses: total economic potential of 60-plus organizational use cases and labor productivity potential across detailed work activities. It highlights the value and economic benefits of generative AI in various business functions and occupations.
This page discusses the potential economic impact of generative AI, estimating its ability to enhance labor productivity and create additional value beyond what traditional AI and analytics can achieve. The chart illustrates the incremental economic impact of generative AI in various scenarios, ranging from 15-40% and 35-70%, and compares it with advanced analytics and total AI economic potential.
The document discusses the economic benefits of generative AI, estimating its potential value at $6.1 to $7.9 trillion annually. It highlights the use of a proprietary McKinsey database and expert insights to assess the value potential, focusing on significant improvements in key outputs. The analysis excludes cases where the sole benefit is natural language use, emphasizing the potential for generative AI to enhance productivity in sales and marketing. The document also notes the ongoing development of generative AI and its potential to open new frontiers in creativity and innovation.
This page discusses the value potential of generative AI across various business functions, highlighting that customer operations, marketing and sales, software engineering, and research and development account for about 75% of the total annual value. A graph illustrates the impact of generative AI in different functions, showing that manufacturing and supply chain functions have lower potential value compared to previous AI applications.
Generative AI can revolutionize internal knowledge management systems, enabling employees to access information quickly and make informed decisions. It can also reduce the time spent searching for information, increasing efficiency and effectiveness. Examples of operational benefits as a virtual expert are provided.
Generative AI can revolutionize customer operations by enhancing productivity, improving issue resolution, and personalizing customer interactions. It benefits less-experienced agents while offering self-service, instant data retrieval, reduced response times, and increased sales opportunities.
Generative AI in marketing and sales offers efficient content creation, enhanced data use, SEO optimization, and personalized product discovery. It reduces time and effort, improves consistency, and leverages customer data for better marketing strategies, while requiring careful consideration of risks like plagiarism and bias.
Generative AI can enhance marketing productivity by 5-15% and sales productivity by 3-5%, offering personalized product descriptions, higher-quality data insights, and improved lead development. It can also act as a virtual collaborator, accelerating productivity and enhancing knowledge work.
Generative AI can significantly boost software engineering productivity by 20-45% through accelerated coding, reduced time on tasks, and improved code quality. Large tech companies like GitHub and OpenAI are already integrating these tools, enhancing efficiency and work experience for developers.
Generative AI in R&D can boost productivity by 10-15% of R&D costs, accelerating product development and enhancing design quality. It pairs well with deep learning surrogates for testing and has potential in multimodal applications beyond text.
Deep learning surrogates are revolutionizing product design by emulating physics-based simulations at higher speeds and lower costs. Generative AI advances in image, audio, and video generation are transforming marketing and media industries. These technologies have significant value potential across various industries, with estimated economic impact ranging from $2.6 to $4.4 trillion.
This page presents a detailed analysis of the impact of generative AI on various business functions across different industries. It highlights the varying percentages of industry revenue impacted and the total potential economic value, ranging from 2,600 to 4,400 billion dollars. Industries like high tech and banking show significant potential, while others like agriculture and public sector have lower impacts. The data is sourced from multiple reputable databases and McKinsey analysis.
Generative AI is estimated to add $310 billion in value to the retail industry by enhancing marketing and customer interactions. In high tech, its main value lies in accelerating software development.
This chapter explores how generative AI will impact work activities, economic growth, and productivity. It highlights the historical role of technology in augmenting human capabilities and suggests that generative AI may follow a similar pattern, though affecting different types of activities and occupations.
This page discusses the impact of technological automation on work activities, emphasizing the gradual adoption of technology and its potential to shift work activities globally. It highlights historical and demographic factors influencing labor markets and the role of generative AI in accelerating automation and enhancing workforce capabilities.
This page discusses how generative AI has accelerated technology performance, enabling it to match or exceed human capabilities sooner than expected. It highlights a shift in the timeline for achieving median human performance in natural-language understanding from 2027 to 2023. The exhibit illustrates expert assessments on various technical capabilities, showing advancements in areas like creativity, logical reasoning, and social and emotional reasoning.
The advent of generative AI has accelerated the potential for technical automation, increasing the percentage of automatable hours from 50% to 60-70%. The technical potential curve is steep due to advancements in natural-language capabilities. The range between early and late scenarios has compressed, reflecting greater confidence in technological capabilities. Global economic growth has slowed, with declining birth rates and aging populations posing challenges. Employment decline is a significant obstacle, with compound annual growth in the workforce slowing significantly.
Productivity growth, a key driver of GDP over the past 30 years, has slowed recently. Generative AI and other technologies could accelerate productivity growth, compensating for declining employment growth and boosting economic growth. Automation could provide an annual productivity boost of 0.5 to 3.4 percent from 2023 to 2040, with generative AI contributing 0.1 to 0.6 percentage points, depending on automation adoption rates and workers' ability to shift to new activities.
Generative AI can boost productivity growth by expanding automation potential and offsetting aging workforce impacts. However, it requires effective labor redeployment and worker support for transitioning to new activities.
This page discusses the potential of generative AI to reshape businesses and society, highlighting its economic benefits and transformative impact. It also addresses the challenges and risks, including concerns about content accuracy, bias, and intellectual property infringement, urging stakeholders to act swiftly to address these issues.
This page discusses the responsible use of generative AI, highlighting various risks such as fairness, intellectual property, privacy, security, explainability, reliability, organizational impact, and social and environmental impact. It also poses critical questions for companies and business leaders on managing these risks while capturing the potential value of the technology.
This page discusses the challenges and opportunities presented by generative AI for policy makers and individuals. It explores workforce planning, retraining programs, human-centric AI policies, and the balance between AI's benefits and risks. The text emphasizes the need for collaboration among stakeholders to ensure AI's positive impact on society and the economy.
This page discusses the potential and challenges of generative AI (gen AI), emphasizing its impact on productivity and innovation. It highlights the debate around gen AI's transformative capabilities versus its risks, estimating its economic potential and the need for CEOs to consider strategic questions. The text also underscores the importance of viewing gen AI as part of broader technology trends like Web 3.0 and AR/VR, suggesting a comprehensive approach to leveraging emerging technologies.
This page discusses the strategic opportunities and challenges of generative AI for telco companies, emphasizing the need for value creation, leveraging disintermediation, and exploring new platforms. It highlights the importance of combining technology with proprietary data, finding underserved segments in the value chain, and addressing talent needs for automation. The page also notes the potential for new entrants to lead in the gen AI market.
This page discusses the challenges and requirements for successfully scaling AI, emphasizing the need for exceptional human capital, proper design, and a holistic approach to risk management. It outlines six dimensions for creating a digitally capable organization and highlights the importance of addressing intermediate and ESG risks.
This page discusses the pragmatic approach for CEOs to manage AI-related risks by setting up cross-functional teams, establishing ethical guidelines, and continuously monitoring AI systems. It emphasizes the importance of CEOs leading thorough discussions on AI strategy to transform organizations and industries, advocating for big thinking and clear road maps.
This page introduces the sector view focusing on telecom operators, likely discussing their role, challenges, and opportunities in the context of AI and gen AI in TMT.
AI is transforming industries, including telecoms, by enhancing customer service, personalization, and employee performance. However, telcos lag behind in AI adoption due to disjointed strategies and lack of top-level sponsorship. Transitioning to AI-native organizations can drive growth and renewal, requiring holistic AI integration and aligned investments.
This page discusses the case for telcos becoming AI-native, highlighting factors such as increasing accessibility of AI technology, rapid data explosion, proven use cases, technology investments as business drivers, and the need for hypercharging operator bets. It emphasizes the importance of AI in driving revenue, transforming costs, enhancing customer experience, and meeting new demands.
This page discusses how telcos can use AI to protect their core business and improve margins by leveraging user-level data for hyperpersonalization in sales and engagement. It also explores how AI can enable proactive service through autonomous resolution and predictive capabilities, enhancing customer experience and reducing churn.
This page discusses AI-driven innovations in telco service and retail, highlighting case studies of AI reducing troubleshooting calls, virtual retail assistants enhancing customer experience, and self-healing networks optimizing operations.
The AI-native telco uses AI for network performance monitoring, frontline productivity improvement, and intelligent internal operations. AI tools enhance workforce planning, provide personalized coaching, and offer insights for decision-making across various business functions.
This page discusses the success factors of AI-native transformation, emphasizing the importance of building AI capabilities in a modular and reusable way, integrating AI models, and leveraging digital twins for a single source of truth. It highlights the benefits of AI in decision-making and execution, supported by a case study and best practices for developing transformative AI.
The page discusses best practices for managing AI, including building propensity models, using digital twins, implementing MLOps, rethinking tech talent strategies, treating AI as a product, setting up AI labs, refreshing AI tech stacks, speeding up IT and data modernization, and ensuring trustworthy AI solutions.
This page discusses the next steps for building an AI-native telco, emphasizing the importance of change management, user involvement, and executive alignment. It highlights the need for operators to learn from other industries, invest in AI, and create a strategic vision for AI deployment. The journey requires commitment and leadership to overcome organizational inertia and drive successful AI-native transformation.
The document discusses the potential of generative AI for telcos to reignite growth, detailing early successes in customer service and cost savings. It highlights the industry's cautious optimism and the need for a holistic AI-native approach to achieve sustainable growth and competitive advantage.
The document highlights significant cost reductions achieved by telcos using generative AI in various domains, including customer service, network, IT, marketing and sales, and support functions. It discusses the potential for AI to unlock $100 billion in incremental value and $140-$180 billion in productivity gains. The article explores how telco leaders can leverage AI for transformation, addressing challenges and providing insights from research and industry surveys.
Generative AI can significantly enhance AI capabilities and create new value sources in telecommunications. It improves customer service, marketing, and network operations, reducing costs and increasing productivity through hyperpersonalization and optimized technology configurations.
This page discusses the significant impact of generative AI on telcos, highlighting its use cases and value in customer service, marketing and sales, network optimization, IT support, and back-office functions. It emphasizes the potential to improve operational planning, software development, and employee productivity, supported by examples and data from telco companies.
The page discusses the challenges and opportunities telcos face in adopting generative AI, including improving employee productivity, creating new products, and facing competitive pressures. It highlights the need for a holistic approach, including talent acquisition, quality data, and change management, to achieve successful AI integration.
The page discusses the focus of small and large operators on generative AI use cases for customer service and IT. It highlights the challenges and strategies for telcos in adopting generative AI, emphasizing the importance of aligning vision, value, and road map. The text also advises on choosing between building, buying, or fine-tuning solutions, cautioning against the pitfalls of building common AI solutions from scratch.
This page discusses the importance of upskilling and expanding internal expertise in generative AI for telcos, emphasizing the need for collaboration with solution providers and internal training programs. It highlights the benefits of building in-house AI expertise and the shift towards centralized decision-making and reusable services in the operating model.
This page discusses the importance of creating a technology blueprint for reusability, innovation, and excellence in gen AI transformation. It emphasizes the need for a control tower to monitor and manage AI models, LLMOps for streamlined management, and comprehensive data collection for responsible use. Organizations should develop frameworks for scaling pilots, reusing AI capabilities, and establishing innovation labs to stay ahead in the industry.
This page discusses responsible use and change management in gen AI, emphasizing data governance, validation processes, and the importance of upskilling and change management for successful implementation. It highlights examples from telcos and outlines future opportunities with gen AI.
The page discusses how generative AI can enhance telcos' profitability through cognitive chatbots, improving efficiency and customer experience. It highlights the challenges telcos face in adopting AI and the potential for those who embrace it to gain a competitive edge.
Generative AI's impact on telecom operators is estimated between $60-100 billion. Successful implementation requires strategic road maps across key areas, prioritizing governance, data, talent, and technologies. Use cases promise incremental improvements and radical reimagining of the telco sector, driving productivity and innovation.
This page outlines how generative AI can accelerate the telco industry's future by enhancing productivity, sales, customer service, IT, support functions, and network operations. It details specific improvements in B2B and B2C marketing, customer service, IT productivity, automated HR tasks, and network capital expenditures. Early adopters are seeing significant returns with minimal investment, with potential margin increases of 3-4 percentage points in two years and 8-10 percentage points in five years.
This page outlines various AI use cases for telcos across different departments, including marketing, sales, customer care, network, support, and new businesses. It highlights the commercial boosters, cost optimizations, and key impacts of implementing AI in each area, such as personalized campaigns, AI chatbots, and enhanced call center operations.
This page discusses how Gen AI can boost sales through personalized content creation, detailing various B2C marketing use cases such as hyper-personalized content, intelligent content generation, enhanced global marketing, tailored product offerings, and customer feedback analysis. Each use case is explained with potential applications and impacts in the Telco/TMT sector.
This page discusses how Gen AI can optimize call center efficiencies and enhance customer experience by supporting agents with relevant data, personalized recommendations, and best practices. It details prioritized use cases for both sales and customer service, highlighting potential impacts such as increased conversion rates and reduced call volumes.
This page outlines various use cases for generative AI in the telecommunications and TMT sectors, detailing potential applications and impacts. It covers automation in after-call logging, personalized customer service chatbots, invoice-focused chatbots, and customer interaction databases, highlighting improvements in efficiency and customer experience.
This page discusses how generative AI can enhance network operations and reduce call center costs by addressing technical issues more efficiently. It outlines various use cases, including circuit inventory management, chatbots for network data, root-cause identification, self-healing networks, and mobile care, detailing their potential impacts on cost reduction, productivity increase, and customer care ticket reduction.
This page discusses the application of generative AI in optimizing network usage and IT operations, highlighting potential impacts such as reduced third-party network consumption and increased productivity in software development. It details specific use cases and their future states, emphasizing the role of AI in enhancing code debugging, optimization, and development processes.
This page discusses two prioritized use cases for generative AI in the telco/TMT sector: code migration for legacy languages and a query assistant. Both use cases aim to increase productivity by 20-30%, with the former focusing on code interpretation and translation, and the latter on efficient data querying and retrieval.
The telecom industry is rapidly evolving, driven by emerging technologies like AI, 5G, and VR. This transformation demands new talent strategies for telcos, who face increasing competition for technical skills. The document outlines seven tech trends reshaping the industry and emphasizes the need for diverse, adaptable talent pipelines to meet future challenges.
The document discusses the evolving role of telcos in meeting customer expectations and the need for telcos to adapt to new technologies. It highlights the importance of hiring the right talent to embrace seven tech trends, which will reduce the need for skills specific to outdated infrastructure. The ever-expanding connectivity through 5G and 6G infrastructure is paving the way for innovative services and experiences. The demand for connectivity is expected to increase with the growth in connected devices and remote work. Additionally, the demand for tech talent critical to telcos is also growing in other industries.
This page discusses the evolving demands on telcos due to remote work and 5G/6G expansion, emphasizing the need for skilled talent in network design, engineering, and innovation. It highlights edge computing's role in enhancing data processing and its implications for various industries. The page also touches on the rise of next-generation transportation technologies.
The page discusses the potential of edge computing in the transportation industry, highlighting its efficiency and sustainability. It emphasizes the growing interest of telcos in various edge computing use cases, as shown in Exhibit 2. The chart illustrates the level of interest among telco executives in different applications, such as video monitoring, augmented reality, and autonomous vehicles. The data suggests a strong inclination towards adopting these technologies to enhance mobility and emergency services, especially in remote areas.
This page discusses the need for telcos to develop skills in network design, engineering, automation, IoT, UX, and data science to support vehicle connectivity and xRAN technologies. It highlights the benefits of xRAN, including flexibility, cost reduction, and vendor competition. The page also emphasizes the importance of trust architecture and digital identity in building consumer trust and privacy.
This page discusses the importance of investing in cybersecurity solutions and the skills needed for digital identity development, cybersecurity, automation, privacy engineering, network engineering, and DevOps. It highlights the potential of AI and generative AI in optimizing networks, addressing maintenance issues, minimizing churn, and enhancing customer experience. It also covers the strategic value of quantum technology in developing secure networks and protecting data.
This page discusses the impact of quantum computing on encryption methods and the need for telcos to develop talent strategies to address emerging tech trends. It outlines the skills required in quantum technology, cybersecurity, network engineering, and product management. The page also emphasizes the importance of aligning investments with business goals and conducting business impact assessments to identify the most relevant tech trends.
This page discusses how telcos can prioritize different technology trends based on their strategic goals, assess talent gaps, and design a tech talent strategy. It highlights the importance of understanding talent demand, demographic variations, and market scarcity to effectively prioritize talent pools and invest in critical skills.
This page discusses the importance of long-term thinking in tech talent management, highlighting the ongoing shortage despite layoffs. It emphasizes the need for telcos to expand talent pipelines, address diversity issues, and reimagine career development to attract top talent. Building holistic university partnerships is also crucial for sustainable talent acquisition.
This page discusses holistic university partnerships and tech talent consortia as strategies for telcos to capture tech talent. It highlights Qualcomm's investment in UC San Diego, Apple's HBCU C2 initiative, and Lockheed Martin's partnership with the University of Colorado Boulder. It also emphasizes the importance of launching or joining tech talent consortiums and adapting strategies based on rigorous evaluations for telcos' future success.
This page introduces the section on deploying generative AI, focusing on strategies and considerations for integrating Gen AI into TMT sectors.
This page discusses the impact of generative AI on organizations and the economy, emphasizing the need for business leaders to understand and strategically implement gen AI. It highlights the technology's accessibility, potential for automation, and the importance of addressing employee concerns. The text also stresses the necessity for leaders to demystify gen AI, build a compelling narrative, and identify high-impact applications to enhance employee experience and stay competitive.
This page discusses the implications of generative AI on organizational culture, business models, and talent management. It emphasizes the need for leaders to consider the wide-ranging effects of AI, from operational transparency to cultural adaptability, and highlights the importance of having the right technical talent and infrastructure in place.
This page discusses the increasing demand for tech talent skilled in generative AI, emphasizing the need for business leaders to identify necessary applications and talent types. It highlights the challenges of building and maintaining gen AI applications and the importance of career development, advancement, and learning opportunities in retaining tech talent. The page also explores the impact of gen AI on apprenticeship and skill-building programs.
This page discusses the potential risks and benefits of incorporating generative AI into business strategies, emphasizing the need for leaders to understand and address risks such as biases, intellectual property exposure, and malicious content creation. It also highlights the importance of employee training and organizational considerations in leveraging gen AI effectively.
This page discusses how generative AI can enhance employee experience, empower middle managers, and help organizations reinvent talent management practices. It also highlights the role of senior leaders in guiding the implementation and adoption of gen AI within the organization.
This page discusses the importance of senior leaders understanding and implementing generative AI in their organizations. It emphasizes the need for ongoing education, forward-thinking strategies, and the identification of high-impact use cases. It also highlights the necessity of building necessary roles, skills, and capabilities for the future, ensuring employees can effectively use gen AI in their daily work.
This page discusses the rapid advancement of gen AI applications and emphasizes the importance of leaders utilizing this intelligence effectively. It highlights the need for organization-specific tailoring and experimentation in integrating gen AI. The authors, Sandra Durth, Bryan Hancock, Dana Maor, and Alexander Sukharevsky, acknowledge contributors and editors involved in the article.
This page outlines seven key actions for data leaders to consider when scaling generative AI, emphasizing the importance of data readiness, value-driven strategies, data architecture capabilities, data quality, data security, talent development, and performance tracking.
This page discusses the roles of Shaper, Maker, and Taker businesses in the context of generative AI, emphasizing the CDO's role in supporting the Shaper approach. It highlights the importance of data management, labeling, and prioritizing initiatives that provide broad business benefits. The page also stresses the need for a comprehensive view on value, considering traditional AI, business intelligence, and machine learning alongside generative AI.
The page discusses building specific capabilities into data architecture to support generative AI use cases. It highlights the need for CDOs to focus on fixing data architecture foundations and determining necessary upgrades. Key components include unstructured data stores, data preprocessing, vector databases, and LLM integrations, emphasizing the importance of a strong data foundation and cost-effective management.
This page discusses the need for upgrades in existing data architecture to enable generative AI, covering data sources, ingestion, repositories, services, and consumption. It emphasizes the importance of prompt engineering and the integration of knowledge graphs for effective AI output.
This page discusses the importance of data quality in generative AI models, emphasizing the need for CDOs to extend data observability programs and develop interventions across the data life cycle. It highlights the challenges posed by unstructured data and outlines four key areas: source data, preprocessing, prompt quality, and output governance. Additionally, it addresses the need to protect sensitive data and adapt quickly to emerging regulations, focusing on security risks and managing access to personally identifiable information (PII).
This page discusses strategies for managing generative AI in enterprises, including setting up protection systems, tracking regulations, building data engineering talent, using generative AI for data management, and rigorously tracking progress. It highlights the need for specialized training, focusing on data engineers and architects, and integrating generative AI into business processes.
This page outlines generative AI use cases along the data value chain, including data discovery, ingestion, storage, processing, access, consumption, governance, and interpretation. It also discusses key performance indicators (KPIs) for measuring the cost, revenue, time-to-market, and end-user satisfaction of generative AI applications, as well as operational KPIs for tracking data usage, model performance, and data quality.
CDOs need to develop FinOps-like capabilities to manage generative AI costs, optimize expenses, and establish data-performance metrics for real-time decision-making. Data is crucial for capturing value from generative AI, requiring CDOs who can lead with data, not just manage it.
This page outlines nine key actions for CIOs and CTOs to harness the potential of generative AI, emphasizing rapid adoption, business reimagining, technology function enhancement, leveraging existing services, upgrading enterprise architecture, developing data architecture, creating a centralized AI team, investing in upskilling, and evaluating new risks.
This page discusses the strategic steps CIOs and CTOs should take regarding generative AI adoption, including determining the company's posture, identifying valuable use cases, and reimagining the technology function. It emphasizes balancing risk with innovation, establishing guidelines, and estimating costs and returns.
This page discusses strategies for CIOs and CTOs to leverage generative AI in software development, technical debt reduction, and IT operations. It emphasizes the importance of focusing on areas like code development, refactoring, and documentation. The page also explores the decision-making process for adopting generative AI capabilities, highlighting the 'Taker' and 'Shaper' archetypes for utilizing existing services or adapting open-source models.
This page discusses strategies for integrating generative AI models into enterprise technology architectures, highlighting the Shaper and Maker archetypes. It explains the 'bring the model to the data' and 'bring data to the model' approaches, the costs and complexities of building foundation models, and the need for CIOs and CTOs to upgrade their technology architecture to integrate and scale generative AI capabilities. Recent integration and orchestration frameworks are also mentioned as tools to facilitate this integration.
This page details the estimated total cost of ownership for different AI archetypes, including Taker, Shaper, and Maker, with specific use cases and cost breakdowns for onetime and recurring expenses. The costs cover various aspects such as model development, data and model pipeline building, fine-tuning, and maintenance.
This page illustrates how generative AI integrates at key touchpoints in a customer journey using a travel agent bot. It shows the interaction between the customer, chatbot, AI model, back-end applications, data sources, and infrastructure. The process includes logging in, reviewing options, requesting live support, and completing booking changes, with AI facilitating each step.
This page outlines five essential elements for integrating generative AI effectively: context management and caching, policy management, model hub, prompt library, and MLOps platform. It also discusses the importance of developing a data architecture to enable access to quality data, emphasizing the need for collaboration between CIOs, CTOs, and data officers to optimize data usage for generative AI models.
This page illustrates the emerging tech stack for generative AI, detailing components like apps-as-a-service, data sources, platforms, infrastructure, experience layer, context management, model hubs, foundation models, MLOps, enterprise platforms, QA, observability, policy management, and prompt libraries, all interconnected for efficient AI operations.
The page discusses the creation of a centralized, cross-functional generative AI platform team and the need to tailor upskilling programs by roles and proficiency levels. It emphasizes the importance of integrating generative AI capabilities into the existing infrastructure and highlights the potential productivity gains and challenges associated with different skill levels.
This page discusses the importance of upskilling employees in the use of generative AI, focusing on software developers and non-technical staff. It highlights the need for training in code review, understanding AI-generated code, and ethical considerations. The text also addresses the new risk landscape introduced by generative AI, including ethical questions, data privacy, and compliance issues, and suggests mitigation practices such as adjusting AI models and implementing data protection protocols.
This page discusses the importance of privacy safeguards and transparency in managing generative AI risks. It highlights the need for CIOs and CTOs to address access control and intellectual property concerns. The text also emphasizes the rapid growth of generative AI and the necessity for tech leaders to develop a strategic approach. Contributions from various McKinsey partners and consultants are acknowledged.
This page discusses the rapid advancement of generative AI, its regulatory challenges, and the need for a strategic roadmap for risk functions. It highlights the economic potential of gen AI, the risks associated with its adoption, and the current international regulatory landscape for AI.
The document discusses global variations in AI governance regulations, highlighting common themes such as transparency, human agency, accountability, technical robustness, diversity, privacy, and social well-being. It outlines different policy types and countries' approaches, emphasizing the challenges organizations face in navigating these evolving rules.
This page outlines global AI governance policies and regulatory efforts from 2019 to 2023, including nonbinding principles, general AI legislation, and vertical-specific AI regulations. It highlights key initiatives by various countries and organizations, such as South Korea's Ethical Guidelines, the EU AI Act, and China's draft provisions on internet information services.
Organizations face legal, reputational, and financial risks if they do not act swiftly on AI regulations. Preemptive actions include transparency in AI usage and governance structures to ensure oversight and adaptability to evolving technology and regulations.
This page discusses data, model, and technology management for AI and gen AI, emphasizing data quality, model fairness, cybersecurity, and ethical considerations. It highlights the need for robust principles, risk management, and user education to ensure responsible AI use.
This page discusses six major trends in gen AI for 2024, including multimodal capabilities, interaction with data systems, easier model control, democratization of development, platform play, and cost decline. It also emphasizes the importance of a top-down gen AI strategy for CEOs to ensure at-scale value creation.
This page discusses the importance of reimagining entire domains rather than isolated use cases in gen AI strategies. It emphasizes the need for organizations to focus on the full software delivery life cycle, aligning gen AI with business outcomes. The text also highlights the strategic decision between buying and building gen AI solutions, advocating for selective investment and strategic building. Additionally, it stresses the importance of building products rather than proofs of concept, ensuring scalability and performance through engineering and experimentation.
This page discusses the acceleration of AI efforts through reusable code components, the shift from hype to real business value in 2024, and the strategic importance of digital and analytics transformations for lasting competitive advantages.
This appendix discusses the practical applications of generative AI solutions, showcasing various tools developed by McKinsey. It highlights their benefits in different industries, such as tech services, media, billing, and customer support. The appendix encourages readers to explore these solutions further and stay ahead in the evolving AI landscape.
This page provides definitions for various AI and machine learning concepts, including machine learning, modality, productivity from labor, prompt engineering, self-attention, structured data, transformers, technical automation potential, use cases, and unstructured data. It explains how these concepts relate to AI capabilities, data processing, and potential applications.

pages.abstract: This executive summary discusses the potential for decarbonizing the built environment, highlighting the need for industry collaboration and the benefits of cost-effective solutions. It analyzes 1,000 levers for reducing emissions, focusing on six asset archetypes. The report identifies 17 opportunities for industry players and emphasizes the importance of partnerships and regional factors in achieving a net-zero world.
pages.title: Executive summary

pages.page_path: library_pages\Building value by decarbonizing the built environment_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_6.jpg
pages.abstract: The built environment significantly contributes to global emissions, with 26% of GHG emissions and 37% of combustion-related emissions linked to construction and operation. Solutions for decarbonization exist but require urgent implementation. Operational emissions from existing structures and embodied emissions from materials are key challenges. Decarbonization efforts can particularly target space and water heating in residential buildings.
pages.title: A serious challenge

pages.page_path: library_pages\Building value by decarbonizing the built environment_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_7.jpg
pages.abstract: This page details the significant contribution of water and space heating to operational emissions in multifamily homes, showing a breakdown of emissions by energy source and usage. It highlights the potential of various levers to reduce these emissions, emphasizing cost-effectiveness and scalability by 2030.
pages.title: Most operational emissions in multifamily homes are caused by water and space heating.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Building value by decarbonizing the built environment_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_8.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the challenges and opportunities of industrializing decarbonization solutions in the built environment. It highlights the need for ecosystem players to address challenges like regional variations, established practices, and potential shortages of labor and materials. Despite these challenges, industrialization can reduce input costs and create value through consistent supply chains, process efficiencies, and stable customer demand. Early movers can capture significant value by leading the industrialization and commercial adoption of decarbonization solutions, benefiting various stakeholders in the built-environment ecosystem.
pages.title: Twenty-two levers can reduce operational emissions by up to 90 percent and embodied emissions by up to 60 percent for the built environment.

pages.title: 4. Design and engineer both green and cost-effective structures

pages.page_path: library_pages\Building value by decarbonizing the built environment_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_47.jpg

The text also emphasizes the importance of standardization and regional knowledge in scaling modular businesses.
pages.title: Build and scale electrified offerings and on-site charging infrastructure for equipment

pages.page_path: library_pages\Building value by decarbonizing the built environment_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_48.jpg

The text also emphasizes the role of green materials and solutions, the benefits of a 'carbon passport,' and the potential for increased asset value and better financial terms for those who decarbonize.

The text also explores the concept of energy-as-a-service financing as a solution to reduce upfront costs for green technologies.
pages.title: Finance the green transition

pages.page_path: library_pages\Building value by decarbonizing the built environment_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_50.jpg

pages.title: Scale offerings of green insurance underwriting

It highlights the use of inert anodes in aluminum smelting and other decarbonization levers, noting that while significant reductions are possible, the cost-effectiveness and scale of these measures vary between the two archetypes.
This page discusses the potential for reducing emissions from large infrastructure projects and operational emissions in buildings. It highlights that about 10% of emissions from infrastructure projects can be abated with cost-effective measures today or by 2030. Additionally, operational emissions from buildings, especially multifamily dwellings, can be significantly reduced using ROI-positive levers. The page emphasizes the importance of circularity in materials and other mechanisms to further decarbonize the built environment.
Circular technologies, including alternative fuels and carbon curing, can help decarbonize 80% of cement and concrete emissions by 2050. While value-positive by 2050, these technologies face challenges in scaling and industrializing in the near to medium term.
This page discusses the potential business opportunities in decarbonizing the built environment, emphasizing the need to unlock barriers and accelerate adoption of abatement technologies. It highlights pathways to cost-effective decarbonization, the role of industrialization, and the push for deep renovations in the European Union. It also stresses the importance of creating a collaborative ecosystem involving various stakeholders to fully realize these opportunities.
This page discusses the opportunities for ecosystem players to industrialize the production of green materials, such as low-carbon cement, through partnerships and decarbonization efforts. It highlights the potential for cost-effective solutions and the role of biomass and waste in reducing emissions in the cement production process.
This page outlines an ecosystem for decarbonizing the built environment, detailing various solutions, providers, and enablers. It covers low-carbon materials, energy-efficient technologies, and financial mechanisms, emphasizing the roles of different stakeholders in achieving sustainability goals.
This page discusses decarbonization opportunities in cement production, including CCUS retrofitting, low-carbon concrete production, and the use of SCMs like fly ash and GGBFS. It highlights the potential of modern grinding technologies and upcycled concrete as fillers or SCMs, and the role of waste management firms in sourcing clinker substitutes. The page also mentions carbon curing as a method to further decarbonize concrete.
This page discusses strategies for steel producers to reduce emissions in construction steel production, including DRI-EAF technology, green hydrogen, CCUS integration, and industry clustering. It highlights partnerships and agreements for green hydrogen and biojet fuel, emphasizing the role of hydrogen and CCUS hubs in accelerating decarbonization efforts.
This page discusses the scale manufacturing of low-cost engineered wood and low-carbon insulation, highlighting their potential to reduce emissions in construction. It emphasizes the benefits of engineered wood as an alternative to concrete and steel, and the opportunities for insulation manufacturers to use recycled materials and improve production processes. The page also introduces the need to industrialize energy-efficient building technology, focusing on heat pumps to decarbonize space cooling, heating, and water heating.
This page discusses scaling the production of low-cost and high-efficiency heat pumps and the need for efficient energy and electrification upgrades. It highlights the opportunities for large appliance and commercial manufacturers and the benefits of standardizing designs, diversifying suppliers, and vertically integrating supply chains. The page also addresses the challenges of fragmented energy upgrade services and proposes the development of comprehensive energy upgrade services to ease transaction costs and maximize energy savings.
This page discusses strategies for designing and engineering green and cost-effective structures, emphasizing the role of D&E firms in minimizing emissions and waste. It highlights the importance of expanding green design capabilities, leveraging off-site construction methods, and enhancing cost estimation tools. The page also explores the potential of generative design AI and the electrification of construction equipment to support decarbonization efforts.
This page discusses the opportunities in electrifying construction equipment and developing off-site modular construction solutions. It highlights the need for partnerships to expand charging infrastructure for electric construction equipment and the benefits of modular construction in reducing costs, waste, and construction time. The text also emphasizes the importance of standardization and regional knowledge in scaling modular businesses.
This section discusses the importance of validating and certifying low-carbon actions and solutions, establishing trustworthy green credentials, and accurately verifying and tracking emissions in the built environment. It highlights the need for transparency, accountability, and partnerships between auditing, environmental, and engineering firms to measure emissions accurately. The text also emphasizes the role of green materials and solutions, the benefits of a 'carbon passport,' and the potential for increased asset value and better financial terms for those who decarbonize.
The document discusses the importance of financing the green transition, highlighting the need for new approaches to overcome barriers such as high capital expenditures and limited insurance offerings. It emphasizes the role of upskilling professionals and establishing partnerships between training academies and companies. The text also explores the concept of energy-as-a-service financing as a solution to reduce upfront costs for green technologies.
The document discusses energy as a service and project financing for green solutions, highlighting the benefits of partnerships across the energy value chain and the need for new technologies and processes to support decarbonization. It emphasizes the importance of financial levers and long-term savings in green projects.
This page discusses the challenges and opportunities for insurers in underwriting green buildings and infrastructure, emphasizing the need for expertise in assessing risks and facilitating the transition to green assets. It highlights the potential for partnerships and investments to drive the adoption of green solutions and decarbonization efforts in the built environment.
This page illustrates the integration of human infrastructure with nature, highlighting the importance of sustainable practices in the built environment. The image of a road winding through a dense forest symbolizes the balance between development and environmental preservation.
This page discusses strategies for companies in the built environment to decarbonize and create value through new green businesses. It emphasizes assessing current models, identifying opportunities, and partnering for upscaling solutions. Smaller players can prove potential solutions, while larger companies can support industrialization and secure demand for green technologies.
This page discusses the need for significant efforts to decarbonize the built environment, highlighting the viability of transformative technologies and the importance of collaboration among stakeholders. It acknowledges contributions from various individuals and organizations, including the Net Zero Built Environment Council, which aims to accelerate decarbonization through transparency, green growth, and collaboration.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Closing the loop_ Increasing fashion circularity in california_McKinsey_2022_03_31\page_11.jpg
pages.abstract: The fashion industry faces a critical decision to either degrade habitats or reinvent operations for sustainability. Circularity, involving reduce, reuse, and recycle dimensions, can reshape the industry. The closed-loop fashion lifecycle, consisting of eight stages, focuses on recycling materials and building a sustainable value chain in California.
pages.title: The closed-loop fashion lifecycle

pages.page_path: library_pages\Closing the loop_ Increasing fashion circularity in california_McKinsey_2022_03_31\page_12.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the need for a local model in achieving full circularity in the fashion industry, emphasizing the benefits of textile-to-textile recycling within a region. It highlights the current linear and global nature of the fashion value chain, with most materials being virgin and sourced from natural resources. The industry's reliance on countries like China, India, Vietnam, and the US for yarn production and finished apparel exportation is also noted.
pages.title: Achieving full circularity requires a local model

pages.page_path: library_pages\Closing the loop_ Increasing fashion circularity in california_McKinsey_2022_03_31\page_13.jpg
pages.abstract: This page illustrates the global fashion value chain, mapping the origins and pathways of materials for typical cotton and synthetic garments worn in the US. pages.title: The fashion value chain is global

pages.page_path: library_pages\Closing the loop_ Increasing fashion circularity in california_McKinsey_2022_03_31\page_14.jpg
pages.abstract: The production of a polyester t-shirt has significant environmental impacts, including 11 kg of CO2e emissions, 380 liters of water consumption, 1+ pounds of chemicals, and 2-7 m2 of land use. The front-end activities of the apparel value chain, such as raw material production and garment manufacturing, account for the majority of these impacts. Reducing these impacts requires actions in sourcing, manufacturing, and waste management, with circularity being a key approach.
pages.title: Producing a garment can be resource-intensive

pages.page_path: library_pages\Closing the loop_ Increasing fashion circularity in california_McKinsey_2022_03_31\page_15.jpg

pages.title: Material production creates the greatest climate impact across the fashion lifecycle

pages.page_path: library_pages\Closing the loop_ Increasing fashion circularity in california_McKinsey_2022_03_31\page_16.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the manufacturing and recycling processes in the apparel industry, emphasizing the importance of circularity to reduce environmental impact. It outlines the challenges and strategies for achieving full circularity in manufacturing, waste management, collecting, sorting, and recycling. The potential economic, environmental, and social benefits of circularity are highlighted, along with the need for investment in technology and infrastructure. The focus on California's apparel industry and the use of polyester as a case study provides a blueprint for global circularity initiatives.
pages.title: Manufacturing and Recycling in the Apparel Industry

pages.page_path: library_pages\Closing the loop_ Increasing fashion circularity in california_McKinsey_2022_03_31\page_17.jpg

pages.page_path: library_pages\Closing the loop_ Increasing fashion circularity in california_McKinsey_2022_03_31\page_19.jpg

pages.page_path: library_pages\Closing the loop_ Increasing fashion circularity in california_McKinsey_2022_03_31\page_20.jpg

pages.page_path: library_pages\Closing the loop_ Increasing fashion circularity in california_McKinsey_2022_03_31\page_22.jpg

pages.page_path: library_pages\Closing the loop_ Increasing fashion circularity in california_McKinsey_2022_03_31\page_23.jpg

pages.abstract: Textile-to-textile recycling, including mechanical and chemical methods, offers opportunities to reduce waste, conserve resources, and approach full circularity in the fashion industry. Mechanical recycling shreds and re-spins fibers, while chemical recycling breaks down textiles into monomers for reconstruction. Both methods aim to reduce landfill waste and conserve resources.
pages.title: Textile-to-textile recycling

Despite these issues, these recycling methods contribute to a more circular economy for textiles by reducing waste and environmental impact.

pages.abstract: This page discusses Californians' current and future intentions to purchase apparel made from recycled materials, highlighting that younger consumers are more willing to pay a premium for such items. pages.abstract: This page discusses strategies for ensuring sustainable economics for textile circularity, including charging a premium for recycled materials, increasing scale and purchasing power, and considering policy interventions. pages.page_path: library_pages\Closing the loop_ Increasing fashion circularity in california_McKinsey_2022_03_31\page_38.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses consumer willingness to pay for recycled materials in apparel, highlighting differences in preferences for various types of recycled materials. Factors like intent versus actual behavior and the role of receiving organizations in landfilling donations are explored.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Closing the loop_ Increasing fashion circularity in california_McKinsey_2022_03_31\page_40.jpg

pages.page_path: library_pages\Closing the loop_ Increasing fashion circularity in california_McKinsey_2022_03_31\page_43.jpg
pages.abstract: This chapter discusses strategies and initiatives to advance fashion circularity in California, focusing on sustainable practices and innovations in the fashion industry.
pages.title: Chapter 5 Advancing fashion circularity in California

pages.abstract: This chapter outlines major obstacles to closed-loop textile recycling, focusing on collection, sorting, and deconstruction challenges. It highlights the need for selective garment acceptance, improved sorting by textile type, standardized guidelines, and increased deconstruction efforts. pages.page_path: library_pages\Closing the loop_ Increasing fashion circularity in california_McKinsey_2022_03_31\page_45.jpg
pages.abstract: Closed-loop recycling faces technical barriers, uncertain feedstock availability, and insufficient demand risks. These obstacles hinder scaling recycling capacity and investment in textile recycling facilities. A five-step methodology was developed to evaluate the potential benefits of overcoming these challenges.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Closing the loop_ Increasing fashion circularity in california_McKinsey_2022_03_31\page_46.jpg
pages.abstract: The methodology outlines a five-step approach to define solutions for closed-loop textile recycling, assessing economic, environmental, and social impacts. It includes defining metrics, identifying initiatives, estimating costs and benefits, comparing initiatives, and estimating total impact in California and the US.
pages.title: Our methodology for defining potential solutions to achieve closed-loop textile recycling and evaluating their collective holistic impact

pages.page_path: library_pages\Closing the loop_ Increasing fashion circularity in california_McKinsey_2022_03_31\page_47.jpg
pages.abstract: The document outlines 12 initiatives to advance fashion circularity, focusing on polyester recycling. It covers input materials, manufacturing, retail, collection, sorting, and recycling. The rationale highlights polyester's dominance in the fiber market, growing demand, and the potential of chemical recycling. Challenges include microplastics pollution.
pages.title: 12 potential initiatives to advance fashion circularity

pages.page_path: library_pages\Closing the loop_ Increasing fashion circularity in california_McKinsey_2022_03_31\page_48.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses eight core initiatives for advancing fashion circularity in California, focusing on recycled polyester, consumer engagement, waste collection partnerships, and curbside textile collection. It highlights the potential of these initiatives to reduce waste and promote sustainable practices in the fashion industry.
pages.title: Focus on eight core initiatives

pages.page_path: library_pages\Closing the loop_ Increasing fashion circularity in california_McKinsey_2022_03_31\page_49.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the need for a highly automated facility to sort and deconstruct polyester textiles for efficient recycling, emphasizing the importance of chemical recycling facilities to process polyester textiles. It highlights the potential holistic economic impact of closed-loop textile recycling in California, estimating a $7-9 billion annual impact.
pages.title: Holistic impact of closed-loop recycling in California

pages.page_path: library_pages\Closing the loop_ Increasing fashion circularity in california_McKinsey_2022_03_31\page_50.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the potential holistic impact of advancing closed-loop recycling of polyester in California, estimating a $3.5-4.5 billion impact by 2030. It details environmental, social, and economic benefits, including CO2e emissions reduction, water use reduction, job creation, and GDP growth. The analysis considers factors like water and land prices, chemical components of polyester, and Californians' willingness to pay a premium for recycled products.
pages.title: Total holistic impact

pages.page_path: library_pages\Closing the loop_ Increasing fashion circularity in california_McKinsey_2022_03_31\page_51.jpg
pages.abstract: Recycled polyester reduces environmental impact by lowering carbon emissions, water use, land use, and chemical use compared to virgin polyester. In California, scaling up closed-loop recycling could create 17,000-18,000 jobs in collection, sorting, and recycling, significantly boosting the waste management sector.
pages.title: Environmental and social impact

pages.page_path: library_pages\Closing the loop_ Increasing fashion circularity in california_McKinsey_2022_03_31\page_52.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the cost versus holistic impact of initiatives for a circular textiles economy, focusing on polyester. It estimates the investment needed and the potential value created, highlighting challenges and cost implications for various initiatives. Closed-loop recycling of polyester is shown to generate significant holistic impact relative to its cost.
pages.title: Cost vs. holistic impact of each initiative

pages.page_path: library_pages\Closing the loop_ Increasing fashion circularity in california_McKinsey_2022_03_31\page_53.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses self-sustaining core initiatives for fashion brands, including purchasing recycled polyester, promoting recycled apparel, and building chemical recycling facilities. It highlights the economic impacts and capital costs associated with these initiatives, emphasizing the need for support beyond initial investments for long-term success.
pages.title: Self-sustaining core initiatives

pages.page_path: library_pages\Closing the loop_ Increasing fashion circularity in california_McKinsey_2022_03_31\page_54.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses challenges in collecting pre-consumer and post-consumer polyester waste for closed-loop recycling in California. It highlights the need for partnerships with manufacturers and retailers, additional incentives, and infrastructure improvements to scale collection efforts. The current feedstock prices do not cover the costs, leading to a significant revenue shortfall. Expanding post-consumer waste collection is crucial for achieving large-scale closed-loop recycling.
pages.title: Challenged core initiatives

pages.page_path: library_pages\Closing the loop_ Increasing fashion circularity in california_McKinsey_2022_03_31\page_55.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses scaling curbside textile collection in densely populated areas of California, potential revenues and costs, and strategies to address challenges in closed-loop recycling, including consumer fees, public funding, and business model innovation.
pages.title: Scale curbside textile collection in Los Angeles, San Francisco, and select Bay Area counties
