pages.title: 3.1 Green hydrogen

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_143.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the potential for green hydrogen to become cost-competitive by 2030, driven by declining electrolyser costs and renewable energy. It outlines scenarios for green hydrogen adoption in various sectors, including chemicals, trucking, power storage, and steel production. The page also highlights the benefits of early adoption, such as cost savings, revenue generation, and export opportunities, while emphasizing the need for significant investment and policy support.
pages.title: Key takeaways

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_144.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of green hydrogen for India's decarbonisation and energy independence. It highlights global momentum towards a hydrogen economy, with over 30 governments announcing hydrogen strategies. The page also provides an overview of global green H2 policies, including domestic production and import strategies, and end-uses in various countries.
pages.title: Overview of global green H2 policies.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_145.jpg
pages.abstract: This section discusses the competitiveness of green hydrogen, focusing on its substitution for grey hydrogen in various sectors, the development scenarios (LoS and Accelerated), and the expected decline in production costs, making it cost-competitive by 2030.
pages.title: Competitiveness of green hydrogen

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_146.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the projected cost competitiveness of green hydrogen production by 2030-2035, highlighting factors such as declining electrolyser and renewable electricity costs, and government support. It emphasizes the role of scale-up, automation, and local production in reducing costs and improving efficiency.
pages.title: Green hydrogen likely to be the most competitive production route by 2030-2035.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_147.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the competitiveness of green hydrogen in various use-cases by 2030, considering carbon pricing and policy scenarios. It highlights the expected cost competitiveness of green hydrogen against conventional technologies, with specific timelines for different sectors. The bar chart illustrates the required hydrogen production costs for breakeven, showing the impact of carbon taxes on cost competitiveness.
pages.title: Green hydrogen could become competitive for a majority of the use-cases by 2030.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_148.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the competitiveness of green hydrogen in various use cases under two scenarios: LoS and Accelerated. By 2030, most use cases become cost-competitive with a carbon price of $50 per tonne under the Accelerated scenario. The use cases include refining, methanol, ammonia, CGD, long-haul trucking, power storage, and steel production. The Accelerated scenario shows earlier competitiveness compared to the LoS scenario.
pages.title: Competitiveness of green hydrogen in different use-cases

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_149.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the projected demand for green hydrogen in various sectors, comparing the LoS and Accelerated scenarios. It highlights the early adoption of green hydrogen in existing use cases like refineries, methanol production, and fertiliser production. The demand forecast shows a gradual increase in green hydrogen usage, with refineries and methanol production expected to be significant adopters. The total demand is projected to be 0.6-0.7 MMTPA by 2030 and 11-12 MMTPA by 2050 in the Accelerated scenario.
pages.title: Demand development for hydrogen in the LoS and Accelerated scenarios

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_150.jpg
pages.abstract: The Accelerated scenario projects significantly higher hydrogen demand in hard-to-abate sectors like steel, trucking, and power by 2040 and 2050. Steel and automotive sectors are expected to become major green hydrogen consumers due to cost competitiveness. Hydrogen plays a minor role in power storage but is crucial for grid balancing and energy storage as India transitions to renewable energy sources.
pages.title: Hard-to-abate sectors drive disproportionate demand for hydrogen in the Accelerated scenario.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_151.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the benefits of accelerating green hydrogen adoption in India's steel industry, comparing the LoS and Accelerated scenarios. It highlights the potential for reducing carbon emissions and the risks associated with high carbon assets. The crude steel capacity by route is illustrated, showing the shift towards green hydrogen-based steel in the Accelerated scenario.
pages.title: Benefits from accelerated adoption of green hydrogen

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_152.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the CO2e abatement potential from green hydrogen under LoS and Accelerated scenarios, showing significant reductions in carbon emissions and energy import reliance, with detailed data visualized in bar charts.
pages.title: Annual CO2e abatement potential from Green hydrogen.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_153.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the potential forex savings from green hydrogen in India under two scenarios: LoS and Accelerated. It highlights India's opportunity to export green hydrogen derivatives and the substantial investment required for green hydrogen infrastructure in the Accelerated scenario.
pages.title: Forex savings on account of green hydrogen.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_154.jpg
pages.abstract: The document compares the landed cost of green hydrogen from India, Australia, and Saudi Arabia to Japan in 2030 under the LoS scenario. India has a total cost of $4.13/Kg, Australia $4.01/Kg, and Saudi Arabia $4.11/Kg, indicating India's competitive position in meeting Japan's import demand.
pages.title: India likely to be a strong contender to meet the import demand for Japan and South Korea.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_155.jpg
pages.abstract: The document outlines the substantial investment required in the green hydrogen value chain under different scenarios, emphasizing the accelerated scenario's higher investment needs. It details the decade-wise capital expenditure, highlighting the front-loaded nature of investments, particularly in the accelerated scenario.
pages.title: $432 billion would be needed in investment in the green hydrogen value chain in the Accelerated scenario by 2050, 1.8x of LoS scenario.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_156.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses proposed enablers for accelerating hydrogen adoption in India, including blending mandates and market-making mechanisms. It highlights Germany’s H2 Global scheme, a €900 million investment to incentivize global players through a double auction mechanism, aiming to support low-cost green hydrogen production and eliminate price/demand uncertainty.
pages.title: Proposed enablers to accelerate hydrogen adoption

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_157.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses strategies for decarbonising India's steel and manufacturing industries, including carbon pricing, local equipment industry development, and international partnerships for green hydrogen. It highlights the importance of policy certainty, subsidies, R&D, and attracting global technology players.
pages.title: Decarbonising India: Charting a pathway for sustainable growth

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_158.jpg
pages.abstract: This page illustrates a community cleanup activity, highlighting the importance of material circularity and environmental stewardship through volunteer participation.
pages.title: 3.2 Material circularity

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_159.jpg
pages.abstract: India's waste management and material circularity can significantly reduce emissions and generate economic benefits. The Accelerated scenario aims for higher recycling rates, requiring policy support and substantial investment in infrastructure. This transition could lead to substantial emission reductions and cost savings by 2070.
pages.title: Key takeaways on India's waste management and material circularity

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_160.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the transition from a linear to a circular economy, emphasizing the importance of closed-loop systems to minimize waste and resource depletion. It highlights the benefits of material circularity in regenerating nature and reducing carbon emissions. The page also introduces biological and technological approaches to circularity and outlines four strategies for creating value from circular systems.
pages.title: Circularity requires a holistic value-chain transformation.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_161.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the substantial emission reduction potential when using recycled raw materials compared to virgin materials across sectors like steel, plastics, aluminium, and cement. It highlights India's low recycling rates and identifies weak demand signals and inadequate enforcement of regulations as key factors hindering recycling efforts.
pages.title: Substantial emission reduction potential in using recycled raw materials vs. virgin materials across sectors.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_162.jpg
pages.abstract: This page details the current recycling rates and targets for various waste streams in India, including construction & demolition, plastics, municipal solid waste, fashion/textile, e-waste, automotive, tyres and rubber, and agriculture. It compares current recycling percentages with global benchmarks and outlines the LoS scenario for 2050. The page also highlights current regulations and applications for each waste stream.
pages.title: Current scenario and recycling targets assumed in the LoS scenario for India's 750-800 million tons of annual waste generation.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_163.jpg
pages.abstract: India faces challenges in waste management due to insufficient infrastructure and reliance on unorganised sectors, leading to low recycling rates for certain waste streams. Improving infrastructure could significantly increase recycling rates and reduce emissions, but this requires substantial investment and consumer-habit changes.
pages.title: India's Waste Management Challenges and Recycling Potential

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_164.jpg
pages.abstract: This page illustrates the potential for emissions reduction through material circularity across various sectors under two scenarios: LoS and Accelerated. The LoS scenario projects a 22 GtCO2e reduction, while the Accelerated scenario aims for a 34 GtCO2e reduction by 2070. Key sectors include steel, cement, solid waste, agriculture, and chemicals, with significant contributions from waste management and crop residue utilization.
pages.title: Emissions reduction by driving material circularity across sectors.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_165.jpg
pages.abstract: This page details the cross-sector utilisation of recycled raw materials from various waste streams, including construction, plastics, municipal waste, fashion, e-waste, automotive, tyres, and agriculture. It highlights annual waste generation and examples of applications in different industries, promoting material circularity and sustainable growth.
pages.title: Cross-sector utilisation of recycled raw materials could accelerate material circularity across waste streams.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_166.jpg
pages.abstract: The Accelerated scenario discusses the potential to enhance material circularity and recycling rates through policy, technology, and infrastructure improvements. It aims to significantly reduce emissions by 2050 and 2070, with a focus on increasing recycling across various waste streams in India. The scenario emphasizes the need for policy changes, consumer awareness, and collaboration among stakeholders to achieve sustainable waste management.
pages.title: The Accelerated scenario

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_167.jpg
pages.abstract: This page outlines the current recycling rates and 2070 target recycling percentages for various waste streams, including construction waste, plastics, municipal waste, fashion/textile, e-waste, automotive, tyres, and agriculture. It identifies key demand drivers, waste management strategies, and technological processes needed to achieve material circularity. The table provides specific measures such as policy revisions, labeling guidelines, and technological innovations for each waste stream.
pages.title: Unlocks across demand drivers, waste management and technology needed for material circularity to reach full potential.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_168.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the significant capital and operational expenditures required for material circularity, focusing on waste collection, sorting, and processing. It highlights the projected Capex and Opex costs under different scenarios and emphasizes the potential for recycled materials to offset these costs. The text also mentions the creation of a green premium for recycled materials and the reduction of imported materials.
pages.title: Material circularity investment and implications

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_169.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the potential to save billions in imports by 2070 through recycling hubs for EV batteries. It highlights the need for early investment in technology, regulations, and infrastructure for cell-level recycling. The page also proposes enablers for accelerating material circularity, including policy shifts, infrastructure investment, and technological support. It emphasizes the importance of demand signals like landfill levies and EPR frameworks. A graph illustrates the contribution of recycled precious metals to total precious-metal demand for batteries in an accelerated scenario.
pages.title: Proposed enablers for accelerating material circularity

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_170.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses policies and regulations for waste management, emphasizing stringent enforcement of existing rules and new policies for emerging waste streams. It highlights the importance of technological innovations, such as chemical recycling and digitization of waste collection, and the need for infrastructure investment in waste management. The text also mentions the potential benefits of dedicated zones for waste recovery and recycling, aiming to move towards a sustainable, closed-loop circular economy.
pages.title: Policies and regulations for waste management

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_171.jpg
pages.abstract: This page outlines global policies and steps taken to drive material circularity across various waste streams, including construction & demolition waste, plastics, municipal solid waste, fashion/textile, e-waste, automotive, tyres and rubber, and agriculture. It compares regulations in different countries/regions and suggests potential actions for India.
pages.title: Global policies & steps taken to drive material circularity.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_172.jpg
pages.abstract: This page illustrates natural climate solutions through an image of a person planting a tree, emphasizing sustainable practices in decarbonizing India.
pages.title: 3.3 Natural climate solutions

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_173.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the potential of natural climate solutions in India, highlighting the sequestration capacity under different scenarios and the need for new solutions, investments, and policies to achieve net zero emissions by 2050. It emphasizes the benefits of accelerating NCS adoption and the challenges in a fast-growing economy.
pages.title: Key takeaways

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_174.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the role of natural climate solutions (NCS) in mitigating greenhouse gas emissions and adapting to climate change. It highlights the importance of conserving and restoring natural ecosystems like forests, mangroves, and peatlands. The page also provides an overview of the United Kingdom's comprehensive NCS commitments across key segments, including land-based solutions, croplands, blue carbon, and oceans. These commitments aim to plant forests, halt deforestation, manage agricultural soil sustainably, restore peatlands, and protect marine areas.
pages.title: Natural solutions for carbon sequestration and climate change mitigation

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_175.jpg
pages.abstract: India's forests, wetlands, and mangroves act as key natural carbon sinks, sequestering 345 MtCO2e annually. However, urbanization and agricultural expansion threaten these ecosystems. The LoS scenario projects an increase to 411 MtCO2e by 2050, with agroforestry playing a crucial role. The Accelerated scenario aims for an additional 233 MtCO2e sequestration by 2050, largely through forest conservation and agroforestry.
pages.title: India's forests and croplands act as key natural carbon sinks.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_176.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the potential of regenerative agriculture and forest restoration to achieve nearly 85% of the NCS potential. It details various land-based and blue carbon solutions, their abatement potential in 2020 and 2050, and the land area required. Solutions include avoided deforestation, reforestation, agroforestry, urban tree plantations, wetland restoration, mangrove restoration, and seagrass protection.
pages.title: Regenerative agriculture and restoration of forests could lead to nearly 85% of the NCS potential.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_177.jpg
library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_178.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses strategies for decarbonising India's agriculture sector, including agroforestry, regenerative farming, and coastal blue-carbon solutions. It highlights the potential of zero or low tillage in reducing agricultural emissions and provides a detailed table on regenerative agriculture's abatement potential and required adoption.
pages.title: Decarbonising India: Charting a pathway for sustainable growth

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_179.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses various blue-carbon solutions in India, categorized into established, emerging, and nascent NCS. It outlines their descriptions, scopes, and implications, emphasizing the need for investment in marine conservation and the potential benefits of accelerating NCS implementation.
pages.title: There are several blue-carbon solutions emerging in India.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_180.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the financial and environmental impacts of Natural Climate Solutions (NCS) under two scenarios: LoS and Accelerated. It highlights the decade-wise investments required, totaling $160 billion by 2070, with $63 billion under the LoS scenario and an additional $100 billion for the Accelerated scenario. It also shows that accelerated NCS could sequester an additional 12 GtCO₂e by 2070, with a significant reduction in emissions compared to the LoS scenario.
pages.title: Maximising the potential of NCS will likely require an expected $160 billion in cumulative investments by 2070.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_181.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the economic feasibility of achieving CO2 abatement through nature-based solutions (NCS) at a carbon price below $50/tCO2e by 2050. It highlights the potential for generating significant carbon credits and the need for accelerated action. The abatement cost curve illustrates various NCS options and their associated costs, demonstrating that many solutions are cost-effective. The page emphasizes the importance of integrating NCS into domestic carbon markets for a net-positive outcome.
pages.title: CO2 abatement through NCS can be achieved below a carbon price of $50/tCO2e.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_182.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses actions to accelerate natural climate solutions (NCS) in India, highlighting environmental co-benefits and specific proposed unlocks for various segments like forests, cropland, urban settlements, coastlines, and oceans. It includes a detailed table outlining the benefits, implementation scores, and proposed state-led unlocks for each solution, emphasizing economic feasibility, maturity, and resource availability.
pages.title: Actions to accelerate NCS

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_183.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the integration of NCS projects with carbon markets, emphasizing the benefits of setting up a domestic carbon market for India. It outlines the carbon-reduction project development process, including design, funding, development, certification, and selling offsets, using a reforestation project in Colombia as an example.
pages.title: NCS projects and carbon market integration

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_184.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses various investment products related to natural capital solutions (NCS), including convertible forest bonds, stormwater retention credits, green municipal bonds, blended finance investments, and sustainability-linked loans. Each product is described with its underlying asset class, example, country, players involved, and a detailed description of its implementation and impact.
pages.title: Natural resources could become investible assets.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_185.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses creating regional and local road maps for NCS projects in India, highlighting four major projects in Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Assam, and Andhra Pradesh. It also emphasizes the importance of unlocking blue carbon potential through regulatory support and investments in marine protected areas. The page includes an exhibit summarizing the abatement potential and required areas for these projects.
pages.title: Creating regional and local road maps and Unlocking blue carbon

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_186.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses carbon capture, utilisation, and storage, featuring an image of storage tanks in a field at sunset, symbolising sustainable growth efforts in India.
pages.title: 3.4 Carbon capture, utilisation and storage

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_187.jpg
pages.abstract: India's CCUS potential is significant, with an estimated reduction of 329 MtCO2e by 2050 and 403 MtCO2e by 2070. Developing storage hubs near emission sources and leveraging existing oil fields for storage are key strategies. However, high costs and economic viability remain challenges, necessitating carbon pricing, R&D investments, and exploration for saline aquifers.
pages.title: Key takeaways on India's CCUS potential and challenges

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_188.jpg
pages.abstract: India's carbon capture technologies, particularly CCUS, are crucial for decarbonisation. By 2050, CCUS could capture 329 MtCO2e annually, with potential to increase to 403 MtCO2e by 2070. This growth is driven by expanding CCUS into sectors like cement, chemicals, and oil and gas, aiming to reduce hard-to-abate emissions.
pages.title: CCUS could capture almost 330 MtCO2e per annum by 2050 and help achieve decarbonisation.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_189.jpg
pages.abstract: This page outlines four key steps for delivering CCUS: identifying CO2 sources, capturing CO2, compressing and transporting CO2, and using or storing CO2. It discusses various types of carbon-emission sources based on CO2 purity and explains the technological requirements for carbon capture. The page also includes an image of a worker in a red uniform at an industrial facility.
pages.title: Four key steps required to deliver CCUS

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_190.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how the purity of CO₂ in its source influences the technology requirements and capture chemistry. It categorizes CO₂ sources into high-purity and low-purity point sources, as well as direct air capture, detailing the mechanisms, descriptions, and maturity levels of various capture technologies.
pages.title: Purity of CO₂ in source determines the technology requirements and capture chemistry.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_191.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the cost of carbon capture technologies in India, highlighting that costs are inversely proportional to CO2 concentration. It mentions the decline in costs due to technological advancements and the maturation of various capture technologies. The exhibit illustrates capture costs for different CO2 sources, showing high-purity sources have lower costs compared to low-purity and diffuse sources.
pages.title: Cost of capture is inversely proportional to concentration of CO2 source.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_192.jpg
pages.abstract: The page illustrates the development of carbon capture technologies, showing their technology readiness levels (TRL) from 2014 to 2020. It highlights advancements in various capture methods, including liquid solvents, solid adsorbents, and novel concepts. Typically, a TRL of 7 or above is required for concept deployment.
pages.title: Momentum in technology advancement could make CCUS a cost-effective decarbonisation option.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_193.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the transportation and storage potential for captured carbon in India, emphasizing the cost-effectiveness of pipelines and the need for additional compression stages. It highlights India's existing storage potential in oil fields and the need for further exploration of saline aquifers. The CCUS hub model is proposed as a cost-effective solution, with five hubs strategically located to capture a significant portion of point-source emissions within specified distances.
pages.title: Transportation and Storage Potential for Carbon Capture in India

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_194.jpg
pages.abstract: This page details various end uses of captured carbon, including enhanced oil recovery, construction materials, fuel, plastics/chemicals, and other uses. It evaluates the advantages, disadvantages, technological status, and implementation requirements for each use case, highlighting the maturity and potential of different applications.
pages.title: Captured carbon can be used in multiple ways.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_195.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the potential of CCUS utilisation in India, driven mainly by construction materials by 2050. It highlights investment implications, proposed enablers like policy interventions, technological advancements, and storage potential exploration. Innovative business models and carbon removal technologies are also considered to support CCUS adoption.
pages.title: Most of India's CCUS utilisation potential could be driven by construction materials in 2050.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_196.jpg
pages.abstract: The document details the capital expenditure (Capex) required for carbon capture, transportation, and storage over different decades. The majority of the investment is needed for capture, followed by transportation and storage. The total Capex is broken down into different categories, with capture requiring the most investment at $527 billion. The document also includes assumptions and sources for the data.
pages.title: Most of the Capex investment would be needed in carbon capture and transportation.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_197.jpg
pages.title: Decarbonising India: Charting a pathway for sustainable growth

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_198.jpg
pages.abstract: This page introduces the implications of India's decarbonisation pathways, focusing on their effects on emissions, energy systems, land use, people, and benefits. The image of a smiling boy symbolizes the human aspect of these changes.
pages.title: 4. Implications of India’s decarbonisation pathways on emissions, energy systems, land use, people and benefits

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_199.jpg
pages.title: Water in Hands

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_200.jpg
pages.abstract: India's GHG emissions are projected to increase significantly by 2070 unless drastic measures are taken. The Accelerated scenario could lead to substantial carbon savings and significant changes in energy systems, land use, and employment. While there may be some economic impacts, the overall benefits include energy security, job creation, and leadership in green technologies.
pages.title: Key takeaways

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_201.jpg
pages.abstract: India's emissions intensity has reduced but absolute emissions are projected to rise. The LoS scenario shows a 90% reduction by 2070, while the Accelerated scenario aims for net-zero by 2070 through policy, technology, and demand shifts.
pages.title: Possible pathways for India to decarbonise.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_202.jpg
pages.abstract: India's GHG economic emissions intensity is projected to decrease significantly under various scenarios, aiming for net-zero by 2070. Challenges include rapid decarbonization in sectors like renewables, EVs, and hydrogen, requiring substantial capacity additions and scaling of raw material manufacturing. The automotive sector needs to transition to electric vehicles, and green hydrogen will require subsidies for widespread adoption. Steel production is expected to grow with hydrogen usage.
pages.title: Economic emissions intensity reduction for India.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_203.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses emission curves for LoS and Accelerated scenarios, projecting sectoral GHG emissions up to 2070. It highlights the potential for net-zero emissions through technological advancements. The text also covers the transition in the power sector from coal to renewable energy, changes in refining capacities, and the need for additional land for various purposes, emphasizing the importance of efficient land use practices.
pages.title: Emission curves for LoS and Accelerated scenarios.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_204.jpg
pages.abstract: The document outlines challenges for India's decarbonisation across power, energy & hydrogen, and automotive sectors. It projects capacity additions, land requirements, storage, coal power generation, refining capacity, coal consumption, green hydrogen costs, electrolyser capacity, battery costs, charger numbers, and EV sales switchovers under different scenarios.
pages.title: Challenges for India's decarbonisation.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_205.jpg
pages.abstract: This page outlines the challenges for India's decarbonisation across agriculture, steel and cement industries, and circularity & financing. It includes data on improved rice straw management, electrification of on-farm equipment, land requirements for trees and regenerative agriculture, steel production capacities, recycling rates for plastics, construction & demolition, and municipal solid waste, as well as average annual investment needs. Key points include a carbon price of $50 by 2030, a reduction in the clinker to cement ratio, and the need for CCUS to capture emissions.
pages.title: Challenges for India's decarbonisation.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_206.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses seven key levers for accelerating decarbonisation, focusing on expanding renewable energy capacity and increasing EV penetration. It highlights the potential for significant emissions reduction through these measures, with detailed analysis on cost, capacity, and technological advancements.
pages.title: Seven key levers that could help accelerate decarbonisation

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_207.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses strategies for decarbonising India, including transitioning to electric vehicles, ramping up green hydrogen, reforming agriculture and dietary systems, driving material circularity, and using natural climate solutions. It highlights the need for policy support, investment in infrastructure, and technological advancements to achieve these goals.
pages.title: Decarbonising India: Charting a pathway for sustainable growth

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_208.jpg
pages.abstract: The primary energy mix is projected to shift towards renewable sources, with a significant decrease in fossil fuel dependence. CCUS technologies could help reduce industrial emissions, particularly in hard-to-abate sectors. Decarbonization efforts in transportation and industry sectors will require a transition to electric vehicles and a mix of electricity, hydrogen, and biomass for manufacturing processes.
pages.title: The primary energy mix would likely shift to renewable sources of energy.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_209.jpg
pages.abstract: India's oil consumption is projected to grow until 2030 and then decline, with the Accelerated scenario showing a halving by 2050. The shift towards electric vehicles and renewable energy sources will significantly impact oil demand, particularly in the transportation sector. Refining capacity and fuel demand will peak in the coming decades before declining due to electrification and increased recycling activity.
pages.title: India's oil consumption in different scenarios

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_210.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the impact of decarbonisation on refining capacity, highlighting the need for repurposing or stranding of refining capacity due to the shift towards electric vehicles and increased demand for petrochemicals. It also explores opportunities for refiners to integrate into petrochemical complexes and chemicals manufacturing to maintain profitability.
pages.title: Decarbonising India: Charting a pathway for sustainable growth

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_211.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the potential growth in naphtha demand driven by petrochemicals, detailing refinery product demand projections and recycling impacts. It highlights refiners' strategies to adjust production for increasing chemical demand, including ethylene, propylene, and aromatics. The text also explores repurposing refineries for green hydrogen, ammonia, and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), and the role of coal in India's energy mix, with a focus on its decline and transition to renewable sources.
pages.title: Demand for petrochemicals could drive growth in Naphtha demand.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_212.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses India's coal consumption under two scenarios: LoS and Accelerated. It projects a significant decline in coal usage by 2050, especially in power generation, steel, and cement sectors. The transition to green fuels and alternative uses for coal, such as coal gasification, is explored. Challenges and opportunities in the petrochemical sector are also highlighted, including the potential for coal-based chemicals and the need for carbon capture and storage.
pages.title: Coal consumption could decline to 8% of current consumption by 2050 in the Accelerated scenario.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_213.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the potential decommissioning of 91 GW of coal power generation capacity by 2040 under an Accelerated scenario. It highlights the importance of using carbon-neutral biomass, especially agricultural crop residue, for decarbonizing India. The National Policy on Biofuels aims to blend bioethanol and biodiesel into petrol and diesel by 2030. The Accelerated scenario projects 600 Mt of crop residue by 2050, with specific allocations for cattle feed, soil carbon sequestration, and biomass-based power generation.
pages.title: 91 GW of coal power generation capacity could be decommissioned in the Accelerated scenario by 2040.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_214.jpg
pages.abstract: India's land use implications in the Accelerated scenario by 2070 require an additional 45 million hectares, with solutions focusing on increasing agricultural productivity and utilizing barren land for renewable energy and industrial purposes.
pages.title: Implications for land use

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_215.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses strategies for meeting carbon-sink goals through denser forests and urban forests, vertical urbanisation, and efficient land use. It explores the implications of accelerated decarbonisation on household spending and jobs, highlighting potential shifts in employment and the need for workforce transition support. The analysis suggests minimal overall spending impact by 2040 and a transformation of over 30 million jobs by 2050.
pages.title: Decarbonising India: Charting a pathway for sustainable growth

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_216.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the decarbonisation-driven household spending impact on the Empowerment Line in 2040, detailing normative spending, accelerated scenario impacts, and factors not considered. It also highlights macro trends affecting India's workforce, including digital adoption, demographic changes, and the green transition.
pages.title: Decarbonisation-driven household spending impact for households on the Empowerment Line (in 2040)

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_217.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the resultant benefits of decarbonisation, including energy import reduction, substantial Forex savings, and leadership opportunities for India. It also outlines pathway uncertainties, such as technology evolution, policy implementation, and other factors that could influence the decarbonisation scenarios.
pages.title: Resultant benefits accrued from decarbonisation

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_218.jpg
pages.abstract: This page introduces the topic of financing India's decarbonisation efforts, emphasizing the importance of financial mechanisms in supporting sustainable development and reducing carbon emissions.
pages.title: 5. Financing India’s decarbonisation

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_219.jpg
pages.title: 农业技术交流

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_220.jpg
pages.abstract: India faces significant challenges in financing decarbonisation, requiring substantial green investments by 2050. Despite potential cost savings, financing is constrained by risks and structural issues. An aligned, cross-sectoral plan and supportive policies are needed to accelerate green investment and transition to greener technologies.
pages.title: Key takeaways

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_221.jpg
pages.abstract: India's decarbonisation requires substantial investment in green technologies, with $7.2 trillion needed for the LoS scenario and $4.9 trillion for the Accelerated scenario by 2050. Investments focus on power, industry, mobility, and agriculture sectors, with 70% allocated to power and automotive. Accelerated decarbonisation could lead to operational cost savings, offsetting 45% of capital investments.
pages.title: Proposed investment needed for India's decarbonisation

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_222.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the investment required for decarbonising India's power and mobility sectors under two scenarios: LoS and Accelerated. It highlights the cost savings and investments across various sectors, including power, transportation, agriculture, and industry. The cost of decarbonisation is expected to decline as technologies mature, with solar energy, wind power, and EVs presenting positive investment cases. High-cost levers like advanced agriculture practices, offshore wind, and CCUS may require demand signals to be set up.
pages.title: 70% of total investment would likely be required to decarbonise the power and mobility sectors.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_223.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the financial implications of accelerating decarbonisation in an Accelerated scenario. It highlights that decarbonisation could offset 45% of incremental capital investments, with a total spending of $50 trillion over 30 years. The cost of decarbonisation is expected to decline as technologies mature, but some emission abatement levers may still require additional support. The document also emphasizes the role of policy and external demand drivers in facilitating decarbonisation efforts.
pages.title: In the Accelerated scenario, decarbonisation could offset 45% of incremental capital investments.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_224.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the potential for mobility to contribute significantly to operating cost savings across various sectors. It highlights challenges in financing the green transition, including delayed benefits, uneconomic business cases, capital formation challenges, mismatched investor expectations, and limited banking sector participation. The text emphasizes the need for incentivizing capital providers and addressing financial and structural constraints.
pages.title: Mobility alone could contribute to more than half of total savings in operating cost.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_225.jpg
pages.abstract: The page presents a cost curve illustrating cumulative abated emissions across sectors. It shows that two-thirds of emissions can be reduced at low or negative costs, with significant potential for economic benefits. The graph highlights the abatement costs and cumulative abatement levels for sectors like Sequestration, Waste, Transport, Power, Industry, Buildings, and Agriculture.
pages.title: Two-thirds of the emissions can be abated at low or negative cost (<10 $/tCO2).

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_226.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses interventions to accelerate financing for India's green transition, including a national decarbonisation plan, carbon markets, and regulatory enablers. It highlights the importance of carbon pricing mechanisms like ETS and VCMs, and suggests strategies for building a robust carbon market in India, such as creating demand, ensuring a supply pipeline, and designing a VCM open to international participation.
pages.title: Proposed interventions could be considered to accelerate financing to support the green transition

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_227.jpg
pages.abstract: India can accelerate its compliance carbon markets by defining an ambitious purpose, implementing a carbon price, setting up clear guidelines, conducting competitiveness assessments, building a private ecosystem for MRV, and using CCM proceeds for capacity building. This approach can ensure a just transition and boost participation in carbon markets.
pages.title: Compliance carbon markets (CCMs) for the longer-term

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_228.jpg
pages.abstract: The EU ETS, a large-scale compliance market, has achieved significant emissions reductions, transitioning through four phases. Phase IV, starting in 2020, targets a 2.2% yearly reduction, aiming for 43% below 2005 levels by 2030, with an expanding coverage and stricter penalties.
pages.title: Case study on EU ETS

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_229.jpg
pages.abstract: This page outlines methods for obtaining and distributing CO2 allowances under ETS, including auction, market trade, and free allowance. It also explains methodologies like grandparenting and benchmarking for allowance distribution based on historical emissions and sector-specific emission factors.
pages.title: Methods for obtaining and distributing allowances under ETS

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_230.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the role of Indian financial institutions in supporting the nation's decarbonisation efforts, consistent with the national plan. It highlights the impact of climate change on banks, the commitment of banks to the 2050 net-zero emissions target, and the need for Indian banks to define net-zero ambitions. It also proposes regulatory actions to enable banks and outlines four key ingredients for a sustainable finance agenda, including setting ambitions, capturing business opportunities, strengthening resilience, and ensuring capabilities for execution.
pages.title: Active and visible support lent by Indian financial institutions to the nation's decarbonisation, consistent with the national plan

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_231.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the opportunity to create long-term value through a comprehensive sustainable finance strategy, which can offset climate change risks. It highlights the importance of disclosure guidelines, green banks, and green transition banks in mobilizing low-carbon investments and supporting sustainable development. The page also mentions the challenges faced by small projects in attracting funding and the role of green transition banks in addressing these challenges.
pages.title: Opportunity to create long term value via a comprehensive sustainable finance strategy could be considered to offset risk from climate change.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_232.jpg
pages.abstract: The European Central Bank (ECB) leads in climate risk initiatives by issuing guidelines, developing stress-testing methodologies, requiring transition plans, and promoting public risk reporting. It also adapts market solutions, establishes sustainability infrastructure, and builds knowledge and capability in sustainable finance.
pages.title: Case example: ECB leads the way in climate risk related initiatives.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_233.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the barriers to funding green projects and proposes the role of governments in accelerating the green transition through strategic interventions. It introduces the concept of an ESG Transition bank, which aims to mobilize private sector capital, reduce risks and costs, and enable sustainable financing. The bank would unlock project finance, create green bonds, act as a market maker, and institutionalize market innovations to scale up ESG financing.
pages.title: Green Transition Banks could enable governments to support infrastructure finance whilst at the same time stimulating other policy goals.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_234.jpg
pages.abstract: Two workers are installing solar panels on a roof, highlighting bold actions towards sustainable energy solutions.
pages.title: 6. Ten bold actions

pages.title: Sunset Over Rooftops

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_236.jpg
pages.abstract: This page outlines ten urgent actions for India's decarbonisation, emphasizing the need for a detailed medium-term plan, accelerating a compliance carbon market, and enabling banks through a green transition bank. It highlights the importance of stakeholder collaboration, policy support, and technological advancements to ensure an orderly and economically viable transition.
pages.title: Ten urgent actions to accelerate India's decarbonisation

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_237.jpg
pages.abstract: This page outlines strategies for India's decarbonisation, including accelerating renewable adoption, empowering land use planning, boosting indigenous manufacturing, evaluating CCS hubs, creating a circularity mission, and enhancing the National Hydrogen Mission. It emphasizes market reforms, efficient land use, local R&D investment, carbon capture storage, recycling initiatives, and green hydrogen adoption to achieve sustainable growth.
pages.title: Decarbonising India: Charting a pathway for sustainable growth

pages.page_path: library_pages\Decarbonising India_ Charting a pathway for sustainable growth_McKinsey_2022_10_01\page_238.jpg
pages.abstract: Companies should evaluate green investment opportunities aligned with India's plans and global decarbonisation trends. Strategic alignment, capital reallocation, and government engagement are crucial. Policy support and consumer behaviour shifts can drive decarbonisation, with the LiFE mission being a key component. India must act thoughtfully now for a sustainable transition.
pages.title: Aiming to play on the front foot, companies
