pages.title: Contents

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_5.jpg
pages.abstract: This page highlights key demographic trends, including falling fertility rates, aging populations, and economic challenges, emphasizing the need for societal and economic adjustments to address these shifts.
pages.title: At a glance

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_6.jpg
pages.abstract: This introduction discusses the global decline in fertility rates, leading to demographic shifts with fewer young people and more older people. It highlights the economic and social challenges this poses, especially in aging economies, and the need for rethinking work and retirement systems. The report explores these shifts and their economic consequences, concluding with recommendations for stakeholders.
pages.title: Introduction

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_7.jpg
pages.title: Playground Seesaw

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_8.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the global trend of declining fertility rates and its impact on population structures. It highlights that more than half of the world's countries now have fertility rates below the replacement level, leading to a demographic shift characterized by fewer young people. The text explores how this phenomenon, termed 'youth scarcity,' is reshaping populations worldwide, with higher-income regions experiencing its effects first. It also notes that Sub-Saharan Africa is an exception, with fertility rates remaining high.
pages.title: 1. The age of youth scarcity

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_9.jpg
pages.abstract: This page explains the concept of fertility rates in demography, distinguishing between colloquial and technical definitions. It discusses how fertility rates are measured, their potential inaccuracies, and their importance in predicting population size. It also touches on the replacement fertility rate and the various factors influencing fertility changes globally.
pages.title: Sidebar: What is the fertility rate?

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_10.jpg
pages.abstract: The document illustrates the global decline in fertility rates from 1950 to 2023, showing regional variations and highlighting that most regions have fertility rates below the replacement level. It also depicts the first and later waves of fertility decline across different regions.
pages.title: Fertility rates are declining everywhere.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_11.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses how falling fertility rates account for 80% of changes in today's total population, with life expectancy explaining the remaining 20%. It highlights Germany's population decrease due to fewer births and increased life expectancy, Japan's unique pattern due to low fertility and higher life expectancy, and dramatic fertility rate drops in emerging economies like Brazil. A bar chart illustrates the impact of fertility and life expectancy changes on various countries' populations.
pages.title: Falling fertility rates explain about 80 percent of the changes in today's total population resulting from the demographic shift sweeping the world.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_12.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the transformation of population pyramids into obelisks due to demographic shifts, focusing on declining fertility and rising longevity. It analyzes population structures across ten global regions, showing how these structures are evolving over time, with economically advanced regions resembling obelisks by 2100.
pages.title: Populations morph from pyramids into obelisks

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_13.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the economic implications of changing demographics, focusing on the impact of aging populations on pension systems and economic growth. It introduces a methodological approach using UN population forecasts and data from various sources to analyze demographic shifts across different regions and countries. The analysis employs a ceteris paribus approach to isolate the effects of demographic change, acknowledging limitations and uncertainties in data and projections.
pages.title: Dependency and depopulation?

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_14.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the challenges in predicting future population trends due to complex factors like fertility, life expectancy, and migration. It highlights the UN medium scenario as a global consensus but notes the wide variation in projections across different scenarios and sources. The content includes a graph (Exhibit A) showing global population projections under various UN scenarios and other data sources, emphasizing the uncertainty and differing methodologies used by research centers.
pages.title: Sidebar: Predicting the future is hard, and demographers don't agree

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_15.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the challenges in predicting future population trends, emphasizing the unpredictability of migration patterns. It highlights the UN's medium scenario predictions for fertility rates, which have not yet plateaued or rebounded as expected. The page also introduces the concept of working-age populations peaking and declining in three waves, impacting economic outcomes.
pages.title: Sidebar: Predicting the future is hard, and demographers don't agree (continued)

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_16.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the demographic shifts across three waves of regions, highlighting the working-age population trends. Developed economies in the first wave are experiencing a decline in working-age population share, while the second wave in emerging regions is still growing. Sub-Saharan Africa, in the third wave, will see a peak in working-age population later in the century. Variations within countries and regions are also noted.
pages.title: Working-age populations peak in three waves.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_17.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the significant variation in fertility rates across and within countries, highlighting subnational data from the United States and India. It shows that while the overall fertility rates are below replacement levels, some states exceed this level, reflecting urban-rural disparities. A subnational approach is suggested for addressing declining fertility rates.
pages.title: Fertility rates vary significantly across regions and within countries

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_18.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the decline in support ratios globally, indicating fewer working-age people will support each senior by 2050. It highlights the impact of youth scarcity and the need for preparation in later wave regions, excluding Sub-Saharan Africa.
pages.title: Support ratios will continue to fall

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_19.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the declining global support ratio and population trends in first wave economies, highlighting the peak and decline of populations in these regions. It also contrasts this with the increasing populations in later wave regions, particularly Sub-Saharan Africa.
pages.title: First wave countries' populations have already peaked

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_20.jpg
pages.abstract: The document projects global population trends, highlighting that the world population will peak at over ten billion in 2084. First wave regions have already peaked, while later wave regions, particularly Sub-Saharan Africa, will see significant growth. By 2100, Sub-Saharan Africa will account for all net global population increase, doubling its share to 34%, while Greater China's share will shrink from 18% to 6%. The population balance is shifting decisively to later wave countries.
pages.title: World population is projected to peak at more than ten billion in 2084, but populations in first wave regions have already peaked.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_21.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the projected shift in global population distribution by 2100, highlighting that less than 20% will live in first wave regions. It analyzes labor market trends, predicting a significant increase in work hours in later wave regions, especially Sub-Saharan Africa. It also explores the economic opportunities for these regions due to growing young populations and increasing global consumption.
pages.title: By 2100, less than 20 percent of the world's population will live in first wave regions.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_22.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the shift in global consumption from North America and Western Europe to Emerging Asia and India, highlighting the implications for businesses and the challenges of depopulation in first wave regions. It emphasizes the need for companies to adapt to changing local tastes and the potential complexities of operating in later wave countries. The text also explores the long-term effects of declining fertility rates and population shrinkage on various sectors of the economy and global balance.
pages.title: Consumption pools are shifting from North America and Western Europe to Emerging Asia and India.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_23.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses projected population declines by 2100, highlighting significant decreases in first wave regions and countries, with some later wave countries experiencing growth. It introduces the 'replacement floor hypothetical' to explore the impact of increased fertility rates on future population trends, emphasizing the long-term effects of current fertility choices on economic growth and sustainability.
pages.title: Based on current projections of fertility and longevity, many countries are headed toward population collapse by 2100.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_24.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the potential impact of raising fertility rates to the replacement level on population growth and support ratios by 2050 and 2100. It presents data comparing UN medium scenarios with a hypothetical replacement floor scenario for various regions. The text highlights the challenges in boosting fertility rates in high-income countries and the need for countries to adapt to demographic shifts in the near future.
pages.title: Raising fertility rates today to match the replacement rate could increase populations and support ratios by 2050 and 2100.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_25.jpg
pages.title: Family Gathering in the Park

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_26.jpg
pages.abstract: This chapter discusses the challenges faced by first wave economies due to depopulation and increasing dependency, analyzing impacts on labor markets, GDP per capita growth, savings trends, and public finances. It explores potential solutions through labor intensity, productivity growth, and demographic shifts.
pages.title: 2. A lower-growth, higher-dependency future in first wave regions

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_27.jpg
pages.abstract: This section discusses how demographic shifts, particularly an aging population, can slow economic growth by reducing hours worked and GDP per capita. It analyzes the impact of these changes on labor intensity and productivity, suggesting that countries need to adjust age mix, labor intensity, and productivity to maintain economic growth.
pages.title: 2.1. Demographic shifts, slower economic growth

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_28.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the factors driving GDP per capita growth, focusing on productivity, labor intensity, and age mix. It highlights the impact of demographic changes, particularly aging populations, on economic growth. The analysis uses Western Europe as an example, showing how labor intensity and productivity have influenced GDP growth. The page also outlines the methodology for assessing the impact of age mix on hours worked and the necessary adjustments in productivity and labor intensity to maintain past GDP growth rates.
pages.title: Our approach to sizing the impact of demographic changes and how to counteract them

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_29.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the impact of demographic changes on GDP per capita growth, focusing on labor intensity and productivity growth. It provides examples from Western Europe, China, and South Korea, and highlights the decline in labor intensity among older age groups before official retirement, affecting labor force participation and hours worked.
pages.title: Our approach to sizing the impact of demographic changes and how to counteract them

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_30.jpg
pages.abstract: The document illustrates how labor intensity, measured by weekly hours per capita, declines as workers enter their 50s across various regions. Graphs show trends for average first wave regions, advanced Asia, North America, Central and Eastern Europe, Greater China, and Western Europe, highlighting a consistent decrease in labor intensity for workers aged 50 and older.
pages.title: Labor intensity starts declining when workers are in their 50s.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_31.jpg
pages.abstract: Japan's aging population and declining fertility rate offer lessons on labor intensity and productivity. As support ratios decline, Japan's labor force participation, especially among older adults, is higher than in other developed countries. However, higher labor intensity alone is insufficient for economic growth, as Japan's GDP per capita growth is lower than in Western Europe and the United States. Boosting productivity growth is crucial to counter the demographic drag.
pages.title: Sidebar: Learning from Japan

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_32.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses how demographic shifts, particularly the aging population, will lead to a decline in hours worked per capita, impacting economic growth. It highlights that the number of older people is increasing while other age groups are shrinking, which will slow the growth in hours worked per capita by 2.2 hours on average, affecting GDP per capita growth.
pages.title: Demographic headwinds will be a drag on hours per capita.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_33.jpg
pages.abstract: The age mix effect has been neutral or slightly negative from 1997 to 2023, but it will slow GDP per capita growth by 0.4% annually in most first wave regions from 2023 to 2050, except North America. This will result in a cumulative reduction of 2.2 hours per capita per week across these economies, with significant economic impacts in Western Europe and Greater China.
pages.title: Demographic shifts will slow GDP per capita growth across first wave economies.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_34.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses how demographic shifts, particularly aging populations, have affected labor intensity and productivity growth. It highlights the increased participation of women and older people in labor markets, which has supported past growth. Despite these positive trends, most regions have experienced stagnant or falling aggregate labor intensity due to fewer young people working, except for Western Europe.
pages.title: More women and older people working—and productivity—have supported past growth

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_35.jpg
pages.abstract: This page presents data on how labor intensity has evolved over time, comparing weekly hours per capita across different age groups and regions from 1997 to 2023. It includes graphs for total first wave regions, advanced Asia, North America, Central and Eastern Europe, Greater China, and Western Europe. The data also breaks down the hours by sex, showing trends for males and females. The analysis is based on comprehensive population data, not just workers, and sources include ILOSTAT, World Population Prospects 2024, United Nations, and McKinsey Global Institute.
pages.title: How has labor intensity evolved?

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_36.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses Spain's economic growth driven by labor intensity and productivity. It highlights the shift in labor force participation among females and the potential challenges in sustaining high labor intensity. The page also presents data on the contribution of various factors to GDP per capita growth across different regions and countries, emphasizing productivity as the main driver.
pages.title: Productivity growth was the main driver of growth in GDP per capita in the past quarter century.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_37.jpg
pages.abstract: This section discusses the need for more workers, hours, and productivity to counteract the effects of a declining youth population on economic growth. It explores three levers: labor intensity, productivity, and age mix, focusing on migration as a viable solution. The conclusion emphasizes the necessity of combining all three levers to sustain growth and improve living standards.
pages.title: 2.2. More workers, more hours, and more productivity needed

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_38.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the need for a combination of changes in age mix, labor intensity, and productivity to sustain GDP per capita growth from 2023 to 2050. It provides data on labor intensity, productivity growth, and migration needs for various countries, emphasizing the importance of balancing these factors. The analysis considers historical trends and future projections, highlighting the unique challenges faced by countries like China and South Korea. The conclusion stresses the necessity of a tailored approach for each country based on its specific circumstances.
pages.title: Changing the age mix, labor intensity, or productivity alone cannot sustain growth—a combination of all three is needed.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_39.jpg
pages.abstract: To sustain Germany's GDP per capita growth, labor intensity must increase by 2.2 hours per capita per week by 2050. This can be achieved by boosting labor participation or hours worked per worker, with significant impacts on different age groups. For example, males aged 20-49 would need to increase hours by 12.7 hours per week, while females aged 20-49 would need 13.2 hours. The analysis highlights the challenges and potential solutions for maintaining economic growth amidst demographic shifts.
pages.title: Both labor intensity and productivity must rise

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_40.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the challenges countries face in sustaining past GDP per capita growth, focusing on labor intensity and participation. It highlights Germany's high labor force participation rates and the need for significant increases in older workers' participation. The analysis compares various countries' requirements for additional hours worked per capita by 2050, emphasizing the varying difficulties based on demographic and productivity growth assumptions.
pages.title: Some countries need to increase hours worked more than others to sustain past GDP per capita growth.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_41.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the need for countries to increase productivity growth to match past GDP per capita growth rates. It highlights the challenges of relying solely on increased labor intensity and emphasizes the importance of boosting productivity. The analysis shows that countries like Germany and Spain would need to significantly increase their productivity growth rates to sustain economic growth, especially if labor intensity remains constant.
pages.title: Productivity growth would have to accelerate substantially to match GDP per capita growth rates from 1997 to 2023.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_42.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the challenges and opportunities in productivity growth across various countries, highlighting the slowdown in productivity in first wave countries and the unique demographic challenges faced by China. It also explores the potential combinations of labor intensity and productivity growth to counteract demographic shifts.
pages.title: Productivity Growth Challenges and Opportunities

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_43.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses various combinations of productivity and labor intensity growth that could sustain past GDP per capita growth. It includes a graph showing different countries' potential paths to sustaining growth, considering productivity and weekly hours per capita. The analysis highlights that China and South Korea have adjusted growth targets due to their development stages in 1997. The page concludes that most countries will likely need to rely on both productivity and labor intensity growth to achieve past growth levels.
pages.title: Many combinations of productivity and labor intensity growth could sustain past GDP per capita growth.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_44.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses how 'isoquants' illustrate potential paths for sustaining economic growth, using Spain as an example. It explains the relationship between productivity growth, labor intensity, and GDP per capita growth, highlighting the need for increased productivity or hours worked to offset demographic challenges.
pages.title: Sidebar: 'Isoquants' help plot the many potential paths to sustaining growth

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_45.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the challenges of altering age mix to counter demographic drag, emphasizing the limited impact of increased fertility rates by 2050. It highlights the role of migration in boosting working-age populations but notes the significant increase needed to sustain GDP per capita growth. Using the UK as an example, it calculates the necessary migrant influx and considers factors like workforce participation and dependents.
pages.title: The age mix can be changed, but with insufficient impact by 2050

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_46.jpg
pages.abstract: This section discusses the growing societal cost of dependency as older people consume more than younger people, creating a senior gap. Funding this gap through public or private means is necessary, with pensions and in-kind services being major sources. As the older population grows, sustaining these funding sources becomes a challenge. Older individuals consume marginally more, even as their income decreases, with both direct and in-kind consumption growing with age. In 2023, those 65 and older had the highest consumption per capita in first wave regions.
pages.title: 2.3. A growing societal bill for dependency

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_47.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how older people consume marginally more than younger cohorts, highlighting the aggregate senior gap that grows as labor income decreases but consumption remains high in retirement. It includes a graph showing average consumption per person in 2023 across different age groups in various regions.
pages.title: Older people consume marginally more than younger cohorts.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_48.jpg
pages.abstract: The senior gap, measuring the difference between labor income and consumption for individuals aged 65 and older, is projected to widen significantly by 2050. In North America, the gap was 26% in 2023 and is expected to rise to 34% by 2050. This trend is also observed in Western Europe and Advanced Asia, with the gap increasing from 33% to 46% and 48%, respectively. The analysis highlights the growing financial burden on labor income to support senior consumption.
pages.title: The senior gap measures the difference between labor income and consumption among individuals 65 years and older.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_49.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the projected increase in the senior gap across regions, highlighting the varying consumer preferences and funding sources for retirement. It emphasizes the role of public pensions and asset price appreciation in supporting seniors' consumption and the increasing pressure on government finances.
pages.title: The aggregate senior gap will increase between 1.3 and 1.5 times across regions.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_50.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the coverage of senior gaps by government pensions in 2023, showing percentages for various countries. It highlights the sustainability challenges of public pensions due to falling support ratios and increasing life expectancy, leading to discussions on pension reforms.
pages.title: Government pensions in 2023 covered between 40 and 80 percent of the senior gap in the countries we analyzed.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_51.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses pension systems globally, highlighting their forms, challenges, and evolving strategies. It covers pay-as-you-go, defined-contribution, and personal savings systems, emphasizing the strain on public pensions due to economic factors and longevity. It also explores adjustments in retirement ages and funding strategies in various countries to address pension gaps and sustainability.
pages.title: Sidebar: Pension tensions: Sense on the dollar?

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_52.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the economic dynamics in Spain, the UK, and the US, focusing on the intergenerational social contract. It highlights the disparity between tax contributions and government spending among different age groups, emphasizing the strain on the social contract when the balance between younger and older populations is disrupted.
pages.title: Dependency and depopulation

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_53.jpg
pages.abstract: This page illustrates government expenditure and tax revenue patterns across different age groups in Spain, the United Kingdom, and the United States. It highlights that government transfers are highest for the young and elderly, while tax payments peak in middle age. The data also shows the government primary surplus/deficit per capita by age, revealing significant variations among the countries.
pages.title: Government transfers peak in young and old age, while tax payments peak in middle age.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_54.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the financial impact of aging populations on government expenditures and deficits in the United States, Spain, and the United Kingdom. It highlights the projected increase in per capita deficits due to demographic shifts and age-related expenditures, with detailed projections for each country. The text also addresses the strain on government finances and the growth in age-related public expenditures exceeding tax revenues.
pages.title: Seniors are the largest group of net recipients of government expenditures.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_55.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how asset appreciation, particularly in real estate, has supported senior consumption. It highlights the uneven distribution of wealth in the US, with older households holding a significant portion of the country's wealth. The page also presents data showing the growth in wealth among older households compared to younger ones, largely attributed to rising real estate values.
pages.title: Asset appreciation, especially in real estate, has supported senior consumption—so far

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_56.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the significant role of real estate in wealth accumulation for older Americans, highlighting homeownership benefits and challenges. It also explores the impact of rising home prices on younger generations and the need for sustainable pension systems in aging populations.
pages.title: Real Estate and Wealth in the United States

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_57.jpg
pages.abstract: This section discusses the demographic shift towards an older workforce and its implications for businesses. By 2050, the share of people aged 65 and older in first wave countries will rise significantly. Businesses must adapt strategies to harness the skills and experiences of older workers while addressing their unique needs. This includes adapting career planning, reorganizing teams, and encouraging lifelong learning. The trend is particularly stark for people aged 50 and older, whose contribution to total hours worked is expected to increase substantially.
pages.title: 2.4. Older workers, older consumers

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_58.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses how the age profile of worked hours will flatten in the future compared to the past's youth-centric structures. It highlights the growing share of consumption from seniors, with consumption increasing with age. The effects of age shifts on overall consumption appear slowly, but the share of consumption by seniors is expected to rise significantly by 2050 in various regions.
pages.title: The age profile of worked hours will flatten in the future compared with the youth-centric structures of the past.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_59.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the projected shift in consumption patterns by age groups, particularly highlighting the increase in consumption share by those aged 65 and older in first wave regions from 21% to 31% by 2050. It also notes the decrease in consumption among those under 30 due to falling fertility rates, offset by rising incomes. The focus shifts towards increased spending on health and wellness for older populations and decreased education spending for younger ones.
pages.title: If 2023 spending patterns are maintained, the share of consumption by those 65 years and older in first wave regions will rise from 21 to 31 percent.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_60.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the consumption patterns by category over a lifecycle across different countries. It highlights the significant differences in education and healthcare spending between younger and older age groups. The data shows that healthcare expenditure increases substantially with age, while education spending is higher for younger individuals. The graphs illustrate similar consumption trends across various categories like food, housing, and health for different age groups in the US, Japan, China, and Germany.
pages.title: All countries we analyzed have similar patterns of consumption by category over a lifecycle.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_61.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how demographic shifts, particularly age mix changes, will impact consumption patterns across various categories in China, Germany, Japan, and the United States. Healthcare spending is expected to rise significantly, while education spending will likely decrease. The table provides detailed projections for per capita consumption changes by 2050 compared to 2023, highlighting the most affected categories.
pages.title: Age mix shifts will drive increased healthcare expenditures and shrink spending on education on a per capita basis.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_62.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how population growth, per capita income changes, and demographic shifts will influence future consumption patterns. It highlights projections for Japan, the United States, and China, emphasizing the role of income growth in driving consumption. Businesses must adapt to these changes to improve competitiveness and counteract demographic challenges.
pages.title: Factors Influencing Future Consumption

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_63.jpg
pages.title: Domino Game in Public Square

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_64.jpg
pages.abstract: Later wave regions face the challenge of 'getting rich' before they 'get old'. They need to increase wealth before their populations age, as many have first wave population structures but lower GDP per capita. Fertility rates are declining, and support ratios will fall, requiring accelerated economic growth to sustain living standards.
pages.title: 3. Anticipating demographic shifts in later wave regions

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_65.jpg
pages.abstract: Later wave countries with lower GDP per capita are significantly behind in demographic changes compared to first wave regions. Many face challenges in achieving high-income status, with projections indicating that most may not reach this threshold before their populations age similarly to first wave regions.
pages.title: Countries in later wave regions, with lower GDP per capita, are one to two generations behind the demographic changes in first wave regions.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_66.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the economic challenges faced by later wave countries, particularly in reaching high-income status before their populations age. It highlights the diminishing demographic dividend in most regions except Sub-Saharan Africa and provides specific examples of countries like India, Latin America, and Mexico. The content includes a detailed chart comparing GDP per capita across different regions and timeframes.
pages.title: Two-thirds of later wave countries are not expected to 'get rich' before they 'get old', and even more will miss the target if growth slips by 1 percent.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_67.jpg
pages.abstract: The demographic dividend is diminishing in most regions except Sub-Saharan Africa, where the working-age population will grow significantly. However, realizing the benefits depends on creating good jobs, as many currently work in low-productivity sectors.
pages.title: The demographic dividend of the last quarter century will diminish or disappear by 2050 in all later wave regions except Sub-Saharan Africa.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_68.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the importance of boosting productivity in later wave economies to raise living standards and close the productivity gap with high-income countries. It highlights the need for increased investment and innovation to achieve catch-up growth. The exhibit illustrates the GDP per hour, prime age female labor force participation rate, and employment/population ratios across different regions.
pages.title: Boosting productivity is key to raising living standards ahead of demographic shifts

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_69.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the disparity in productivity between first wave and later wave regions, highlighting the potential for later wave regions to improve productivity. It presents data on total employment growth and productivity levels across various regions, emphasizing the impact of demographic shifts on global productivity. The importance of increasing productivity in later wave regions is underscored, with a focus on the challenges faced by emerging economies in narrowing the productivity gap.
pages.title: Labor pools and global productivity

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_70.jpg
pages.abstract: Later wave countries can boost productivity and GDP per capita by leveraging their youthful population, investing in human capital, and developing robust infrastructure. They can also capitalize on opportunities and sidestep foreseeable problems by learning from first wave countries' experiences.
pages.title: Later wave countries can capitalize on opportunities and sidestep foreseeable problems

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_71.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of designing sustainable support systems for the elderly and society, learning from first wave countries' successes and failures. It emphasizes the need for fiscal sustainability in retirement systems and the importance of investing in healthcare and education to promote healthy longevity. It also highlights the role of companies and infrastructure in navigating demographic changes successfully.
pages.title: Support Systems and Healthcare for Aging Populations

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_72.jpg
pages.title: Group Collaboration

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_73.jpg
pages.abstract: This section discusses the profound impact of demographic shifts on various aspects of society, including economic growth, labor markets, and social norms. It highlights the interconnectedness of these factors and the potential for significant knock-on effects as fertility rates decline and populations age. The text also explores the challenges posed by depopulation and the need for businesses and policymakers to adapt to these changes.
pages.title: 4. Responding to a new demographic reality

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_74.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the challenges societies face as they address changing population dynamics, including fertility rates, aging, and migration. It highlights the need for dialogue on family structures and caregiving roles, the limited success of policy interventions to boost fertility, and the potential for scientific and cultural shifts. Short-term options for businesses and policymakers include improving childcare and eldercare programs and implementing tailored migration policies.
pages.title: Societies are entering uncharted waters as they address changing population trajectories

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_75.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses economic responses to societal aging, focusing on enhancing productivity through investment, managing older workforces, and tapping the potential of senior consumers. It highlights the need for innovation in productivity, flexible work arrangements for seniors, and tailored products and services for the aging population.
pages.title: Economic responses to societal aging are already visible and will intensify

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_76.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses strategies for managing dependency through increased workforce participation and evolving fiscally sustainable systems for an aging world. It highlights policy reforms, age-friendly workplaces, and initiatives for women's participation. It also emphasizes the importance of innovation, affordable healthcare, and urban design to address demographic challenges.
pages.title: Managing dependency through increased workforce participation

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_77.jpg
pages.title: Acknowledgments

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_78.jpg
pages.title: Glossary

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_79.jpg
pages.title: Endnotes

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_80.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the impact of demographic changes on consumption, labor force participation, and housing markets. It highlights the role of aging populations, asset prices, and income growth in shaping economic outcomes. The text also explores the challenges and opportunities presented by demographic shifts, such as the increasing homeownership rates among older adults and the potential for higher labor force participation among the elderly.
pages.title: Dependency and depopulation?

pages.page_path: library_pages\Dependency and depopulation_ Confronting the consequences of a new demographic reality_McKinysey_2025_01_01\page_81.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the impact of demographic changes on consumption patterns, healthcare expenditure, and economic growth. It highlights the challenges and opportunities presented by aging populations and declining fertility rates, with a focus on Sub-Saharan Africa and emerging economies. The content also includes references to various reports and studies on productivity growth, social protection, and demographic trends.
pages.title: Dependency and depopulation?

pages.title: McKinsey Global Institute

42.file_desc:
This page highlights key demographic trends, including falling fertility rates, aging populations, and economic challenges, emphasizing the need for societal and economic adjustments to address these shifts.
This introduction discusses the global decline in fertility rates, leading to demographic shifts with fewer young people and more older people. It highlights the economic and social challenges this poses, especially in aging economies, and the need for rethinking work and retirement systems. The report explores these shifts and their economic consequences, concluding with recommendations for stakeholders.
The page discusses the global trend of declining fertility rates and its impact on population structures. It highlights that more than half of the world's countries now have fertility rates below the replacement level, leading to a demographic shift characterized by fewer young people. The text explores how this phenomenon, termed 'youth scarcity,' is reshaping populations worldwide, with higher-income regions experiencing its effects first. It also notes that Sub-Saharan Africa is an exception, with fertility rates remaining high.
This page explains the concept of fertility rates in demography, distinguishing between colloquial and technical definitions. It discusses how fertility rates are measured, their potential inaccuracies, and their importance in predicting population size. It also touches on the replacement fertility rate and the various factors influencing fertility changes globally.
The document illustrates the global decline in fertility rates from 1950 to 2023, showing regional variations and highlighting that most regions have fertility rates below the replacement level. It also depicts the first and later waves of fertility decline across different regions.
The page discusses how falling fertility rates account for 80% of changes in today's total population, with life expectancy explaining the remaining 20%. It highlights Germany's population decrease due to fewer births and increased life expectancy, Japan's unique pattern due to low fertility and higher life expectancy, and dramatic fertility rate drops in emerging economies like Brazil. A bar chart illustrates the impact of fertility and life expectancy changes on various countries' populations.
The document discusses the transformation of population pyramids into obelisks due to demographic shifts, focusing on declining fertility and rising longevity. It analyzes population structures across ten global regions, showing how these structures are evolving over time, with economically advanced regions resembling obelisks by 2100.
This page discusses the economic implications of changing demographics, focusing on the impact of aging populations on pension systems and economic growth. It introduces a methodological approach using UN population forecasts and data from various sources to analyze demographic shifts across different regions and countries. The analysis employs a ceteris paribus approach to isolate the effects of demographic change, acknowledging limitations and uncertainties in data and projections.
This page discusses the challenges in predicting future population trends due to complex factors like fertility, life expectancy, and migration. It highlights the UN medium scenario as a global consensus but notes the wide variation in projections across different scenarios and sources. The content includes a graph (Exhibit A) showing global population projections under various UN scenarios and other data sources, emphasizing the uncertainty and differing methodologies used by research centers.
This page discusses the challenges in predicting future population trends, emphasizing the unpredictability of migration patterns. It highlights the UN's medium scenario predictions for fertility rates, which have not yet plateaued or rebounded as expected. The page also introduces the concept of working-age populations peaking and declining in three waves, impacting economic outcomes.
The document discusses the demographic shifts across three waves of regions, highlighting the working-age population trends. Developed economies in the first wave are experiencing a decline in working-age population share, while the second wave in emerging regions is still growing. Sub-Saharan Africa, in the third wave, will see a peak in working-age population later in the century. Variations within countries and regions are also noted.
This page discusses the significant variation in fertility rates across and within countries, highlighting subnational data from the United States and India. It shows that while the overall fertility rates are below replacement levels, some states exceed this level, reflecting urban-rural disparities. A subnational approach is suggested for addressing declining fertility rates.
The document discusses the decline in support ratios globally, indicating fewer working-age people will support each senior by 2050. It highlights the impact of youth scarcity and the need for preparation in later wave regions, excluding Sub-Saharan Africa.
The document discusses the declining global support ratio and population trends in first wave economies, highlighting the peak and decline of populations in these regions. It also contrasts this with the increasing populations in later wave regions, particularly Sub-Saharan Africa.
The document projects global population trends, highlighting that the world population will peak at over ten billion in 2084. First wave regions have already peaked, while later wave regions, particularly Sub-Saharan Africa, will see significant growth. By 2100, Sub-Saharan Africa will account for all net global population increase, doubling its share to 34%, while Greater China's share will shrink from 18% to 6%. The population balance is shifting decisively to later wave countries.
The document discusses the projected shift in global population distribution by 2100, highlighting that less than 20% will live in first wave regions. It analyzes labor market trends, predicting a significant increase in work hours in later wave regions, especially Sub-Saharan Africa. It also explores the economic opportunities for these regions due to growing young populations and increasing global consumption.
The document discusses the shift in global consumption from North America and Western Europe to Emerging Asia and India, highlighting the implications for businesses and the challenges of depopulation in first wave regions. It emphasizes the need for companies to adapt to changing local tastes and the potential complexities of operating in later wave countries. The text also explores the long-term effects of declining fertility rates and population shrinkage on various sectors of the economy and global balance.
The document discusses projected population declines by 2100, highlighting significant decreases in first wave regions and countries, with some later wave countries experiencing growth. It introduces the 'replacement floor hypothetical' to explore the impact of increased fertility rates on future population trends, emphasizing the long-term effects of current fertility choices on economic growth and sustainability.
This page discusses the potential impact of raising fertility rates to the replacement level on population growth and support ratios by 2050 and 2100. It presents data comparing UN medium scenarios with a hypothetical replacement floor scenario for various regions. The text highlights the challenges in boosting fertility rates in high-income countries and the need for countries to adapt to demographic shifts in the near future.
This chapter discusses the challenges faced by first wave economies due to depopulation and increasing dependency, analyzing impacts on labor markets, GDP per capita growth, savings trends, and public finances. It explores potential solutions through labor intensity, productivity growth, and demographic shifts.
This section discusses how demographic shifts, particularly an aging population, can slow economic growth by reducing hours worked and GDP per capita. It analyzes the impact of these changes on labor intensity and productivity, suggesting that countries need to adjust age mix, labor intensity, and productivity to maintain economic growth.
This page discusses the factors driving GDP per capita growth, focusing on productivity, labor intensity, and age mix. It highlights the impact of demographic changes, particularly aging populations, on economic growth. The analysis uses Western Europe as an example, showing how labor intensity and productivity have influenced GDP growth. The page also outlines the methodology for assessing the impact of age mix on hours worked and the necessary adjustments in productivity and labor intensity to maintain past GDP growth rates.
This page discusses the impact of demographic changes on GDP per capita growth, focusing on labor intensity and productivity growth. It provides examples from Western Europe, China, and South Korea, and highlights the decline in labor intensity among older age groups before official retirement, affecting labor force participation and hours worked.
The document illustrates how labor intensity, measured by weekly hours per capita, declines as workers enter their 50s across various regions. Graphs show trends for average first wave regions, advanced Asia, North America, Central and Eastern Europe, Greater China, and Western Europe, highlighting a consistent decrease in labor intensity for workers aged 50 and older.
Japan's aging population and declining fertility rate offer lessons on labor intensity and productivity. As support ratios decline, Japan's labor force participation, especially among older adults, is higher than in other developed countries. However, higher labor intensity alone is insufficient for economic growth, as Japan's GDP per capita growth is lower than in Western Europe and the United States. Boosting productivity growth is crucial to counter the demographic drag.
The document discusses how demographic shifts, particularly the aging population, will lead to a decline in hours worked per capita, impacting economic growth. It highlights that the number of older people is increasing while other age groups are shrinking, which will slow the growth in hours worked per capita by 2.2 hours on average, affecting GDP per capita growth.
The age mix effect has been neutral or slightly negative from 1997 to 2023, but it will slow GDP per capita growth by 0.4% annually in most first wave regions from 2023 to 2050, except North America. This will result in a cumulative reduction of 2.2 hours per capita per week across these economies, with significant economic impacts in Western Europe and Greater China.
The page discusses how demographic shifts, particularly aging populations, have affected labor intensity and productivity growth. It highlights the increased participation of women and older people in labor markets, which has supported past growth. Despite these positive trends, most regions have experienced stagnant or falling aggregate labor intensity due to fewer young people working, except for Western Europe.
This page presents data on how labor intensity has evolved over time, comparing weekly hours per capita across different age groups and regions from 1997 to 2023. It includes graphs for total first wave regions, advanced Asia, North America, Central and Eastern Europe, Greater China, and Western Europe. The data also breaks down the hours by sex, showing trends for males and females. The analysis is based on comprehensive population data, not just workers, and sources include ILOSTAT, World Population Prospects 2024, United Nations, and McKinsey Global Institute.
This page discusses Spain's economic growth driven by labor intensity and productivity. It highlights the shift in labor force participation among females and the potential challenges in sustaining high labor intensity. The page also presents data on the contribution of various factors to GDP per capita growth across different regions and countries, emphasizing productivity as the main driver.
This section discusses the need for more workers, hours, and productivity to counteract the effects of a declining youth population on economic growth. It explores three levers: labor intensity, productivity, and age mix, focusing on migration as a viable solution. The conclusion emphasizes the necessity of combining all three levers to sustain growth and improve living standards.
The document discusses the need for a combination of changes in age mix, labor intensity, and productivity to sustain GDP per capita growth from 2023 to 2050. It provides data on labor intensity, productivity growth, and migration needs for various countries, emphasizing the importance of balancing these factors. The analysis considers historical trends and future projections, highlighting the unique challenges faced by countries like China and South Korea. The conclusion stresses the necessity of a tailored approach for each country based on its specific circumstances.
To sustain Germany's GDP per capita growth, labor intensity must increase by 2.2 hours per capita per week by 2050. This can be achieved by boosting labor participation or hours worked per worker, with significant impacts on different age groups. For example, males aged 20-49 would need to increase hours by 12.7 hours per week, while females aged 20-49 would need 13.2 hours. The analysis highlights the challenges and potential solutions for maintaining economic growth amidst demographic shifts.
The document discusses the challenges countries face in sustaining past GDP per capita growth, focusing on labor intensity and participation. It highlights Germany's high labor force participation rates and the need for significant increases in older workers' participation. The analysis compares various countries' requirements for additional hours worked per capita by 2050, emphasizing the varying difficulties based on demographic and productivity growth assumptions.
The document discusses the need for countries to increase productivity growth to match past GDP per capita growth rates. It highlights the challenges of relying solely on increased labor intensity and emphasizes the importance of boosting productivity. The analysis shows that countries like Germany and Spain would need to significantly increase their productivity growth rates to sustain economic growth, especially if labor intensity remains constant.
This page discusses the challenges and opportunities in productivity growth across various countries, highlighting the slowdown in productivity in first wave countries and the unique demographic challenges faced by China. It also explores the potential combinations of labor intensity and productivity growth to counteract demographic shifts.
This page discusses various combinations of productivity and labor intensity growth that could sustain past GDP per capita growth. It includes a graph showing different countries' potential paths to sustaining growth, considering productivity and weekly hours per capita. The analysis highlights that China and South Korea have adjusted growth targets due to their development stages in 1997. The page concludes that most countries will likely need to rely on both productivity and labor intensity growth to achieve past growth levels.
The page discusses how 'isoquants' illustrate potential paths for sustaining economic growth, using Spain as an example. It explains the relationship between productivity growth, labor intensity, and GDP per capita growth, highlighting the need for increased productivity or hours worked to offset demographic challenges.
The page discusses the challenges of altering age mix to counter demographic drag, emphasizing the limited impact of increased fertility rates by 2050. It highlights the role of migration in boosting working-age populations but notes the significant increase needed to sustain GDP per capita growth. Using the UK as an example, it calculates the necessary migrant influx and considers factors like workforce participation and dependents.
This section discusses the growing societal cost of dependency as older people consume more than younger people, creating a senior gap. Funding this gap through public or private means is necessary, with pensions and in-kind services being major sources. As the older population grows, sustaining these funding sources becomes a challenge. Older individuals consume marginally more, even as their income decreases, with both direct and in-kind consumption growing with age. In 2023, those 65 and older had the highest consumption per capita in first wave regions.
This page discusses how older people consume marginally more than younger cohorts, highlighting the aggregate senior gap that grows as labor income decreases but consumption remains high in retirement. It includes a graph showing average consumption per person in 2023 across different age groups in various regions.
The senior gap, measuring the difference between labor income and consumption for individuals aged 65 and older, is projected to widen significantly by 2050. In North America, the gap was 26% in 2023 and is expected to rise to 34% by 2050. This trend is also observed in Western Europe and Advanced Asia, with the gap increasing from 33% to 46% and 48%, respectively. The analysis highlights the growing financial burden on labor income to support senior consumption.
The document discusses the projected increase in the senior gap across regions, highlighting the varying consumer preferences and funding sources for retirement. It emphasizes the role of public pensions and asset price appreciation in supporting seniors' consumption and the increasing pressure on government finances.
The document discusses the coverage of senior gaps by government pensions in 2023, showing percentages for various countries. It highlights the sustainability challenges of public pensions due to falling support ratios and increasing life expectancy, leading to discussions on pension reforms.
This page discusses pension systems globally, highlighting their forms, challenges, and evolving strategies. It covers pay-as-you-go, defined-contribution, and personal savings systems, emphasizing the strain on public pensions due to economic factors and longevity. It also explores adjustments in retirement ages and funding strategies in various countries to address pension gaps and sustainability.
This page discusses the economic dynamics in Spain, the UK, and the US, focusing on the intergenerational social contract. It highlights the disparity between tax contributions and government spending among different age groups, emphasizing the strain on the social contract when the balance between younger and older populations is disrupted.
This page illustrates government expenditure and tax revenue patterns across different age groups in Spain, the United Kingdom, and the United States. It highlights that government transfers are highest for the young and elderly, while tax payments peak in middle age. The data also shows the government primary surplus/deficit per capita by age, revealing significant variations among the countries.
This page discusses the financial impact of aging populations on government expenditures and deficits in the United States, Spain, and the United Kingdom. It highlights the projected increase in per capita deficits due to demographic shifts and age-related expenditures, with detailed projections for each country. The text also addresses the strain on government finances and the growth in age-related public expenditures exceeding tax revenues.
This page discusses how asset appreciation, particularly in real estate, has supported senior consumption. It highlights the uneven distribution of wealth in the US, with older households holding a significant portion of the country's wealth. The page also presents data showing the growth in wealth among older households compared to younger ones, largely attributed to rising real estate values.
This page discusses the significant role of real estate in wealth accumulation for older Americans, highlighting homeownership benefits and challenges. It also explores the impact of rising home prices on younger generations and the need for sustainable pension systems in aging populations.
This section discusses the demographic shift towards an older workforce and its implications for businesses. By 2050, the share of people aged 65 and older in first wave countries will rise significantly. Businesses must adapt strategies to harness the skills and experiences of older workers while addressing their unique needs. This includes adapting career planning, reorganizing teams, and encouraging lifelong learning. The trend is particularly stark for people aged 50 and older, whose contribution to total hours worked is expected to increase substantially.
The document discusses how the age profile of worked hours will flatten in the future compared to the past's youth-centric structures. It highlights the growing share of consumption from seniors, with consumption increasing with age. The effects of age shifts on overall consumption appear slowly, but the share of consumption by seniors is expected to rise significantly by 2050 in various regions.
The document discusses the projected shift in consumption patterns by age groups, particularly highlighting the increase in consumption share by those aged 65 and older in first wave regions from 21% to 31% by 2050. It also notes the decrease in consumption among those under 30 due to falling fertility rates, offset by rising incomes. The focus shifts towards increased spending on health and wellness for older populations and decreased education spending for younger ones.
This page discusses the consumption patterns by category over a lifecycle across different countries. It highlights the significant differences in education and healthcare spending between younger and older age groups. The data shows that healthcare expenditure increases substantially with age, while education spending is higher for younger individuals. The graphs illustrate similar consumption trends across various categories like food, housing, and health for different age groups in the US, Japan, China, and Germany.
This page discusses how demographic shifts, particularly age mix changes, will impact consumption patterns across various categories in China, Germany, Japan, and the United States. Healthcare spending is expected to rise significantly, while education spending will likely decrease. The table provides detailed projections for per capita consumption changes by 2050 compared to 2023, highlighting the most affected categories.
This page discusses how population growth, per capita income changes, and demographic shifts will influence future consumption patterns. It highlights projections for Japan, the United States, and China, emphasizing the role of income growth in driving consumption. Businesses must adapt to these changes to improve competitiveness and counteract demographic challenges.
Later wave regions face the challenge of 'getting rich' before they 'get old'. They need to increase wealth before their populations age, as many have first wave population structures but lower GDP per capita. Fertility rates are declining, and support ratios will fall, requiring accelerated economic growth to sustain living standards.
Later wave countries with lower GDP per capita are significantly behind in demographic changes compared to first wave regions. Many face challenges in achieving high-income status, with projections indicating that most may not reach this threshold before their populations age similarly to first wave regions.
The page discusses the economic challenges faced by later wave countries, particularly in reaching high-income status before their populations age. It highlights the diminishing demographic dividend in most regions except Sub-Saharan Africa and provides specific examples of countries like India, Latin America, and Mexico. The content includes a detailed chart comparing GDP per capita across different regions and timeframes.
The demographic dividend is diminishing in most regions except Sub-Saharan Africa, where the working-age population will grow significantly. However, realizing the benefits depends on creating good jobs, as many currently work in low-productivity sectors.
The document discusses the importance of boosting productivity in later wave economies to raise living standards and close the productivity gap with high-income countries. It highlights the need for increased investment and innovation to achieve catch-up growth. The exhibit illustrates the GDP per hour, prime age female labor force participation rate, and employment/population ratios across different regions.
The document discusses the disparity in productivity between first wave and later wave regions, highlighting the potential for later wave regions to improve productivity. It presents data on total employment growth and productivity levels across various regions, emphasizing the impact of demographic shifts on global productivity. The importance of increasing productivity in later wave regions is underscored, with a focus on the challenges faced by emerging economies in narrowing the productivity gap.
Later wave countries can boost productivity and GDP per capita by leveraging their youthful population, investing in human capital, and developing robust infrastructure. They can also capitalize on opportunities and sidestep foreseeable problems by learning from first wave countries' experiences.
This page discusses the importance of designing sustainable support systems for the elderly and society, learning from first wave countries' successes and failures. It emphasizes the need for fiscal sustainability in retirement systems and the importance of investing in healthcare and education to promote healthy longevity. It also highlights the role of companies and infrastructure in navigating demographic changes successfully.
This section discusses the profound impact of demographic shifts on various aspects of society, including economic growth, labor markets, and social norms. It highlights the interconnectedness of these factors and the potential for significant knock-on effects as fertility rates decline and populations age. The text also explores the challenges posed by depopulation and the need for businesses and policymakers to adapt to these changes.
This page discusses the challenges societies face as they address changing population dynamics, including fertility rates, aging, and migration. It highlights the need for dialogue on family structures and caregiving roles, the limited success of policy interventions to boost fertility, and the potential for scientific and cultural shifts. Short-term options for businesses and policymakers include improving childcare and eldercare programs and implementing tailored migration policies.
This page discusses economic responses to societal aging, focusing on enhancing productivity through investment, managing older workforces, and tapping the potential of senior consumers. It highlights the need for innovation in productivity, flexible work arrangements for seniors, and tailored products and services for the aging population.
This page discusses strategies for managing dependency through increased workforce participation and evolving fiscally sustainable systems for an aging world. It highlights policy reforms, age-friendly workplaces, and initiatives for women's participation. It also emphasizes the importance of innovation, affordable healthcare, and urban design to address demographic challenges.
This page discusses the impact of demographic changes on consumption, labor force participation, and housing markets. It highlights the role of aging populations, asset prices, and income growth in shaping economic outcomes. The text also explores the challenges and opportunities presented by demographic shifts, such as the increasing homeownership rates among older adults and the potential for higher labor force participation among the elderly.
This page discusses the impact of demographic changes on consumption patterns, healthcare expenditure, and economic growth. It highlights the challenges and opportunities presented by aging populations and declining fertility rates, with a focus on Sub-Saharan Africa and emerging economies. The content also includes references to various reports and studies on productivity growth, social protection, and demographic trends.

library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_3.jpg
pages.abstract: The document introduces the McKinsey Global Institute, its mission, research themes, and independence. It also highlights McKinsey's Real Estate Practice, its focus on sustainable growth, and its unique capabilities.
pages.title: McKinsey Global Institute

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_4.jpg
pages.title: Unfinished Interior Space

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_5.jpg
pages.title: Contents

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_6.jpg
pages.abstract: This research highlights the lasting impact of COVID-19 on real estate in major global cities, emphasizing the shift to hybrid work, reduced demand for office and retail space, and the need for cities to adapt through hybrid approaches.
pages.title: At a glance

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_7.jpg
pages.abstract: The exhibit illustrates the projected change in demand for office, residential, and retail space in urban cores between 2019 and 2030, showing significant declines driven by pandemic behavior, with variations across cities like San Francisco, London, and New York City.
pages.title: In a moderate scenario, demand for office and retail space falls sharply between 2019 and 2030.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_8.jpg
pages.title: Urban Street Scene

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_9.jpg
pages.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic altered urban living and working patterns, leading to shifts in real estate demand in superstar cities. McKinsey Global Institute's research models future demand for office, residential, and retail spaces, predicting lower demand by 2030. Factors like automation, employee coordination, and shopping trends were considered. Despite macroeconomic uncertainties, the research highlights opportunities for cities to adapt and thrive through hybrid urban spaces.
pages.title: Executive summary

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_10.jpg
pages.abstract: The pandemic has led to a significant shift in work patterns, with hybrid work becoming the norm and office attendance dropping by 30%. Urban cores have seen a decrease in population and retail spending, with few people returning. The report focuses on real estate in superstar cities, defining them as areas with a large share of global GDP and GDP growth. The urban core and suburbs are analyzed separately, with data collected from 17 cities in six countries. Office attendance varies by industry and neighborhood, influenced by factors like housing costs and local culture.
pages.title: How hybrid work has changed the way people work, live, and shop
