pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_11.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses office attendance trends in various industries and firm sizes, highlighting that larger firms in knowledge-based sectors have lower attendance. It explains factors influencing these trends, including stability since mid-2022, employee preferences, and potential shifts due to labor market dynamics or research findings.
pages.title: Office attendance is lower in large firms in the knowledge economy.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_12.jpg
pages.abstract: The pandemic accelerated suburbanization trends, with urban cores losing population while suburban areas grew or shrank less. This shift was more pronounced in the US compared to European and Japanese cities. The exhibit highlights the difference in growth rates between urban and suburban areas across various metro regions.
pages.title: During the pandemic, most suburbs grew more quickly than their urban cores.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_13.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the out-migration trends from urban cores of superstar cities, influenced by factors like expensive housing, high office density, and limited retail presence. Hybrid work and housing conditions have contributed to these trends. Shopping in urban cores remains depressed due to shifts in consumer behavior during the pandemic, with foot traffic still lower than pre-pandemic levels. Retailers in urban cores face challenges in attracting customers as people visit offices less frequently.
pages.title: Out-migration from urban cores of superstar cities seems to have slowed, but it is still above pre-pandemic levels.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_14.jpg
pages.abstract: The page presents data showing that foot traffic near stores has recovered more quickly in suburban areas compared to urban cores across various cities. Graphs illustrate the change in foot traffic from January 2020, with suburban areas generally showing a faster recovery trend. The data is sourced from Google's Community Mobility Reports and analyzed by the McKinsey Global Institute.
pages.title: Foot traffic near stores is recovering more quickly in the suburbs than in urban cores.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_15.jpg
pages.abstract: The pandemic has led to lower office attendance, out-migration from cities, and reduced shopping in office-heavy neighborhoods, pushing down demand for real estate in superstar cities. By 2030, demand for office and retail space is projected to be lower than in 2019. Residential space is less affected, with price differences between urban cores and suburbs narrowing. The exhibit shows a moderate scenario where demand for office and retail space falls sharply between 2019 and 2030.
pages.title: The impact on real estate

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_16.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the decline in demand for office space due to remote work and economic challenges, leading to increased vacancy rates and decreased transaction volumes. By 2030, demand could be 20-38% lower than in 2019, impacting office values and leading to a surplus of lower-quality office space.
pages.title: There will be 13 percent less demand for office space in the median city we studied

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_17.jpg
pages.abstract: The pandemic has led to muted demand growth for residences in urban cores compared to suburbs. Vacancy rates and prices have increased less in urban cores, with a global phenomenon observed. By 2030, demand for residences in urban cores is projected to be 10% lower than pre-pandemic levels. Retail space demand is also expected to decline by 9% in median cities due to reduced foot traffic and increased online shopping. Adjustments in prices and rents are likely, but urban cores remain attractive for residential space.
pages.title: Demand growth for residences will be muted, especially in urban cores

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_18.jpg
pages.abstract: Cities strongly affected by the pandemic in real estate demand share characteristics like a high knowledge economy workforce, large firms, and office-dense structures. These factors reduce office attendance, retail shopping, and residential demand. Neighborhoods with more office-occupied real estate experience higher out-migration.
pages.title: What strongly affected neighborhoods and cities have in common

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_19.jpg
pages.abstract: This page presents data showing that expensive, office-dense neighborhoods in San Francisco and Manhattan experienced higher out-migration rates during 2020-2022. It includes maps illustrating the share of real estate occupied by office buildings, typical home values, and net out-migration percentages, highlighting the correlation between high office density and migration trends.
pages.title: Expensive, office-dense neighborhoods have tended to suffer more out-migration.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_20.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how business mix and urban structure influence real estate demand at neighborhood and city levels, comparing Manhattan neighborhoods, San Francisco, Paris, and Tokyo. Factors like knowledge economy prevalence, office density, and home prices are analyzed in relation to pandemic-driven changes in demand and migration patterns.
pages.title: Business mix and urban structure make a difference at the neighborhood level

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_21.jpg
pages.abstract: Superstar cities face challenges from hybrid work, leading to vacancy and reduced urban vibrancy. Mixed-use development, incorporating diverse real estate types, can help adapt neighborhoods. Mobilizing stakeholders, including governments, investors, and developers, is crucial for successful redevelopment. Suburbs can also benefit from hybrid approaches, with multifamily housing and greener spaces attracting urban dwellers.
pages.title: Thriving in hybrid places

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_22.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the benefits of multifamily housing and adaptable building spaces, emphasizing energy efficiency, flexibility, and the potential for hybrid buildings to address changing demands and protect against unpredictable shifts in preferences. It also explores the challenges and opportunities of converting office spaces into other types of demand-driven spaces.
pages.title: Turning empty spaces into hybrid places could be a way to transform superstar cities and prepare them for a dynamic, prosperous future.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_23.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of adaptable and modular design in retail and office spaces to cater to changing tenant needs. It highlights the need for spaces that can serve multiple purposes, attract visitors, and integrate with their environments. The text also explores the concept of hybrid floors combining offices, residences, and stores to counter the pandemic's impact and prepare cities for a prosperous future.
pages.title: At the floor level, design space that is modular and multiuse

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_24.jpg
pages.title: Home Office Scene

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_25.jpg
pages.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic led to a significant shift to remote work, altering where people work, live, and shop. This hybrid work model has permanently changed urban dynamics, with office attendance stabilizing at lower rates and urban out-migration continuing, though at a slower pace. Shopping in cities remains weaker than before the pandemic.
pages.title: 1. How hybrid work has changed the way people work, live, and shop

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_26.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the shift from remote to hybrid work, highlighting that as of fall 2022, workers were in the office an average of 3.5 days per week, 30% below pre-pandemic norms. It includes a survey showing 37% of respondents go to the office daily, 56% have hybrid arrangements, and 7% work fully remotely. A chart illustrates office attendance by city.
pages.title: Most office employees report having hybrid work arrangements.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_27.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how office attendance varies among metropolitan areas, influenced by factors like housing costs and the proportion of knowledge-economy workers. It highlights that higher housing costs and a larger share of knowledge-economy workers correlate with lower office attendance. Cultural and policy factors, such as China's '996' work culture and city lockdowns, also impact attendance. The page includes an exhibit showing the relationship between office attendance and these factors in US counties.
pages.title: Office attendance is lower in metropolitan areas with expensive housing and a large share of knowledge-economy workers

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_28.jpg
pages.abstract: Employees in larger firms report lower office attendance compared to smaller firms due to more resources for remote work and a stronger sense of community in smaller companies. Client meetings are less of a reason for office visits in larger firms. Knowledge-economy employees go to the office less often, possibly due to digitization and remote work suitability.
pages.title: Office attendance is lower in large firms in the knowledge economy

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_29.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses how office attendance varies subtly by age, income, and seniority. Millennials work 3.4 days per week in the office, while Generation X and baby boomers work 3.5 days. Millennials in senior positions work 3.7 days per week. Baby boomers are more likely to work five days per week compared to younger workers. The data is presented in Exhibit 4, showing reported attendance by age, income, and job seniority.
pages.title: Office attendance varies in subtle ways by age, income, and seniority

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_30.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the reasons employees choose to work from home or the office, highlighting that saving commuting time is the top reason for working from home, while working with teams is the top reason for going to the office. It also presents data on the top reasons for both options, showing variations by country and the importance of productivity.
pages.title: Employees work from home to save commuting time, and they work from the office to see their teams

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_31.jpg
pages.abstract: The current rate of office attendance appears to have stabilized in major US cities since mid-2022, with slight seasonal variations. The data, indexed to March 2020, shows trends across various cities, indicating that while attendance has stabilized, it remains below pre-pandemic levels.
pages.title: The current rate of office attendance may persist

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_32.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses employees' preferences for working from the office versus working from home. It shows that employees already work close to their ideal number of days in the office. Additionally, it highlights that employees who prefer working from home are generally more senior and better compensated.
pages.title: Employees already work nearly as few days in the office as they would like.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_33.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the preferences of office workers for remote work, the potential impact on office attendance, and the relationship between hybrid work and productivity. It highlights that a significant group of senior and well-paid workers prefer remote work, and improvements in hybrid work technology may reduce the need for office attendance. The page also mentions the limited success of employer perks in attracting workers back to the office and the positive perception of hybrid work on productivity.
pages.title: Office workers' preferences for remote work and its impact on productivity

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_34.jpg
pages.abstract: The pandemic significantly reduced population growth in most cities, with urban cores experiencing population decline due to hybrid work and out-migration. Munich's growth slowed from 1.0% to 0.3%, while New York City's urban core lost 5% of its population. Out-migration remains higher than pre-pandemic levels, and suburban growth has surpassed urban growth in many cities.
pages.title: The pandemic reduced population growth in most cities.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_35.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses how suburban population growth outpaced urban growth during the pandemic in many cities, with notable differences between US, European, and Japanese cities. It includes a detailed exhibit comparing growth rates across various metro areas.
pages.title: During the pandemic, most suburbs grew more quickly than their urban cores.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_36.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses population trends in Beijing and compares suburbanization effects in US superstar cities with European and Japanese urban cores. It highlights the office-dense and retail-poor nature of US urban cores and the mixed-use model in European and Japanese cities. The analysis of US counties and zip codes during the pandemic reveals patterns of out-migration influenced by factors like expensive homes, high office density, and limited retail presence.
pages.title: The urban cores of US superstar cities tend to be office-dense and retail-poor, whereas the European and Japanese urban cores tend to follow a mixed-use model.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_37.jpg
pages.abstract: The exhibit illustrates that counties with high housing costs, dense office environments, a strong knowledge economy, and weak retail sectors experienced greater out-migration during the pandemic. The data, presented through four scatter plots, shows a correlation between these factors and net migration trends in various metropolitan areas. The analysis is based on data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, US Census Bureau, and Zillow Home Value Index.
pages.title: Counties that were expensive, office-dense, knowledge economy-oriented, and retail-weak suffered greater out-migration during the pandemic.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_38.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses how hybrid work encouraged out-migration during the pandemic, with young caregivers who valued remote work being the primary drivers. It highlights that respondents who moved were younger, more likely to quit jobs if forced to attend the office five days a week, more likely to be caregivers, and had larger households. The data shows that remote work made employees more willing to live farther from the office.
pages.title: Hybrid work encouraged the out-migration

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_39.jpg
pages.abstract: Out-migration from US urban cores has slowed but continues, with rural and suburban areas near non-superstar cities benefiting. Pandemic-related movers prefer hybrid work and are unlikely to return to urban cores.
pages.title: Out-migration has since slowed, but people are still leaving urban cores

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_40.jpg
pages.abstract: The pandemic significantly reduced foot traffic near urban stores, especially in London and Paris, due to lockdowns and shifts to online shopping. While foot traffic has partially recovered, it remains lower than pre-pandemic levels, impacting retailers.
pages.title: Shopping remains depressed, especially in urban cores

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_41.jpg
pages.abstract: The pandemic accelerated online retail spending growth, with the largest spikes in China and the UK. Online spending as a share of total retail spending increased significantly from 2019 to 2020, with China experiencing a 9.9 percentage point increase. The trend has since returned to pre-pandemic levels, but the shift to online shopping has been lasting.
pages.title: Online retail spending spiked in 2020, though it has since returned to pre-pandemic trends.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_42.jpg
pages.abstract: Shopping behavior is returning to pre-pandemic trends, but foot traffic and in-store spending remain lower. Online spending has stabilized, while foot traffic and in-store spending have decreased, with foot traffic down 10-20% and in-store spending down 10% in most areas. Shoppers are making fewer trips but spending more per visit.
pages.title: Shopping behavior has started to return to pre-pandemic trends, yet foot traffic and purchasing in stores remain lower

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_43.jpg
pages.abstract: The pandemic initially shifted consumer spending towards goods, but since 2021, there has been a gradual return to spending on services. This trend poses challenges for brick-and-mortar stores, as online sales continue to grow and foot traffic declines. Retailers need to adapt by improving marketing and integrating in-store and online experiences.
pages.title: The pandemic led consumers to spend more on goods, but since 2021, they have been shifting their spending to services.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_44.jpg
pages.abstract: Foot traffic near stores is recovering more quickly in suburban areas compared to urban cores. Urban cores and office-dense neighborhoods have experienced significant and persistent declines in foot traffic, with some areas like the City of London seeing a nearly 50% decrease. Tourism declines have also impacted foot traffic, but to a lesser extent in tourist-popular areas.
pages.title: Foot traffic near stores is recovering more quickly in the suburbs than in urban cores.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_45.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses how employees in the U.S. who work fewer days in the office tend to spend more on online retail. It includes a detailed bar chart showing the share of weekly retail spending based on the number of days worked in the office. The data reveals that those working less in the office spend less near the workplace but more online and near home. This trend is linked to the decline in foot traffic in office-dense neighborhoods and potential opportunities for suburban stores.
pages.title: In the United States, employees who work less in the office spend more online.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_46.jpg
pages.title: 建筑玻璃幕墙

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_47.jpg
pages.abstract: The pandemic altered office workers' habits, leading to reduced demand for office and retail space, increased suburban migration, and higher vacancy rates in superstar cities. A model projects lower demand in 2030 compared to 2019, with significant impacts on office space vacancy rates, especially in cities like San Francisco.
pages.title: 2. The impact on real estate

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_48.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the increase in office vacancy rates in major cities between 2019 and 2022, with a focus on the impact of lower office attendance on rents. It highlights significant rent declines in US cities like San Francisco and New York, while European cities showed more resilience. Occupancy and rents may continue to fall as employers downsize office spaces, and macroeconomic uncertainty adds to the challenges. Some landlords have offered incentives to maintain occupancy, but effective rent has decreased.
pages.title: Office vacancy rates in superstar cities increased between 2019 and 2022.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_49.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the historical context of falling rents and declining demand for office space, influenced by macroeconomic conditions and remote work trends. It highlights the dramatic fall in transaction volumes, rising capitalization rates, and projected lower demand for office space by 2030, especially in cities like San Francisco, due to remote work and flexible arrangements.
pages.title: Demand for office space in the median city we studied is projected to be 13 percent lower in 2030 than in 2019

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_50.jpg
pages.abstract: The document projects a decrease in office space demand in most major cities by 2030 compared to 2019, with Houston being an exception due to high office attendance and population growth. The moderate and severe scenarios highlight varying impacts of pandemic-driven behavior on demand.
pages.title: Projected change in office space demand before prices adjust, 2019–30, %

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_51.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses a severe scenario for office-space demand, projecting a significant decrease in demand and increase in vacancy rates in major cities. It highlights that San Francisco will face the worst impact, with a 38% lower demand in 2030 compared to 2019, while Houston will fare better. The excess supply of office space, defined as the percentage of space vacant beyond structural vacancy, is projected to be highest in San Francisco, Shanghai, Beijing, London, and Munich. The factors causing excess supply include decreasing demand and continued supply growth.
pages.title: Excess supply in superstar cities is highest in San Francisco, Shanghai, Beijing, London, and Munich.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_52.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the projected high vacancy rates and declining office space value in various cities by 2030, with Tokyo having the lowest vacancy rate due to its transit-oriented design. It explores ways to reduce excess supply, including boosting demand and shrinking supply. The total value of office space is at risk, with potential declines of 26% to 42% depending on the scenario. Factors like rising interest rates and financial institutions' actions could exacerbate the impact. The decline in value is already evident, with capitalization rates rising and potential 'doom loops' affecting property values. Shorter leases and tenants' preference for higher-quality spaces further complicate the situation.
pages.title: A 'doom loop' could be exacerbated by office tenants' increased preference for higher-quality spaces.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_53.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the trend of tenants preferring high-quality office spaces, especially Class A spaces, over Class B spaces since 2020. This shift is driven by factors such as the suitability of older spaces for hybrid work, the desire for better audiovisual equipment, and the reduced need for large spaces due to hybrid work. Employers are willing to invest in smaller, higher-quality spaces to encourage office attendance and reduce commuting time. A survey indicates that even those least inclined to work in the office are attracted to quality spaces.
pages.title: The ‘flight to quality’ in office space

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_54.jpg
pages.abstract: The pandemic reversed the pre-pandemic trend of faster housing price growth in urban cores compared to suburbs. Residential vacancy rates increased more quickly in urban cores during the pandemic, with the highest increase in London and the lowest in Tokyo. The average increase in vacancy rates was higher in urban cores than in suburbs.
pages.title: Demand growth for residences will be muted, especially in urban cores

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_55.jpg
pages.abstract: The vacancy rate for residences increased more in urban cores than in suburbs due to suburbanization. Home prices rose more slowly in US superstar urban cores compared to their suburbs and non-superstar urban cores. This trend was observed globally outside major city centers.
pages.title: Home prices in the United States have risen far more slowly in superstar urban cores than elsewhere.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_56.jpg
pages.abstract: San Francisco exhibits the 'doughnut effect' in housing prices, with rising prices in suburbs and falling prices in the city center. From 2019 to 2022, nominal prices in affected neighborhoods fell by 12%, resulting in urban core residences being worth $750 billion less than the national average rate.
pages.title: San Francisco has demonstrated the ‘doughnut effect’: rising prices in the suburbs and falling prices in city centers.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_57.jpg
pages.abstract: The document projects that by 2030, demand for residential real estate in most superstar urban cores will surpass 2019 levels, despite pandemic effects. Houston, Munich, and Tokyo show the strongest growth, while Paris and San Francisco are exceptions due to urban core population decline. The pandemic significantly impacts demand in only three cities: London, New York City, and San Francisco. The exhibit details projected changes in residential space demand and excess supply for various cities, highlighting the effects of pandemic-driven behavior.
pages.title: Projected demand for residential real estate in 2030

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_58.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the projected growth in demand for residential space, highlighting the impact of population growth and pandemic-induced migration on urban cores and suburbs. It presents a moderate scenario for London, showing that while both areas expect population and home size growth, migration patterns differ, driving demand up in suburbs and down in urban cores.
pages.title: Demand for residential space is largely driven by population growth, which has been affected by pandemic-induced out-migration.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_59.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the projected change in residential space demand in major cities from 2019 to 2030, considering pandemic-driven behavior and other factors. It highlights that even in a severe scenario, demand for residential space is expected to be higher in 2030 compared to 2019 in most superstar cities, with variations between urban cores and suburbs.
pages.title: Even in a severe scenario, demand for residential space is higher in 2030 than it was in 2019 in most superstar cities.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_60.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the impact of the pandemic on retail space in urban cores, highlighting increased vacancy rates and declining rents, especially in office-dense locations. It also addresses the challenges faced by retail real estate and the projected lower demand for retail space in urban cores by 2030.
pages.title: A great deal of retail space in urban cores became vacant during the pandemic, and there is reason to think that vacancy rates will keep rising.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_61.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the increase in retail vacancy rates and decrease in asking rents in urban cores from 2019 to 2022, with specific data for cities like London, Paris, and Shanghai. It also notes a significant rise in U.S. home prices during the same period.
pages.title: Retail space in urban cores became more vacant from 2019 to 2022, and rents fell.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_62.jpg
pages.abstract: Retail rents grew most slowly in office-dense neighborhoods in the New York City metropolitan area from 2019 to 2022. This trend is attributed to factors such as retailers' lease renewals, landlord concessions, and economic uncertainty affecting consumer spending.
pages.title: In the New York City metropolitan area, retail rents grew most slowly in office-dense neighborhoods.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_63.jpg
pages.abstract: The document projects a significant decline in retail space demand across major urban cores by 2030, with moderate and severe scenarios showing decreases of up to 22% and 31%, respectively, compared to 2019. Factors unrelated to the pandemic and pandemic-driven behavior both contribute to this decline.
pages.title: Demand for retail space in the median city we studied is projected to be 9 percent lower in 2030 than in 2019

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_64.jpg
pages.abstract: The ongoing shift toward online shopping is the main factor reducing demand for retail space in London. Population growth and consumer spending growth have minimal impact, while increased online shopping significantly decreases demand. The urban core and suburbs both experience a decline in retail space demand by 2030, with the urban core seeing a larger decrease.
pages.title: In London, the main factor pushing down demand for retail space is the ongoing shift toward online shopping.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_65.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses how population shifts and changes in consumer behavior due to remote work and online shopping have impacted retail space demand in Paris. The urban core is projected to see a decrease in demand, while the suburbs are expected to experience an increase. Net migration and foot traffic changes are key factors in this variation.
pages.title: In Paris, a shifting population reduces demand for retail space in the urban core but increases it in the suburbs.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_66.jpg
pages.title: Cityscape at Sunset

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_67.jpg
pages.abstract: This chapter examines the characteristics of neighborhoods and cities strongly affected by the pandemic, focusing on business mix and urban structure. Factors like a higher share of knowledge workers, large firms, and expensive housing correlate with greater demand impact. The analysis also explores neighborhood-level effects in Manhattan, San Francisco, Paris, and Tokyo.
pages.title: 3. What strongly affected neighborhoods and cities have in common

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_68.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how business mix and urban structure influence real estate demand at neighborhood and city levels, comparing the Financial District and Lower East Side in Manhattan, and cities like San Francisco, Paris, and Tokyo. It highlights the impact of the pandemic on demand, influenced by factors like remote work and mixed-use development.
pages.title: Business mix and urban structure make a difference at the neighborhood level

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_69.jpg
pages.abstract: This page explains how differences in business mix and urban structure influenced city responses to the pandemic. Cities with higher shares of knowledge workers and large firms, like New York City, London, and San Francisco, were more disrupted. Cities with lower shares, like Munich, Tokyo, and Houston, were less affected. Urban structure, including residences, offices, price gradients, and green spaces, also played a role.
pages.title: Differences in the business mix and urban structure of cities help explain why they were affected differently by the pandemic.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_70.jpg
pages.abstract: San Francisco's real estate market has been significantly impacted by the pandemic, with higher vacancy rates and slower home price growth compared to other cities. The city's technology-focused economy and high housing costs contributed to these changes. The outlook for San Francisco's future is dire, with projected increases in vacancy rates and decreases in demand for office and retail space.
pages.title: San Francisco, a bastion of the knowledge economy, has been strongly affected by the pandemic

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_71.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses how high housing costs in Paris's urban core are driving residents to move elsewhere. It highlights the diverse industry mix in Paris, which helped it weather the pandemic better than San Francisco. However, the urban structure, with significantly higher home prices in the core compared to suburbs and national average, has led to out-migration since 2010. The page also projects future demand shifts in office, retail, and residential spaces.
pages.title: Expensive housing in Paris's urban core gives people a reason to move elsewhere.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_72.jpg
pages.abstract: Tokyo experienced minimal pandemic-induced behavioral shifts due to its diverse industry mix, cultural emphasis on office presence, and lower technology adoption. Real estate demand remained stable, with modest changes in office and retail vacancy rates. Future projections indicate healthier real estate demand compared to other cities.
pages.title: Tokyo, industrially diverse and relatively inexpensive, was affected only lightly by the pandemic

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_73.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses housing prices in Tokyo, showing that they have grown slightly faster than the national average since the pandemic. It includes graphs comparing home prices and population trends in various prefectures. Additionally, it highlights that urban core home prices in Tokyo are 2.1 times higher than the national average, contrasting with Paris and San Francisco.
pages.title: Housing prices in Tokyo have grown only slightly faster than the national average rate since the start of the pandemic.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_74.jpg
pages.title: Parisian Street Scene

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_75.jpg
pages.abstract: The pandemic has led to higher vacancy rates in urban cores due to hybrid work trends. To thrive, cities should adopt hybrid approaches, including mixed-use development, to enhance neighborhood vibrancy and resilience. Mobilizing stakeholders, reforming zoning policies, and considering diverse user journeys are crucial for successful redevelopment.
pages.title: 4. Thriving in hybrid places

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_76.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the potential financial impact of declining urban real estate demand, emphasizing the importance of recognizing property losses and the challenges and opportunities for investors and financiers. It highlights the need for recapitalization and rethinking property valuation in a hybrid work world. Examples from Lower Manhattan and the High Line illustrate successful mixed-use developments, while suburban areas can benefit from hybridity and multifamily housing.
pages.title: Investing in the future of urban real estate

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_77.jpg
pages.abstract: The report discusses the potential for pandemic-induced shifts to improve affordability and sustainability in real estate. Residents are moving to suburbs and non-superstar cities, where housing is cheaper and easier to build. Developers can convert vacant office buildings into residences in urban cores, but the impact on affordability is limited. Sustainability can be improved by replacing older buildings with energy-efficient ones and reducing commutes, but suburban migration may lead to less efficient housing. Transit-oriented and mixed-use developments can help.
pages.title: Affordable, sustainable real estate after the pandemic

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_78.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the need for adaptable and flexible building spaces in response to declining demand for traditional office and retail spaces. It explores the concept of hybrid buildings, their advantages, and the challenges of converting offices into other types of spaces. It also highlights the importance of adaptability in retail spaces and the potential for new store formats.
pages.title: At the building level, construct space that is adaptable and flexible

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_79.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the need for modular and multiuse design in urban spaces, emphasizing the importance of creating attractive experiences for office workers and shoppers. It highlights the role of flexible and adaptable thinking in designing spaces that cater to various uses, including omnichannel retail and experiential retail, to earn the commute and transform cities for a prosperous future.
pages.title: At the floor level, design space that is modular and multiuse

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_80.jpg
pages.title: Cityscape at Dusk

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_81.jpg
pages.abstract: This appendix details a survey conducted in 2022 to understand pandemic-induced behavioral shifts among office workers in six countries. It describes the survey methodology, including respondent selection, weighting, and overrepresentation of specific groups to ensure comprehensive data on targeted cities and migration patterns.
pages.title: Technical appendix

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_82.jpg
pages.abstract: This page outlines the survey areas covering respondents' characteristics, employment, office attendance, work-from-home factors, space needs, retail spending, recent moves, and preferences. It also introduces models for projecting real estate demand in 2030, focusing on office space factors like employment and attendance.
pages.title: Survey Areas and Models for Real Estate Demand Projections

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_83.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses employee coordination and space per seat in office demand scenarios, including reversion, moderate, and severe scenarios. It also introduces a residential space model considering population, average household size, and average home size.
pages.title: Employee coordination and space per seat in office demand scenarios

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_84.jpg
pages.abstract: The document outlines three scenarios for estimating demand in retail spaces, considering factors like population, remote work impact, e-commerce penetration, sales productivity, in-store retail sales, and commuters. It discusses how these factors vary in reversion, moderate, and severe scenarios, affecting population growth, retail spending, and e-commerce trends.
pages.title: Estimating demand in three scenarios

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_85.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the severe scenario's impact on retail spending, population assumptions, office attendance, e-commerce penetration, and sales productivity in various cities, highlighting trends and expectations post-pandemic.
pages.title: In the severe scenario

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_86.jpg
pages.title: Urban Plaza with Outdoor Seating

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_87.jpg
pages.title: Acknowledgments

pages.page_path: library_pages\Empty spaces and hybrid places_ The pandemic’s lasting impact on real estate_McKinsey_2023_01_01\page_88.jpg
pages.title: McKinsey Global Institute

43.file_desc:
The document introduces the McKinsey Global Institute, its mission, research themes, and independence. It also highlights McKinsey's Real Estate Practice, its focus on sustainable growth, and its unique capabilities.
This research highlights the lasting impact of COVID-19 on real estate in major global cities, emphasizing the shift to hybrid work, reduced demand for office and retail space, and the need for cities to adapt through hybrid approaches.
The exhibit illustrates the projected change in demand for office, residential, and retail space in urban cores between 2019 and 2030, showing significant declines driven by pandemic behavior, with variations across cities like San Francisco, London, and New York City.
The COVID-19 pandemic altered urban living and working patterns, leading to shifts in real estate demand in superstar cities. McKinsey Global Institute's research models future demand for office, residential, and retail spaces, predicting lower demand by 2030. Factors like automation, employee coordination, and shopping trends were considered. Despite macroeconomic uncertainties, the research highlights opportunities for cities to adapt and thrive through hybrid urban spaces.
The pandemic has led to a significant shift in work patterns, with hybrid work becoming the norm and office attendance dropping by 30%. Urban cores have seen a decrease in population and retail spending, with few people returning. The report focuses on real estate in superstar cities, defining them as areas with a large share of global GDP and GDP growth. The urban core and suburbs are analyzed separately, with data collected from 17 cities in six countries. Office attendance varies by industry and neighborhood, influenced by factors like housing costs and local culture.
The document discusses office attendance trends in various industries and firm sizes, highlighting that larger firms in knowledge-based sectors have lower attendance. It explains factors influencing these trends, including stability since mid-2022, employee preferences, and potential shifts due to labor market dynamics or research findings.
The pandemic accelerated suburbanization trends, with urban cores losing population while suburban areas grew or shrank less. This shift was more pronounced in the US compared to European and Japanese cities. The exhibit highlights the difference in growth rates between urban and suburban areas across various metro regions.
The document discusses the out-migration trends from urban cores of superstar cities, influenced by factors like expensive housing, high office density, and limited retail presence. Hybrid work and housing conditions have contributed to these trends. Shopping in urban cores remains depressed due to shifts in consumer behavior during the pandemic, with foot traffic still lower than pre-pandemic levels. Retailers in urban cores face challenges in attracting customers as people visit offices less frequently.
The page presents data showing that foot traffic near stores has recovered more quickly in suburban areas compared to urban cores across various cities. Graphs illustrate the change in foot traffic from January 2020, with suburban areas generally showing a faster recovery trend. The data is sourced from Google's Community Mobility Reports and analyzed by the McKinsey Global Institute.
The pandemic has led to lower office attendance, out-migration from cities, and reduced shopping in office-heavy neighborhoods, pushing down demand for real estate in superstar cities. By 2030, demand for office and retail space is projected to be lower than in 2019. Residential space is less affected, with price differences between urban cores and suburbs narrowing. The exhibit shows a moderate scenario where demand for office and retail space falls sharply between 2019 and 2030.
The document discusses the decline in demand for office space due to remote work and economic challenges, leading to increased vacancy rates and decreased transaction volumes. By 2030, demand could be 20-38% lower than in 2019, impacting office values and leading to a surplus of lower-quality office space.
The pandemic has led to muted demand growth for residences in urban cores compared to suburbs. Vacancy rates and prices have increased less in urban cores, with a global phenomenon observed. By 2030, demand for residences in urban cores is projected to be 10% lower than pre-pandemic levels. Retail space demand is also expected to decline by 9% in median cities due to reduced foot traffic and increased online shopping. Adjustments in prices and rents are likely, but urban cores remain attractive for residential space.
Cities strongly affected by the pandemic in real estate demand share characteristics like a high knowledge economy workforce, large firms, and office-dense structures. These factors reduce office attendance, retail shopping, and residential demand. Neighborhoods with more office-occupied real estate experience higher out-migration.
This page presents data showing that expensive, office-dense neighborhoods in San Francisco and Manhattan experienced higher out-migration rates during 2020-2022. It includes maps illustrating the share of real estate occupied by office buildings, typical home values, and net out-migration percentages, highlighting the correlation between high office density and migration trends.
This page discusses how business mix and urban structure influence real estate demand at neighborhood and city levels, comparing Manhattan neighborhoods, San Francisco, Paris, and Tokyo. Factors like knowledge economy prevalence, office density, and home prices are analyzed in relation to pandemic-driven changes in demand and migration patterns.
Superstar cities face challenges from hybrid work, leading to vacancy and reduced urban vibrancy. Mixed-use development, incorporating diverse real estate types, can help adapt neighborhoods. Mobilizing stakeholders, including governments, investors, and developers, is crucial for successful redevelopment. Suburbs can also benefit from hybrid approaches, with multifamily housing and greener spaces attracting urban dwellers.
This page discusses the benefits of multifamily housing and adaptable building spaces, emphasizing energy efficiency, flexibility, and the potential for hybrid buildings to address changing demands and protect against unpredictable shifts in preferences. It also explores the challenges and opportunities of converting office spaces into other types of demand-driven spaces.
This page discusses the importance of adaptable and modular design in retail and office spaces to cater to changing tenant needs. It highlights the need for spaces that can serve multiple purposes, attract visitors, and integrate with their environments. The text also explores the concept of hybrid floors combining offices, residences, and stores to counter the pandemic's impact and prepare cities for a prosperous future.
The COVID-19 pandemic led to a significant shift to remote work, altering where people work, live, and shop. This hybrid work model has permanently changed urban dynamics, with office attendance stabilizing at lower rates and urban out-migration continuing, though at a slower pace. Shopping in cities remains weaker than before the pandemic.
The page discusses the shift from remote to hybrid work, highlighting that as of fall 2022, workers were in the office an average of 3.5 days per week, 30% below pre-pandemic norms. It includes a survey showing 37% of respondents go to the office daily, 56% have hybrid arrangements, and 7% work fully remotely. A chart illustrates office attendance by city.
This page discusses how office attendance varies among metropolitan areas, influenced by factors like housing costs and the proportion of knowledge-economy workers. It highlights that higher housing costs and a larger share of knowledge-economy workers correlate with lower office attendance. Cultural and policy factors, such as China's '996' work culture and city lockdowns, also impact attendance. The page includes an exhibit showing the relationship between office attendance and these factors in US counties.
Employees in larger firms report lower office attendance compared to smaller firms due to more resources for remote work and a stronger sense of community in smaller companies. Client meetings are less of a reason for office visits in larger firms. Knowledge-economy employees go to the office less often, possibly due to digitization and remote work suitability.
The document discusses how office attendance varies subtly by age, income, and seniority. Millennials work 3.4 days per week in the office, while Generation X and baby boomers work 3.5 days. Millennials in senior positions work 3.7 days per week. Baby boomers are more likely to work five days per week compared to younger workers. The data is presented in Exhibit 4, showing reported attendance by age, income, and job seniority.
This page discusses the reasons employees choose to work from home or the office, highlighting that saving commuting time is the top reason for working from home, while working with teams is the top reason for going to the office. It also presents data on the top reasons for both options, showing variations by country and the importance of productivity.
The current rate of office attendance appears to have stabilized in major US cities since mid-2022, with slight seasonal variations. The data, indexed to March 2020, shows trends across various cities, indicating that while attendance has stabilized, it remains below pre-pandemic levels.
The page discusses employees' preferences for working from the office versus working from home. It shows that employees already work close to their ideal number of days in the office. Additionally, it highlights that employees who prefer working from home are generally more senior and better compensated.
This page discusses the preferences of office workers for remote work, the potential impact on office attendance, and the relationship between hybrid work and productivity. It highlights that a significant group of senior and well-paid workers prefer remote work, and improvements in hybrid work technology may reduce the need for office attendance. The page also mentions the limited success of employer perks in attracting workers back to the office and the positive perception of hybrid work on productivity.
The pandemic significantly reduced population growth in most cities, with urban cores experiencing population decline due to hybrid work and out-migration. Munich's growth slowed from 1.0% to 0.3%, while New York City's urban core lost 5% of its population. Out-migration remains higher than pre-pandemic levels, and suburban growth has surpassed urban growth in many cities.
The document discusses how suburban population growth outpaced urban growth during the pandemic in many cities, with notable differences between US, European, and Japanese cities. It includes a detailed exhibit comparing growth rates across various metro areas.
This page discusses population trends in Beijing and compares suburbanization effects in US superstar cities with European and Japanese urban cores. It highlights the office-dense and retail-poor nature of US urban cores and the mixed-use model in European and Japanese cities. The analysis of US counties and zip codes during the pandemic reveals patterns of out-migration influenced by factors like expensive homes, high office density, and limited retail presence.
The exhibit illustrates that counties with high housing costs, dense office environments, a strong knowledge economy, and weak retail sectors experienced greater out-migration during the pandemic. The data, presented through four scatter plots, shows a correlation between these factors and net migration trends in various metropolitan areas. The analysis is based on data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, US Census Bureau, and Zillow Home Value Index.
The page discusses how hybrid work encouraged out-migration during the pandemic, with young caregivers who valued remote work being the primary drivers. It highlights that respondents who moved were younger, more likely to quit jobs if forced to attend the office five days a week, more likely to be caregivers, and had larger households. The data shows that remote work made employees more willing to live farther from the office.
Out-migration from US urban cores has slowed but continues, with rural and suburban areas near non-superstar cities benefiting. Pandemic-related movers prefer hybrid work and are unlikely to return to urban cores.
The pandemic significantly reduced foot traffic near urban stores, especially in London and Paris, due to lockdowns and shifts to online shopping. While foot traffic has partially recovered, it remains lower than pre-pandemic levels, impacting retailers.
The pandemic accelerated online retail spending growth, with the largest spikes in China and the UK. Online spending as a share of total retail spending increased significantly from 2019 to 2020, with China experiencing a 9.9 percentage point increase. The trend has since returned to pre-pandemic levels, but the shift to online shopping has been lasting.
Shopping behavior is returning to pre-pandemic trends, but foot traffic and in-store spending remain lower. Online spending has stabilized, while foot traffic and in-store spending have decreased, with foot traffic down 10-20% and in-store spending down 10% in most areas. Shoppers are making fewer trips but spending more per visit.
The pandemic initially shifted consumer spending towards goods, but since 2021, there has been a gradual return to spending on services. This trend poses challenges for brick-and-mortar stores, as online sales continue to grow and foot traffic declines. Retailers need to adapt by improving marketing and integrating in-store and online experiences.
Foot traffic near stores is recovering more quickly in suburban areas compared to urban cores. Urban cores and office-dense neighborhoods have experienced significant and persistent declines in foot traffic, with some areas like the City of London seeing a nearly 50% decrease. Tourism declines have also impacted foot traffic, but to a lesser extent in tourist-popular areas.
The page discusses how employees in the U.S. who work fewer days in the office tend to spend more on online retail. It includes a detailed bar chart showing the share of weekly retail spending based on the number of days worked in the office. The data reveals that those working less in the office spend less near the workplace but more online and near home. This trend is linked to the decline in foot traffic in office-dense neighborhoods and potential opportunities for suburban stores.
The pandemic altered office workers' habits, leading to reduced demand for office and retail space, increased suburban migration, and higher vacancy rates in superstar cities. A model projects lower demand in 2030 compared to 2019, with significant impacts on office space vacancy rates, especially in cities like San Francisco.
The document discusses the increase in office vacancy rates in major cities between 2019 and 2022, with a focus on the impact of lower office attendance on rents. It highlights significant rent declines in US cities like San Francisco and New York, while European cities showed more resilience. Occupancy and rents may continue to fall as employers downsize office spaces, and macroeconomic uncertainty adds to the challenges. Some landlords have offered incentives to maintain occupancy, but effective rent has decreased.
The document discusses the historical context of falling rents and declining demand for office space, influenced by macroeconomic conditions and remote work trends. It highlights the dramatic fall in transaction volumes, rising capitalization rates, and projected lower demand for office space by 2030, especially in cities like San Francisco, due to remote work and flexible arrangements.
The document projects a decrease in office space demand in most major cities by 2030 compared to 2019, with Houston being an exception due to high office attendance and population growth. The moderate and severe scenarios highlight varying impacts of pandemic-driven behavior on demand.
The document discusses a severe scenario for office-space demand, projecting a significant decrease in demand and increase in vacancy rates in major cities. It highlights that San Francisco will face the worst impact, with a 38% lower demand in 2030 compared to 2019, while Houston will fare better. The excess supply of office space, defined as the percentage of space vacant beyond structural vacancy, is projected to be highest in San Francisco, Shanghai, Beijing, London, and Munich. The factors causing excess supply include decreasing demand and continued supply growth.
The document discusses the projected high vacancy rates and declining office space value in various cities by 2030, with Tokyo having the lowest vacancy rate due to its transit-oriented design. It explores ways to reduce excess supply, including boosting demand and shrinking supply. The total value of office space is at risk, with potential declines of 26% to 42% depending on the scenario. Factors like rising interest rates and financial institutions' actions could exacerbate the impact. The decline in value is already evident, with capitalization rates rising and potential 'doom loops' affecting property values. Shorter leases and tenants' preference for higher-quality spaces further complicate the situation.
The document discusses the trend of tenants preferring high-quality office spaces, especially Class A spaces, over Class B spaces since 2020. This shift is driven by factors such as the suitability of older spaces for hybrid work, the desire for better audiovisual equipment, and the reduced need for large spaces due to hybrid work. Employers are willing to invest in smaller, higher-quality spaces to encourage office attendance and reduce commuting time. A survey indicates that even those least inclined to work in the office are attracted to quality spaces.
The pandemic reversed the pre-pandemic trend of faster housing price growth in urban cores compared to suburbs. Residential vacancy rates increased more quickly in urban cores during the pandemic, with the highest increase in London and the lowest in Tokyo. The average increase in vacancy rates was higher in urban cores than in suburbs.
The vacancy rate for residences increased more in urban cores than in suburbs due to suburbanization. Home prices rose more slowly in US superstar urban cores compared to their suburbs and non-superstar urban cores. This trend was observed globally outside major city centers.
San Francisco exhibits the 'doughnut effect' in housing prices, with rising prices in suburbs and falling prices in the city center. From 2019 to 2022, nominal prices in affected neighborhoods fell by 12%, resulting in urban core residences being worth $750 billion less than the national average rate.
The document projects that by 2030, demand for residential real estate in most superstar urban cores will surpass 2019 levels, despite pandemic effects. Houston, Munich, and Tokyo show the strongest growth, while Paris and San Francisco are exceptions due to urban core population decline. The pandemic significantly impacts demand in only three cities: London, New York City, and San Francisco. The exhibit details projected changes in residential space demand and excess supply for various cities, highlighting the effects of pandemic-driven behavior.
The document discusses the projected growth in demand for residential space, highlighting the impact of population growth and pandemic-induced migration on urban cores and suburbs. It presents a moderate scenario for London, showing that while both areas expect population and home size growth, migration patterns differ, driving demand up in suburbs and down in urban cores.
This page discusses the projected change in residential space demand in major cities from 2019 to 2030, considering pandemic-driven behavior and other factors. It highlights that even in a severe scenario, demand for residential space is expected to be higher in 2030 compared to 2019 in most superstar cities, with variations between urban cores and suburbs.
The document discusses the impact of the pandemic on retail space in urban cores, highlighting increased vacancy rates and declining rents, especially in office-dense locations. It also addresses the challenges faced by retail real estate and the projected lower demand for retail space in urban cores by 2030.
The page discusses the increase in retail vacancy rates and decrease in asking rents in urban cores from 2019 to 2022, with specific data for cities like London, Paris, and Shanghai. It also notes a significant rise in U.S. home prices during the same period.
Retail rents grew most slowly in office-dense neighborhoods in the New York City metropolitan area from 2019 to 2022. This trend is attributed to factors such as retailers' lease renewals, landlord concessions, and economic uncertainty affecting consumer spending.
The document projects a significant decline in retail space demand across major urban cores by 2030, with moderate and severe scenarios showing decreases of up to 22% and 31%, respectively, compared to 2019. Factors unrelated to the pandemic and pandemic-driven behavior both contribute to this decline.
The ongoing shift toward online shopping is the main factor reducing demand for retail space in London. Population growth and consumer spending growth have minimal impact, while increased online shopping significantly decreases demand. The urban core and suburbs both experience a decline in retail space demand by 2030, with the urban core seeing a larger decrease.
The document discusses how population shifts and changes in consumer behavior due to remote work and online shopping have impacted retail space demand in Paris. The urban core is projected to see a decrease in demand, while the suburbs are expected to experience an increase. Net migration and foot traffic changes are key factors in this variation.
This chapter examines the characteristics of neighborhoods and cities strongly affected by the pandemic, focusing on business mix and urban structure. Factors like a higher share of knowledge workers, large firms, and expensive housing correlate with greater demand impact. The analysis also explores neighborhood-level effects in Manhattan, San Francisco, Paris, and Tokyo.
This page discusses how business mix and urban structure influence real estate demand at neighborhood and city levels, comparing the Financial District and Lower East Side in Manhattan, and cities like San Francisco, Paris, and Tokyo. It highlights the impact of the pandemic on demand, influenced by factors like remote work and mixed-use development.
This page explains how differences in business mix and urban structure influenced city responses to the pandemic. Cities with higher shares of knowledge workers and large firms, like New York City, London, and San Francisco, were more disrupted. Cities with lower shares, like Munich, Tokyo, and Houston, were less affected. Urban structure, including residences, offices, price gradients, and green spaces, also played a role.
San Francisco's real estate market has been significantly impacted by the pandemic, with higher vacancy rates and slower home price growth compared to other cities. The city's technology-focused economy and high housing costs contributed to these changes. The outlook for San Francisco's future is dire, with projected increases in vacancy rates and decreases in demand for office and retail space.
The page discusses how high housing costs in Paris's urban core are driving residents to move elsewhere. It highlights the diverse industry mix in Paris, which helped it weather the pandemic better than San Francisco. However, the urban structure, with significantly higher home prices in the core compared to suburbs and national average, has led to out-migration since 2010. The page also projects future demand shifts in office, retail, and residential spaces.
Tokyo experienced minimal pandemic-induced behavioral shifts due to its diverse industry mix, cultural emphasis on office presence, and lower technology adoption. Real estate demand remained stable, with modest changes in office and retail vacancy rates. Future projections indicate healthier real estate demand compared to other cities.
The page discusses housing prices in Tokyo, showing that they have grown slightly faster than the national average since the pandemic. It includes graphs comparing home prices and population trends in various prefectures. Additionally, it highlights that urban core home prices in Tokyo are 2.1 times higher than the national average, contrasting with Paris and San Francisco.
The pandemic has led to higher vacancy rates in urban cores due to hybrid work trends. To thrive, cities should adopt hybrid approaches, including mixed-use development, to enhance neighborhood vibrancy and resilience. Mobilizing stakeholders, reforming zoning policies, and considering diverse user journeys are crucial for successful redevelopment.
This page discusses the potential financial impact of declining urban real estate demand, emphasizing the importance of recognizing property losses and the challenges and opportunities for investors and financiers. It highlights the need for recapitalization and rethinking property valuation in a hybrid work world. Examples from Lower Manhattan and the High Line illustrate successful mixed-use developments, while suburban areas can benefit from hybridity and multifamily housing.
The report discusses the potential for pandemic-induced shifts to improve affordability and sustainability in real estate. Residents are moving to suburbs and non-superstar cities, where housing is cheaper and easier to build. Developers can convert vacant office buildings into residences in urban cores, but the impact on affordability is limited. Sustainability can be improved by replacing older buildings with energy-efficient ones and reducing commutes, but suburban migration may lead to less efficient housing. Transit-oriented and mixed-use developments can help.
This page discusses the need for adaptable and flexible building spaces in response to declining demand for traditional office and retail spaces. It explores the concept of hybrid buildings, their advantages, and the challenges of converting offices into other types of spaces. It also highlights the importance of adaptability in retail spaces and the potential for new store formats.
This page discusses the need for modular and multiuse design in urban spaces, emphasizing the importance of creating attractive experiences for office workers and shoppers. It highlights the role of flexible and adaptable thinking in designing spaces that cater to various uses, including omnichannel retail and experiential retail, to earn the commute and transform cities for a prosperous future.
This appendix details a survey conducted in 2022 to understand pandemic-induced behavioral shifts among office workers in six countries. It describes the survey methodology, including respondent selection, weighting, and overrepresentation of specific groups to ensure comprehensive data on targeted cities and migration patterns.
This page outlines the survey areas covering respondents' characteristics, employment, office attendance, work-from-home factors, space needs, retail spending, recent moves, and preferences. It also introduces models for projecting real estate demand in 2030, focusing on office space factors like employment and attendance.
This page discusses employee coordination and space per seat in office demand scenarios, including reversion, moderate, and severe scenarios. It also introduces a residential space model considering population, average household size, and average home size.
The document outlines three scenarios for estimating demand in retail spaces, considering factors like population, remote work impact, e-commerce penetration, sales productivity, in-store retail sales, and commuters. It discusses how these factors vary in reversion, moderate, and severe scenarios, affecting population growth, retail spending, and e-commerce trends.
This page discusses the severe scenario's impact on retail spending, population assumptions, office attendance, e-commerce penetration, and sales productivity in various cities, highlighting trends and expectations post-pandemic.

pages.title: Europe's fintech opportunity
Europe's fintech opportunity
Contents

pages.abstract: The executive summary discusses the challenges faced by European fintechs due to a deteriorating macroeconomic environment, highlighting their resilience and potential for growth. It focuses on founding, funding, and scaling aspects of the fintech sector, emphasizing the modernization of the financial ecosystem and the substantial performance gaps among European countries.
pages.title: Executive Summary

pages.abstract: The page discusses the variable fintech performance across Europe, highlighting leading countries like the United Kingdom, Sweden, and northern European nations. It presents a ranking of countries by fintech performance and discusses potential growth in jobs, funding, and valuations if the bottom two-thirds of countries catch up with the top third. The text also outlines challenges and imperatives for the fintech sector in Europe, including market maturity, access to capital, regulatory frameworks, talent mobility, and customer openness.
pages.title: Fintech performance is variable across Europe, with the United Kingdom, Sweden, and northern European countries leading.

pages.abstract: This page discusses the rapid growth and mainstream adoption of fintechs in Europe, highlighting their contributions to customer satisfaction, financial sector modernization, and economic development. It emphasizes the competitive pricing and superior service offered by fintechs compared to traditional banks, supported by customer satisfaction scores and survey data.
pages.title: Fintechs are a force for growth, modernization, and customer satisfaction in Europe’s financial-services sector

pages.abstract: Customers prioritize pricing and easy access when using fintechs and digital banks. Fintechs contribute to the financial ecosystem by creating new revenue pools and challenging incumbents. Their agility and speed enable them to launch products faster and tap into emerging markets. Fintechs also provide innovative features and services, such as investment platforms and cryptocurrencies.
pages.title: Customers cite pricing and customer experience as their primary reasons for banking with fintechs.

pages.abstract: Fintechs act as bellwethers for incumbent banks, signaling successful innovations and enhancing competitiveness. They contribute to economic growth by creating jobs and fostering innovation, especially in vibrant start-up hubs across Europe. Despite some recent staff reductions, the overall upward trend in fintech employment is expected to continue.
pages.title: Fintechs can serve as a bellwether for incumbents, signaling which innovations are successful.

pages.abstract: European fintechs, valued at €430 billion, face challenges from rising interest rates. They must shift focus from growth to profitability and operational maturity. With €57 billion in venture capital, they invest in IT for cost advantages and scalability. Opportunities exist in B2B services, data monetization, and ESG investments, with open banking fostering innovation.
pages.title: Europe's fintech opportunity

pages.abstract: This page discusses the varying performance of European fintech ecosystems, highlighting leaders like the UK and Sweden, and factors influencing performance such as geography, market size, and digital bank usage. It also notes the strong performance of smaller economies and the correlation with international rankings.
pages.title: The divergent national performance of fintech ecosystems in Europe points to considerable untapped potential

pages.abstract: This page ranks European countries by their relative strength in five fintech KPIs across three growth stages. It highlights that countries like the UK, Sweden, and Malta performed well, while others like Greece, Bulgaria, and Slovakia lagged. The data is categorized by GDP levels and includes metrics like fintech funding per capita and unicorns per million capita.
pages.title: By the end of 2021, a few European countries outperformed others across all dimensions.

pages.abstract: This page analyzes fintech performance in Europe using five KPIs across founding, funding, and scaling stages. It highlights performance gaps, with some countries excelling despite lower GDP. The analysis focuses on countries with GDP over $100 billion, acknowledging limitations for smaller economies.
pages.title: Our analysis of fintech performance

pages.abstract: The page presents data on fintechs per million capita in 2021 for various European countries and the United States, showing significant variation. Countries like Ireland and Switzerland have the highest fintech density, while Greece has none. The data highlights the relationship between entrepreneurial attitudes and fintech development.
pages.title: The number of fintechs per capita varies widely among European countries.

pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of funding growth in fintech ecosystems, highlighting that countries like Sweden and the UK lead in per capita funding. It also notes disparities among European countries, with some experiencing significant funding increases while others lag behind due to low total funding volumes.
pages.title: Funding growth
