pages.abstract: The United Kingdom led in both early- and late-stage fintech funding in 2021, with €1.3 billion and €8.3 billion respectively. It outperformed other countries, including the US, despite a smaller GDP. Several European countries, especially in eastern Europe, had limited early-stage funding and no late-stage funding.
pages.title: The United Kingdom led in both early- and late-stage funding in 2021.

pages.abstract: The United States outperforms Europe in fintech metrics due to a large market, harmonized regulations, mature venture capital ecosystem, and strong talent attraction. Despite some European countries excelling in funding, the US ranks in the top third for all evaluated performance indicators in 2021.
pages.title: How fintech in Europe compares with the United States

pages.abstract: The limited scale of fintechs in Europe is linked to low internationalization of business models. Leading countries like the UK and Sweden have global footprints, with the UK having 32 unicorns. Factors affecting ecosystem performance include market structure, access to capital, regulatory frameworks, talent mobility, scaling requirements, and customer openness. Mature markets benefit from experienced founders and clustering effects around successful fintechs.
pages.title: The limited scale of fintechs may be related to the relatively low level of internationalization of business models, which can serve as a constraint on growth.

pages.abstract: This page discusses the fintech funding landscape in Europe, highlighting the uneven distribution of capital across different stages and countries. It emphasizes the importance of access to capital for early-stage fintechs and the role of foreign funding in underserved markets. The page also compares European and US pension fund investments in private markets and highlights regulatory support for fintechs in France.
pages.title: A tale of two countries: Fintech lessons from France and the United Kingdom

pages.abstract: This page discusses fintech lessons from France and the UK, focusing on business creation simplification, innovation enablement, and sustainability. It highlights regulatory changes, government initiatives, and strategies for fostering fintech growth, including policy, investments, international collaboration, and national connectivity.
pages.title: A tale of two countries: Fintech lessons from France and the United Kingdom (continued)

pages.abstract: The regulatory and legal landscape for fintechs in Europe varies, with some countries adapting existing frameworks to support innovation while others face challenges. Collaboration with regulators is crucial but often lacks optimal structure. Talent acquisition remains a significant issue due to skills gaps, visa requirements, and competition. Remote work and university support are key factors in attracting talent.
pages.title: The regulatory and legal landscape

pages.abstract: This page discusses the challenges and opportunities for European fintechs to scale up by expanding beyond their home markets. It highlights the need for fintechs to navigate language, regulatory, and cultural barriers, and the role of export agencies in supporting their international growth. The text also addresses customer openness, digital maturity, and regulatory differences as factors influencing fintech adoption. Finally, it outlines the potential benefits of scaling up, including more jobs, larger funding volumes, and higher valuations.
pages.title: To scale up, fintechs in Europe need to be able to expand beyond their home market.

pages.abstract: The page discusses the potential growth of European fintech jobs, funding, and valuation if countries align with the best in the region. It highlights the UK's relative strength and the need for collective action to achieve significant growth.
pages.title: European fintechs could have significant growth potential if all countries caught up with the best in region.

pages.abstract: This chapter discusses strategic areas for European countries to catch up with fintech leaders, emphasizing the alignment of market structures within the EU, encouraging diverse capital, and the role of local political players and regulators in shaping investment restrictions.
pages.title: A focused push along six strategic areas could help all European countries catch up with fintech leaders

pages.abstract: This page discusses fostering regulation with an innovative mindset and attracting global talent for fintechs. It emphasizes the importance of regulatory frameworks that support innovation, customer-friendly implementation, and modern work cultures. Examples include regulatory sandboxes, remote work options, and tax incentives.
pages.title: Foster regulation with an innovative mindset

pages.abstract: This page discusses enabling fintechs to thrive in target markets by creating support hubs for market insights and legal advice. It emphasizes increasing customer choices and access through safe and high-quality fintech offerings. The text highlights the importance of product safety, regulatory compliance, and partnerships between fintechs and incumbent banks. It also suggests Europe-wide initiatives and official recognitions to enhance fintech credibility and customer trust.
pages.title: Enable fintechs to thrive in target markets
About the authors
October 2022

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_3.jpg
pages.abstract: African fintech is experiencing rapid growth, with digital transactions increasing and revenues projected to reach $30 billion by 2025. Challenges include reaching scale, navigating uncertainty, managing scarcity, and building governance. Market leaders focus on value proposition, user acquisition, monetization, offline market understanding, and regulatory engagement. Growth varies across countries, with key markets driving significant GDP and population impact.
pages.title: The rise and rise of African fintech

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_4.jpg
pages.abstract: The executive summary highlights the booming fintech industry in Africa, with a tripling of tech startups and significant revenue growth. It discusses the continent's fintech eruption, attracting investors and bringing economic growth. Despite funding slowdowns, the sector shows potential for massive growth, especially in financial services. The structural shift in African financial services, driven by trends like smartphone ownership and declining internet costs, is creating a fertile environment for fintech companies, which offer cheaper and more efficient solutions.
pages.title: Executive summary

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_5.jpg
pages.abstract: African fintech markets are poised for exponential growth, with key markets like South Africa, Ghana, and Nigeria leading the way. Opportunities vary by digital maturity, with advanced services in mature economies and foundational advancements in developing ones. Sustainability and profitability remain challenges.
pages.title: Fintech in Africa: The end of the beginning

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_6.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses four key challenges African fintechs face in their growth: reaching scale and profitability, navigating a fragmented regulatory environment, managing scarce resources, and building robust corporate governance. It highlights infrastructure constraints, regulatory complexities, and funding challenges as major hurdles.
pages.title: Four challenges African fintechs may face in their next stage of growth

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_7.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the challenges faced by African fintechs, including limited local venture financing, talent concentration in specific countries, and the need for robust corporate governance. It emphasizes the importance of strong organizational culture, stakeholder engagement, and talent strategy to navigate the uncertain landscape and achieve long-term success.
pages.title: Building robust corporate governance foundations

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_8.jpg
pages.abstract: Africa's leading fintechs share characteristics that align with successful global companies, adapting to local economic realities. They achieve scale through various routes, including evolving from consumer products or financial products to digital banks, and building country-specific payment infrastructure. Sustainable growth is driven by rapid customer acquisition, overcoming infrastructure and purchasing power challenges.
pages.title: Africa's leading fintechs share a set of winning characteristics

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_9.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses successful African fintechs' strategies, including monetization, adapting to low ARPU, offline client reach, and regulatory compliance, highlighting their unique approaches to economic realities and customer needs.
pages.title: The most successful African tech startups share six characteristics with features that mirror those of successful global companies, and have also adapted their business models to the unique economic realities and customer needs of Africa.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_10.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the growth of the African fintech industry, its potential to create jobs and wealth, and the need for stakeholders to collaborate to support sustainable growth. It highlights the importance of digital skills, regulatory support, and partnerships in driving financial inclusion and innovation.
pages.title: Unlocking the potential of fintech in Africa

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_11.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the importance of partnerships in bank-led countries for fintech success, highlighting faster go-to-market and regulatory reassurance. It also mentions that 300 million Africans came online for the first time between 2010 and 2019.
pages.title: Fintech Entrepreneur Insights

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_12.jpg
pages.abstract: The maturation of Africa's fintech sector is underway, driven by technology advances and regulatory improvements. If penetration levels reach those of market leaders like Kenya, fintech revenues could grow eightfold by 2025, significantly impacting social and economic gains.
pages.title: 1. Laying down the path

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_13.jpg
pages.abstract: Fintech innovation in Africa is rapidly expanding financial services through digital wallets, lending platforms, and remittance solutions, offering cheaper and more accessible options compared to traditional banks. These innovations are particularly beneficial during the COVID-19 pandemic, addressing financial gaps and creating new job opportunities.
pages.title: Fintech innovation is delivering an all-access pass to financial services

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_14.jpg
pages.abstract: Fintech growth drives social benefits across financial inclusion, education, gender equality, public health, and agriculture. It enables financial inclusion for the unbanked, promotes female adoption of financial services, and provides access to healthcare. Innovations in fintech are reshaping African financial services, creating opportunities for populations and investors.
pages.title: Fintech growth will drive social benefits over time.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_15.jpg
pages.abstract: Financial services revenues in Africa are projected to grow by 10% annually until 2025, with payments and wallets leading the growth. The market is concentrated in South Africa but expected to expand rapidly in Ghana and Francophone West Africa. Eleven key countries will drive the market's evolution, offering favorable conditions for fintechs. Digital and mobile penetration is increasing, with data costs falling and internet usage growing, accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic.
pages.title: Financial services revenues are expected to grow by 10% p.a. until 2025, with payments and wallets being the fastest growing products.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_16.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses key trends driving digital expansion in Africa, including financial inclusion, dethroning cash, increased funding for innovation, fast growth in spending, a young and urbanizing population, increasing digital penetration, and COVID-19 acceleration. These trends present significant opportunities for fintechs to migrate Africa's cash-based customers to new solutions.
pages.title: Key trends driving digital expansion in Africa

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_17.jpg
pages.abstract: The funding for African startups has surged 18.5x over six years, with fintech contributing 45%. Africa's rapid population growth and urbanization, coupled with a young, digitally-savvy consumer base, make it an attractive market for foreign investors. Despite a dip in 2020 due to COVID-19, startup funding grew by over 200% between 2020 and 2021, outpacing global growth.
pages.title: Funding for African startups has grown 18.5x over the last six years, 45% of which was attributable to fintech.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_18.jpg
pages.abstract: African fintechs have experienced significant growth, with substantial funding and regulatory support. Despite challenges, they are poised to expand into advanced financial services, driven by digital transformation and regulatory innovations. Opportunities vary across markets, with advanced economies focusing on B2B liquidity and regulatory tech, while emerging markets innovate in insurance, banking-as-a-service, and embedded finance.
pages.title: African fintech is primed to expand into more advanced financial services

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_19.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses emerging white spaces in the market, focusing on various financial services and technologies. It highlights opportunities in account management, wallets, payments, remittances, lending, insurance, wealth management, blockchain/crypto, and operations/infrastructure. The text also notes the rapid growth of blockchain and cryptocurrency in Africa, emphasizing the potential for blockchain in enabling foreign exchange and remittance payments.
pages.title: White spaces are emerging across the market, typically in distribution, acquisition, lending, and advanced infrastructure.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_20.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses fintech penetration in African markets, highlighting that some countries exceed global benchmarks. It presents a bar chart showing revenue penetration percentages and analyzes the growth opportunities and challenges for fintech in Africa, including funding, unicorns, and market penetration compared to other regions.
pages.title: Fintech penetration in some African markets exceeds global benchmarks.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_21.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the current state of African fintech, highlighting its growth and potential. It outlines various fintech services, from basic payments to advanced lending and wealth management, emphasizing the need for consolidation and focus in the next phase of development.
pages.title: Today's players have laid the foundations and the next stage of the journey is beginning to unlock.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_22.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the low data penetration in Africa, emphasizing the importance of USSD as a payment channel. It highlights a 15% annual decrease in data costs from 2015 to 2019, suggesting potential growth in mobile payments.
pages.title: Mobile Payment in Africa

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_23.jpg
pages.abstract: African fintechs face challenges in scaling and growing, including reimagining target audiences, adapting revenue streams, and monetizing customer bases. Corporate governance issues and limited risk management capabilities are also concerns. Four key hurdles include reaching scale and profitability, navigating complex regulatory environments, building robust governance, and managing scarcity. The success of fintechs in Africa depends on adapting to unique characteristics and overcoming infrastructure and market constraints.
pages.title: 2. All things excellent are as difficult as they are rare

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_24.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the challenges faced by fintech in Africa, including low internet penetration, limited payment infrastructure, and the dominance of telcos in fintech revenues. It highlights the importance of USSD as a channel and the advantages telcos have due to high mobile phone penetration and access to customer data.
pages.title: Fintech in Africa: The end of the beginning

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_25.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the varying fintech landscapes across African regions, emphasizing the need for tailored strategies. It highlights opportunities in markets with mature banking systems and low mobile payment penetration, as well as in mobile-money specialist markets. It also addresses disruption-ready markets like Nigeria and Egypt, and the challenges in countries with high unregistered populations and limited internet penetration.
pages.title: Fintechs in Africa: Regional Discrepancies and Opportunities

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_26.jpg
pages.abstract: African markets are categorized into four archetypes based on banking, mobile money, disrupted markets, and crossroads markets. Each archetype presents unique opportunities and challenges for fintechs, with considerations for customer loyalty, monetization, and infrastructure development. Achieving scale requires addressing customer acquisition costs and adapting to regional economic conditions.
pages.title: African markets can be clustered into four discrete archetypes to achieve scale.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_27.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the complex regulatory environment for fintechs in Africa, highlighting the fragmented legislative rules and guidelines across regions. It explains the varying stages of regulatory development in 11 key African countries, focusing on aspects like open banking, cryptocurrency wealth management, and digital authentication. The page also includes an exhibit summarizing the regulatory status of these countries in various fintech-related areas.
pages.title: Navigating a complex regulatory environment

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_28.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the challenges fintechs face due to regulatory variability and the need for harmonization of licensing requirements. It highlights the impact of currency volatility and exchange controls on African businesses and the delicate balance required in managing risk exposure.
pages.title: The harmonization and streamlining of licensing requirements, potentially across borders, could go a long way toward enhancing the speed and scale of fintech growth.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_29.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the challenges African fintech startups face in securing funding, including limited exit opportunities and global funding fluctuations. It highlights the importance of targeting specific investors and understanding the venture capital ecosystem abroad. Despite some positive trends, a significant capital allocation gap between men and women persists.
pages.title: Managing scarcity

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_30.jpg
pages.abstract: African investors dominate seed funding for fintechs, while non-African investors lead later stages. Africa faces a talent shortage, with skilled workers concentrated in a few countries and many seeking opportunities abroad due to wage disparities and STEM capability gaps.
pages.title: African investors play a key role in seed funding, while late stages are led by non-African investors.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_31.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of robust corporate governance foundations for fintech businesses, emphasizing the need for a strong culture, stakeholder engagement, and talent strategy. It highlights three interrelated factors: culture and capability building, stakeholder engagement, and talent strategy & HR, which collectively support a healthy corporate governance model.
pages.title: Building robust corporate governance foundations

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_32.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of a strong business culture and robust talent strategy for fintechs. It highlights the need for clear HR processes, stakeholder engagement, and effective risk management as firms scale up. The text also emphasizes the challenges of navigating uncertain environments and the importance of learning from market leaders.
pages.title: A robust talent strategy and clear HR processes are a critical part of world-class capability building

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_33.jpg
pages.abstract: This page highlights the underpayment of Africa's talented individuals and emphasizes the need for fair compensation. It also provides a statistic that 50% of Africa's software developers are concentrated in just five countries, indicating a regional disparity in the tech industry.
pages.title: Africa's Talent and Software Developers

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_34.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the challenges and strategies for African fintechs to achieve long-term success, emphasizing the need for understanding local markets, adapting business models, and expanding offerings to meet specific financial needs.
pages.title: 3. African fintech’s winning formula for long-term success

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_35.jpg
pages.abstract: This page outlines six key characteristics of market leaders in Africa, focusing on global and African-specific strategies. It emphasizes matching value propositions, acquiring users quickly, clear monetization strategies, managing revenue expectations, understanding local needs, and aligning with regulators. Examples include M-Pesa, Tala, and FairMoney, showcasing successful fintech models in Africa.
pages.title: Market leaders share six characteristics.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_36.jpg
pages.abstract: Fintechs evolve through unique distribution, local consumer/MSME markets, and payment infrastructure strategies. They start with non-financial products, grow user bases, add financial services, and build ecosystems. Infrastructure-focused fintechs like Interswitch and Flutterwave address specific needs, leading to mobile money growth and digital wallet innovation in Africa.
pages.title: Fintechs have typically evolved through 3 different scenarios.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_37.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the challenges faced by fintechs in Africa, particularly in mobile money services, due to established telcos. It highlights the growth opportunities in lending and saving services, noting the low credit penetration in Africa compared to global standards. The text also explains how fintechs are leveraging alternative data to offer credit services, contrasting with traditional banking models.
pages.title: Fintech in Africa: The end of the beginning

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_38.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how large African fintechs have entered the payments market by addressing infrastructure needs in their home markets. It highlights the timeline of market-entry services and additional services offered by various fintechs in different African countries. The page also emphasizes the importance of acquiring a large base of active users quickly, despite infrastructure and purchasing power challenges. Examples like OPay and PalmPay illustrate strategies for overcoming these obstacles.
pages.title: Large African fintechs have entered the payments market by solving infrastructure needs across their home market.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_39.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of clear monetization strategies for fintechs in Africa. It highlights the use of aggressive pricing strategies for customer acquisition and the need for diversification to ensure long-term sustainability. It also compares B2C and B2B fintech models, emphasizing the better unit economics of B2B players.
pages.title: Have clear monetization strategies that are rolled out effectively

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_40.jpg
pages.abstract: Leading B2B players are exploring B2C services to boost revenues. In Africa, low personal consumption expenditure limits revenue potential, prompting fintechs to adjust strategies. Innovations include cloud-based technologies, alternative data sources, and pay-as-you-go models to reduce costs and serve customers effectively.
pages.title: 4. Manage lower expected revenue per customer

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_41.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses strategies for fintechs to address Africa's offline market, highlighting the use of pre-existing infrastructure, mobile networks, and agent networks to increase financial access. Examples include TymeBank's partnership with retail stores and the extensive agent networks in Nigeria and Kenya.
pages.title: 5. Understand and address Africa’s offline market

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_42.jpg
pages.abstract: This section discusses the importance of fintechs engaging with regulators and governments to achieve sustainable growth and support national economic development. It highlights successful partnerships, such as Fawry in Egypt and Safaricom in Kenya, and warns of the risks of neglecting regulatory alignment, exemplified by Dash's shutdown in Ghana.
pages.title: 6. Actively engage, align with, and work with regulators

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_43.jpg
pages.title: Fintech Eruption in Africa

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_44.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the growth of Africa's fintech sector, emphasizing the roles of regulators and fintechs in promoting predictability, flexibility, and scalability. It highlights the importance of partnerships between fintechs and incumbents, focusing on talent development and regulatory alignment to drive long-term success and economic growth.
pages.title: 4. Let there be digital: Building Africa’s fintech future

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_45.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of reducing costs and increasing access in financial services, highlighting the roles of incumbents and fintechs in reaching underserved populations. It emphasizes the vital role of investors in identifying growth opportunities, focusing on value over valuation, and supporting sustainable investments. The page concludes with a positive outlook on Africa's fintech industry, noting its strong foundations and future potential despite challenges.
pages.title: Investors: A focus on value over valuation

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_46.jpg
pages.title: About the authors

pages.page_path: library_pages\Fintech in Africa_ The end of the beginning_McKinsey_2022_08_01\page_47.jpg

This page discusses the growth of Africa's fintech sector, emphasizing the roles of regulators and fintechs in promoting predictability, flexibility, and scalability. This page discusses the importance of reducing costs and increasing access in financial services, highlighting the roles of incumbents and fintechs in reaching underserved populations. pages.abstract: This page discusses the increasing influence of Asian and Pacific Islanders in the film and television industry, highlighting their achievements and the need for more authentic representation. pages.title: Introduction

pages.page_path: library_pages\From margins to mainstream_ Asians and Pacific Islanders in media_McKinsey_2024_04_01\page_5.jpg
pages.abstract: This chapter examines the evolution of API representation in media, highlighting the progress and persistent stereotypes. It discusses historical casting practices, breakthroughs like Bruce Lee and The Joy Luck Club, and the ongoing challenges in authentic representation.
pages.title: The evolution of API representation in media

pages.page_path: library_pages\From margins to mainstream_ Asians and Pacific Islanders in media_McKinsey_2024_04_01\page_6.jpg
pages.abstract: Despite recent progress in media representation, less than 30% of API consumers feel authentically represented in US-produced media. The survey highlights dissatisfaction across subgroups, with East Asians, Southeast Asians, and Pasifika respondents showing more negative perceptions. There is an opportunity to shift neutral respondents to positive perceptions.
pages.title: API consumers don’t perceive their portrayals in media as authentic

pages.page_path: library_pages\From margins to mainstream_ Asians and Pacific Islanders in media_McKinsey_2024_04_01\page_7.jpg
pages.abstract: This page defines key terminologies related to Asian and Pacific Islander (API) populations, including AANHPI, APAC, and various ethnic subgroups. It also outlines roles in media production and discusses the underrepresentation of API experiences in US media, setting the stage for further analysis.
pages.title: Terminology

pages.page_path: library_pages\From margins to mainstream_ Asians and Pacific Islanders in media_McKinsey_2024_04_01\page_8.jpg
pages.abstract: This chapter examines API representation in film and television, highlighting that while overall numbers appear strong due to content from outside the US, API actors are underrepresented in US productions. The increase in API representation is largely driven by films from the Asia-Pacific region, with API actors concentrated in certain genres. The chapter also discusses the mutual reinforcement between off-screen talent and on-screen representation.
pages.title: Examining API representation in film and television

pages.page_path: library_pages\From margins to mainstream_ Asians and Pacific Islanders in media_McKinsey_2024_04_01\page_9.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the increased representation of API actors in films, particularly those produced outside the US, and the impact on box office revenues. It highlights the difference in reception between US and non-US produced content with API leads, noting that non-US films with API leads account for 1.6% of US box office receipts, while US-produced films with API leads account for 7.8%. The page also includes a graph showing the trend of API representation in US-distributed films from 2002 to 2022.
pages.title: API on-screen representation in film has increased, propelled by films produced outside the United States.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From margins to mainstream_ Asians and Pacific Islanders in media_McKinsey_2024_04_01\page_10.jpg
pages.abstract: Streaming services have expanded programming and democratized content access, increasing API representation. API actors are underrepresented in US films but find success on social media platforms like YouTube, where they resonate with young Asian Americans.
pages.title: Streaming and API inclusion

pages.page_path: library_pages\From margins to mainstream_ Asians and Pacific Islanders in media_McKinsey_2024_04_01\page_11.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the challenges faced by API content in film and television, focusing on the types of roles API actors play and the impact on consumer perception. It highlights that API actors account for about 3% of lead and supporting roles in US films, with a significant portion of films featuring API leads being race-agnostic. The analysis categorizes films based on race-specific storytelling and provides data on the release patterns of these films.
pages.title: API content faces genre challenges in both film and television

pages.page_path: library_pages\From margins to mainstream_ Asians and Pacific Islanders in media_McKinsey_2024_04_01\page_12.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the underrepresentation of API stories in major film releases, noting that most films with wide theatrical releases are race-agnostic. It highlights that API films are more likely to be action and adventure genres compared to films without API leads. This trend contrasts with Black films, which are more likely to be race-specific. The analysis suggests that the low share of race-specific API stories may contribute to a low perception of authenticity among API consumers.
pages.title: Almost half of wide-release films with API leads are action and adventure films, compared to 30 percent of films without API leads.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From margins to mainstream_ Asians and Pacific Islanders in media_McKinsey_2024_04_01\page_13.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the representation of API actors in films and TV, highlighting the concentration of API stories in limited theatrical releases and the need for specificity in portrayal. It also analyzes the genre distribution of TV episodes with API leads, showing a higher percentage of animated shows compared to other races.
pages.title: API representation in films and TV

pages.page_path: library_pages\From margins to mainstream_ Asians and Pacific Islanders in media_McKinsey_2024_04_01\page_14.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the imbalance in representation of API subgroups in US-produced films, highlighting the disproportionate casting of East Asian actors and the lack of female and nonbinary leads among Pasifika actors. It also explores the mutual reinforcement between off-screen talent and on-screen representation in the entertainment industry.
pages.title: An imbalance across API subgroups

pages.page_path: library_pages\From margins to mainstream_ Asians and Pacific Islanders in media_McKinsey_2024_04_01\page_15.jpg
pages.abstract: The presence of API talent in key off-screen roles correlates with higher on-screen API representation. Films and TV shows with API off-screen professionals are more likely to feature API leads. Directors and writers have a stronger influence on API representation compared to producers. Showrunners and producers in TV have significant impact on API representation over seasons.
pages.title: The presence of API talent in key off-screen roles is consistent with higher on-screen API representation.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From margins to mainstream_ Asians and Pacific Islanders in media_McKinsey_2024_04_01\page_16.jpg
pages.abstract: The document highlights the underrepresentation of API talent in key off-screen roles in both film and television from 2018 to 2022. It provides data on API representation in US-distributed films and TV episodes, showing lower percentages for US-produced content compared to non-US-produced content. The text emphasizes the importance of understanding career barriers for API professionals and the role of successful creators in attracting investment.
pages.title: API talent is underrepresented in key off-screen roles in both film and television.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From margins to mainstream_ Asians and Pacific Islanders in media_McKinsey_2024_04_01\page_17.jpg
pages.abstract: This chapter discusses the spending habits of Asian American consumers, highlighting their higher income but lower spending on film and television compared to other racial groups. It attributes this disparity partly to perceived inauthenticity in media representation. The analysis also shows that Asian Americans allocate a smaller percentage of their income to cable, satellite, and streaming services compared to White and Black consumers.
pages.title: A multibillion-dollar opportunity for the industry and ideas for API representation

pages.page_path: library_pages\From margins to mainstream_ Asians and Pacific Islanders in media_McKinsey_2024_04_01\page_18.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses API consumers' willingness to spend more on authentic media representation, highlighting that nearly half of respondents would increase spending if their experiences were more accurately portrayed. Younger age groups show a stronger inclination towards this behavior.
pages.title: Exhibit 10: Nearly half of API consumers would spend more money or time on more API-authentic film and TV, especially those in younger age brackets.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From margins to mainstream_ Asians and Pacific Islanders in media_McKinsey_2024_04_01\page_19.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses methods to estimate the revenue opportunity for the industry by increasing API representation and authenticity in film and TV. It includes survey results and industry insights, highlighting a $2 to $4 billion annual opportunity. The page also features a visual representation of the estimated opportunity per year.
pages.title: Estimating the opportunity for the industry

pages.page_path: library_pages\From margins to mainstream_ Asians and Pacific Islanders in media_McKinsey_2024_04_01\page_20.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the potential economic benefits of increasing authentic API representation in media, highlighting consumer willingness to spend more on authentic content and the broader market opportunities for studios and streaming services. It emphasizes the importance of authenticity and quality in engaging API audiences.
pages.title: Value of Authentic API Content in Media

pages.page_path: library_pages\From margins to mainstream_ Asians and Pacific Islanders in media_McKinsey_2024_04_01\page_21.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the potential for the film and television industry to unlock a multibillion-dollar opportunity by improving Asian and Pacific Islander (API) representation. It highlights demographic trends, challenges, and external hurdles, and suggests increasing the likelihood of API projects being approved and distributed by promoting API representation in leadership roles and establishing funds for API stories.
pages.title: Five potential ideas could help the industry to unlock the multibillion-dollar opportunity

pages.page_path: library_pages\From margins to mainstream_ Asians and Pacific Islanders in media_McKinsey_2024_04_01\page_22.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses increasing financial support for API projects, investing in API off-screen talent, and expanding evaluation criteria for API projects. It highlights the need for specialized resources, visibility into API content performance, and opportunities for API professionals in creative roles. It also emphasizes the potential of API content in international markets.
pages.title: Increase financial support for API projects and creators

pages.page_path: library_pages\From margins to mainstream_ Asians and Pacific Islanders in media_McKinsey_2024_04_01\page_23.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of understanding and improving API representation in the film and television industry. It highlights the need for tracking data, identifying trends, and recognizing the diversity within the API community. The text emphasizes the potential financial benefits of better representation and the need for decision-makers to allocate resources accordingly.
pages.title: Continue to understand the state of API representation

pages.page_path: library_pages\From margins to mainstream_ Asians and Pacific Islanders in media_McKinsey_2024_04_01\page_24.jpg
pages.abstract: This appendix details the methodology used to collect and analyze data for a report on film and TV representation. It includes data sources, film and TV data selection criteria, and on-screen/off-screen talent representation analysis.
pages.title: Appendix: Methodology

pages.page_path: library_pages\From margins to mainstream_ Asians and Pacific Islanders in media_McKinsey_2024_04_01\page_25.jpg
pages.abstract: This report details the data sources and methodologies used, including film and TV datasets, interviews, focus groups, and surveys, to analyze representation of API individuals in the entertainment industry.
pages.title: Data used in this report

This page discusses the potential economic benefits of increasing authentic API representation in media, highlighting consumer willingness to spend more on authentic content and the broader market opportunities for studios and streaming services. It emphasizes the importance of authenticity and quality in engaging API audiences.
The document discusses the potential for the film and television industry to unlock a multibillion-dollar opportunity by improving Asian and Pacific Islander (API) representation. It highlights demographic trends, challenges, and external hurdles, and suggests increasing the likelihood of API projects being approved and distributed by promoting API representation in leadership roles and establishing funds for API stories.
This page discusses increasing financial support for API projects, investing in API off-screen talent, and expanding evaluation criteria for API projects. It highlights the need for specialized resources, visibility into API content performance, and opportunities for API professionals in creative roles. It also emphasizes the potential of API content in international markets.
This page discusses the importance of understanding and improving API representation in the film and television industry. It highlights the need for tracking data, identifying trends, and recognizing the diversity within the API community. The text emphasizes the potential financial benefits of better representation and the need for decision-makers to allocate resources accordingly.
This appendix details the methodology used to collect and analyze data for a report on film and TV representation. It includes data sources, film and TV data selection criteria, and on-screen/off-screen talent representation analysis.
This report details the data sources and methodologies used, including film and TV datasets, interviews, focus groups, and surveys, to analyze representation of API individuals in the entertainment industry.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_7.jpg
pages.abstract: This research explores the interconnectedness of growth, inclusion, and sustainability, emphasizing the need for economic empowerment and net-zero commitments. It highlights the challenges and tensions between improving living standards and addressing climate change, quantifying the investment gaps and potential solutions through growth and innovation.
pages.title: Key findings

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_8.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the substantial gaps in achieving net-zero spending and the hard choices needed to address them. It highlights the potential of growth and innovation, the risks and benefits of additional societal commitments, and the importance of empowering large populations while pursuing net-zero goals. It emphasizes the need for global collaboration, innovation, and financing to achieve sustainable and inclusive growth.
pages.title: From poverty to empowerment: Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_9.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the financial requirements to achieve minimum living standards and net-zero emissions by 2030, highlighting the need for growth, innovation, and societal commitments. It presents a visual breakdown of the $37 trillion empowerment gap and the $41 trillion net-zero investment gap, along with potential sources to fill these gaps.
pages.title: What would it take for the world to raise everyone to minimum living standards while also getting on a net-zero pathway by 2030?

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_10.jpg
pages.title: Child holding a young plant

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_11.jpg
pages.abstract: This research explores the interconnectedness of growth, inclusion, and sustainability, focusing on global aspirations like the Paris Agreement and SDGs. It examines the economic empowerment needed to meet essential needs by 2030 and the net-zero transition, considering the trade-offs and challenges. The study sizes the empowerment and net-zero gaps and explores scenarios to close them, emphasizing the urgency of addressing both poverty and climate change.
pages.title: Executive summary

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_12.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the essential role of growth and innovation in achieving bold goals, focusing on potential linkages over the next decade. It highlights the impact of growth on economic inclusion and net-zero transition, emphasizing the need for 8% of global GDP annually. The page explores how market forces can contribute to closing economic gaps and the choices societies face in addressing these challenges.
pages.title: Growth and innovation are essential to making progress toward bold goals.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_13.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of economic empowerment in raising living standards, highlighting the need for a complementary benchmark beyond the extreme poverty line. It explains the concept of economic empowerment, its benefits, and the quantification of a higher bar for sustainable and inclusive growth.
pages.title: Economic empowerment raises living standards

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_14.jpg
pages.abstract: The empowerment line defines the threshold where individuals meet essential needs and achieve security. It considers local costs of food, housing, healthcare, and other components. Empowerment thresholds vary globally, ranging from $3 to $50 per capita per day, reflecting purchasing power and local norms. Establishing these thresholds helps measure and address empowerment gaps.
pages.title: The empowerment line is the point at which individuals can meet their essential needs and begin to achieve security.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_15.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses various approaches to measuring economic inclusion and poverty, emphasizing the importance of metrics. It explores monetary and nonmonetary measures, including the World Bank's global extreme poverty line and the concept of economic empowerment. The text also highlights the debate around defining a global middle class and the need for a common definition of basic needs and security worldwide.
pages.title: Measuring economic inclusion

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_16.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how the means to achieve sufficiency in basic needs vary by stage of development, using illustrative examples of daily spending patterns. It highlights the concept of empowerment and its relation to the 'living wage' and economic inclusion, emphasizing the importance of addressing inequality and redistribution.
pages.title: The means required to achieve sufficiency in basic needs vary by stage of development.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_17.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the challenges of economic empowerment globally, highlighting that 4.7 billion people live below the empowerment line. It emphasizes the need for logistical and operational improvements in social benefit programs. The data shows regional disparities in empowerment levels, with Sub-Saharan Africa and India having the highest percentages of populations below the empowerment line.
pages.title: Worldwide, 4.7 billion people live below the empowerment line, with poverty levels that vary across regions.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_18.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the challenges faced by people below the empowerment line, particularly in major cities, where high housing costs impact other priorities. It highlights the global distribution of this population, the implications for education and employment, and the economic impact of achieving universal empowerment by 2030, emphasizing the need to address the empowerment gap.
pages.title: For many people below the empowerment line, especially in the world’s major cities, the high cost of housing eats into other priorities.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_19.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the net-zero investment gap, the incremental low-emissions spending needed by 2030 to change the climate trajectory. It highlights the importance of empowerment in creating a virtuous cycle for sustainable growth. The research quantifies the spending needed based on scenarios from the Network for Greening the Financial System, focusing on power and mobility sectors. It also explains the methodology used to measure the net-zero investment need, including the NGFS scenarios and the McKinsey Transition Finance Model.
pages.title: The net-zero investment gap is the incremental low-emissions spending needed by 2030 to change the climate trajectory

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_20.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the net-zero investment needs across seven major energy and land-use sectors, highlighting a $55 trillion total low-emissions spending need and a $41 trillion net-zero investment gap. It details spending requirements for sectors like power, mobility, buildings, agriculture, forestry, hydrogen, and industry, emphasizing the need for significant investment scaling to achieve net-zero goals.
pages.title: The net-zero investment need in this decade differs across seven major energy and land-use sectors.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_21.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the interplay between empowerment and the net-zero transition, highlighting how higher economic growth and empowerment can increase demand for energy-intensive products, leading to higher emissions. It also addresses the need for policy mechanisms like carbon taxes and subsidies to manage these tensions and protect low-income households during the transition.
pages.title: Empowerment and the net-zero transition affect each other—and some tensions would need to be managed

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_22.jpg
pages.abstract: The net-zero transition's impact on jobs varies globally, with potential job gains in construction and manufacturing. Managing the transition effectively is crucial for supporting affected regions and sectors. Empowerment and net-zero investment gaps differ significantly across regions, with high-income areas facing smaller gaps compared to developing regions. Developing regions face challenges in balancing fossil fuel replacement with energy access needs.
pages.title: The gaps vary widely across regions

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_23.jpg
pages.abstract: This page details the empowerment gap across various regions, showing that lower-income regions have a larger share of the $37 trillion gap. It includes data on the share of the global empowerment gap, annualized GDP equivalent, and the empowerment gap as a share of continued 2020 spending for populations below the empowerment line. The data highlights disparities and the financial needs for achieving empowerment goals by 2030.
pages.title: Lower-income regions generally have larger shares of the $37 trillion empowerment gap.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_24.jpg
pages.abstract: This page details the net-zero investment gaps by region, highlighting the unique share each region has in the $41 trillion net-zero investment gap. It includes a table showing the share of the global net-zero investment gap, the annualized percentage of GDP equivalent, and the increase over 2020 levels of low-emissions spend for various regions. The page also discusses how growth and business-led innovation could drive economic empowerment.
pages.title: Each region has a unique share of the $41 trillion net-zero investment gap.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_25.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how businesses can improve productivity and accelerate global growth, leading to empowerment and poverty reduction. It highlights the importance of upskilling workers, leveraging technology, and creating more productive jobs. The text emphasizes the role of businesses in facilitating skill-building and transitions to better-paying occupations, ultimately aiming to close the global empowerment gap and transform lives on a massive scale.
pages.title: From poverty to empowerment: Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_26.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the potential for unlocking $15 trillion in low-emissions spending through economic growth and innovation, focusing on sub-Saharan Africa's poverty challenges and opportunities in power and mobility sectors in major economies. It highlights the role of private investment and technological advancements in making low-emissions alternatives cost-competitive.
pages.title: Some $15 trillion of new low-emissions spending could be unlocked this decade through growth and innovation

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_27.jpg
pages.abstract: Market forces and current policies could close roughly half of the combined empowerment and net-zero investment gaps. Inclusion and sustainability gaps could be partially addressed through rising incomes, productivity growth, and tech advancements, leaving an unfilled economic gap of ~1% and ~3% of GDP equivalent, respectively.
pages.title: The extent to which growth, innovation, and continued current policies could close the combined gaps varies by region

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_28.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how growth and business-led innovation can reduce the empowerment gap globally, with varying impacts across regions. By 2030, these forces could fill 55-85% of the gap in high-income regions, with the greatest potential in India and China. However, their impact may be lower in other developing countries. The page also highlights the potential of growth and innovation to address the net-zero investment gap, with a focus on regional variations and the need for continued current policies.
pages.title: The portion of the economic gaps that can be filled by growth and business-led innovation varies by region.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_29.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the global unfilled economic gaps in empowerment and net-zero investments, totaling $40 trillion. Sub-Saharan Africa has the highest unfilled gap, followed by the US and China. The regional breakdown shows significant disparities, with developing countries accounting for nearly two-thirds of the residual gap. The analysis is based on specific spending levels and investment scenarios, excluding high-emissions spending.
pages.title: The residual gaps raise fundamental questions

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_30.jpg
pages.abstract: The report discusses Africa's empowerment opportunity, emphasizing the need for growth, innovation, and public-private action. It highlights the continent's diversity and the varying levels of empowerment across countries. With accelerated growth, 770 million people could surpass the 50% empowerment line by 2030, reducing extreme poverty. Strategies like digitization and regional collaboration can drive progress.
pages.title: The empowerment opportunity for Africa

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_31.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the potential for growth and innovation to reduce poverty and empower Africa's population. It presents data on population spending levels and explores different scenarios for achieving empowerment and addressing climate change, emphasizing the trade-offs between economic growth and environmental sustainability.
pages.title: The empowerment opportunity for Africa

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_32.jpg
pages.abstract: This page presents scenarios analyzing the impact of commitments beyond growth and innovation on addressing economic and net-zero investment gaps. It outlines three scenarios (A, B, and C) with varying levels of societal commitment, detailing outcomes such as population empowerment, warming levels, and financial commitments. The scenarios highlight the potential for public commitments to spur private investment but also caution against potential economic distortions.
pages.title: Scenarios show a range of outcomes that depend on commitments to go beyond what growth and innovation can do.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_33.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how societies can close the $13 trillion economic gap for universal empowerment by delivering essential goods and services more affordably, improving work arrangements, and providing more direct support. It presents a scenario for closing the empowerment gap, highlighting the need for increased societal commitments and affordable essentials.
pages.title: How could societies get closer to full empowerment beyond what current market forces can do?

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_34.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses strategies to reduce the price of essential goods and services, improve productivity in housing, healthcare, education, and nutrition, and enhance well-being and human potential. It highlights the potential benefits of improved construction productivity, health outcomes, and learning outcomes. The text also explores policies and incentives for affordable housing, labor-friendly measures, and targeted transfers to households, emphasizing the role of digital tools and international aid in achieving full empowerment.
pages.title: From poverty to empowerment: Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_35.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the residual net-zero investment gap of $26 trillion and the need for combined public-private efforts to address it. It highlights the potential impact of an additional $10 trillion in public funding, which could unlock $17 trillion in positive impact by 2030. The page also explores the role of public support in sectors like building and mobility, and the potential for private investment to contribute significantly to net-zero goals.
pages.title: Question 2: What would it take to get on a true net-zero trajectory beyond what current market forces can do?

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_36.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the scenario for closing the net-zero investment gap, emphasizing the role of public and private commitments. It includes a detailed breakdown of investment needs and potential contributions from various actors, highlighting the importance of growth, innovation, and societal shifts. The page also poses a question about societal capacity and willingness for higher commitments and explores potential solutions.
pages.title: Fully closing the net-zero investment gap relies on the assumption that higher public commitments can activate more private capital.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_37.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the challenges and trade-offs in achieving net-zero emissions and full empowerment, particularly for lower- and middle-income countries. It highlights the importance of productivity-driven growth for closing the empowerment gap and providing fiscal flexibility. The text also addresses the need for global cooperation and innovative financial mechanisms to support sustainable and inclusive growth.
pages.title: We are reaching a fork in the road

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_38.jpg
pages.abstract: Higher growth and innovation can lift 600 million people out of poverty by enhancing productivity, skill development, and technological advancements. This requires institutional reforms, new collaborations, and innovation at scale to address climate change and improve living standards. Innovation can drive down costs, create better jobs, and boost efficiency in various sectors.
pages.title: Higher growth and innovation could bring 600 million more people out of poverty, taking steps on a longer journey toward empowerment.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_39.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the challenges and opportunities in achieving empowerment and net zero, emphasizing the need for collaboration among various stakeholders. It highlights the complexity of financing, consensus-building, and implementation, calling for increased public-private cooperation. The page also includes a note on data sources used in the research, acknowledging contributions from McKinsey and the International Energy Agency.
pages.title: Empowerment and Net Zero Progress

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_40.jpg
pages.title: Family Cooking Moment

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_41.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the significant progress in reducing extreme poverty globally, highlighting achievements in human development outcomes such as reduced child mortality and increased access to education. However, it also addresses the persistent challenges of poverty, especially in developing countries, and the difficulties faced by those just above the poverty line in securing economic stability.
pages.title: 1. Economic empowerment: Higher minimum living standards for everyone

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_42.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the concept of universal empowerment as a higher standard for living, ensuring people can meet essential needs and have some economic security. It explains how empowerment lines are estimated for different countries, ranging from $3 to $50 per capita per day in 2020 US dollars, and highlights the benefits of empowerment in improving quality of life and fueling market growth.
pages.title: Universal empowerment lifts everyone to economic sufficiency

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_43.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the empowerment line, which is the point where individuals meet essential needs and achieve security. It includes a diagram illustrating components of empowerment and characteristics of security and sufficiency. The text provides data on consumption levels needed in various countries and explains the methodology behind these figures, referencing research on global middle-class consumption.
pages.title: The empowerment line is the point at which individuals can meet their essential needs and begin to achieve security.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_44.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how the means to achieve basic needs sufficiency vary by development stage, using detailed cost-of-living data. It includes an illustrative example of daily spending patterns across different income levels, highlighting disparities in spending on food, housing, health, education, and transportation. The data emphasizes the need for adjustments in higher-income countries and acknowledges within-country variations.
pages.title: The means required to achieve sufficiency in basic needs vary by stage of development.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_45.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the calibration of empowerment lines using consumption-based metrics, accounting for taxes, transfers, and public services. It highlights the rise of empowerment thresholds with income levels and the economic insecurity in both wealthy and developing countries. It emphasizes the importance of program design and execution for social benefit programs and defines empowerment as the point where people can make discretionary choices, reflecting well-being and individual agency.
pages.title: Empowerment thresholds and economic insecurity

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_46.jpg
pages.abstract: This page presents two graphs showing the empowerment line across countries, with the first graph using 2017 PPP and the second using 2020 dollars. The empowerment line starts at a global floor of $12 in 2017 PPP and rises across countries, reflecting higher costs and different contexts. The EU floor is set at $32. The graphs illustrate the relationship between GDP per capita and the empowerment line for various countries, categorized by World Bank income levels.
pages.title: The empowerment line starts with a global floor, then rises across countries to reflect higher costs and different contexts.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_47.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the global population living below the empowerment line, highlighting that 4.7 billion people face varying levels of poverty. It details the experiences of the poorest segments, those lacking basic needs, and those closer to the empowerment line but still vulnerable. A chart breaks down the population by spending level and region, showing the highest percentages in Sub-Saharan Africa and India.
pages.title: Worldwide, 4.7 billion people live below the empowerment line, with poverty levels that vary across regions.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_48.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the challenges faced by people living below the empowerment line, including housing, healthcare, and education. It highlights the global empowerment gap of $37 trillion by 2030 and emphasizes the need for full economic empowerment to improve living conditions and opportunities.
pages.title: We calculate the global empowerment gap at $37 trillion, cumulative through 2030

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_49.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the global empowerment gap, estimating it at over $37 trillion over a decade. It analyzes spending levels needed to empower households by 2030, varying by region. High-income regions have smaller gaps compared to developing regions like sub-Saharan Africa. The analysis assumes gradual spending increases for those below the empowerment line.
pages.title: If every household were fully empowered to meet all basic needs by 2030, the generation coming into adulthood by midcentury would be healthier, more educated, and equipped to realize more of their potential.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_50.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses empowerment gaps globally, highlighting that Sub-Saharan Africa and India have the largest gaps. It emphasizes the societal and individual benefits of closing these gaps, such as improved human development outcomes and increased life satisfaction. Achieving full empowerment by 2030 could lead to healthier, more educated, and globally connected children, setting the stage for a more prosperous future.
pages.title: Whether measured in absolute dollar terms or relative to GDP, the empowerment gaps are largest in sub-Saharan Africa and India.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_51.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of empowerment for sustainable growth, emphasizing the need for educated and empowered adults to achieve broad-based prosperity. It highlights the risks of inaction, such as societal instability due to poverty and hunger, and the urgency of prioritizing empowerment alongside sustainability. The text also links empowerment to economic growth and sustainability, stressing the need for investment and spending to reach net-zero emissions.
pages.title: The importance of empowerment for sustainable growth

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_52.jpg
pages.title: 太阳能果园管理

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_53.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the urgent need for net-zero investment to combat climate change. It highlights the necessity of transforming energy and land-use systems, requiring a massive capital infusion of $55 trillion over the decade. This investment, equivalent to 4% of global GDP annually, will fund renewable power, low-emissions energy sources, and electric vehicles. The page also references scientific studies and reports to support the urgency of this transition.
pages.title: 2. The net-zero investment need

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_54.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the necessary $41 trillion investment in low-emissions assets by 2030 to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050. It highlights the challenges and uncertainties in estimating such investments, including factors like warming pathways, technology costs, and input material availability. The page also outlines the current spending on low-emissions assets and the need for significant growth in clean energy investment. It provides a detailed breakdown of the types of low-emissions assets and enabling infrastructure required for the transition.
pages.title: A net-zero trajectory requires a $41 trillion step-up in low-emissions investment, cumulative through 2030

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_55.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the scale of investment needed to achieve net-zero emissions by 2030 and the implications of accelerated economic growth on investment needs. It highlights the net-zero investment gap and the transformation required in energy and land-use systems to reach net zero by 2050.
pages.title: This is a decisive decade for altering the world’s emissions trajectory.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_56.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the net-zero investment gap, defined as the incremental low-emissions spending needed for global energy and land-use systems. It presents a chart showing high- and low-emissions spending needed to achieve a 2050 net-zero pathway. The net-zero spending need varies across sectors, with mobility accounting for over one-third of the gap. The focus is on reducing emissions from road mobility through electric vehicles and building charging infrastructure.
pages.title: Exhibit 6: Net-zero investment gap and spending needs

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_57.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the global low-emissions spending need and net-zero investment gap across seven major energy and land-use sectors from 2021 to 2030. It highlights the significant investment requirements in power, mobility, buildings, agriculture, forestry, hydrogen, and industry. The page emphasizes the need for a substantial step-up in low-emissions spending, particularly in mobility and power sectors, to achieve net-zero goals.
pages.title: The net-zero investment need in this decade differs across seven major energy and land-use sectors.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_58.jpg
pages.abstract: The document outlines three key categories for achieving net-zero emissions: physical building blocks, economic and societal adjustments, and governance, institutions, and commitment. It emphasizes the need for innovation, resource management, capital reallocation, and policy development to support a successful transition.
pages.title: Requirements to reach net-zero emissions

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_59.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the varying net-zero investment gaps across regions and sectors, emphasizing the unique footprints of sectors like mobility and power. It highlights the need for region-specific investment strategies and provides a detailed breakdown of investment gaps by region and sector, showing mobility and power as significant contributors.
pages.title: The size of the gap that would need to be bridged to get on a net-zero pathway varies by region

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_60.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the need to view each region's net-zero investment gap in both absolute and relative terms, highlighting disparities in mobility, power, and agriculture investments across high-income and developing economies. It emphasizes the varying scales of investment required for electrification and renewable energy growth, with specific examples from the United States, India, and sub-Saharan Africa.
pages.title: Each region’s net-zero investment gap needs to be viewed not only in absolute terms but also in relative terms.

pages.page_path: library_pages\From poverty to empowerment_ Raising the bar for sustainable and inclusive growth_McKinsey_2023_09_01\page_61.jpg
