It highlights significant variability in these metrics, with notable differences in transfer rates, Pell-eligible student shares, and completion rate gaps between Q4 and Q1 quartiles. The data underscores disparities among different types of associate colleges and special-focus institutions.
This page discusses strategies for improving graduation rates and expanding access in higher education. It highlights the importance of prioritizing completion strategies for existing students and the potential benefits of increasing completion rates by one percentage point annually. The page also addresses the need to expand enrollment and the Pell Grant-eligible student population for institutions with high completion rates.
This page presents data on the distribution of two- and four-year educational institution capacities based on Pell-eligible student share and completion rates. It highlights that only 11% of available capacity is at institutions with above-average completion rates and high Pell-eligible student shares. The data is visualized through graphs for 4- and 2-year institutions, showing the proportions of high and low Pell-eligible students with corresponding completion rates.
This page discusses the challenges and costs associated with increasing college access and completion, emphasizing the need for bold investments and interventions. It highlights the importance of addressing affordability, financial resources, mindset, preparedness, and support services. Examples of successful interventions include small grants and discounted transportation passes, which have shown positive impacts on student retention and graduation rates.
This page discusses the investment and returns of adding ten million more graduates by 2042, highlighting the significant costs and potential benefits. It details the average costs for different educational levels and the impact on lifetime earnings, emphasizing the need for additional support and initiatives for adult learners.
This page discusses initiatives for affordable education and student success, emphasizing the importance of mental health services, childcare, and cultural events. It highlights the need to consider additional costs like opportunity costs and student loan debt. The text also covers information accessibility, career resources, and the role of mindset and preparedness in student outcomes.
This page discusses support services and networks for students, emphasizing the importance of academic, family, and social support systems. It highlights successful programs like CUNY ASAP and C2C, which have significantly improved graduation rates. The page also outlines key actions to begin, including prioritizing adult learners, filling excess capacity in schools, and deploying data-driven interventions to enhance access and completion rates.
This page discusses strategies to improve higher education completion rates, including counseling students toward high-employment pathways, exploring cost efficiency and new financing models, and implementing sectorwide actions for greater transparency and support. It emphasizes the need for immediate action to address skilled job shortages, civic engagement, and economic growth.

It also addresses the potential labor shortages and the challenges faced by employers in a tighter labor market.

It highlights the decline in food services, customer service, office support, and production roles, while growth is observed in health, business, STEM, and education sectors. The data also reveals the impact of COVID-19 on certain occupations and the educational background of workers in various fields.

pages.abstract: The US labor market has recovered strongly post-COVID-19, with a significant wave of job switching. About 48 million people quit their jobs in 2021 and 51 million in 2022. Many sought better pay or alignment with priorities. The pandemic altered employment mix, favoring remote-capable roles like managerial and STEM jobs, while e-commerce boosted warehousing jobs. These trends are expected to continue.
pages.title: A robust recovery marked by job switching and labor shortages

pages.page_path: library_pages\Generative AI and the future of work in America_McKinsey_2023_07_01\page_24.jpg
pages.abstract: The document details employment changes across various occupational categories from 2019 to 2022, highlighting that customer-facing jobs suffered the most during the pandemic. Business, transportation, and STEM roles showed resilience. Food services and customer service roles declined significantly, while healthcare employment saw a nuanced recovery. Automation and consumer preference shifts contributed to these trends.
pages.title: Employment change by occupational category, 2019–22

pages.page_path: library_pages\Generative AI and the future of work in America_McKinsey_2023_07_01\page_25.jpg
pages.abstract: The United States experienced a labor shortage in the economic recovery, with total employment exceeding pre-pandemic levels but labor force participation lagging. The shortage disproportionately affected workers without college degrees and people of color. Despite white-collar layoffs, the job market remained robust, especially for blue-collar workers. Factors contributing to the shortage include retirement, early exits from the workforce, and workers quitting without new jobs lined up.
pages.title: In the economic recovery, the United States developed a labor shortage

pages.abstract: The net-zero transition could reallocate a substantial number of American jobs, with an estimated net gain of 700,000 jobs by 2030. Job growth is expected in renewable energy sectors, while carbon-intensive industries may see job reductions. Training and retraining will be crucial to ensure a smooth transition and address geographic mismatches.
pages.title: The net-zero transition could reallocate a substantial number of American jobs.

The McKinsey Global Institute (MGI) provides fact-based research on critical economic and business issues, focusing on productivity, resources, human potential, global connections, and future technologies. It operates independently, funded by McKinsey partners, and shares results publicly. The McKinsey Center for Government (MCG) supports government leaders in delivering better outcomes through an independent and analytical approach.
The US labor market experienced significant shifts during the pandemic, with automation and structural changes expected to alter job categories by 2030. Federal investments in climate and infrastructure will shift employment, while workforce development and hiring strategies need to adapt to evolving needs.
The document projects 12 million occupational transitions by 2030, categorizing job growth into resilient, stalled, and declining occupations. Resilient occupations, driven by healthcare, technology, and infrastructure investments, are expected to grow by 17%. Stalled occupations, influenced by automation and e-commerce, will rise by 7%. Declining occupations, impacted by reduced customer-facing roles, will decrease by 10%. The analysis highlights the need for reskilling and the role of generative AI in accelerating automation.
The US labor market is rapidly evolving due to automation, generative AI, and long-term trends. 8.6 million occupational shifts occurred from 2019 to 2022, with an expected 12 million more by 2030. The pandemic accelerated trends affecting customer-facing and office support roles, leading to potential declines in certain sectors.
The document discusses the resilience of certain occupations during the pandemic and the expected occupational shifts by 2030. It highlights the temporary impact of the pandemic on employment in various sectors and the need for continuous education and lifelong learning. The text emphasizes the urgency of solving occupational and geographic mismatches and the willingness of workers to change career paths. It also addresses the potential labor shortages and the challenges faced by employers in a tighter labor market.
The infographic illustrates the significant occupational shifts in the US from 2019 to 2022, with over 8.6 million workers transitioning between sectors. It highlights the decline in food services, customer service, office support, and production roles, while growth is observed in health, business, STEM, and education sectors. The data also reveals the impact of COVID-19 on certain occupations and the educational background of workers in various fields.
The document discusses the significant occupational shifts during the pandemic, highlighting the move from lower-wage to higher-wage jobs and the role of automation and generative AI in reshaping the labor market. It emphasizes the dynamic movement in the US labor market and the potential of generative AI in various business applications.
This page discusses the impact of generative AI on automation adoption, estimating that by 2030, 30% of work hours could be automated. It provides a detailed breakdown of automation adoption percentages across various sectors in the US, comparing scenarios with and without generative AI acceleration.
This page discusses various forces affecting future labor demand, including federal investment in net-zero emissions and infrastructure, major infrastructure projects, the CHIPS and Science Act, and other structural trends like rising incomes and education levels. It highlights the anticipated changes in job mix, with a focus on healthcare, STEM, and managerial positions, and the impact of generative AI on employment. The page concludes that while generative AI may disrupt some jobs, it is likely to significantly change the mix of work activities for knowledge workers.
The chart illustrates the estimated labor demand change and generative AI automation acceleration by occupation in the US from 2022 to 2030. It shows that while STEM, healthcare, builders, and professional fields are expected to add jobs, generative AI could significantly change work activities for many occupations. The chart categorizes occupations based on changes in labor demand and the degree of work activity change, highlighting increasing and decreasing labor demand with varying levels of automation adoption.
The document discusses the projected growth in healthcare and STEM jobs, alongside declining roles in office support and manufacturing. By 2030, an estimated 11.8 million workers may need to transition to new occupations, with a significant shift towards roles requiring higher education and skills.
The document discusses estimated future US job growth by occupational category under a midpoint automation scenario with generative AI acceleration. It highlights that healthcare, STEM, and builder roles are expected to grow, while demand for office support and customer service roles could decline. Workers in jobs with lower wages and educational requirements are the most affected, with a higher likelihood of needing to change occupations by the end of the decade.
This page discusses the disproportionate impact of job changes on lower-wage workers, particularly women and people of color, and the potential for inclusive growth through automation and generative AI. It highlights the need for reskilling, innovative hiring strategies, and support for workers transitioning to new roles. Generative AI is seen as a key driver of productivity growth, with potential benefits for knowledge work and economic growth if managed well.
This page discusses the importance of skills development through work experience, the need for inclusive labor market practices, and strategies to address structural issues such as childcare and caregiving. It emphasizes the role of reskilling partnerships and digital microcredentials in adapting to job market changes.
This report examines the evolving US labor market, focusing on the impact of generative AI and other technological advancements. It highlights the need for preparing workers for future job shifts and emphasizes the importance of long-term structural changes over short-term forecasts.
The US labor market has recovered strongly post-COVID-19, with a significant wave of job switching. About 48 million people quit their jobs in 2021 and 51 million in 2022. Many sought better pay or alignment with priorities. The pandemic altered employment mix, favoring remote-capable roles like managerial and STEM jobs, while e-commerce boosted warehousing jobs. These trends are expected to continue.
The document details employment changes across various occupational categories from 2019 to 2022, highlighting that customer-facing jobs suffered the most during the pandemic. Business, transportation, and STEM roles showed resilience. Food services and customer service roles declined significantly, while healthcare employment saw a nuanced recovery. Automation and consumer preference shifts contributed to these trends.
The United States experienced a labor shortage in the economic recovery, with total employment exceeding pre-pandemic levels but labor force participation lagging. The shortage disproportionately affected workers without college degrees and people of color. Despite white-collar layoffs, the job market remained robust, especially for blue-collar workers. Factors contributing to the shortage include retirement, early exits from the workforce, and workers quitting without new jobs lined up.
This page discusses the significant impact of health concerns and immigration on the US labor force, highlighting the decline in foreign-born workers and the rebound in 2022. It also addresses the Great Attrition, where millions of workers changed jobs and took up new occupations, with a 50% increase in occupational shifts between 2019 and 2022.
The document analyzes recent occupational shifts in the U.S., showing that over 8.6 million workers transitioned between jobs from 2019 to 2022, with a 50% faster rate of change. It categorizes these shifts into four groups and provides detailed data on various sectors, highlighting the number of shifts, low-wage jobs, and workers without a college degree.
The page discusses the shift in employment patterns post-pandemic, highlighting an increase in higher-wage jobs and a decline in lower-wage jobs. It suggests that improvements in job quality, pay, benefits, career advancement, or automation are needed to address labor shortages in lower-wage occupations.
This page discusses job gains and losses through 2030, considering factors like automation, remote work, and generative AI. It estimates 11.8 million occupational transitions by 2030 and explores the impact of generative AI on white-collar jobs, suggesting a mix of gains and losses.
This page discusses the impact of generative AI on labor demand and work activities across various occupations in the US from 2022 to 2030. It highlights that while STEM, healthcare, and professional fields are adding jobs, generative AI could significantly alter work activities. The content includes a detailed analysis of labor demand changes and automation adoption, emphasizing the varying effects on different occupations.
The page discusses the resilient growth in healthcare, STEM, construction, and business/legal professions, predicting significant job gains. Healthcare jobs are expected to grow by 30%, driven by an aging population. STEM jobs will increase by 23% by 2030, fueled by digitization and the CHIPS and Science Act. Transportation and construction sectors will also see growth due to e-commerce and infrastructure projects.
The document outlines estimated future US job growth and educational attainment by occupational category under a midpoint automation scenario with generative AI acceleration. It highlights resilient and growing occupations like healthcare and STEM, while noting declining roles in customer service and office support. The data includes net labor demand changes, educational attainment levels, and employment figures for various occupations.
The document discusses expected declines in office support, customer service, and food services jobs due to automation, estimating losses of 1.6 million clerical jobs, 830,000 retail salespeople, and 630,000 cashiers. It highlights the shift in manufacturing towards high-tech roles and the need for nearly 12 million workers to transition to new occupations by 2030, with many moving into higher-wage jobs.
The page presents a comparative analysis of labor demand changes for various occupations between 2022 and 2030 under a midpoint automation scenario with generative AI acceleration. It highlights robust growth in occupations like personal care aides and registered nurses, while showing a decline in roles such as retail salespersons and office clerks. The data underscores the impact of automation and AI on the job market.
This page details the estimated number of occupational transitions by category from 2022 to 2030 under a midpoint automation scenario with generative AI acceleration. It categorizes occupations into resilient and growing, stalled but rising, and hit and declining, providing absolute transition numbers and 2022 employment figures. Key sectors like office support and customer service face significant shifts, while business and legal professionals show resilience. The data highlights the impact of automation and AI on various job categories.
This page discusses the impact of generative AI and federal investment on labor demand, highlighting the rapid adoption of tools like ChatGPT and their potential to transform work activities. It explains what generative AI is and how it can generate various types of content, including text and images.
Generative AI is advancing natural language capabilities, impacting a wide range of work activities. Automation potential has increased from 44% to 62%, but actual adoption lags due to various barriers. Generative AI accelerates automation adoption, potentially increasing automated tasks from 21.5% to 29.5% by 2030.
The graph illustrates how generative AI accelerates automation adoption in the US under different scenarios. By 2030, the early scenario with generative AI shows a 15 percentage point difference compared to the scenario without it. The late scenario shows a 1 percentage point difference. The scenarios reflect varying assumptions about technical capabilities and adoption timelines.
This page discusses how generative AI could automate 30% of work hours by 2030, affecting high-skilled workers. It highlights the shift from skill-biased automation to knowledge-worker automation and presents a chart showing automation adoption across various occupations in the US.
This page discusses the significant impact of generative AI on white-collar jobs, particularly lawyers and civil engineers. It explains how generative AI can enhance productivity by automating tasks like legal research and design processes. The page includes Exhibit 9, a chart showing the potential automation adoption by 2030 for various occupations, highlighting the acceleration due to generative AI.
This page discusses how generative AI and automation are changing work processes, enhancing productivity, and shifting employment demands. It highlights the need for workers to adapt to new technologies and use freed time for higher-value tasks. The page also touches on federal investments in greener sectors and the net-zero transition, emphasizing the role of policy in shaping the future of work.
The net-zero transition could reallocate a substantial number of American jobs, with an estimated net gain of 700,000 jobs by 2030. However, the transition may involve significant job churn, with 3.5 million jobs lost and 4.2 million gained. Job growth is expected in renewable energy sectors, while carbon-intensive industries may see job reductions. Training and retraining will be crucial to ensure a smooth transition and address geographic mismatches.
This page illustrates how transferable skills can help workers transition into higher-paying jobs in growing industries. It provides examples of career paths from automotive technician to wind turbine technician and from building maintenance technician to HVAC contractor. The page also discusses the importance of renewing America's infrastructure and the potential impact of the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law on employment and productivity.
This page discusses the shift towards electric vehicles (EVs) in the US, highlighting the federal government's goals, the impact on the automotive industry, and the need for tech-oriented workers. It also covers the CHIPS and Science Act, the Inflation Reduction Act, and the potential job growth in states like California, Georgia, and Michigan. The page emphasizes the challenges and opportunities in the transition to EVs, including the need for new skills and infrastructure development.
The construction sector faces significant labor demand, especially for skilled trades, due to infrastructure spending and natural disaster rebuilding. Shortages exist, with unfilled positions exceeding unemployed workers. The workforce is aging, reliant on immigrants, and lacks diversity. Competition for skilled workers is high, requiring diversification and training to meet future needs.
This page discusses the vulnerability of workers to automation, highlighting the need for retraining and job-matching systems. It emphasizes the decline of low- and middle-wage jobs and the potential for better-paying jobs with skills training and employer willingness to take hiring risks.
The document discusses the projected changes in US employment across different wage bands from 2022 to 2030. It highlights that high-wage jobs are expected to increase by 2.6 percentage points, while middle-wage jobs will decline by 0.3 percentage points and low-wage jobs by 2.3 percentage points. The employment distribution across various occupational categories is also provided, showing the percentage of jobs in high, middle, and low wage categories.
The page discusses the potential shift in the US economy toward higher-wage jobs, highlighting the vulnerability of low-wage workers and the need for training and flexible hiring. It also notes the importance of upgrading low-paying but essential jobs like home healthcare and childcare to meet societal needs.
The chart illustrates that women are underrepresented in high-growth and high-wage jobs, with significant disparities in representation across various occupations. High female representation is observed in health-related and personal care roles, while low representation is seen in technology and managerial positions.
This page discusses the likelihood of workers in low-wage jobs and those without college degrees needing to change occupations by 2030. It highlights the vulnerability of these groups to job displacement and the need for support in making successful job transitions. The page provides specific statistics and examples of the most affected groups, including workers in the lowest wage brackets, those without college degrees, the youngest and oldest workers, women, Hispanic workers, and Black workers.
This page discusses the likelihood of job displacement and occupational changes by 2030, highlighting that low-wage workers, those with less education, younger individuals, women, and certain racial/ethnic groups are more susceptible. It provides a detailed breakdown by wage, education, age, gender, and race/ethnicity, showing the national average transition rate and specific factors affecting each group.
The future workforce will require more technological and people skills, with social and emotional skills and technological skills seeing the biggest increase in demand by 2030. Skill shifts within occupations offer opportunities for higher-value work, such as retail employees focusing on customer experience and healthcare workers interacting more with patients.
The demand for basic cognitive and physical skills is declining due to automation. Workers need to develop social, emotional, and technological skills to move into higher-wage occupations. The share of physical work in the US economy is expected to decrease slightly by 2030. Despite this, some jobs requiring physical skills will endure, and technology will continue to alter daily tasks, necessitating continuous learning.
This section discusses the importance of preparing for the future of work by enhancing employee skills, promoting workforce mobility, and leveraging workplace experiences to develop human capital. It highlights the role of leaders in fostering an inclusive and dynamic work environment and emphasizes the need for clear pathways into critical roles. The text also underscores the significance of work experience in career advancement and the benefits of evaluating candidates based on their learning capacity and transferable skills.
The document discusses the need for the United States to boost productivity growth through automation, particularly generative AI. It highlights the importance of a sustained strategy for implementation, responsible use guidelines, and evolving job roles. Workers can benefit from AI by focusing on higher-value activities, while leaders and researchers can enhance their productivity through automation tools.
The document illustrates how generative AI can enhance a software developer's productivity by automating routine tasks, enabling focus on valuable activities, and expanding the company's capabilities through advanced technology infrastructure.
The document discusses strategies to build a more inclusive economy by addressing challenges in the US labor market, including removing unnecessary credential requirements, broadening opportunities for workers without college degrees, and removing barriers for women by expanding access to affordable childcare.
The page discusses strategies to boost women's participation in the labor market, including reexamining hiring biases, implementing returnship programs, and keeping experienced older workers engaged. It highlights the need for flexible work arrangements and skills development for low-wage workers to transition into growing jobs.
This page discusses strategies to activate historically overlooked populations in the labor force, including remote work opportunities for people with disabilities and residents of rural areas. It also addresses eliminating traditional hiring barriers and the need for American workers to acquire new skills in demand, emphasizing the role of employers and government initiatives in facilitating career transitions.
This page discusses initiatives for preparing different groups (pre-college students, college students, unemployed individuals, and displaced workers) for the future workforce. It highlights the importance of collaboration between employers, educational institutions, and other organizations to address labor market challenges and emphasizes the value workers place on flexibility and positive work experiences.
This page discusses strategies for employee retention, emphasizing meaningful work, flexibility, and career development. It highlights the benefits of hybrid work models and the importance of offering learning opportunities. It also explores the potential of rural areas in attracting workers through remote work and financial incentives. The page concludes by addressing the impact of automation on jobs and the need for skill development and job redesign.
This page outlines the methodology for analyzing the impact of net-zero emissions and infrastructure spending on jobs in the US, using updated models and data sources like the Current Population Survey.
This page explains the terminology used for occupational shifts, detailing how employment declines are calculated and interpreted. It discusses the methodology for estimating baseline employment, automation impact, and productivity changes, considering various scenarios and assumptions.
This page discusses the GDP impact of automation, long-term labor market trends influenced by macroeconomic factors, trends accelerated by COVID-19, and the demand for various workforce skills, emphasizing the need for digital skills.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Geopolitics and the geometry of global trade_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_5.jpg
pages.abstract: This page highlights key trends in global trade, including the binding effect of concentrated products on distant economies, ongoing trade reconfiguration among major economies, shifting investment patterns in developing countries, trade-offs between geopolitical distance and concentration, and the need for businesses to adapt to uncertainty.
pages.title: At a glance

pages.page_path: library_pages\Geopolitics and the geometry of global trade_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_6.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses trade reconfiguration, highlighting shifts in trade patterns, geopolitical influences, and emerging trade terms. It analyzes the impact of sanctions, tariffs, and global trade restrictions, emphasizing the changing geometry of global trade connections.
pages.title: Introduction

pages.page_path: library_pages\Geopolitics and the geometry of global trade_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_7.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the relationship between geopolitical alignment and trade shifts, using UN General Assembly voting records. It highlights changes in US, China, and Germany's trade patterns and explores potential future trade reconfigurations, including trade fragmentation and diversification, and their implications for business leaders.
pages.title: Geopolitical Alignment and Trade Shifts

pages.page_path: library_pages\Geopolitics and the geometry of global trade_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_8.jpg
pages.title: Mining Site Aerial View

pages.page_path: library_pages\Geopolitics and the geometry of global trade_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_9.jpg
pages.abstract: The world is interconnected, with major regions relying on imports for over 25% of their consumption. Global goods trade is concentrated among a few economies. Trade profiles vary among economies, influenced by trade intensity, geographic and geopolitical distances, and supply network breadth. ASEAN and Germany are highly integrated regional manufacturing hubs.
pages.title: 1. Trade connects the world across geopolitical differences

pages.page_path: library_pages\Geopolitics and the geometry of global trade_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_10.jpg
pages.abstract: This page illustrates how large economies vary in their trade relations across four dimensions: trade intensity, geographic distance, geopolitical distance, and import concentration. It uses visual representations to compare these factors among ASEAN, Brazil, China, Germany, India, the UK, and the US, highlighting differences from global averages.
pages.title: Large economies differ in the nature of their goods trade relations on four dimensions.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Geopolitics and the geometry of global trade_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_11.jpg
pages.abstract: This sidebar explains the methodology for measuring geopolitical distance using UN General Assembly votes, defining a one-dimensional spectrum and discussing its limitations. It highlights the positions of major economies and notes that voting practices may not fully represent countries' global issue stances. The analysis includes robustness checks and compares trade intensity and geographical trade patterns of the US, Germany, and China.
pages.title: Sidebar 1. Measuring geopolitical distance and its limitations

pages.page_path: library_pages\Geopolitics and the geometry of global trade_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_12.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the trade patterns of major economies, focusing on Brazil's trade with China, India's global average trade geometry, and the tendency of larger economies to trade over wider geopolitical distances. It highlights the economic vulnerabilities associated with trade between geopolitically distant partners and the concentration of trade in globally concentrated goods.
pages.title: Geopolitics and the geometry of global trade

pages.page_path: library_pages\Geopolitics and the geometry of global trade_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_13.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how many large economies engage in trade with partners that are geopolitically different from them. It highlights the geopolitical distances and voting patterns of countries in the UN General Assembly. Examples include iron ore, soybeans, and flat-panel displays, showing trade flows between geopolitically distant economies. China plays a significant role as a global processing hub.
pages.title: Many large economies have trade relationships with partners that are relatively different from them in geopolitical terms.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Geopolitics and the geometry of global trade_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_14.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the value of global goods trade by geopolitical distance, highlighting that nearly 20% of trade occurs between distant economies. It includes data on all products and globally concentrated products, showing significant trade flows from China. The text also addresses the risks and challenges of relying on geopolitically distant partners for concentrated products, emphasizing the importance of supply security and potential disruptions.
pages.title: Nearly 20 percent of global goods trade is between geopolitically distant economies.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Geopolitics and the geometry of global trade_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_15.jpg
pages.abstract: This page illustrates the trade dynamics between geopolitically distant economies, showing that nearly 20% of global goods trade occurs between such partners. It uses a scatter plot to depict the geopolitical position of exporters and the share of trade between distant partners, highlighting products like iron ore, laptops, and cell phones. The data reveals varying levels of supply concentration and geopolitical alignment with the US or China.
pages.title: Trade between geopolitically distant economies accounts for nearly 20 percent of global goods trade.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Geopolitics and the geometry of global trade_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_16.jpg
pages.abstract: This page illustrates that nearly 40% of trade in globally concentrated products occurs between geopolitically distant economies. It uses a scatter plot to show the relationship between the geopolitical position of exporters and the share of trade between distant partners, highlighting products like iron ore, laptops, and soybeans. The data emphasizes the significant trade value and geopolitical diversity in these products.
pages.title: Nearly 40 percent of trade in globally concentrated products is between geopolitically more distant economies.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Geopolitics and the geometry of global trade_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_17.jpg
pages.abstract: The page illustrates the concentration of product trade at the economy level between geopolitically distant partners, showing that around 13 percent of such trade occurs between distant economies. It highlights various goods like airplanes, human vaccines, and photovoltaic cells, with their geopolitical positions and trade shares depicted in a scatter plot. The data is sourced from UN Comtrade and McKinsey Global Institute analysis.
pages.title: Around 13 percent of concentrated product trade at the economy level is between geopolitically more distant economies.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Geopolitics and the geometry of global trade_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_18.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the trade in products that are not concentrated, highlighting that around 15 percent of such trade occurs between geopolitically distant economies. It includes a scatter plot showing the relationship between the geopolitical position of exporters and the share of trade between distant partners, with examples like refined petroleum, skincare cosmetics, and crude oil. The data is based on 2021 trade values and geopolitical positions calculated from UN General Assembly voting records.
pages.title: Around 15 percent of trade in products that are not concentrated is between geopolitically more distant economies.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Geopolitics and the geometry of global trade_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_19.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the prevalence of concentrated products in trade corridors between geopolitically distant partners, highlighting the top ten largest goods trade corridors in 2021. It also delves into the global concentration of neodymium magnets, their importance in the energy transition, and the challenges in diversifying their supply chain.
pages.title: The prevalence of concentrated products varies widely among trade corridors that link geopolitically distant partners.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Geopolitics and the geometry of global trade_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_20.jpg
pages.title: 工厂工作场景

pages.page_path: library_pages\Geopolitics and the geometry of global trade_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_21.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses gradual shifts in global trade since 1995, with individual countries gaining or losing minimal export share. Recent geopolitical and geographic changes in trade patterns are analyzed, highlighting the United States' diversification and reduced dependency on critical imports. ASEAN, Brazil, and India are increasingly participating in global trade with distant partners, while nearshoring remains limited.
pages.title: 2. Trade reconfiguration is under way

pages.page_path: library_pages\Geopolitics and the geometry of global trade_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_22.jpg
pages.abstract: The exhibit illustrates changes in trade intensity, geographic and geopolitical distances, and import concentration for various economies between 2013-17 and 2017-23. It shows a trend towards closer geopolitical partners, with notable shifts in trade patterns for countries like China, the US, and India.
pages.title: Trade may be reconfiguring toward geopolitically closer partners for some economies.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Geopolitics and the geometry of global trade_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_23.jpg
pages.abstract: This page illustrates how China's trade relationships have shifted towards developing economies globally between 2017 and 2023, with notable increases in trade shares with regions like ASEAN and Latin America, while decreasing with developed economies like the US and Japan.
pages.title: China’s trade geometry has reoriented toward developing economies around the world.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Geopolitics and the geometry of global trade_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_24.jpg
pages.abstract: The United States has diversified its imports away from China in various manufacturing sectors between 2017 and 2023. pages.title: Global balance sheet 2022: Enter volatility
McKinsey Global Institute
Contents

pages.abstract: The document discusses the evolution of global net worth and balance sheets, highlighting a 170 percentage point increase in assets and net worth relative to GDP from pre-2000 levels, driven by asset price inflation. It also details the balance sheet expansion across various sectors during the pandemic, noting a $100 trillion addition to global wealth.
pages.title: After growing net worth and 'pandemic' acceleration, now what?

pages.abstract: The global balance sheet grew faster than GDP for three decades, accelerating during the pandemic. In 2022, signs of volatility emerged, with the first overall shrinkage in decades. Real estate, debt, and US equities drove growth, with asset price inflation playing a key role. Inflation and interest rate rises in 2022 led to declines in equity and bond prices, while debt continued to grow. Future outcomes depend on productivity growth and capital reallocation or unwinding via inflation or asset price corrections.
pages.title: Global balance sheet 2022: Enter volatility

pages.abstract: The global balance sheet experienced significant growth and volatility from 2000 to 2022, with notable changes in financial corporations' liabilities, household and government liabilities, and net worth. The data highlights the impact of the pandemic and the shift from unconsolidated to consolidated financial data in 2020.
pages.title: Evolution of the global balance sheet, consolidated data

pages.abstract: The document discusses the expansion of the global balance sheet in the Era of Markets, highlighting its role in assessing economic prosperity, health, and resilience. It updates the balance sheet to reflect the pandemic's impact, the war in Ukraine, inflation, and interest rate shocks, providing a lens for evaluating economic wealth and health.
pages.title: The global balance sheet expanded inexorably in the Era of Markets

pages.abstract: The global balance sheet assesses economic health by analyzing real and financial assets and liabilities across sectors. It includes real assets like real estate and financial assets like stocks, bonds, and cash. Financial institutions play a key role in intermediating these assets and liabilities. The balance sheet helps gauge wealth, capital allocation, and financial fragilities.
pages.title: The global balance sheet: Taking stock of economic health and wealth

pages.abstract: The global balance sheet is divided into three interlocking balance sheets, each valued at approximately $500 to $600 trillion. The financial sector creates and intermediates assets, the financial system separates wealth from investment, and the real economy drives growth and wealth. The data includes consolidated financial assets and liabilities, with key percentages for debt, equity, currency, and other financial assets.
pages.title: The global balance sheet consists of three interlocking balance sheets of—coincidentally—~$500 trillion to $600 trillion each.

pages.abstract: The global balance sheet has quadrupled since 2000, with net worth exceeding six times GDP. Asset price inflation, driven by declining interest rates, has fueled this growth, with only 23% of it reflecting new investment. Real assets and net worth are at their highest levels relative to GDP since the two world wars, while liabilities and debt surpass pre-crisis peaks.
pages.title: Real assets and net worth rose to their highest levels relative to GDP since the two world wars, while liabilities and debt are now above the peaks reached around the global financial crisis.

pages.abstract: The page illustrates the rise in assets and net worth relative to GDP from pre-2000 levels, driven by asset price inflation. It shows a graph comparing net worth/GDP percentages across various countries from 1970 to 2021, highlighting a 170 percentage point increase. The components of net worth growth from 2000 to 2021 are detailed, with asset price increases above inflation contributing significantly.
pages.title: Assets and net worth rose 170 percentage points relative to GDP from pre-2000 averages, fueled by asset price inflation.

pages.abstract: The document discusses the historical trends of wealth-to-GDP ratios, highlighting disruptions during the early 20th century and the subsequent recovery and growth post-1950. It emphasizes the role of urbanization, suburban development, and the shift to services in elevating real estate as a primary store of value, especially in the context of declining interest rates and rising asset prices.
pages.title: Net worth is now at levels relative to GDP last seen before the world wars in several economies

pages.abstract: This page discusses how net worth relative to GDP has reached unprecedented levels in several economies since before the two world wars. Real estate and US equities have been key drivers of asset growth globally, with rising real estate values significantly impacting household balance sheets. Countries like South Korea, France, and New Zealand have seen substantial growth in real estate net worth, while resource exporters such as Australia, Canada, and Norway have also benefited from rising resource wealth.
pages.title: Net worth is now at levels relative to GDP not seen since before the two world wars in several economies.

pages.abstract: This page presents data on country net worth growth from 2000 to 2021, showing the growth of real estate, equities, and other assets relative to GDP. It also includes liabilities such as debt and other liabilities, and the resulting net worth. The data reveals that real estate grew relative to GDP almost universally, and so did debt and equity. The table includes data for various countries, with South Korea having the highest net worth growth at 3.9, and Ireland having the lowest at -2.3.
pages.title: Real estate grew relative to GDP almost universally, and so did debt and equity.

pages.abstract: This page discusses the rapid increases in real estate prices and net worth trends in various countries, highlighting China's property boom, Japan's bubble collapse, and the US's household wealth growth. It also examines the impact of financial crises on countries like Greece, Ireland, and Portugal, and the role of pension systems and foreign investments in expanding net worth in Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands, and Norway. Australia leads in household net worth due to high land prices.
pages.title: Real Estate Prices and Net Worth Trends

pages.abstract: This page presents a detailed comparison of household sector balance sheets across various countries, highlighting Australia's leading position in household net worth relative to GDP due to high land prices. The data includes real and financial assets, liabilities, and net worth per capita, providing insights into global economic disparities.
pages.title: Australia leads the world in household net worth relative to GDP due to high land prices.

pages.abstract: This page discusses the expansion of debt and equity liabilities relative to GDP since 2000, highlighting global trends and regional differences. It explains the risks associated with high debt levels and provides specific examples from the United States, Europe, China, and Japan. The page also notes variations in debt growth across countries and sectors, emphasizing the potential financial fragilities as interest rates rise.
pages.title: Debt and equity liabilities have expanded relative to GDP since 2000 and are now higher than before the global financial crisis

pages.abstract: The document compares debt and equity liabilities relative to GDP across countries from 1990 to 2021, showing significant increases in debt levels since 2000, with China experiencing the largest rise. Equity liabilities also increased, with the United States showing the highest growth. The data highlights the global financial crisis's impact on debt levels.
pages.title: In 2021, liabilities and debt were higher relative to GDP than they were before the global financial crisis.

pages.abstract: The exhibit illustrates the growth of debt across various sectors in China, Europe, Japan, and the US from 2000 to 2021. It shows the nominal values of debt liabilities relative to GDP for financial corporations, governments, households, and nonfinancial corporations. The data reveals significant increases in debt levels, particularly in government and financial sectors, with notable fluctuations in household and nonfinancial corporation debt.
pages.title: Debt grew from 2000 to 2021 across sectors in China, Europe, Japan, and the United States.

pages.abstract: This exhibit illustrates the growth in liabilities relative to GDP and net investment across various countries from 2000 to 2021. It highlights significant variations in net new debt, equity liabilities growth, and other new liabilities. The ratio of new debt to new investment also varies widely, with some countries like Greece and Portugal showing high ratios, while others like Mexico and New Zealand have lower ratios.
pages.title: Growth in liabilities relative to GDP and net investment varies significantly among countries.

pages.abstract: The global balance sheet saw significant growth during the pandemic, with wealth and liabilities increasing sharply due to government and central bank actions. The global economy added $100 trillion to wealth, and debt creation accelerated, reflecting economic stimulus efforts.
pages.title: Growth in the global balance sheet accelerated during the pandemic

pages.abstract: During the pandemic, global wealth grew by $100 trillion due to asset price growth. Household net worth increased by $110 trillion, while governments added $19 trillion in debt. The expansion was driven by fiscal and monetary stimulus, leading to growth in home prices, equity markets, and currency holdings. However, the distribution of wealth was highly unequal, and its sustainability was tested in 2022.
pages.title: During the pandemic, net worth growth accelerated, adding $100 trillion to global wealth 'on paper.'

pages.abstract: This page discusses the significant increase in debt and financial liabilities during the pandemic, highlighting the rise in real estate value relative to GDP in specific countries. It also explains the role of financial institutions in expanding balance sheets and the complex relationship between debt and investment.
pages.title: Real estate accelerated its rise relative to GDP, most notably in Australia, Austria, Canada, France, New Zealand, and Portugal.

pages.abstract: The page discusses the rapid growth of balance sheets globally, especially during the pandemic, with a focus on the disproportionate increase in debt compared to net investment. It highlights country-specific trends in real estate, equity, and debt growth.
pages.title: Balance sheet growth accelerated across countries

pages.abstract: This page presents a detailed analysis of balance sheet growth across various countries from 2019 to 2021, excluding financial assets and liabilities. It highlights changes in assets and liabilities by asset type, showing significant variations among countries. The data is sourced from multiple international organizations and statistical offices.
pages.title: Balance sheet growth accelerated across countries.

pages.abstract: The first three quarters of 2022 saw rising rates and inflation, leading to volatility and a pause in the global balance sheet's rise. Amid geopolitical and economic turbulence, all three global balance sheets shrank relative to GDP for the first time since the global financial crisis.
pages.title: Is 2022 a pause or an inflection point in the rise of the global balance sheet?

pages.abstract: The page discusses significant macroeconomic changes in 2022, including rising interest rates, inflation, and declines in equities, debt, and housing prices. The global balance sheet experienced its first decline since the financial crisis, with a $20 trillion reduction in financial assets and liabilities. Investors became wary of debt, and real estate prices and security valuations declined. The balance sheet contracted relative to GDP, with decreases in equities, debt securities, and real estate.
pages.title: Several factors that drove sustained balance sheet expansion have turned (for now)

pages.abstract: The page presents a series of graphs showing changes in key macroeconomic indicators from 1980 to Q3 2022. It highlights inflection points in 2022, including global nominal interest rates, inflation, equity growth, bond prices, real estate prices, and oil prices. The data reveals significant shifts, such as a rise in inflation and a decline in equity and bond prices.
pages.title: Inflection points were evident in 2022 on a range of key macroeconomic indicators.

pages.abstract: The global balance sheet declined in the first three quarters of 2022, with financial sector liabilities decreasing at market value. Non-financial corporations and government debt showed mixed trends, while declining equity prices impacted household wealth and corporate equity liabilities.
pages.title: In the first three quarters of 2022, the global balance sheet declined for the first time since the global financial crisis.

pages.abstract: The balance sheet contracted relative to GDP in most countries, with Australia and Sweden experiencing the largest declines in real estate worth. Rising mineral prices positively impacted Australia's net worth. The financial balance sheet changes varied across countries, with some experiencing declines in net worth and others seeing increases.
pages.title: The balance sheet contracted in most countries; real assets and net worth in Australia and Sweden felt the most impact

pages.abstract: This page discusses potential future scenarios for economic health and wealth, focusing on the relationship between balance sheets and GDP. It highlights a new paper to be released in 2023 that will explore four different directions for this relationship up to 2030.
pages.title: What is next for economic health and wealth?

pages.abstract: This page discusses potential scenarios for the balance sheet's relationship with GDP, including secular stagnation, productivity acceleration, inflationary pressures, and asset price correction. Each scenario outlines trends in GDP growth, interest rates, and inflation, along with their impacts on the balance sheet and historical precedents.
pages.title: Will the balance sheet resume its rise relative to GDP or start to unwind?

pages.abstract: This page outlines four potential economic pathways: the rise resumes, productivity acceleration, inflationary way out, and asset price correction and deleveraging. Each scenario explores different economic conditions and their impacts on growth, inflation, and balance sheets. The page also highlights regional variations and the implications for households, governments, and corporations.
pages.title: Possible pathways for different economies

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_1.jpg

pages.abstract: The executive summary highlights the banking sector's recent challenges and favorable shifts, noting the best 18 months for global banking since 2007. It discusses the movement of balance sheets and transactions to nontraditional institutions and the tipping point of traditional banking assets.
pages.title: Executive summary

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_4.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the 'Great Banking Transition,' focusing on the banking sector's performance improvements in 2022-23, the impact of rising interest rates, and the need for financial institutions to adapt through technology, balance sheet flexibility, and risk management. It highlights the varied performance across categories, the importance of operational excellence, and the geographical divergence in banking performance.
pages.title: The Great Banking Transition

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_5.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the challenges and future trends in the banking sector, focusing on the Great Banking Transition. It highlights the impact of macroeconomic shifts, technological advancements, regulatory changes, and systemic risks on financial institutions. The text emphasizes the importance of adapting to these changes and outlines five priorities for banks, including leveraging technology and AI.
pages.title: The Great Banking Transition

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_6.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses key strategies for banks to adapt in the evolving financial landscape, including leveraging technology, flexing balance sheets, scaling transaction businesses, enhancing distribution methods, and managing evolving risks. It emphasizes the importance of innovation, scale, and risk management in a dynamic macroeconomic environment.
pages.title: The Great Banking Transition

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_7.jpg
pages.abstract: The past 18 months have been a time of extremes for the banking industry, with some institutions experiencing record highs while others faced significant lows. Key indicators like ROE and capital ratios have improved globally, particularly in Europe and the United States, due to higher interest rates and revenue growth.
pages.title: The highest highs, the lowest lows

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_8.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the Great Banking Transition, highlighting the reinvention and innovation in banking, the impact of technological advancements, and the challenges faced by traditional banks. It also analyzes the upturn in net interest margins and profit margins in Europe and North America, driven by rising interest rates, and the varying performance across different financial segments.
pages.title: The Great Banking Transition

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_9.jpg
pages.abstract: The document highlights the exceptional performance of global banks in 2022-2023, with ROE reaching 13%, significantly above the 13-year average. It also notes the doubling of net income to $1.4 trillion and an increase in capital ratios, alongside a drop in the cost-income ratio, indicating improved efficiency and profitability.
pages.title: Banks globally posted their best return on equity and profits in a decade in 2022–23.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_10.jpg
pages.abstract: The financial services sector intermediated $400 trillion in assets and generated $6.8 trillion in revenue in 2022, with intermediation growing faster than the overall economy. Intermediation revenues were concentrated in corporate, commercial, and retail banking, while wealth and asset management, capital markets infrastructure, and payments were the most profitable sectors. Higher interest rates improved margins in corporate and commercial banking, while wealth and asset management saw declines in profitability. Capital markets revenue pools grew on the buy side but remained stagnant on the sell side. Retail banking embraced new technologies, and payments saw rapid growth in Asia with the shift to digital payments.
pages.title: The global figures mask wide variations within individual subsectors

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_11.jpg
pages.abstract: The global financial industry intermediates $400 trillion in funds, generating $7 trillion in revenue. The funds are sourced from personal deposits, banks' bonds, corporate deposits, and retail AUM, among others. The use of funds includes retail loans, securities, corporate loans, and other investments. The share of total annual revenue is dominated by retail banking (33%) and corporate banking (28%).
pages.title: The global financial industry intermediates $400 trillion in funds to generate about $7 trillion in revenue.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_12.jpg
pages.abstract: The document highlights the wide variations in financial institutions' performance across subsectors, emphasizing the importance of operational excellence and strategic decisions. It discusses disruptions affecting the banking sector and presents a distribution of institutions by return on equity, showing successful institutions exist in every subsector with significant dispersion.
pages.title: Successful institutions exist in every subsector, albeit with much dispersion.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_13.jpg
pages.abstract: The banking sector faces regulatory constraints and valuation challenges, with a 70% gap in price-to-book ratio compared to other industries. This highlights the need for evolving business models to enhance shareholder value and stability.
pages.title: The banking valuation gap highlights different regulatory constraints and a need for business models to evolve.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_14.jpg
pages.abstract: The banking industry is evolving due to economic pressures and new market entrants. The divergence among three categories of banks has grown, with North Stars declining and challenges for long-term value creation increasing. Competition from nonincumbents and regulatory requirements are impacting the industry's ROE.
pages.title: The banking industry is evolving in response to economic pressures and new entrants into the market, including specialist players.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_15.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses global trends impacting financial institutions, including uneven macroeconomic outlooks, tighter regulations, technology disruption, and systemic risks. It highlights the shift in technology and macroeconomics, increased industry velocity due to connectivity, and the potential economic scenarios influenced by interest rates. The text also mentions the turbulence in US regional banks and the cautious optimism about the short-term economic outlook.
pages.title: Global trends bring a new outlook for financial institutions

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_16.jpg
pages.abstract: The macroeconomic outlook varies across economies, with differing GDP growth, inflation, and policy rate changes. Historical interest rate hikes are shown for the US and Eurozone. GDP growth is expected to be around 3% in 2023-2024, with improved sentiment in developing countries and less concern about recession in the US and Europe. Global executives are more positive about the economy, with a survey highlighting geographic divergence in economic optimism.
pages.title: The macroeconomic outlook is uneven, with varying growth expectations and rapid increases in interest rates.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_17.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the tightening of regulation and government supervision in the financial sector, highlighting the impact of Basel III proposals on capital requirements and the growing importance of technology in enhancing competitive advantage and customer experience. It also touches on the challenges and opportunities presented by open banking, ESG requirements, and the emergence of generative AI.
pages.title: Tighter regulation and government supervision

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_18.jpg
pages.abstract: Gen AI has the potential to revolutionize banking by enhancing productivity, customer experience, and operational efficiency. It can personalize content, improve chatbots, accelerate software development, and automate risk reports. However, challenges like errors and untested value judgments must be addressed before widespread adoption.
pages.title: Generative AI and banking

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_19.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the impact of generative AI on banking, systemic risks due to geopolitical tensions and trade restrictions, and other trends like changing customer preferences and structural shifts in lending. It highlights the increased velocity of trends affecting the industry due to technological innovation and economic interdependencies.
pages.title: The trends are affecting the industry with increased velocity.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_20.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the impact of evolving corporate needs and ESG trends on the banking sector, focusing on the issuance of sustainable bonds and the long-term pressure on bank profitability. It highlights the expected compression of banking margins and the potential effects of Basel III proposals on banks' capital requirements.
pages.title: Impact on the banking sector

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_21.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses how economic profits are diverging among different banking business models. Retail and wholesale banking are the largest contributors to the industry's $1 trillion in annual average profits. The chart shows the global banking average net income and ROE for various banking sectors, highlighting the differences in profitability and return on equity.
pages.title: Economic profits are diverging among business models

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_22.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the varying abilities of financial institutions to create economic and shareholder value, highlighting the strong performance of payment providers and the challenges faced by mid-tier banks. It also notes the shift in banking revenues towards Asia, Latin America, and the Middle East and Africa, rather than the BRICS countries.
pages.title: There is wide divergence in financial institutions' ability to create economic and shareholder value.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_23.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the wide divergence in financial institutions' ability to create economic and shareholder value, highlighting differences in P/E ratios and earnings per share. It notes the trend of revenue growth in specific geographic pockets, particularly in the Middle East and Africa, and the misleading nature of lumping all emerging-market banks together.
pages.title: There is wide divergence in financial institutions' ability to create economic and shareholder value.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_24.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the growth of global financial intermediation revenue, focusing on specific markets. It highlights the revenue by region and the assets of the largest 100 banks. The Indo Crescent region is expected to experience accelerated growth in banking, with innovative institutions like HDFC and StashAway playing significant roles.
pages.title: Growth of global financial intermediation revenue is likely to be focused on specific markets.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_25.jpg
pages.abstract: The Indo-Crescent region holds 8% of global banking assets and 51% of top-performing banks, driven by factors like GDP growth and ecosystem plays. It includes both advanced and developing economies, with expected banking revenue growth rates varying across countries. The region's share in global assets and best-performing banks is significant.
pages.title: The Indo-Crescent region now is home to half of best-performing banks that are achieving breakthrough growth.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_26.jpg
pages.abstract: China's banking sector faces unique challenges, including high nonperforming loans, real estate overhang, and declining real estate values. Banks are exploring cost-saving measures like digitization and salary adjustments. Government ownership provides protection, but tighter fintech regulations are in place. Opportunities exist in digital technologies, AI, infrastructure funding, and expanding financial access.
pages.title: China's banking sector faces tighter times

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_27.jpg
pages.abstract: Assets and clients are shifting from traditional capital-heavy banks to capital-light nontraditional institutions, impacting the balance sheet and reshaping banking's core functions. Technological innovation is driving this transition, enabling scalability and cost reduction.
pages.title: The great banking transition

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_28.jpg
pages.abstract: The Great Banking Transition is reshaping the banking industry, affecting balance sheets, transactions, and distribution. Banks face pressure from rising interest rates and shifting economic scenarios, while financial assets migrate to off-balance-sheet vehicles. Institutions must assess their competitive advantages in a tech-driven, geopolitically complex world.
pages.title: How the transition affects banking

pages.page_path: library_pages\Global Banking Annual Review 2023_ The Great Banking Transition_McKinsey_2023_10_01\page_29.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the shift of bank assets from balance sheet to off-balance-sheet activities due to various business models and client service factors. It highlights the rapid growth of private credit and the ability of some institutions to better meet client needs.
