pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of human capital in economies and organizations, emphasizing career mobility as a mechanism for skill expansion and earnings growth. It analyzes job histories of four million workers across four countries, highlighting that strategic role moves can significantly boost lifetime earnings. The text also underscores the role of organizations in maximizing the 'experience effect' and the continuous learning throughout a working life.
pages.title: Executive summary

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_12.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how work experience builds on formal education, enhancing human capital and lifetime earnings. It explains the methodology for tracking new skills acquired through role changes and their impact on earnings, using a detailed dataset from four countries. The page also introduces the concept of 'skill distance' and its role in measuring the acquisition of new skills.
pages.title: Modeling the link between role moves and the addition of skills to lifetime earnings

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_13.jpg
pages.abstract: Work experience significantly contributes to an individual's human capital, accounting for 40-60% of their total wealth. Skills acquired through work experience contribute an average of 46% of human capital value. The analysis shows that work experience contributes 40% of lifetime earnings in the US and 43% in Germany and the UK. Exhibit E1 illustrates the skill distance and new skills acquired with each role change, highlighting the increasing specialization and new skill requirements as individuals progress in their careers.
pages.title: Work experience contributes 40 to 60 percent of a worker’s human capital

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_14.jpg
pages.abstract: The document illustrates the significant impact of work experience on lifetime earnings across advanced economies and India. It shows that work experience contributes more to earnings over time, with India having the highest percentage. The data is presented through graphs showing salary multiples at different career stages.
pages.title: Work experience accounts for 40 to 43 percent of average lifetime earnings in the advanced economies we studied, and 58 percent in India

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_15.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how work experience significantly influences lifetime earnings, especially for those starting in occupations with low educational requirements. It highlights the varying impact of experience across different jobs and countries, noting that some individuals can overcome educational disadvantages to achieve higher earnings. The content emphasizes the importance of work experience in signaling employability and career progression.
pages.title: Work experience is a bigger determinant for people who start in occupations without significant credentialing barriers

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_16.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how work experience significantly contributes to lifetime earnings, especially in occupations with lower education requirements. It highlights the disparity between upwardly mobile groups and those who remain stagnant or decline, attributing this to structural and social barriers. The exhibit compares the share of lifetime earnings associated with work experience in the United States and India, showing variations by occupational category and educational attainment.
pages.title: Work experience accounts for a greater share of lifetime earnings in occupations with lower education requirements.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_17.jpg
pages.abstract: The document illustrates how individuals in various occupations rely differently on work experience for salary growth. It compares restaurant servers, commercial pilots, maintenance and repair workers, and physicians, showing the share of earnings attributed to work experience versus entry-level skills over a 30-year career. Commercial pilots and physicians see the highest reliance on work experience, with significant salary multipliers over time.
pages.title: Individuals starting in different occupations have varying degrees of reliance on work experience.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_18.jpg
pages.abstract: Role moves significantly boost earnings and skills, with 30-45% average pay increase for those changing roles. Most moves involve switching employers, indicating limited internal advancement tracks. Bolder moves with higher skill distances yield greater rewards, enhancing capabilities over a working life.
pages.title: Role moves bring new skills and can unlock higher earnings—and in most cases, people are moving to new organizations

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_19.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how 'experience seekers' and 'early movers' boost their earnings through effective career moves. It highlights the movement patterns and outcomes of these archetypes, with 'experience seekers' frequently changing roles to enhance their skills and wages, and 'early movers' making significant leaps early in their careers. The page includes an exhibit showing how experience and role moves enable workers to move into higher earning quintiles in the United States.
pages.title: 'Experience seekers' and 'early movers' boost their earnings through effective career moves

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_20.jpg
pages.abstract: Employers can attract and retain talent by recognizing potential, embracing mobility, and strengthening learning. Companies with strong organizational health, structured training, and internal advancement opportunities stand out. They help employees build experience capital and establish themselves as learning organizations. Employers should understand potential, remove biases, and embrace mobility by providing clear paths for future roles.
pages.title: Employers can attract and retain talent by recognizing potential, embracing mobility, and strengthening learning

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_21.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of early exposure to effective organizations and bold role moves in building individuals' experience capital. It highlights the role of internal digital platforms, mobility, and coaching in skills development. The page includes an exhibit showing the drivers of experience capital variation and characteristics of effective organizations, emphasizing the impact of training, internal moves, and organizational health.
pages.title: Most of the differences in individuals' experience capital are associated with early exposure to an effective organization, followed by bold role moves.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_22.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of foundational career years and effective onboarding. It highlights the need for ongoing learning opportunities and the impact of organizational health on career growth. The pandemic has prompted job reevaluation, with many workers seeking better opportunities. Bold role moves can propel workers forward, but constraints such as health and family responsibilities may limit options. Strategic job choices should focus on learning and growth potential.
pages.title: Workers should choose their moves (and their employers) carefully

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_23.jpg
pages.abstract: This page compares the career paths of two architects, Jeanne and Jane, highlighting how different workplace experiences influenced their professional development. Jane's mentorship and exposure to advanced tools gave her a competitive edge, leading to better career opportunities.
pages.title: A tale of two architects

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_24.jpg
pages.title: Truck Driver Preparing for Journey

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_25.jpg
pages.abstract: This chapter discusses the development of human capital across life stages, emphasizing the influence of context. It reviews seminal research, empirical findings, and the concept of human capital as an economic value. It explores how work experience enhances human capital and its implications for employers, workers, and policymakers.
pages.title: Human capital development in context

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_26.jpg
pages.abstract: Human capital develops dynamically from childhood through education and working life, influenced by innate and instilled characteristics. Early education fosters critical thinking and societal contributions. Childhood advantages and disadvantages shape future career choices. Family, community, and institutional contexts significantly impact human potential, with early childhood education and public health investments yielding lifelong benefits.
pages.title: Human capital develops over much of an individual's lifetime and is heavily influenced by contextual settings

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_27.jpg
pages.abstract: This page illustrates the framework of human capital evolution across three stages: early childhood development, education, and work experience. It highlights the importance of work experience in shaping knowledge, skills, and attributes. The individual and institutional contexts are also discussed, emphasizing the roles of family, education, and work environments in human capital development.
pages.title: Work experience is an essential component of human capital development.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_28.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how work experiences enhance human capital, detailing how individuals acquire skills and knowledge throughout their careers. It highlights the role of employers in skill development and the impact of organizational practices on productivity. The text also explains how human capital, combined with other forms of capital, benefits both companies and workers.
pages.title: Experience gained in the work environment activates and augments human capital

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_29.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how work experience serves as a crucial signal of human capital's value in the labor market. It highlights the challenges of hiring due to information asymmetry and explains how educational qualifications are often used as proxies for skills. A case study of a US sports reporter illustrates how practical experience, developed over time, significantly enhances career progression and income potential.
pages.title: Work experience is an important signal of human capital's value

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_30.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the role of work experience as a signaling mechanism in job markets, comparing it to education. It highlights the challenges in measuring human capital due to its dynamic nature and long-term payoff. Two main approaches to measuring human capital are explored: focusing on indicators and measuring monetary value. The page also introduces the concept of the 'residual' in macroeconomic models and the importance of human capital in economic growth.
pages.title: Measuring human capital remains a challenge

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_31.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the role of job matching in discovering human capital's value, emphasizing the dynamics between employers and job seekers. It explains how job matching theory captures labor market outcomes and the factors influencing job-worker matches. The text highlights the importance of information, the costs of the matching process, and the concept of jobs as 'experience goods.' It also explores turnover as a result of new information and the benefits of better evaluation methods for both employers and job seekers.
pages.title: The role of job matching in discovering human capital’s value

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_32.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the role of education and health in human capital, highlighting their correlation with economic growth. It emphasizes the importance of health as a durable capital stock and its impact on productivity. The text also underscores the need for a holistic view that includes skill formation and workplace experiences in understanding human capital.
pages.title: The role of education and health in human capital

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_33.jpg
library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_34.jpg
pages.title: Firefighting Training Session

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_35.jpg
pages.abstract: This chapter discusses how work experience builds human capital, estimating that accumulated experience accounts for roughly half of lifetime earnings. It highlights the importance of learning through jobs, formal training, and observation, and notes that the 'experience effect' varies across different contexts. People with lower education rely more on work experience to grow earnings, while those with higher education benefit more from formal education. Factors like economic growth and personal choices influence career opportunities and earnings.
pages.title: 2. How the 'experience effect' builds human capital

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_36.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the value of human capital, approximated by lifetime earnings, and its significance in wealth per capita. It explains how human capital is not traditionally recognized as a capital asset but generates economic benefits through work. The capitalized value of human capital is estimated for the United States and other countries, highlighting its substantial contribution to total wealth. The page also mentions the importance of non-marketized services and personal attributes in enhancing human capital value.
pages.title: The value of human capital can be approximated by lifetime earnings

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_37.jpg
pages.abstract: This page illustrates the wide variation in lifetime earnings across different occupations within the same occupational category in the United States. It provides indexed lifetime earnings for the highest- and lowest-earning starting occupations within each category, showing significant disparities. The data is sourced from various professional profiles and job posting records.
pages.title: Lifetime earnings vary widely by occupation, even within the same occupational category.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_38.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how role moves and skill acquisition contribute to lifetime earnings, using a detailed dataset of workers' career histories. It explains the methodology for estimating future earnings and acknowledges the limitations of using wages as a measure of human capital. The text highlights the importance of understanding the dynamic of human capital accumulation through individual career journeys.
pages.title: We trace role moves and the addition of skills, modeling their link to lifetime earnings

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_39.jpg
pages.abstract: This page illustrates the skill distance and new skills acquired by individuals as they transition between roles. It compares the weighted share of non-overlapping skills required in each new role, showing the skill distance and the number of new skills gained. Examples include transitions from a welder to a maintenance supervisor and from an office clerk to a store manager, highlighting the increasing specialization and complexity of skills required in higher roles.
pages.title: We identify new skills individuals acquire or begin to deploy with each role move.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_40.jpg
pages.abstract: This page details the scope and limitations of the data sample used in the research, including data sources, sample creation, and analysis methods. It highlights the focus on role changes, skill distances, and salary changes across four countries, with a subset of profiles for entry-level jobs. The data is harmonized and reweighted for accurate comparisons.
pages.title: Our data sample: Scope and limitations

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_41.jpg
pages.abstract: The analysis faces limitations including self-reporting biases, imperfect representation of low-paid workers, generalized salary assumptions, inability to fully separate experience effects, and limited personal and demographic data.
pages.title: Limitations of the Analysis

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_42.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how work experience contributes significantly to lifetime earnings, estimating that it accounts for about half of human capital value in four focus countries. It explains the methodology used to attribute salary increases to work experience and highlights the importance of education as a foundational factor. The analysis shows that work experience contributes 40-43% of lifetime earnings in advanced economies, with variations across countries.
pages.title: Skills gained through work experience contribute about half of lifetime earnings, varying by country

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_43.jpg
pages.abstract: This page illustrates the impact of work experience on lifetime earnings across the US, Germany, UK, and India. It shows that work experience contributes significantly to earnings, with the highest impact in India. The data is presented through graphs showing the share of earnings associated with work experience versus entry-level skills over time.
pages.title: Work experience accounts for 40 to 43 percent of average lifetime earnings in the advanced economies we studied, and 58 percent in India

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_44.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how work experience significantly influences lifetime earnings, especially for those starting in occupations with low educational barriers. It highlights the importance of on-the-job learning and training in emerging economies and compares the experience effect across different occupations in the United States, emphasizing the role of initial education versus work experience in determining lifetime earnings.
pages.title: Work experience is a bigger determinant for people who start in occupations without significant credentialing barriers

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_45.jpg
pages.abstract: This page compares the share of lifetime earnings associated with work experience in the United States and India, categorized by starting occupational roles. It highlights that in occupations with lower education requirements, work experience contributes more significantly to lifetime earnings. The data also shows differences in educational attainment levels between the most and least experience-driven occupations.
pages.title: Work experience accounts for a greater share of lifetime earnings in occupations with lower education requirements.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_46.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses how the experience effect varies widely by occupation in the United States. It highlights that individuals in different starting occupations have varying lifetime earnings and reliance on work experience. For instance, physicians earn significantly more than waiters and are less reliant on work experience, while commercial pilots derive a significant share of their earnings from skills learned through work experience. Maintenance and repair workers earn less-than-average wages over their lifetimes. The document also notes that starting occupations with higher lifetime earnings have a smaller share attributable to work experience, and similar patterns are observed in other countries like the United Kingdom, Germany, and India.
pages.title: The experience effect varies widely by occupation.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_47.jpg
pages.abstract: The document compares the reliance on work experience versus entry-level skills for different occupations over time. It shows that commercial pilots and physicians have a higher reliance on work experience, with their salaries increasing significantly over 30 years. In contrast, restaurant servers and maintenance workers have a higher reliance on entry-level skills, with smaller salary increases over time.
pages.title: Individuals starting in different occupations have varying degrees of reliance on work experience.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_48.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how occupations significantly influence the role of work experience in building human capital more than sectors do. It highlights the varying shares of lifetime earnings from work experience across different sectors and occupations in countries like the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, and India, emphasizing the importance of specific occupations within sectors.
pages.title: Occupations matter more than sectors in determining the role of work experience in building human capital

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_49.jpg
library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_50.jpg
pages.title: Man riding a bicycle in urban setting

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_51.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of movement in career roles for maximizing experience and earnings. It highlights that changing roles, especially into positions that stretch skills, can significantly boost lifetime earnings. It also notes that while education generally correlates with higher earnings, some individuals defy this trend through strategic career moves. The page emphasizes the need for employers to recognize the potential within people beyond traditional educational credentials.
pages.title: 3. Movement matters

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_52.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how some individuals defy educational disadvantages to achieve higher lifetime earnings than their peers with more education. It highlights that 28% of high school graduates and 37% of associate degree holders earn more than the median of those with higher degrees. The page also presents a chart showing lifetime earnings by education level, emphasizing the potential for upward mobility despite initial disadvantages.
pages.title: Although higher education generally leads to higher lifetime earnings, some people defy the odds.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_53.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how role moves, especially job switching, can unlock higher earnings. It highlights that 60-80% of lifetime earnings for upwardly mobile cohorts are linked to work experience, compared to 35-55% for others. More than 80% of role moves involve joining a new employer. The page also notes that while some moves result in lower-paying roles, many lead to significant wage increases, with 40-50% of observed moves involving salary boosts of 30-45%.
pages.title: Role moves can unlock higher earnings—and most job changes involve people moving to new organizations

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_54.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how workers' role moves boosted earnings by up to 30 to 45 percent and added significant new skills. It analyzes data from the United States, Germany, United Kingdom, and India, showing the average increase in salary and median skill distance for all moves and income-increasing moves. The content highlights the importance of bold moves for higher rewards and the need for individuals to reinvent themselves in new environments for senior roles.
pages.title: Moves made by workers in our sample boosted earnings by up to 30 to 45 percent while adding significant new skills.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_55.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the dynamics of upward career moves, emphasizing the value of skills and opportunities. It highlights the challenges faced by individuals in making bold career changes and the factors influencing their decisions. The page also presents data on the frequency and skill distance of moves made by upwardly mobile workers in the US, Germany, and the UK. A hypothetical billing clerk's career progression is used as an example to illustrate the potential benefits of strategic career moves.
pages.title: How a billing clerk made moves to move up

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_56.jpg
pages.abstract: The document illustrates how experience and role moves significantly contribute to workers moving into higher earning quintiles in the United States and Germany. It provides detailed data on the share of individuals, experience capital, role moves, and average skill distance across different quintiles. The analysis shows that 30% of workers in the United States and 32% in Germany are on track to move into a higher quintile. The data is presented in a visual format with flow diagrams and tables, highlighting the progression of workers from their starting points to their final positions.
pages.title: In each country we studied, experience and role moves enable a significant share of workers to move into higher earning quintiles.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_57.jpg
pages.abstract: This page presents data on how experience and role moves enable workers in the United Kingdom and India to move into higher-earning quintiles. It includes detailed statistics on the share of individuals, experience capital, role moves, and average skill distance for each quintile, showing that a significant percentage of workers are on track to move into higher quintiles.
pages.title: Exhibit 11 (continued): Experience and role moves enable workers to move into higher-earning quintiles

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_58.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the career progression of UK customer service representatives, highlighting that 58% of those who started in the lowest earnings bracket moved roles frequently, acquiring new skills like digital design and solution architecture. This upward mobility led them to roles such as web administrators and sales managers, with a significant skill distance between their starting and final roles.
pages.title: A quarter of the UK customer service reps who started in the lowest earnings bracket are on a path to move into the top two quintiles.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_59.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the career progression of service sales representatives in India who started in the bottom quintile of earnings. Half of this group remains at the bottom, while the other half advances into higher lifetime earnings brackets by acquiring new skills such as leadership, process management, and strategic thinking. The exhibit illustrates the distribution of these representatives across different earnings quintiles and the skills they acquire.
pages.title: Almost half of the service sales reps in India who started in the bottom quintile of earnings are on a trajectory that puts them into higher quintiles.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_60.jpg
pages.abstract: The document examines the career trajectories of individuals in computer occupations in the US, focusing on those who started in the third quintile of earnings. It highlights that those who moved to higher quintiles made more frequent role changes with greater skill distances, often acquiring higher-level technical skills. Conversely, those who dropped to lower quintiles also experienced significant skill shifts, though their roles were less specialized and lower-paying. The analysis underscores the importance of skill acquisition and role mobility in career progression.
pages.title: A US occupational example shows that moves into both higher and lower earning quintiles involve significant skill distances.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_61.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses four archetypes of career movers—Experience seekers, Early movers, Late movers, and Lock-ins—based on their career trajectory patterns. Experience seekers make the most moves and bold moves, resulting in strong wage growth. Early movers make bolder moves early in their careers. Late movers make incremental moves early and bolder moves later. Lock-ins make only incremental moves. The data is consistent across Germany, the US, UK, and India, highlighting the impact of career moves on lifetime earnings.
pages.title: 'Experience seekers' and 'early movers' boost their earnings through effective career moves

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_62.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses career movement strategies, categorizing individuals into early movers, late movers, and lock-ins. It highlights the impact of automation on career trajectories and the need for facilitating learning and role transitions. The COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated remote and hybrid work, intensifying opportunities and challenges for learning through experience.
pages.title: The future of work creates new urgency for facilitating learning and role moves

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_63.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses how occupations with high reliance on work experience and lower lifetime earnings are more susceptible to automation. It highlights that 134 occupations, contributing to 15% of the labor force, have high remote work potential and high reliance on experience. These roles include credit analysts, data entry keyers, and editors, offering new opportunities for workers as companies expand hiring beyond traditional boundaries.
pages.title: Occupations that are more reliant on work experience and have lower lifetime earnings are more susceptible to automation.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_64.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the challenges of remote work in a distributed world, highlighting the limited remote work potential for lower-pay, experience-reliant occupations. It emphasizes the need for workers to acquire new skills and make seamless transitions in the face of ongoing technological change.
pages.title: Remote Work Potential and Career Mobility

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_65.jpg
pages.abstract: The exhibit illustrates that occupations with higher reliance on work experience and lower lifetime earnings have limited potential for remote work. It shows a correlation between the share of lifetime earnings associated with work experience and the potential for remote work, with food servers and agricultural workers having a lower share of earnings and low remote work potential, while lawyers and financial managers have a higher share of earnings and higher remote work potential.
pages.title: Occupations that are more reliant on work experience and have lower lifetime earnings have limited potential for remote work.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_66.jpg
pages.abstract: Alice, a young UK worker, transitions from odd jobs to sales, then to computer support, and finally to marketing. She enhances her skills through online courses and job moves, eventually becoming a senior marketing manager with a fulfilling career.
pages.title: Alice: The early mover

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_67.jpg
pages.abstract: Karla, a high school graduate, transitions from administrative roles to become a successful regional sales manager in real estate. Dhruv, a taxi driver, dreams of a sales job to better support his family but struggles due to his busy schedule.
pages.title: Karla: The late mover

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_68.jpg
pages.abstract: Bill, an Indiana-born warehouse worker, transitions through various roles, from quality control to electrician, and eventually founds an energy-efficiency consultancy. His journey highlights continuous learning and adapting to new challenges, culminating in a successful business venture.
pages.title: Bill: The experience seeker

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_69.jpg
library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_70.jpg
pages.title: Engineering Collaboration

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_71.jpg
pages.abstract: This chapter discusses how individuals and employers can maximize the value of work experience. It highlights the importance of effective organizations that prioritize learning and development, especially early in a career. It also explores the role of employers in recognizing potential in candidates and creating opportunities for skill development. The chapter emphasizes the benefits of worker mobility for both individuals and the broader economy, while noting the challenges posed by tight labor markets and rapid technological changes.
pages.title: 4. Shaping experience: Opportunities for employers and workers

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_72.jpg
pages.abstract: Effective organizations, particularly those with strong organizational health, offer significant upward mobility for employees through structured learning, development programs, and internal advancement opportunities. Top quintile companies provide more training hours and internal moves, leading to higher earning brackets and career growth compared to bottom quintile companies.
pages.title: Healthy organizations that emphasize employee development are engines of upward mobility

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_73.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses how early exposure to effective organizations and bold role moves significantly influence individuals' experience capital. Effective organizations are characterized by higher training hours, more internal moves, and better organizational health. Workers in top-quintile firms are more likely to move into higher earning quintiles compared to those in bottom-quintile firms.
pages.title: Most of the differences in individuals' experience capital are associated with early exposure to an effective organization, followed by bold role moves.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_74.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of employee happiness, health, and welfare in the workplace. It highlights the need for organizations to assess their offerings, including compensation, work environment, and benefits, to meet employees' needs. The text also emphasizes the role of good management practices and the impact of family care demands on employee decisions.
pages.title: A new spotlight on employees' happiness, health, and welfare

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_75.jpg
pages.abstract: Employers can attract and retain talent by recognizing potential, embracing mobility, and strengthening learning. This involves understanding the potential in people beyond their current skills, selecting candidates based on their potential, and challenging the status quo of hiring practices. By doing so, organizations can boost productivity and engagement, and retain top talent for longer.
pages.title: Employers can attract and retain talent by recognizing potential, embracing mobility, and strengthening learning

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_76.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the shift towards skills-based hiring, emphasizing the need for new assessment techniques and digital tools. It highlights the importance of hiring unconventional candidates, embracing employee mobility, setting expectations for managerial development, and celebrating the movement of talented workers.
pages.title: Make skills assessment fit for purpose

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_77.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of lateral opportunities, defining future career pathways, prioritizing coaching and apprenticeship, and strengthening coaching for employee development. It highlights the benefits of mobility, internal digital platforms, AI-driven career suggestions, and day-to-day training for skill enhancement.
pages.title: Emphasize lateral opportunities as much as linear progression

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_78.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses strategies for employee learning and development, emphasizing structured onboarding, personalized coaching, and effective formal learning programs. It highlights the importance of a multichannel approach and measuring outcomes for successful corporate learning initiatives.
pages.title: Learning and Development Strategies for Employees

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_79.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the value of external learning opportunities for employees, highlighting partnerships between large employers and educational institutions. It also addresses the issue of job switching, distinguishing between healthy career development and dysfunctional churn, and emphasizes the importance of addressing job churn to maintain organizational health.
pages.title: Consider offering employees external learning opportunities

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_80.jpg
pages.abstract: The pandemic has led to the Great Resignation, with millions quitting bad jobs for better opportunities. However, not everyone can make such moves due to financial, housing, and social constraints. The labor market is dynamic, but challenges remain for women, minorities, and those in low-wage jobs. Workers are reassessing their lives, considering factors like work-life balance and growth potential. Transparency about employer opportunities and flexible hiring practices can help workers make informed decisions.
pages.title: Workers should navigate their careers with intention—and choose their employers carefully

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_81.jpg
pages.abstract: Policy makers should recognize the role of companies in cultivating workforce skills by supporting workforce training and encouraging nationally recognized credentials. Governments can incentivize corporate investment in human capital and play a convening role for coalitions. Initiatives like the Pact for Skills and Rework America Alliance aim to train workers and enable career advancement. Systems like Europass Digital Credentials and T3 Innovation Network enhance skill verification and transparency.
pages.title: Policy makers should recognize and encourage the role of companies in cultivating workforce skills

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_82.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the need to reassess labor market regulations for healthy worker mobility and the importance of investing in health and education in developing economies. It highlights challenges such as licensing barriers, noncompete contracts, high housing costs, and the reliance on informal jobs in poorer countries. The text emphasizes the role of education in reducing informal employment and the need for early-stage human capital development.
pages.title: Reassess whether labor markets enable healthy worker mobility

pages.title: Technical appendix

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_86.jpg
pages.abstract: This page explains occupational categories, occupations, and role trajectories, detailing how they are defined and categorized based on knowledge, skills, abilities, and career paths.
pages.title: Occupational categories, occupations, and role trajectory

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_87.jpg
pages.abstract: This appendix details the methodology for analyzing lifetime earnings, skill distances, salary changes, and experience shares using data from millions of professional profiles and job postings across four countries. It explains the creation of a worker data set and the harmonization of data for accurate role, salary, and skill comparisons.
pages.title: B. Methodology

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_88.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the estimation of lifetime earnings for a subset of workers across four countries, using online professional profiles and reweighted data to reflect the 2019 occupational mix. It explains the methodology for calculating earnings, including the use of job postings and government statistics, and the harmonization of occupation codes.
pages.title: Lifetime earnings

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_89.jpg
pages.abstract: This page explains the methodology for estimating salaries per occupation using a log-linear model and projecting future earnings. It also details the estimation of skill distance per role move using job posting data and online professional profiles.
pages.title: Salaries per occupation are estimated using a log-linear model with the following specification

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_90.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the calculation of skill distance and salary change per role move, emphasizing the importance of specialized skills and their impact on upward mobility. It also explores the experience share of lifetime earnings, attributing earnings to work experience and entry-level skills.
pages.title: Skill distance and salary change per role move

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_91.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the experience share of lifetime earnings, attributing salary increases to work experience and measuring it in absolute terms. It explains the conservative assumption of average salary increases based on terminal occupation and the impact of role moves on earnings. The experience capital is calculated as a percentage of lifetime earnings, and factors affecting the share of earnings from entry-level skills are detailed.
pages.title: Experience share of lifetime earnings

pages.page_path: library_pages\Human capital at work_ The value of experience_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_92.jpg
pages.abstract: This page details the observed work history and projections of earnings for a marketing assistant over 30 years, showing the progression in salary, skills, and experience. It highlights the decreasing proportion of entry-level skills and increasing experience as roles change, with a final projection of earnings and skill distribution.
pages.title: Observed work history and projections of earnings

pages.abstract: This page discusses the drivers of experience capital, analyzing data from 65,554 individuals across 362 companies. It explores the impact of organizational practices, role mobility, and bolder role moves on experience capital, finding significant statistical associations. The study uses regression analysis and control variables to measure these effects.
pages.title: 5. Drivers associated with experience capital
