The page presents data on M&A deals, including total deal value by size, share of deal volume by size, and share of cross-border deals. It also lists the top 10 global deals by value, highlighting major acquirers and targets. The data is sourced from Dealogic and McKinsey analysis.
The document provides an overview of M&A activity in the TMT sector in 2024, highlighting significant investments, regional focus, and deal sizes. It discusses trends in technology, media, and telecommunications subsectors, emphasizing software, infrastructure, and visual media deals. The outlook for 2025 includes increased M&A growth, cost pressures, new technologies, and regulatory changes, with a focus on market leadership and capital-expenditure-fueled growth in the technology sector.
This page discusses trends in M&A activity, focusing on AI investments, bolt-on acquisitions, the role of private equity in tech, and media subsector activity. It highlights shifts in AI spending, the importance of specialized skills, PE investments, and emerging trends in media separations and consolidation.
The telecommunications sector faces regulatory limits on consolidation but continues to pursue strategic partnerships and M&A activities. Operators aim to share network costs, diversify into new revenue streams, and streamline core businesses. Infrastructure deals, especially in 5G and data centers, are prominent, with PE and sovereign-wealth funds playing key roles. Future consolidation and partnerships will address capital-intensive growth challenges.
This page discusses the new normal of uncertainty in M&A, highlighting six key perspectives: historical macroeconomic comparisons, deal metrics, cross-border M&A, deal synergies, alternative deal types, and private equity. It emphasizes the need for a multifaceted approach to understand the complexities and challenges in the current M&A landscape.
This page discusses historical macroeconomic comparisons, highlighting similarities and differences between current and past economic downturns. It emphasizes that while deal prices have declined, uncertainties related to the US presidential election year in 2024 are a factor. The page also notes that recent economic challenges are not isolated incidents but part of a broader pattern of forces and shocks affecting various industries and regions.
The document discusses how M&A activity lags behind economic downturns due to heightened uncertainty. It highlights the impact of various crises, such as the Dot-com bubble, the Financial and eurozone crisis, the COVID-19 pandemic, and the 2022 invasion of Ukraine by Russia, on M&A transactions. The text also addresses regulatory changes affecting M&A, particularly in the United States, and the uncertainty surrounding these changes.
The page discusses the impact of uncertainty on M&A transactions, highlighting declining foreign direct investment in Europe, changes in tariff policy, global supply chain strains, geopolitical tensions, and carbon constraints. It presents data on M&A transaction values, oil prices, leverage ratios, inflation, and political stability from 2000 to 2024, showing how various crises have affected these metrics.
The document discusses the decline in deal volume and multiples in recent years, attributing it to economic uncertainties and shocks. It highlights the impact of macroeconomic challenges, customer sentiment, funding costs, and market volatility on M&A activity. The analysis also notes the global nature of these trends and the varied dynamics across industries and geographies.
This page presents key M&A metrics from 2000 to 2024, including transaction values, enterprise value to EBITDA ratios, federal funds rates, customer sentiment, IPO net proceeds, and IPO numbers. It highlights that while some M&A data points like reduced IPO proceeds are stark, other trend lines are not as clear. The page also discusses cross-border M&A, noting that companies have pivoted to gain access to the Americas despite global uncertainty.
The Americas led global M&A activity in 2024, with cross-border deals increasing in value and volume. Approximately 60% of intercontinental deals over $500 million involved EMEA and the Americas, while APAC and Americas deals accounted for 26%. Cross-border M&A is trending up, bringing higher valuations despite declining trends in individual countries.
The document discusses the increasing trend of announced synergies in M&A transactions, particularly in 2024, despite uncertainties. It highlights the significant rise in cost and revenue synergies since 2015, influenced by factors like the COVID-19 pandemic and market uncertainties. The text also mentions the need for boards to be more convinced by M&A deals and the role of proficient corporate acquirers.
Alternative deal types, such as joint ventures and alliances, have become more prevalent in recent years, reflecting a shift towards earlier-stage acquisitions and access to functional capabilities. These structures help reduce dependencies on interest rate fluctuations and manage funding gaps, especially in uncertain times. The share of minority investments has also increased following recent economic shocks.
Private equity funds are holding more dry powder in 2024, with their share of M&A deals below historical highs. Increased pressure to exit and deliver higher returns is driving PE firms to engage in more dealmaking, despite the uncertainty in recent years.
Dealmakers are adopting cautious strategies, slowing M&A activities due to limited risk appetite, selective deal sourcing, holistic assessments, and a sentiment of decline in the current economic climate. Industries exposed to exogenous factors are particularly affected.
Dealmakers are adopting a more deliberate approach to M&A, focusing on rigorous due diligence and strategic criteria. Amid uncertainty, they seek opportunities through a bolder stance, leveraging less active markets for value-accretive deals and creative deal structuring. Companies with a programmatic approach to M&A are more likely to create value, showing greater resilience and alignment with strategic plans. Purposeful M&A, despite challenges, offers higher excess TSR and no-regret actions for value creation.
This page discusses the importance of effective separations for companies to outperform their peers. It highlights the opportunities and complexities involved in achieving a successful separation, based on the latest survey.
This page discusses how successful companies recognize the need for business separations, anticipate challenges, and take practical steps to execute them effectively. It highlights key findings from a survey of experienced leaders, emphasizing the importance of speed and the complexity of separations. The page aims to share compelling lessons learned from the survey.
Companies that regularly refresh their business portfolio through a programmatic approach achieve better outcomes in separations, with higher success rates and better resource control compared to single separation approaches. This underscores the value of accumulated experience and strategic management in corporate separations.
The page discusses programmatic separators' plans to continue separations, highlighting that 69% will increase or maintain their separation activities. It emphasizes the importance of speed in separation success, with faster closures leading to better TSR outcomes. Board deliberations are identified as a critical source of delay, often leading to resource overruns and project setbacks. The text underscores the need for early board clarity and addresses various concerns that boards consider during separations.
This page discusses the importance of addressing board concerns early in separation processes to avoid delays and resource overruns. It highlights the impact of board delays on project timing and resources, common concerns that delay decision-making, and provides a case study of ChemCo. The text emphasizes the need for clear, data-driven arguments and thorough planning to ensure successful separation.
This page discusses the challenges faced by companies during separations, highlighting the most common sticking points such as TSA duration and pricing, talent allocation, and technology architecture. It emphasizes the need for proactive management of discussions between RemainCo and NewCo to ensure a successful transition.
This page discusses the challenges of negotiating transitional service agreements (TSAs) and long-term agreements (LTAs) during business separations. It highlights that 42% of survey respondents identified TSAs as a top challenge, with difficulties in defining scope, pricing, and governance. The page also presents data on significant sticking points and challenges in finalizing TSAs and LTAs, emphasizing the complexity of these negotiations.
This page discusses the challenges of negotiating long-term agreements (LTAs) in divestitures and the importance of talent allocation. It highlights the need for effective leadership to frame separations as opportunities for all employees, not just top performers. The text emphasizes the critical role of talent retention mechanisms and the survey findings on the success of talent strategies.
The document discusses the importance of talent retention programs in separations, showing that both NewCo and RemainCo benefit from such programs, though the impact is more pronounced for NewCo. It highlights common retention levers like retention bonuses and leadership opportunities, noting that the use of these levers is fairly equal between the two entities, except for acknowledgment and salary review.
Survey responses highlight the importance of proactive management, strategic use of TSAs, and comprehensive planning in achieving successful separations. Delays can cause setbacks and overruns, emphasizing the need for early data-driven arguments to address board concerns.
This page discusses the importance of proactive risk management and strategic leadership in successful corporate separations. It highlights the need for identifying disruptions, mitigating risks, and structured planning to achieve better business outcomes. The authors emphasize the role of steering committees and separation management offices in orchestrating separation processes. The page concludes with acknowledgments to contributors.
This page discusses the challenges of M&A in the automotive industry and highlights creative solutions for dealmaking. It introduces the authors and sets the stage for lessons learned from the industry.
The document discusses the challenges faced by the automotive sector in M&A activities, highlighting a 20-year low in 2023 and the impact of global transitions such as the rise of Chinese OEMs and battery electric vehicles. It also addresses broader industry challenges like competitive markets and regulatory conditions.
The article discusses the challenges and opportunities in automotive M&A deals, emphasizing the importance of acting swiftly. It highlights the industry's transformative shifts, including digitalization, electric vehicles, and geopolitical factors, and their implications for dealmaking.
The document discusses the low valuation multiples in the automotive industry due to high exposure to sunset assets. Traditional buyers and financial investors are showing limited interest in acquisitions, except for a few funds focused on restructurings. The median global-forward market multiples for top companies are robust compared to challenged automotive segments.
Automotive companies face challenges in divesting assets due to a lack of buyers. Effective dealmakers expand the universe of potential buyers beyond traditional competitors, targeting geographies like India, the Middle East, and Greater China, and identifying partners with complementary capabilities for synergies. This approach helps in achieving expansion opportunities and managing declining assets.
This page discusses strategies for sellers to enhance their business value before transactions, including transformation initiatives, tailored deal narratives, and alternative financing methods to attract a broader range of buyers.
This page discusses how sellers can expand potential buyers through alternative financing methods like earn outs, seller financing, and stock swaps. It highlights the benefits and examples of these methods, emphasizing their role in reducing financial burdens and aligning interests. Additionally, it explores alternative transaction structures such as spin-offs and joint ventures, which can enhance strategic flexibility and innovation in the automotive industry.
The automotive industry is witnessing strategic combinations through partnerships and joint ventures, enhancing innovation and resource efficiency. Examples include collaborations for electric vehicles, fuel cell stacks, and battery recycling. Despite challenges, proactive dealmakers find creative solutions for M&A, creating value for all parties involved.
This page discusses the growing role of generative AI in M&A processes, highlighting its potential to enhance various stages of M&A, from target sourcing to integration. It emphasizes the need for a programmatic approach and the benefits of gen AI in improving decision-making and resource allocation, ultimately creating long-term value for organizations.
This page presents a visual representation of energy industry subindustry clusters using generative AI. It highlights potential M&A targets and their specific sets of keywords. The clusters include virtual power plant management, renewable-energy operations, energy monitoring software, building performance management, grid analytics, water monitoring, smart meters, EV-charging software, and carbon management, each with a percentage share of the industry.
This page discusses how Gen AI tools can expedite diligence and negotiation processes in M&A, summarize key documents, and automate various tasks. It also highlights the importance of executing integrations or separations efficiently to capture synergies and avoid value loss. Tools like McKinsey’s myIMO are evolving to provide fast, smart answers and automate post-day-one activities.
This page discusses how senior leaders can enhance their M&A capabilities using Gen AI, focusing on assessing past deals, calculating deal impacts, and generating insights. It emphasizes the importance of prioritizing AI use cases and deciding whether to develop or adopt solutions, while considering the company's M&A strategy and team resources.
This page discusses the importance of establishing appropriate guardrails for generative AI (Gen AI) in business, highlighting risks such as security breaches and intellectual property infringement. It emphasizes the need for human oversight and ethical standards in AI applications. The text also mentions the strategic opportunities that Gen AI presents, such as focusing on high-value activities like relationship building. Finally, it notes the growing role of Gen AI in M&A and the need to monitor its impact.
This page discusses five critical actions CEOs must take during M&A transactions, based on McKinsey research and interviews with global leaders. It highlights the importance of CEO involvement in ensuring successful M&A processes.
The CEO's agenda involves addressing global business concerns and leveraging M&A as a strategic tool. CEOs must focus on strategy, deal size, stakeholder management, capabilities, and culture to ensure M&A success. Defining M&A priorities within the long-term corporate strategy is crucial for identifying opportunities and mounting strategic responses.
This page discusses the role of CEOs in M&A, emphasizing the importance of focusing on strategic considerations and delegating detailed tasks. It highlights the need for CEOs to engage with a shortlist of opportunities that align with corporate strategy and to be directly involved in transformative deals, serving as deal champions throughout all phases.
This page discusses the CEO's role in smaller M&A deals, emphasizing strategic alignment, value creation, and stakeholder management. It highlights the importance of the CEO as a 'chief stakeholder officer,' managing expectations with the target CEO and the board of directors to ensure successful integration and value capture.
The target company CEO plays a crucial role in M&A deals, providing insights into strategies and culture, and aiding the acquiring company's CEO. Effective communication with the board and stakeholders is vital for deal success, fostering trust and transparency throughout the process.
This page discusses the importance of conviction, capacity, and capabilities for successful M&A execution. It highlights the CEO's role in securing organizational conviction and building a management team with the necessary capacity and capabilities. It also emphasizes the significance of a healthy organizational culture for M&A success.
CEOs play a crucial role in M&A by assessing cultures, aligning skills, and ensuring cultural compatibility. They must invest time in due diligence, build relationships, and communicate the vision for the combined company's culture. Establishing guardrails and delegating tasks to a dedicated team is key to successful integration.
This page discusses the importance of organizational culture in M&A transactions, highlighting the risks of cultural misalignment and the benefits of addressing cultural factors. It emphasizes the need for executives to diagnose cultural issues, set priorities, and establish a clear cultural transformation plan to ensure successful integrations.
Leaders should diagnose work processes, set cultural priorities, and support cultural change in M&A discussions. Early involvement of stakeholders and using diagnostics like surveys and interviews can help understand cultural aspects and build common norms.
Leaders must set cultural priorities using data on existing cultures, addressing common friction points like decision-making and communication styles. They should redefine roles, introduce new cultural artifacts, and serve as role models for behavioral changes. Concrete initiatives and KPIs can support desired cultural shifts.
This page discusses the importance of hard-wiring cultural changes into a company's operating model and daily practices. It emphasizes the role of leadership in creating a culture of respect, implementing signature initiatives, empowering change agents, and tracking the implementation of themes and initiatives with the same rigor as financial targets. The page concludes by highlighting the critical role of culture in mergers and acquisitions.
This page discusses a strategy for managing talent during M&A transactions, emphasizing the importance of retaining and engaging top talent throughout the process to create value. It highlights the critical phases of M&A and offers insights into addressing talent needs effectively.
This page discusses the paradox in M&A transactions where top talent may leave, causing operational risks and value loss. It highlights the importance of retaining critical talent through strategic steps before, during, and after integrations, emphasizing communication, incentives, and employee value proposition.
This page discusses the importance of identifying and categorizing crucial employee groups in both the target and parent companies before a deal is announced. It emphasizes the need to consider employees at all levels and highlights the significance of nonfinancial incentives in retaining top talent. The page also stresses the role of senior leaders in shaping messaging and conveying empathy to maintain business continuity and future success.
This page discusses strategies for maintaining stability and focus during the period between a deal announcement and its close in M&A transactions. It emphasizes the importance of effective communication, leadership actions, and the role of frontline managers in retaining top talent and ensuring employee engagement throughout the integration process.
Metrics are crucial for performance management, especially in transitions. Leaders should monitor retention metrics, conduct exit interviews, and use tools like dashboards and toolkits to maintain communication and lower attrition. Post-deal, solidifying engagement involves combating change fatigue and creating unity among employees.
This page discusses the importance of a redesigned Employee Value Proposition (EVP) post-merger and acquisition (M&A) to align with the new company's direction. It highlights a B2B electronic-materials player's large-scale organizational transformation and the need for a revised EVP. The page emphasizes integrating five core elements of the EVP into daily work and the role of 'cultivation leaders' in retaining talent. It concludes by stressing the critical role of talent in deal theses and the need for a fit-for-purpose retention strategy.

pages.title: McKinsey China Auto Consumer Insights 2024

pages.abstract: This page provides an overview of a survey conducted in Q4 2023, involving 2,449 auto buyers across 19 Chinese cities. It details the demographic diversity of respondents and the survey's focus on consumer attitudes, vehicle preferences, and purchasing behaviors.
pages.title: About the survey

pages.abstract: The rapid development in electrification and smartification is shaping Chinese auto consumers' preferences. McKinsey's survey reveals key trends: consumers are trading up to mid-and high-priced smart EVs, perceptions of EV and ICE brands are diverging, and while EV penetration rises, charging anxiety persists due to infrastructure challenges.
pages.title: Executive summary

pages.abstract: This page discusses key trends in the Chinese auto consumer market, including the success of the DTC model, challenges in monetizing autonomous driving technologies, and consumer attitudes toward low-carbon vehicles. It highlights evolving consumer behaviors and the industry's adaptation to meet diverse needs.
pages.title: Key Trends in the Chinese Auto Consumer Market

pages.abstract: Chinese consumers are increasingly choosing to trade up to premium vehicles, with a growing market share. The desire to trade down has decreased compared to a year ago. Despite intense price competition, consumption stimulation remains limited.
pages.title: Consumers are continuing the trend of trading up

pages.abstract: Chinese consumers are increasingly upgrading to premium vehicles, with the market share of premium models rising from 10% in 2016 to 23% in 2023. The desire to trade up is particularly strong among those with existing cars priced below RMB 200,000. Premium smart-EV models are attracting rational consumer groups in higher price segments.
pages.title: The desire to trade up is boosting sales of premium vehicles

pages.abstract: The exhibit shows Chinese consumers' strong desire to upgrade their vehicles, with a detailed comparison of their budget for the next car versus the price of their current car. The data reveals trends in preferences for staying in the same price range, trading up, or paying less, across different price brackets for both 2022 and 2023.
pages.title: Chinese consumers' desire to upgrade their vehicle remains strong

pages.abstract: The share of consumers planning to downgrade their car purchases has significantly decreased in 2023 compared to 2022. Factors contributing to this trend include increased enthusiasm for new cars post-pandemic and the introduction of highly competitive smart EV models with advanced features, shifting consumer attention to higher-priced segments.
pages.title: The share of consumers seeking a downgrade has fallen significantly

pages.abstract: The page discusses the limited impact of price competition on stimulating car consumption in China. Survey results show that 64.1% of consumers are neutral, 16.4% are negatively impacted, and 19.4% are positively impacted by price competition. The majority of consumers report no positive role for price competition in their purchase decisions.
pages.title: Price competition that has been occurring in China has had a limited impact on stimulating consumption

pages.abstract: Price competition has a limited net impact on volume segment consumers, with higher net impact observed in the high-price segment. Consumers in lower price segments are more hesitant, while those in higher price segments respond positively to favorable prices.
pages.title: Price competition have limited net impact for volume segment consumers, and may even result in losses

pages.abstract: This page discusses the diverging perceptions of EV and ICE brands, highlighting how consumer preferences are shifting. Chinese EV brands are gaining traction due to smartification, while traditional MNC brands face challenges. Consumers' views on Chinese car brands are improving, and fewer are willing to pay premiums for MNC brands.
pages.title: Perceptions of EV and ICE brands are diverging

pages.abstract: The Chinese passenger vehicle market is experiencing intense competition as new EV brands gain traction and old brands phase out. Over three years, 16 new brands entered the market, while seven old brands vanished. The market share distribution shows a shift towards newer brands, with significant changes in consumer perceptions.
pages.title: Consumers' brand perceptions have significantly diverged; their initial consideration set differs according to the brand or type of car they own

pages.abstract: Chinese consumers maintain a shallow initial consideration set (ICS) of 2-3 brands when purchasing cars. Despite an increase in optional brands, 85% of final decisions come from the ICS. OEMs can benefit by actively placing their brands in consumers' ICS to capture greater mindshare.
pages.title: Chinese consumers' initial consideration set for car purchases

pages.abstract: The page presents data on the initial consideration set (ICS) of consumers who bought new cars in the past six months, categorized by traditional mass MNC and Chinese brands. It highlights the significant differences in brand preferences between MNC and Chinese buyers, with MNC buyers favoring MNC brands and Chinese buyers favoring Chinese brands.
pages.title: Consumers in the mass brand segment show different consideration in ICS (initial consideration set)

pages.abstract: The page discusses the divergent brand perceptions among mass segment ICE consumers, showing that traditional mass MNC brand owners recognize MNC brands more, while traditional mass Chinese brand owners recognize both Chinese and MNC brands but are less likely to recognize top-ranking MNC brands.
pages.title: A similar perception-diverge is happening to mass segment ICE consumers' brand recognition

pages.abstract: The survey highlights significant differences in ICS mix among premium vehicle buyers, with German brands dominating ICE and EV owners' ICS, while Chinese EV brands are rarely considered by ICE buyers but highly favored by EV buyers.
pages.title: Consumers in the premium vehicle segment also show significantly-different consideration in ICS

pages.abstract: This page discusses the divergent perceptions of premium brands between ICE and EV vehicles among consumers. Traditional MNC brands are seen as premium for ICE vehicles, while emerging EV brands, particularly American and Chinese, are favored for premium EVs. German brands rank lower in premium EV perception despite their strong ICE brand image.
pages.title: The huge difference in ICS-mix among different vehicle groups is caused by consumers' diverging perceptions on premium between ICE vs. EV

pages.abstract: The page discusses how owners of major German car brands view certain EV brands as premium. A bar chart shows the percentage of respondents who consider various EV brands as premium. The text explains that selection criteria for premium EVs differ among owners of different brands, with Chinese EV owners valuing technical advantages, while traditional premium EV owners prefer established brands.
pages.title: Even owners of the 3 major German brand owners consider EV brands more premium in the EV domain

pages.abstract: The page highlights that smart features such as better AD performance and smart cockpit performance are the top reasons consumers choose premium Chinese EV brands over traditional premium MNC brands. The survey also shows that attractive exterior design and native EV platform are significant factors. Traditional branding is less impactful compared to smart features and technology addressing range anxiety.
pages.title: Smart features are core reasons consumers given to buy EV from premium Chinese EV brands

pages.abstract: The page discusses reasons for buying EVs from traditional premium MNC brands versus premium Chinese EV brands, highlighting trust in quality, attractive design, and brand recognition as key factors. It also notes a trend of traditional premium MNC brand owners switching to premium Chinese EVs, with a higher likelihood of this switch compared to the reverse.
pages.title: Reasons for buying EV from traditional premium MNC brands, vs premium Chinese EV brands

pages.abstract: The page discusses the shift in consumer preferences from traditional premium German car brands to premium Chinese EV brands. It highlights that 24% of German brand owners consider Chinese EV brands for their next car, while only 7% of Chinese EV owners consider German brands. The improvement in Chinese car brands' quality, energy efficiency, smart features, and electrification has positively influenced consumer perceptions, challenging the dominance of traditional multinational OEMs.
pages.title: Traditional premium brand owners are almost in a “one-way flow” to be converted to customers of premium Chinese EV brands

pages.abstract: Chinese brands have significantly improved their recognition in traditional dimensions, with a notable increase in the number of Chinese brands in the top 5. In technology-intensive dimensions, Chinese brands are now recognized as market leaders, surpassing traditional MNC brands.
pages.title: Chinese brands are gaining recognition as leading brands in traditional dimensions, a big improvement vs. survey 3-years ago

pages.abstract: Chinese consumers are increasingly reluctant to pay a premium for MNC brands, with 48% of respondents showing this reluctance, up from 43% previously. This trend is evident across ICE and EV owners, with significant increases in reluctance among ICE owners. MNC brands' market share in the ICE segment has also declined, reflecting a shift in consumer preference.
pages.title: Chinese consumers are becoming increasingly reluctant to pay a price premium for MNC brands

pages.abstract: The page discusses consumer willingness to pay a premium for traditional premium MNC EV brands over Chinese EV brands. It highlights a trend where even among those willing to pay more, the acceptable premium is limited. The data shows a decline in willingness to pay premiums for MNC brands, with brand importance decreasing for EV consumers but potentially increasing as EV technology matures.
pages.title: Exhibit 19: Willingness to pay more for EV from traditional premium MNC brands over premium Chinese EV brands

pages.abstract: The document compares key buying factors (KBFs) between ICE car buyers and EV car buyers, highlighting that EV buyers prioritize practical aspects like range and charging time over branding. ICE car buyers place more importance on brand trust and static/dynamic experiences. The data is derived from the McKinsey China Auto Consumer Survey 2024.
pages.title: Not surprisingly, EV buyers are more pragmatic-oriented and have relatively lower rating on the importance of branding

pages.abstract: The survey highlights that as EV technology advances, brand importance for EV consumers may align with ICE consumers. Traditional MNC brands can regain market share if they match Chinese EV brands in smartification and electrification, with 63% of premium Chinese EV owners considering a switch.
pages.title: McKinsey China Auto Consumer Insights 2024

pages.abstract: The page discusses the rapid rise of EV adoption, driven by vehicle performance, but highlights a decline in Chinese consumers' acceptance of EVs. It emphasizes the need for better charging infrastructure to ensure long-term, sustainable EV sector growth.
pages.title: EV penetration is rising fast, with a hidden concern of charging anxiety

pages.abstract: China's EV penetration is rapidly increasing across all city tiers, driven by consumer preference for vehicle performance advantages like low TCO and smartification, rather than policy factors such as free license plates.
pages.title: EV penetration is increasing rapidly in China across all city tiers

pages.abstract: The chart illustrates the reasons consumers consider purchasing an EV, with lower fuel cost and smartification being the top factors. The preference ranking shows a shift over the years, with smartification rising to the second position in 2023. Other factors like lower maintenance cost, attractive appearance, and environmental friendliness also play significant roles.
pages.title: The growing EV penetration is triggered by consumers' stronger recognition of EV's actual benefits like smartification

pages.abstract: The page discusses the preference of Chinese consumers for PHEV and REEV vehicles due to their advantages in range and cost. It highlights a decrease in the proportion of consumers considering these options from 85% in 2022 to 71% in 2023. The reasons for preferring PHEV/REEV over BEV include range anxiety, sufficient daily range, attractive pricing, and concerns about BEV residual value and charging infrastructure.
pages.title: Consumers favor PHEV and REEV mostly based on consideration of TCO and charging

pages.abstract: Chinese consumers prefer EVs over ICE vehicles in terms of satisfaction across various dimensions, including cost, driving experience, and vehicle quality. The survey highlights the importance of addressing charging infrastructure and cost factors for long-term EV adoption.
pages.title: EV owners report greater satisfaction than ICE owners across dimensions

pages.abstract: The document discusses a decline in EV acceptance among Chinese consumers, with 62% considering an EV as their next car compared to 68% in 2022. BEV owners show a significant increase in regret, with 22% not considering another EV. The analysis links this to charging infrastructure quality, with higher regret in less developed cities. Charging experience is identified as a key factor in dissatisfaction.
pages.title: For the first time, responses signal a drop in EV acceptance, mainly in the segment owning BEV

pages.abstract: BEV owners in Tier 3 and 4 cities experience greater dissatisfaction due to limited charging infrastructure. The regret level is significantly higher in these cities compared to Tier 1 and 2 cities. The biggest gap is in charging experience, with net satisfaction lower in Tier 3/4 cities. The building of charging infrastructure in less developed regions is losing momentum. Electrification is an irreversible trend, but efforts are needed to improve and expand the EV charging network for sustainable development.
pages.title: Dissatisfaction of BEV owners is greatest in Tier 3 and 4 cities, where charging experience is hampered by limited infrastructure

pages.abstract: The DTC model enhances consumer trust through high transparency in the customer journey, improving the purchase and usage experience of vehicles.
pages.title: Direct-to-consumers (DTC) model is winning consumer trusts, thanks to its high transparency across customer journey

pages.abstract: The page discusses consumer preferences for emerging car retail models, highlighting dissatisfaction with conventional dealership models. It emphasizes the desire for transparency in various aspects of the car purchasing process, including vehicle information, experience, price, and visibility. A survey reveals that 64% of respondents are dissatisfied with the traditional dealership model, with key improvements needed in transparency of vehicle status, information, experience, price, and visibility.
pages.title: Consumers favor emerging car retail models

pages.abstract: The document highlights that premium Chinese EV brands achieve higher customer satisfaction through a DTC model compared to conventional dealership models, particularly in pre-sales stages. The net satisfaction rates for online and offline information display, as well as test drives, show a clear advantage for DTC models in 2023.
pages.title: Customers are more satisfied with the DTC model than with the conventional dealership model

pages.abstract: The sales stage of premium Chinese EV brands shows higher consumer satisfaction compared to ICE owners, particularly in price negotiation, financing options, and delivery. Premium EV brands excel with one-stop delivery centers and transparent pricing, significantly improving customer experience.
pages.title: In the sales stage, premium Chinese EV brands excel at consumer satisfaction with one-stop delivery centers, transparent pricing, and financing options

pages.abstract: The page discusses the post-sales performance of premium Chinese EV brands, highlighting their success in maintaining customer satisfaction through various engagement strategies. Despite a slight gap in maintenance satisfaction compared to traditional OEMs, the difference is minimal. The data from the McKinsey China Auto Consumer Survey 2024 supports the effectiveness of the DTC model in enhancing the overall consumer experience.
pages.title: In the post-sales stage, premium Chinese EV brands continued to excel; even in maintenance, their gap with traditional brands is marginal

pages.abstract: Consumers are increasingly interested in autonomous driving solutions, but their willingness to pay is decreasing due to pricing strategies of leading OEMs. Consumer preferences in Tier 1 cities may serve as a key indicator for overall changes in AD monetization.
pages.title: Autonomous driving (AD) enjoys great popularity, but chance of monetization is coming under pressure

pages.abstract: Chinese consumers' interest in AD functions has risen, but their willingness to pay has declined, particularly in Tier 1 cities. The importance of autonomous driving is recognized, but aggressive pricing strategies have influenced consumer perceptions and payment willingness.
pages.title: Consumer interest in various AD functions has risen, but willingness to pay has fallen

pages.abstract: The document discusses how consumers in higher-tier cities are more inclined to adopt simple and direct payment methods for AD functions due to greater awareness and experience. Tier 1 cities lead in adopting advanced AD technology, influencing consumers' willingness to pay. Consumers in lower-tier cities prefer cautious payment methods due to limited experience with advanced autonomous driving.
pages.title: Consumers in higher-tier cities are more willing to adopt simple and direct payment methods for AD

pages.abstract: The willingness and monetary amount consumers are willing to pay for AD functions are declining, except for a significant increase in fees for urban ground road AD packages. Leading OEMs' promotion of city NOA is raising consumer enthusiasm. Advanced AD technology, including city NOA, is becoming a must-have for smart EVs, putting pressure on OEMs that have not progressed in AD technology.
pages.title: The monetary amount that consumers are willing to pay for AD functions also is declining

pages.abstract: This page discusses consumer awareness of low-carbon vehicles in China. While many consumers are aware of and willing to pay for these vehicles, there has been a decline in the proportion of consumers willing to pay a premium and the amount they are willing to pay.
pages.title: Consumers are aware of low-carbon vehicles but less willing to pay a premium for them

pages.abstract: The willingness of consumers to pay a premium for low-carbon vehicles has slightly decreased from 71% in 2022 to 66% in 2023. The average premium amount they are willing to pay has also declined from ~RMB 2,660 to ~RMB 1,950. This trend reflects a reduced enthusiasm for premium low-carbon vehicles among consumers.
pages.title: Many consumers are willing to pay a premium for low-carbon vehicles, but the share willing to pay and the acceptable size of the premium have declined

pages.abstract: The page discusses consumer willingness to pay for low-carbon vehicles across different income segments, highlighting that high-income individuals are more willing to pay a premium. The data shows a decline in willingness to pay for low-carbon vehicles, influenced by public perception and urgency of decarbonization.
pages.title: High-income individuals are willing to pay the largest premium for low-carbon vehicles

pages.abstract: The China auto industry has made significant progress but faces intense price competition. While 'involution' describes intense competition, the EV sector's rapid technological and design advancements signify evolution. Despite challenges, embracing evolution is crucial for the industry's future.
pages.title: Conclusion: Involution or evolution?

pages.abstract: This page discusses how Chinese OEMs are adapting to the EV industry's evolution, highlighting shifts in product innovation, brand management, customer touchpoints, and organizational structure. It emphasizes the importance of consumer-focused strategies and value creation in a competitive landscape.
pages.title: Embracing Change in the Chinese EV Industry
McKinsey China Auto Consumer Insights 2024

Chinese consumers are increasingly reluctant to pay a premium for MNC brands, with 48% of respondents showing this reluctance, up from 43% previously. This trend is evident across ICE and EV owners, with significant increases in reluctance among ICE owners. MNC brands' market share in the ICE segment has also declined, reflecting a shift in consumer preference.
The page discusses consumer willingness to pay a premium for traditional premium MNC EV brands over Chinese EV brands. It highlights a trend where even among those willing to pay more, the acceptable premium is limited. The data shows a decline in willingness to pay premiums for MNC brands, with brand importance decreasing for EV consumers but potentially increasing as EV technology matures.
The document compares key buying factors (KBFs) between ICE car buyers and EV car buyers, highlighting that EV buyers prioritize practical aspects like range and charging time over branding. ICE car buyers place more importance on brand trust and static/dynamic experiences. The data is derived from the McKinsey China Auto Consumer Survey 2024.
The survey highlights that as EV technology advances, brand importance for EV consumers may align with ICE consumers. Traditional MNC brands can regain market share if they match Chinese EV brands in smartification and electrification, with 63% of premium Chinese EV owners considering a switch.
The page discusses the rapid rise of EV adoption, driven by vehicle performance, but highlights a decline in Chinese consumers' acceptance of EVs. It emphasizes the need for better charging infrastructure to ensure long-term, sustainable EV sector growth.
China's EV penetration is rapidly increasing across all city tiers, driven by consumer preference for vehicle performance advantages like low TCO and smartification, rather than policy factors such as free license plates.
The chart illustrates the reasons consumers consider purchasing an EV, with lower fuel cost and smartification being the top factors. The preference ranking shows a shift over the years, with smartification rising to the second position in 2023. Other factors like lower maintenance cost, attractive appearance, and environmental friendliness also play significant roles.
The page discusses the preference of Chinese consumers for PHEV and REEV vehicles due to their advantages in range and cost. It highlights a decrease in the proportion of consumers considering these options from 85% in 2022 to 71% in 2023. The reasons for preferring PHEV/REEV over BEV include range anxiety, sufficient daily range, attractive pricing, and concerns about BEV residual value and charging infrastructure.
Chinese consumers prefer EVs over ICE vehicles in terms of satisfaction across various dimensions, including cost, driving experience, and vehicle quality. The survey highlights the importance of addressing charging infrastructure and cost factors for long-term EV adoption.
The document discusses a decline in EV acceptance among Chinese consumers, with 62% considering an EV as their next car compared to 68% in 2022. BEV owners show a significant increase in regret, with 22% not considering another EV. The analysis links this to charging infrastructure quality, with higher regret in less developed cities. Charging experience is identified as a key factor in dissatisfaction.
BEV owners in Tier 3 and 4 cities experience greater dissatisfaction due to limited charging infrastructure. The regret level is significantly higher in these cities compared to Tier 1 and 2 cities. The biggest gap is in charging experience, with net satisfaction lower in Tier 3/4 cities. The building of charging infrastructure in less developed regions is losing momentum. Electrification is an irreversible trend, but efforts are needed to improve and expand the EV charging network for sustainable development.
The DTC model enhances consumer trust through high transparency in the customer journey, improving the purchase and usage experience of vehicles.
The page discusses consumer preferences for emerging car retail models, highlighting dissatisfaction with conventional dealership models. It emphasizes the desire for transparency in various aspects of the car purchasing process, including vehicle information, experience, price, and visibility. A survey reveals that 64% of respondents are dissatisfied with the traditional dealership model, with key improvements needed in transparency of vehicle status, information, experience, price, and visibility.
The document highlights that premium Chinese EV brands achieve higher customer satisfaction through a DTC model compared to conventional dealership models, particularly in pre-sales stages. The net satisfaction rates for online and offline information display, as well as test drives, show a clear advantage for DTC models in 2023.
The sales stage of premium Chinese EV brands shows higher consumer satisfaction compared to ICE owners, particularly in price negotiation, financing options, and delivery. Premium EV brands excel with one-stop delivery centers and transparent pricing, significantly improving customer experience.
The page discusses the post-sales performance of premium Chinese EV brands, highlighting their success in maintaining customer satisfaction through various engagement strategies. Despite a slight gap in maintenance satisfaction compared to traditional OEMs, the difference is minimal. The data from the McKinsey China Auto Consumer Survey 2024 supports the effectiveness of the DTC model in enhancing the overall consumer experience.
Consumers are increasingly interested in autonomous driving solutions, but their willingness to pay is decreasing due to pricing strategies of leading OEMs. Consumer preferences in Tier 1 cities may serve as a key indicator for overall changes in AD monetization.
Chinese consumers' interest in AD functions has risen, but their willingness to pay has declined, particularly in Tier 1 cities. The importance of autonomous driving is recognized, but aggressive pricing strategies have influenced consumer perceptions and payment willingness.
The document discusses how consumers in higher-tier cities are more inclined to adopt simple and direct payment methods for AD functions due to greater awareness and experience. Tier 1 cities lead in adopting advanced AD technology, influencing consumers' willingness to pay. Consumers in lower-tier cities prefer cautious payment methods due to limited experience with advanced autonomous driving.
The willingness and monetary amount consumers are willing to pay for AD functions are declining, except for a significant increase in fees for urban ground road AD packages. Leading OEMs' promotion of city NOA is raising consumer enthusiasm. Advanced AD technology, including city NOA, is becoming a must-have for smart EVs, putting pressure on OEMs that have not progressed in AD technology.
This page discusses consumer awareness of low-carbon vehicles in China. While many consumers are aware of and willing to pay for these vehicles, there has been a decline in the proportion of consumers willing to pay a premium and the amount they are willing to pay.
The willingness of consumers to pay a premium for low-carbon vehicles has slightly decreased from 71% in 2022 to 66% in 2023. The average premium amount they are willing to pay has also declined from ~RMB 2,660 to ~RMB 1,950. This trend reflects a reduced enthusiasm for premium low-carbon vehicles among consumers.
The page discusses consumer willingness to pay for low-carbon vehicles across different income segments, highlighting that high-income individuals are more willing to pay a premium. The data shows a decline in willingness to pay for low-carbon vehicles, influenced by public perception and urgency of decarbonization.
The China auto industry has made significant progress but faces intense price competition. While 'involution' describes intense competition, the EV sector's rapid technological and design advancements signify evolution. Despite challenges, embracing evolution is crucial for the industry's future.
This page discusses how Chinese OEMs are adapting to the EV industry's evolution, highlighting shifts in product innovation, brand management, customer touchpoints, and organizational structure. It emphasizes the importance of consumer-focused strategies and value creation in a competitive landscape.

65.file_name: McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01.pdf

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_1.jpg
pages.title: Private markets turn down the volume

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_2.jpg
pages.title: Disclaimer

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_3.jpg
pages.title: Contents

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_4.jpg
pages.abstract: The 2023 McKinsey report on private markets investing highlights trends such as strong tailwinds since the GFC, a slowdown in deal-making in the second half of 2022, and the impact of the denominator effect on fundraising. Despite challenges, private markets outperformed public markets during downturns.
pages.title: Executive summary

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_5.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses fundraising trends in private markets, highlighting regional disparities and investor behavior. North America showed resilience, while Asia and Europe faced challenges. Investors favored larger, established funds, leading to a significant increase in capital for funds over $5 billion. Dry powder inventory surged, indicating a substantial amount of available capital for deployment. The strengthening dollar and geopolitical factors influenced fundraising outcomes.
pages.title: Amid a pullback in commitments, an outsized share of capital flowed to the largest funds, as investors re-upped with their existing managers but reduced backing smaller and new funds.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_6.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the performance of private markets in 2022, highlighting the contraction of PE multiples, negative PE performance, real estate as an inflation hedge, growth in private debt, infrastructure fundraising, and the scaling of sustainable investing. It covers various sectors and their responses to market volatility and macroeconomic events.
pages.title: Private markets turn down the volume

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_7.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the growing impact of ESG on private markets, highlighting the need for private market firms to improve diversity, equity, and inclusion. It outlines McKinsey's role as a leading adviser and consultant in private markets, detailing the report's structure and data sources. The report emphasizes the importance of diverse deal teams and the need for fresh approaches to hiring, retention, and promotion.
pages.title: Private markets firms still have work to do on diversity

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_8.jpg
pages.abstract: 2022 saw subdued growth in private markets due to macroeconomic disruptions like high inflation and the Ukraine crisis. Fundraising fell by 11%, with regional variations, while performance declined but still outperformed public markets. Assets under management reached $11.7 trillion by June 2022, indicating steady industry growth despite challenges.
pages.title: Private markets lose momentum

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_9.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the global private markets fundraising in 2022, which totaled $1.2 trillion, a decrease of 11.4% from 2021. It analyzes the impact of the denominator effect on fundraising and allocation changes. The exhibit provides detailed fundraising data by region and asset class, showing significant year-over-year changes.
pages.title: Fundraising

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_10.jpg
pages.abstract: North America saw a 2.4% increase in private markets fundraising to $799 billion in 2022, while Europe and Asia experienced declines of 28% and 39%, respectively. Factors such as foreign-exchange effects, economic outlook, and regulatory changes influenced these trends.
pages.title: North America was the only region to record positive fundraising growth in 2022.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_11.jpg
pages.abstract: In 2022, larger funds over $5 billion raised significantly more capital, accounting for 37% of total fundraising, while smaller funds under $1 billion saw a decline. The number of funds under $1 billion decreased by 45%, while those over $5 billion increased by nearly 40%. Established GPs managing larger funds attracted significant investor commitments, with the top 20 fundraisers raising 32% of the total volume.
pages.title: Funds greater than $5 billion raised 37 percent of total fundraising.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_12.jpg
pages.abstract: The private markets AUM reached $11.7 trillion by June 30, 2022, growing at an annual rate of 18% since 2017. The chart shows the distribution of assets across regions and asset classes, with North America leading at 54% and buyout dominating private equity. A deteriorating macro environment slowed exit activity, but net asset value and dry powder continued to grow.
pages.title: Private markets AUM totaled $11.7 trillion.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_13.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the performance of private markets asset classes in 2022, noting a decline compared to 2021. Private equity (PE) experienced negative returns, while natural resources showed strong performance. Private markets outperformed public markets, with PE outperforming public indexes despite turbulent conditions. The document highlights the importance of manager selection in PE and includes a graph (Exhibit 5) showing performance by asset class from 2000 to 2022.
pages.title: Performance

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_14.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the growing importance of non-institutional capital in private markets, highlighting the performance gap between top and bottom quartile PE funds. It explains the appeal of private markets to non-institutional investors and the potential for higher returns. The page also includes an exhibit showing performance by asset class, emphasizing the wider performance gap in private equity compared to other asset classes.
pages.title: Non-institutional capital comes in to focus

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_15.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the growing trend of private markets investing for non-institutional investors, highlighting regulatory changes, structured vehicles like feeder funds, and the role of technology in promoting access. It also addresses the challenges and opportunities for private markets players in this space.
pages.title: Private Markets and Non-Institutional Investors

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_16.jpg
pages.abstract: Private equity faced significant challenges in 2022, with fundraising declining, deal-making momentum slowing, and returns disappointing. Despite these issues, AUM reached $7.6 trillion, and megafunds gained prominence. VC and growth equity saw their second-largest fundraising year, but returns fell sharply due to declining technology valuations.
pages.title: Private equity endures a tough year

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_17.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the decline in global private equity fundraising, with a 15% drop to $655 billion. Major PE strategies saw declines, with buyout down 18%. North America showed resilience with a 2% decline, while Europe and Asia saw significant drops. The shift towards larger funds in North America contributed to its relative stability.
pages.title: Fundraising

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_18.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the decline in fundraising for major private equity (PE) strategies, particularly in Asia, due to macroeconomic conditions, regulatory changes, and the impact of COVID-19. It highlights the significant drop in China-focused fundraising and explains the reasons behind it, including the accumulation of dry powder, new regulations, and logistical challenges. The page also mentions the growth in fundraising in Australia and the Australia-Pacific region, driven by large funds, and discusses the factors contributing to the overall decline in fundraising momentum.
pages.title: Each major PE strategy experienced fundraising declines greater than 10 percent.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_19.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the performance of global buyout funds across different fund sizes, highlighting that median returns were similar but spreads were larger for small-cap buyout funds. It also covers LPs' reactions to overallocation in PE, including slowing or stopping new capital allocation, selling portfolios, and raising targets. The concentration into larger funds is also addressed, noting that top managers consistently account for a significant portion of fundraising.
pages.title: Median returns were similar across fund sizes; spreads were larger for small-cap buyout funds.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_20.jpg
pages.abstract: In 2022, top 25 managers captured the largest share of PE fundraising, while managers outside the top 250 saw a decline. Larger funds saw increased fundraising, while smaller funds experienced a drop. The average fund size increased, and megafunds played a significant role in driving up fund sizes.
pages.title: Top managers captured a greater share of PE fundraising in 2022.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_21.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the decline in small private equity funds in 2022, the concentration of larger funds, and the global PE AUM growth. It highlights the challenges faced by first-time funds and the shift in AUM mix over time, with buyout and VC shares changing significantly. The page also mentions the all-time high of PE dry powder and the regional differences in AUM distribution.
pages.title: The number of small PE funds closed in 2022 fell 51 percent.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_22.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the decrease in fundraising by first-time managers in private equity, with a peak in 2017 and a decline in subsequent years. It also highlights the rebound in global inventories of PE dry powder, showing trends in private equity inventory on hand over time.
pages.title: PE fundraising by first-time managers decreased. Global inventories of PE dry powder rebounded.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_23.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the performance of private equity (PE) in 2022, noting a decline in performance compared to public markets. PE was not the highest-performing asset class for the first time in six years, with a nine-month trailing pooled net IRR of –9.2 percent. Buyout strategies showed the strongest performance, returning –6.0 percent, while venture capital and growth strategies underperformed. The graph illustrates the performance by strategy over time, highlighting the underperformance of venture capital relative to buyout since 2017.
pages.title: Performance

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_24.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the underperformance of Growth and VC strategies in private equity in 2022 compared to buyout strategies. It highlights the impact of tech-oriented strategies on buyout returns and compares public market performance. The best-performing buyout sector was energy, driven by rising commodity prices. Manager selection mattered less in 2022, and the interquartile spread of PE fund returns narrowed. Despite challenges, long-term PE returns remained resilient, outperforming other private markets asset classes over the last 15 years. The median net IRR of 2009–19 PE fund vintages exceeded the top-quartile return of other private asset classes. PE continued to outperform public markets, though valuation discretion may play a role.
pages.title: VC returns outpaced all other PE substrategies across every quartile.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_25.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the decline in private equity deal volume by 26 percent globally, with a detailed analysis of deal activity trends across different regions. It highlights that despite the decline, 2022 remained the second most active year on record for deal activity, with a strong first half. The page includes a graph showing the global private equity deal volume and count over time, emphasizing the significant drop in 2022 compared to the previous year.
pages.title: Private equity deal volume declined 26 percent.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_26.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the decline in global deal activity in the second half of 2022 due to reduced debt availability and economic uncertainty. It highlights significant decreases in deal volumes across North America, Europe, and Asia, with the most substantial impact in Asia. The report also notes the decline in buyout, growth, and VC deal volumes, with energy being the only sector to see an increase in deal volume. The data is supported by Exhibit 16, which shows the global private equity deal volume across different regions and quarters.
pages.title: Deal volume decreased across all regions in the second half of 2022

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_27.jpg
pages.abstract: The chart illustrates the decline in global PE deal volume across various sectors from 2015 to 2022. The total deal volume peaked in 2021 at $3,281 billion and then dropped to $2,420 billion in 2022. Most sectors experienced negative growth rates between 2021 and 2022, with materials and resources showing the most significant decline at -52.0%. The information technology sector had the highest compound annual growth rate (CAGR) from 2017 to 2022 at 17.4%, but still saw a -21.1% decline in 2021-2022.
pages.title: Deal activity declined across almost every sector.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_28.jpg
pages.abstract: Add-on deals have grown in popularity, accounting for 72% of buyouts in 2022. M&A strategies, including industry roll-ups, allow GPs to invest in smaller targets for potential multiples arbitrage. Exits declined significantly in 2022, with the ratio of exits to investments falling to the lowest level since 2008, particularly in North America.
pages.title: Add-on deals and exits in PE buyout activity

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_29.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the decline in global buyout entry multiples, comparing private equity and public equity markets. It highlights sponsor-to-sponsor transactions, reduced IPO volumes, and corporate M&A activity. The median global buyout multiple fell from 13.2 to 12.9 times EBITDA in 2022, while public equity multiples dropped more significantly. Sector-specific changes in multiples are also noted.
pages.title: Global buyout entry multiples declined slightly.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_30.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the consistency of private markets sectors with public markets, highlighting stable leverage levels despite rising debt costs. It focuses on the prominence of the PE secondaries market as a liquidity tool, noting a decline in secondaries deal volume in 2022, influenced by pricing decreases and LP behavior. LP-led secondaries deals still accounted for over 50% of the total volume.
pages.title: Spotlight on secondaries

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_31.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the decline in deal volume for GP-led secondaries and PE secondaries fundraising. It highlights the trend of GPs holding assets within existing vehicles and the concentration of fundraising among the top managers. The exhibit illustrates the decrease in fundraising over the years, with the top 10 managers accounting for a significant portion of the total.
pages.title: A decline in the number of large fund closings reduced PE secondaries fundraising.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_32.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the trends in private equity secondaries fundraising, noting a decline in fundraising totals but growth among smaller managers. It highlights pricing changes, factors influencing secondaries pricing, and the increasing participation of first-time sellers in the market.
pages.title: Private markets turn down the volume

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_33.jpg
pages.abstract: 2022 saw real estate sectors stabilize and top performers slow down. Closed-end funds reached new AUM peaks, while open-end funds in the US grew significantly. Office, retail, and hospitality sectors showed signs of stability. However, real estate experienced a downturn with declining fundraising and deal volume. Cap rates expanded, driving performance lower. Quality-focused trends emerged, with top managers and class A properties favored. Investments in property technology companies decreased.
pages.title: Real estate renovates

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_34.jpg
pages.abstract: Closed-end real estate fundraising declined to $166 billion in 2022, with significant regional and strategy variations. Asia remained stable, North America saw a 22% drop, and Europe experienced a 39% decline. Opportunistic and value-add strategies were relatively resilient, while debt and core/core-plus strategies faced substantial challenges. Returns decreased from 2021, with pooled-net IRR at 2.5% for the first three quarters.
pages.title: Closed-end funds

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_35.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the performance of real estate funds, highlighting consistent long-term returns and the growth of AUM. It also mentions the increase in dry powder and the trend of flight to quality in fundraising and office space demand. The top five managers captured the highest share of fundraising in a decade.
pages.title: The largest five managers accounted for 29 percent of all fundraising, the highest share of the last decade.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_36.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses fundraising trends in closed-end real estate funds, highlighting the concentration of capital among top managers and the shift towards larger funds. It explains the advantages of scale in real estate investments and the impact of these trends on the industry.
pages.title: Fundraising concentration in the top five closed-end funds reached a ten-year high.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_37.jpg
pages.abstract: Larger real estate funds have outperformed smaller ones with less dispersion in returns. Median IRR and percentile spread by fund size are shown for 2009–19 and 2015–19 vintage years. Demand for office space has fallen due to hybrid work models, but class A properties outperformed. Open-end funds in the US saw contributions exceed distributions and redemptions, indicating a shift towards less risky strategies.
pages.title: Larger real estate funds have outperformed, with less dispersion.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_38.jpg
pages.abstract: The exhibit illustrates that Class A properties outperformed Class B in price and demand across most large US cities from 2020 to 2022. Cities like Boston and Seattle showed higher price growth for Class A with little or no demand change. Conversely, cities such as Chicago and Phoenix experienced lower price and demand for Class A compared to Class B. The data highlights varying market dynamics across different cities.
pages.title: Class A outperformed class B in price and demand across a majority of large US cities.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_39.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the performance of private real estate investment trusts (REITs) in 2022, highlighting the challenges faced by open-end funds due to liquidity issues and the impact of cap rate expansion on performance. It compares the returns of open-end and closed-end funds, noting the decline in open-end fund performance but the stark contrast with public markets. The page also mentions the growth in rents across sectors, despite concerns about office attendance.
pages.title: Reversing a long-term trend, the expansion of cap rates was a headwind for performance in 2022.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_40.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the decline in global real estate deal volume by 20 percent in 2022, with the Americas experiencing the highest volume at $698 billion. It highlights the impact of rising interest rates, declining debt availability, and economic uncertainty on deal activity. The net asset value of funds reached $376 billion, marking the highest year-over-year growth in a decade. Deal activity varied across regions and asset classes, with hospitality and retail showing relative resilience.
pages.title: Global deal volume fell 20 percent.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_41.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses global deal volumes across various sectors, highlighting a decline in multifamily deal activity in the US. Despite lower absorption, the US faces a structural shortage of housing units. Industrial sectors saw unprecedented demand due to pandemic-driven shifts, but deal volumes declined in 2022 after a significant increase in 2021.
pages.title: Global deal volume was the second highest on record.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_42.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the performance of various real estate sectors in the US, highlighting improvements in industrial and retail sectors while noting challenges in office spaces. It also examines the impact of e-commerce on retail, noting a slowdown in growth after an initial boost in 2020. The text provides data on e-commerce sales as a percentage of retail sales, showing a significant increase from 2017 to 2020 followed by a slower growth rate.
pages.title: US e-commerce growth slowed significantly after a boost in 2020.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_43.jpg
pages.abstract: The document details the performance of various real estate sectors in the US, focusing on deal volumes, development, occupancy, absorption, RevPAR growth, cap rates, and total returns. Hospitality and retail sectors showed growth, while multifamily and industrial sectors experienced declines. Key metrics include deal volumes, development percentages, occupancy rates, absorption figures, RevPAR growth, cap rates, and total returns for 2022 compared to 2021.
pages.title: Deal volume in US retail and hospitality increased; multifamily and industrial tumbled from all-time highs.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_44.jpg
pages.abstract: The US property technology sector experienced a slowdown in deal volume and activity in 2022, with commercial proptech deals decreasing to $12 billion from a high of $31 billion in 2021. The decline was mainly due to a lack of large transactions. Despite this, demand for underlying technologies remains strong as the real estate industry continues its digital transformation. Various investors, including venture capital funds, traditional VCs, and buyout managers, are still active in the space, and new entrants are emerging.
pages.title: Spotlight on US property technology

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_45.jpg
pages.abstract: Real estate has historically outperformed gold, equities, and fixed income during inflationary periods, driven by factors like contracting cap rates and increased replacement costs, making it a strong inflation hedge.
pages.title: Real estate—an inflation hedge

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_46.jpg
pages.abstract: Private debt maintained growth despite macroeconomic challenges, setting new fundraising records in 2022. Mezzanine strategies were particularly successful, while direct lending saw marginal declines. Deal volumes dropped due to PE slowdown, and performance declined from 2021’s high.
pages.title: Private debt weathers the storm

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_47.jpg
pages.abstract: Global private debt fundraising reached a new high of $224 billion in 2022, growing at an annual rate of 12 percent since 2013. North America-focused fundraising increased by 11 percent, while Europe and Asia saw declines of 10 and 25 percent, respectively. Mezzanine lending fundraising surged 2.4 times to $46 billion, driven by large fund closings and favorable credit cycle positioning.
pages.title: Fundraising

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey Global Private Markets Annual Review_McKinsey_2023_03_01\page_48.jpg
pages.abstract: 2022 saw significant growth in fundraising for special situations strategies, despite a decline in distressed fundraising. The share of loans priced at distressed levels increased in both the US and Europe. Direct lending fundraising remained strong, exceeding $100 billion for the second consecutive year. Investors are shifting towards private loans due to their attractive yields and floating-rate coupons.
