pages.abstract: This introduction welcomes readers to the eighth volume of McKinsey on Investing, highlighting the current challenges in private markets and emphasizing the importance of value creation. It discusses the impact of market conditions on fundraising and transactions, and the need for strategic approaches in uncertain times. The issue aims to provide a long-term perspective on investment firms' evolution and thematic ways of investing, including new research on diversity in private equity.
pages.title: Introduction

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_7.jpg
pages.abstract: This page highlights key financial figures and trends in private markets, including capital deployment, climate tech investments, venture capital in biotech, private funding in space, gender diversity in private equity, and global investment managers' commitment to responsible investment. It also projects future energy investment needs.
pages.title: Notable facts and figures

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_8.jpg
pages.title: Building a better investment firm

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_9.jpg
pages.abstract: This page introduces an interview with Indhira Arrington, Ares Management's first global chief DEI officer, discussing her efforts in developing the company's DEI strategy.
pages.title: 'Making the world a better place never feels like work': An interview with chief DEI officer Indhira Arrington

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_10.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) in business, focusing on Ares Management's approach. It highlights the need for formal DEI structures, embedding DEI into various business aspects, and using data-driven KPIs to drive accountability and long-term performance. The page also emphasizes the role of leadership, procurement processes, and community impact in achieving DEI goals.
pages.title: The business case for diversity, equity, and inclusion

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_11.jpg
pages.abstract: Indhira Arrington, born in 1977, holds an MBA and a bachelor’s degree in economics. She has held various leadership roles in diversity and inclusion at major corporations like Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and Ares Management Corporation. She is a Cornell Certified Diversity Professional and serves on several boards and councils. She emphasizes a pragmatic approach to her role as a Chief Diversity Officer, focusing on data gathering and assessment.
pages.title: Indhira Arrington

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_12.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the implementation of a DEI strategy within Ares, involving team member interviews, external surveys, and strategic planning with portfolio companies. It highlights challenges faced by the CDO, the creation of a three-year DEI plan, and initiatives to increase diversity in management and suppliers. The page also covers changes in recruitment processes to enhance diversity and the launch of the AltFinance Investing in Black Futures initiative.
pages.title: DEI Strategy Implementation and Impact

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_13.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses a $90 million initiative by Apollo Global Management, Oaktree Capital Management, and Ares Management to support HBCU students in joining the asset management industry. It includes partnerships with AltFinance Investing and the Wharton School, aiming to provide scholarships, internships, and career pathways. The page also introduces key figures from Ares Management, McKinsey, and McKinsey's Atlanta office, emphasizing their roles in the initiative.
pages.title: Initiative to support HBCU students in asset management

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_14.jpg
pages.abstract: Sandra Horbach, cohead of US buyout and growth at Carlyle, discusses the importance of diversity and inclusion in private equity and offers advice for building a successful career in the industry.
pages.title: Forging your own path: Sandra Horbach on building a career in private equity

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_15.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the evolution of the private equity industry, focusing on diversity, specialization, and the changing recruitment landscape. It highlights the importance of diverse teams for better investment decisions and the shift towards hiring individuals with varied backgrounds and functional expertise. The conversation also touches on career advancement in private equity, emphasizing the role of industry growth and the increasing sophistication of investment skills.
pages.title: Forging your own path: Sandra Horbach on building a career in private equity

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_16.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the evolving responsibilities of managing directors in complex investment environments, emphasizing the importance of taking on challenging assignments and advocating for oneself. It also highlights the significance of diversity initiatives, particularly at Carlyle, where at least 50% of incoming classes are women or minorities. The role of leadership commitment, policy enforcement, and flexible work arrangements in promoting diversity and work-life balance is also addressed.
pages.title: Managing Director Responsibilities and Diversity Initiatives

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_17.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of flexibility, work-life balance, and inclusive culture in the private equity industry. It highlights the challenges of compressed deal timelines and the need for effective communication and relationship-building. The text emphasizes the role of leaders in fostering an inclusive environment and the benefits of networking for career advancement.
pages.title: Forging your own path: Sandra Horbach on building a career in private equity

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_18.jpg
pages.abstract: This page provides career advice for women in private equity, emphasizing persistence, hard work, and adaptability. It highlights the importance of not taking oneself too seriously and learning from setbacks. The conversation features insights from Sandra Horbach, Alexandra Nee, and Rodney Zemmel, discussing the diverse experiences and opportunities in the industry.
pages.title: Career Advice for Women in Private Equity

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_19.jpg
pages.abstract: Jenny Johnson, CEO of Franklin Templeton, discusses how the acquisition of Legg Mason strengthens the firm's position for future growth.
pages.title: How an acquisition invigorated an asset management leader

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_20.jpg
pages.abstract: Jenny Johnson discusses the challenges and successes of acquiring Legg Mason, emphasizing clear communication, talent integration, and client-focused strategies during the pandemic.
pages.title: Jenny Johnson and Robert Byrne discuss the Legg Mason acquisition

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_21.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the integration challenges and benefits of acquisitions in asset management, focusing on client relationships, cross-selling opportunities, and the importance of cultural alignment for successful mergers. It highlights the strategic decisions made to maintain the independence of acquired investment teams while fostering collaboration.
pages.title: How an acquisition invigorated an asset management leader

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_22.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the impact of blockchain and digital assets on the investment industry, highlighting tokenization, NFTs, and decentralized finance. It explores how these innovations can democratize asset ownership and bring alternative investments to retail investors, while also addressing potential risks and challenges for asset managers and smaller investors.
pages.title: Blockchain and Digital Assets: Disruption and Opportunities

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_23.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the evolving focus on stakeholder capitalism and ESG in the asset management industry. It highlights the importance of data in active management, the role of M&A in driving industry shifts, and the necessity of having the right people in leadership roles. The conversation also touches on the challenges and opportunities presented by ESG data and the expectations of clients regarding returns and impact.
pages.title: Stakeholder Capitalism and ESG in Asset Management

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_24.jpg
pages.abstract: This page introduces a research article on the state of diversity in global private markets in 2022. It highlights regional differences in diversity within private equity and explores the role of institutional investors in driving change. The collaborative effort involves experts from McKinsey's Private Equity and Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Service lines.
pages.title: The state of diversity in global private markets: 2022

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_25.jpg
pages.abstract: This report explores diversity in global private markets, focusing on PE firms and institutional investors. It highlights key findings on gender and ethnic/racial diversity, including allocation preferences, representation at various levels, and geographic differences. The report also discusses the role of institutional investors as catalysts for change in promoting diversity, equity, and inclusion within the industry.
pages.title: The state of diversity in global Private Markets: 2022

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_26.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the role of institutional investors (IIs) in private equity, their challenges with standardized metrics, and the need for diversity improvement in PE firms. It highlights the importance of aligning IIs' priorities with PE firms' actions and the difficulties in data comparison due to lack of standardization.
pages.title: Institutional investors in the private market ecosystem

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_27.jpg
pages.abstract: Institutional investors are increasingly considering diversity in PE firms' investment teams when allocating capital. More diverse teams receive higher allocations, even if they have lower historical performance. Surveyed investors show a preference for gender, ethnic, and racial diversity in investment teams and portfolio companies.
pages.title: Institutional investors' views on PE firms' diversity actions

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_28.jpg
pages.abstract: The document highlights that women are more represented in non-investing roles at every level in private equity firms. Despite achieving near gender parity in entry-level roles, women's representation in investing roles is significantly lower compared to non-investing roles. This disparity is evident across various seniority levels, with women holding only 34% of entry-level investing roles compared to 57% in non-investing roles. The data suggests a cultural dynamic affecting women's career advancement in private equity.
pages.title: Women are more represented in non-investing roles at every level.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_29.jpg
pages.abstract: This page details the job levels in private equity, classifying them into six levels from C-level executives to entry level. It highlights the gender distribution in higher-level roles, showing that women comprise only 9% of investment committees globally, with regional variations. The data is based on responses from 31 private equity firms covering over 11,000 employees.
pages.title: Job levels in private equity

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_30.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the gender diversity in private equity firms, highlighting that leading firms in diversity at the managing director level have a higher representation of women in investing roles compared to the industry average. It also notes regional differences in gender diversity within the PE industry and the impact of women's representation at the top on overall gender diversity in the organization.
pages.title: Globally, private equity firms that lead on diversity at the managing director (L2) level also beat the industry benchmark for all investing roles.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_31.jpg
pages.abstract: This page presents data on gender diversity in private equity roles across different regions. It shows the percentage of women and men in various investment roles, changes in women's representation between levels, and differences in representation from the beginning to the end of 2021. The data highlights regional variations in gender diversity within the private equity sector.
pages.title: Gender diversity in private equity varies by region.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_32.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the gender representation of women in private equity offices across different regions, highlighting the highest shares of women in various roles in the Americas, APAC, and Europe. It also explains the role of investment committees in private equity firms and their significance in decision-making processes.
pages.title: The role of investment committees in the private equity industry

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_33.jpg
pages.abstract: The document highlights the underrepresentation of ethnic and racial minorities in top private equity roles. Despite making up 17% of investing employees, they only constitute 9% of investment committee members. White professionals dominate investing roles, especially at higher levels. Asians, while the largest minority group at the associate level, see a significant decline in representation at the MD level. Black and Hispanic professionals have consistently low representation across all levels, with minimal presence in leadership roles.
pages.title: People from ethnic and racial minority groups are less represented at the top levels in private equity.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_34.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the underrepresentation of Black and Hispanic professionals in private equity (PE) firms, highlighting disparities in leadership roles and gender imbalances. It suggests evaluating investment committee diversity and addressing region-specific challenges to promote inclusivity.
pages.title: The path forward

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_35.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses ethnic and racial diversity in private equity firms in Canada and the United States, showing that leading firms with higher diversity in L2 roles outperform industry benchmarks. It includes data on managing director roles and entry-level to managing director roles, highlighting disparities between leading, average, and lagging firms. The page also suggests strategies for APAC and European offices to improve diversity and retention of women.
pages.title: In Canada and the United States, private equity firms that lead on ethnic and racial diversity in L2 roles also beat the industry benchmark for all investing roles.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_36.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses strategies for increasing diversity in private equity (PE) investing teams, emphasizing the need for intersectional diversity data and standardized diversity metrics. It highlights the importance of creating an inclusive culture and the role of institutional investors (IIs) in promoting diversity. The page also acknowledges contributors and references relevant studies.
pages.title: Increasing diversity in PE investing teams

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_37.jpg
pages.abstract: Bill Gurley discusses the potential and challenges for start-ups in an uncertain economy, emphasizing the current favorable conditions for building from scratch and highlighting hybrid work as a significant technological advancement.
pages.title: If you’re going to build something from scratch, this might be as good a time as in a decade

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_38.jpg
pages.abstract: Bill Gurley discusses the challenges and uncertainties faced by start-ups in the current economic environment, emphasizing the impact of interest rates, layoffs, and macroeconomic factors. He advises start-ups to focus on their circle of influence and competence rather than uncontrollable macro issues.
pages.title: Bill Gurley on Start-ups in Uncertain Times

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_39.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the current start-up environment, the impact of hybrid work on company culture, and the challenges faced by start-ups in terms of funding and valuations. It highlights the benefits of hybrid work in accessing talent and the uncertainties it brings to company culture. The conversation also touches on the differences between the current economic situation and past downturns, emphasizing the need for the venture community to adapt to the new reality.
pages.title: Discussion on Start-up Environment and Hybrid Work

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_40.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the challenges faced by founders and companies during economic downturns, emphasizing the importance of adapting quickly and pragmatically. It highlights the resilience of companies and the potential for growth even in tough times, while also addressing the impact of layoffs and the unique investment strategy of focusing on early-stage companies.
pages.title: McKinsey on Investing: Number 8, December 2022

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_41.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses market strategies, learning from past mistakes, and the evolving role of Silicon Valley in tech. It covers topics like direct listings, market corrections, and the cultural impact of the Bay Area on innovation and talent acquisition.
pages.title: Discussion on Market Strategies and Silicon Valley's Role

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_42.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the potential of Web3 and hybrid work models in enhancing productivity and innovation. It also explores the challenges and opportunities in the crypto industry, emphasizing the need for regulatory clarity and hard-core proof points.
pages.title: Discussion on Web3, Productivity, and Crypto

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_43.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how infrastructure investing is undergoing significant changes due to energy, mobility, and digitization revolutions, urging investors to reevaluate their strategies.
pages.title: Infrastructure investing will never be the same

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_44.jpg
pages.abstract: Infrastructure investing faces new challenges due to economic shifts and technological advancements. Investors must reassess risk profiles and adapt portfolios to emerging opportunities in energy, mobility, and digitization. Traditional low-risk assets may carry hidden risks, while new investments like EV charging and 5G networks offer potential but require significant upfront investment and active management.
pages.title: Infrastructure investing

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_45.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the traditional taxonomy of infrastructure investments, categorizing them into super core, core, and core-plus based on risk and return. It also reassesses the risk and return spectrum due to changes in energy, mobility, and digitization, highlighting the need to reclassify certain assets. A sidebar explains the characteristics of classic infrastructure investments.
pages.title: Infrastructure's traditional taxonomy

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_46.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses recent asset subclass migrations, including gas networks, motorway service areas, digital infrastructure, and power networks. It highlights the need for investors to adapt to changing risk/return profiles in infrastructure investing. The page also includes a graph showing stable returns from infrastructure compared to other asset classes.
pages.title: Examples of recent asset subclass migrations

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_47.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the challenges and changes in infrastructure investing, highlighting the decline in expected returns and the need for investors to adopt a new underwriting approach that considers dynamic factors like EV charging and energy transition impacts.
pages.title: Investors should adopt a new approach to underwriting

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_48.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the recovery of most infrastructure sectors to pre-COVID-19 levels, except for renewables. It emphasizes the need for investors to adopt a proactive approach to asset management and technology to deliver superior returns, given the changing investment environment. The text highlights the importance of reassessing portfolios and managing strategic, operational, and digital initiatives to preserve value and align with evolving risk/return dynamics.
pages.title: Most infrastructure sectors have recovered to pre-COVID-19 levels, except for renewables.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_49.jpg
pages.abstract: Investors need to actively manage assets using operational and digital tools, especially in emerging opportunities like the energy transition. Strong fundraising increases competition, leading to larger fund sizes and intense competition for suitable infrastructure targets. The energy transition requires significant investment, presenting a large-scale opportunity for investors who can adapt.
pages.title: Benefiting from emerging opportunities calls for more active investing

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_50.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses active investing strategies in infrastructure, emphasizing scaling up niche markets, consolidating national champions, and employing roll-up and bolt-on strategies. It highlights the importance of building relationships with utilities and setting up separate funds for early-stage energy transition opportunities. The text also mentions the attractiveness of infrastructure as a long-term investment despite economic pressures.
pages.title: Active Investing Strategies in Infrastructure

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_51.jpg
pages.title: US wealth management: A growth agenda for the coming decade

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_52.jpg
pages.abstract: The US wealth management industry entered 2021 with record-high client assets and healthy pretax margins, but faced challenges like slow revenue growth, declining profit pools, and uneven cost discipline. The industry must prioritize growth, innovate, and improve cost management to thrive in a dynamic environment.
pages.title: Wealth management: A growth industry facing disruptions

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_53.jpg
pages.abstract: The US wealth management industry experienced a 11% decline in profit pools in 2020. Despite near-term challenges, the industry is projected to grow at about 5% annually over the next five years, driven by market performance, net flows, and the shift from brokerage to advisory services. Growth will vary across segments, with digital advice models expected to lead. The industry is also adapting to demographic shifts and innovation, shaping future growth trends.
pages.title: US profit pools declined by 11 percent in 2020.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_54.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the significant growth in three investor segments: women, engaged first-time investors, and hybrid affluent investors. It highlights the increasing financial power of women, the rise of engaged investors due to market and pandemic-related trends, and outlines new growth narratives including fast-growth segments, new needs, products, and business models.
pages.title: Fast-growth segments offer new potential

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_55.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the growth of hybrid affluent investors, combining self-directed accounts with traditional advisors, and the need for wealth managers to integrate direct brokerage and advisor-led offerings. It highlights the increasing demand for omnichannel access, personalized services, and digital capabilities, especially among high-net-worth clients.
pages.title: US wealth management: A growth agenda for the coming decade

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_56.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the growing trend of affluent investors using hybrid accounts, combining self-directed and traditional advisory services. It highlights a 40% increase in direct brokerage accounts since 2020 and the convergence of banking and investing, with clients preferring to consolidate their financial relationships for convenience and better deals.
pages.title: The fastest-growing segment of affluent investors is hybrid—those with self-directed accounts plus a traditional advisor.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_57.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses investors' anticipated preferences for in-person, remote, and digital channels post-COVID-19. It highlights the increased role of digital and remote channels compared to in-person ones. The text also mentions the rise of personalized investing and the need for wealth managers to improve their digital capabilities, with 50% of clients expecting enhancements.
pages.title: Investors anticipate a more modest role for in-person channels than for digital and remote when the pandemic recedes.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_58.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the preference of younger and wealthier retail investors for consolidating banking and investing relationships. It highlights the growth of direct indexing and its potential to expand personalized investment management. The text also mentions the need for innovation in wealth management, particularly in integrating new products like private markets and digital assets.
pages.title: Younger and, to a lesser extent, wealthier segments have a strong preference for consolidating banking and investing.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_59.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses how younger and less affluent investors are more likely to consider ESG factors in their investment choices. It also highlights the growing interest in private markets and digital assets among investors, driven by lower interest rates and new retail investors. The text emphasizes the potential growth in private market investments and the diversification of digital assets beyond cryptocurrencies.
pages.title: Younger and, to a lesser extent, less affluent segments are more likely to consider ESG when choosing investments.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_60.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the challenges and opportunities for wealth managers in embracing digital assets, including regulatory ambiguity, infrastructure requirements, and advisor understanding. It highlights the migration of advisors to registered independent advisors (RIAs) and the potential for new business models in serving RIAs. The trend presents both challenges and opportunities for traditional wealth managers and ecosystem participants.
pages.title: Advisors' desire for independence presents an opportunity to serve RIAs

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_61.jpg
pages.abstract: Digital advice models, including robo-advisors and hybrid models, have shown significant growth in wealth management. Comfort levels with remote advice have increased, especially among younger clients. Wealth managers need to reposition their firms by leveraging growth themes, considering M&A strategies, and enhancing personalized content and solutions to attract more investors.
pages.title: The opportunity for digital advice models

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_62.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the increasing comfort with digital advice models among investors, particularly younger segments. It highlights the percentage of investors using remote and robo advisors by age group. The text also emphasizes the need for firms to redesign offerings, reimagine client engagement, and reallocate resources to support strategic growth in wealth management.
pages.title: Comfort with digital advice models has accelerated in the last three years, especially for younger segments.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_63.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the strategic resource reallocation in wealth management, emphasizing the importance of focusing on priority growth themes and having the right team and operating model. It also highlights the challenge of attracting and retaining talent in the industry, especially in the context of the Great Attrition and the shift towards hybrid working models.
pages.title: Five questions for wealth management executives

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_64.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses key questions for wealth management leaders, focusing on resource reallocation, M&A strategies, and partnership strategies. It highlights the importance of systematic resource allocation, M&A themes for growth, and leveraging partnerships for digital and technological advancements. The industry faces opportunities and challenges in the post-pandemic era, requiring adaptability and innovation.
pages.title: Key Questions for Wealth Management Leaders

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_65.jpg
pages.abstract: This page introduces the concept of becoming a digital investing organization, emphasizing the role of AI and other digital technologies in driving performance differentiation. It sets the stage for strategies to enhance digital capabilities.
pages.title: It's time to become a digital investing organization

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_66.jpg
pages.abstract: Digital technologies and analytics are reshaping industries, offering investors a competitive edge. By leveraging AI and automation, investors can analyze vast data sets, streamline tasks, and generate predictive insights faster and more efficiently. Early adopters have seen significant returns, with analytics users gaining a 5.3% higher ROIC. Embracing digital tools is crucial for investors to stay competitive.
pages.title: Digital and analytics: Practically made for investors

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_67.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of AI and digital technologies in investment organizations, emphasizing the need for a strategic approach, cultural shift, and understanding of technology's strengths and limitations. It highlights common pitfalls to avoid, such as misconceptions about AI's role and setting the wrong goals, to ensure successful digital transformation.
pages.title: Getting started—while avoiding common pitfalls

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_68.jpg
pages.abstract: This page outlines six key components for successful digital and analytics transformations, including strategy and vision, technology, data, talent, agile delivery, and solution delivery and operating-model transition. It emphasizes the importance of prioritizing business domains, leveraging technology and data, attracting talent, implementing agile practices, and ensuring proper execution support.
pages.title: There are six common components to successful digital and analytics transformations.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_69.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how sophisticated investors have improved portfolio performance using AI to identify key stocks. It highlights the importance of technology, data, and talent in digital deployment. It also emphasizes the need to integrate leadership and practitioners through specialized training and a digital-literacy program for the broader organization.
pages.title: Sophisticated investors have seen their portfolio performance in equities improve by more than 50 basis points by allowing AI to identify a basket of stocks where portfolio managers should focus their attention.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_70.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the execution and capability-building pitfalls in digital transformation, emphasizing the importance of agile methodologies, avoiding shiny-object syndrome, and ensuring end-user involvement. It outlines steps for successful technology adoption and highlights the role of AI in providing a competitive edge.
pages.title: Execution and Capability-building Pitfalls in Digital Transformation

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_71.jpg
pages.title: Exploring investment themes

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_72.jpg
pages.title: Highlights from McKinsey's 2022 sector research

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_73.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses how rising inflation has led industrial companies to focus on active price management, which has improved profitability and revenue. Top-quartile companies that actively discussed price management saw significant increases in profitability and revenue compared to those that did not. The data highlights the importance of incorporating pricing strategies into short-, medium-, and long-term plans.
pages.title: Tackling inflation with active price management

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_74.jpg
pages.abstract: Private investors are diversifying their exposure to space-related companies, with growing interest in lunar and beyond orbital regimes. In 2021, about $1 billion in private investment went toward these initiatives, focusing on various areas such as spacecraft components, mining, infrastructure, and robotics.
pages.title: Space investment is diversifying to new orbits and technologies

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_75.jpg
pages.abstract: The global food system faces high risks due to the war in Ukraine, climate change, trade restrictions, and other factors. Grain trade volumes are expected to drop by 5-10% by Q3 2023. Short-term impacts include logistical problems and reduced exports, while medium-term impacts involve fertilizer shortages and decreased harvests. Stakeholders need to enhance resilience by reducing waste and improving efficiency.
pages.title: Global food supply faced converging risks in 2022; next year could be even harder

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_76.jpg
pages.abstract: The European battery cell machinery equipment industry is experiencing significant growth due to the rising demand for electric vehicles. By 2025, the industry is expected to reach an annual business opportunity of €5 billion to €7 billion. To meet this demand, approximately 30 new battery manufacturing facilities will be required across Europe, necessitating up to €100 billion in capital expenditures. Securing equipment supply and avoiding production delays are crucial for businesses to capitalize on this unprecedented opportunity.
pages.title: Unlocking the growth opportunity in battery manufacturing equipment

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_77.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the unprecedented capital investment required between 2022 and 2050 to meet decarbonization and sustainability goals, totaling $9.2 trillion annually. It highlights the need for organizations to address supply chain inefficiencies, outdated project delivery systems, and shortages of labor, equipment, and raw materials. The solution involves adopting a CEO-led approach with advanced analytics for better capital planning. The NGFS Net Zero 2050 scenario projects a $3.5 trillion increase in spending on physical assets for energy and land-use systems.
pages.title: Is your capital strategy ready for the 21st century's first big investment wave?

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_78.jpg
pages.abstract: Chemical companies face challenges in achieving consistent growth. Only 16% of companies, termed growth champions, have managed to outperform global GDP growth and deliver high ROIC. The industry needs to adopt omnichannel strategies, invest in digital and analytics, and reevaluate contracting strategies to protect against inflationary pressures.
pages.title: Cracking the growth code in chemicals

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_79.jpg
pages.abstract: The consumer sector's growth varies significantly by company size. Smaller companies ($300 million to $3 billion in revenue) achieved the fastest growth (5.2% CAGR) between 2009 and 2019, while larger companies (> $10 billion) faced challenges, growing only 2.4%. Strategies for outperformance include expanding core businesses, entering new markets, and launching disruptive innovations.
pages.title: Three pathways to fast and profitable growth in the consumer sector

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_80.jpg
pages.abstract: The building products industry faces challenges like supply chain disruptions and labor shortages. A 2022 global survey of 500 industry players highlights the importance of innovation, digital transformation, and R&D. To stimulate growth, leaders should focus on value creation drivers, including setting clear targets for growth, routine cost interventions, marketing and sales initiatives, and agile resource allocation. The chart illustrates how these drivers can increase a company's value over five years.
pages.title: The building products industry is ripe for innovation

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_81.jpg
pages.abstract: The global insurance industry rebounded in 2021, with brokers showing the highest TSR. North America led in premium growth, profits, and shareholder returns. The report highlights the performance of different insurance segments and regions over the past decade.
pages.title: Creating value and finding focus in the insurance industry

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_82.jpg
pages.abstract: The US healthcare industry is projected to grow at 6% annually from 2019 to 2025, with payers and providers leading the growth. The payer segment will see a shift towards government segments due to the aging population and Medicare Advantage adoption. Providers will benefit from the aging population and changes in care delivery. The chart shows projected EBITDA across segments, highlighting strong growth in payer and services segments post-COVID-19.
pages.title: Profit pools are shifting in the US healthcare industry

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_83.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses biotech investment themes, highlighting venture capital funding trends in innovative platform technologies, cell therapy 2.0, next-generation gene therapies, and precision medicine. It provides funding data from 2019 to 2021, emphasizing the potential impact on long-term drug development despite macroeconomic challenges.
pages.title: What are the biotech investment themes that will shape the industry?

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_84.jpg
pages.abstract: The energy transition demands significant capital allocation, especially in decarbonization technologies and renewable energy sources. Despite fossil fuel demand decline, O&G investments are expected to remain stable. By 2035, global energy investments are projected to double, with decarbonization technologies comprising over a quarter of these investments. Business models in a decarbonized system remain uncertain.
pages.title: Accelerating the energy transition requires more capital allocation

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_85.jpg
pages.abstract: The European consumer goods industry is experiencing rapid growth in circular product demand, driven by sustainability-conscious consumers and regulations. By 2030, circular-economy segments are projected to grow 10-15% annually, reaching €400-650 billion. Companies can capitalize by promoting recycled, refurbished, and reused goods, developing greener supply chains, and calibrating portfolios towards high-demand circular products.
pages.title: Playing offense on circularity can net European consumer goods companies €500 billion

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_86.jpg
pages.abstract: Investors are exploring new growth areas in logistics, with funding for startups almost doubling in 2021. Key areas include last-mile delivery, visibility providers, and road-freight marketplaces. Digitization is crucial for incumbents to stay competitive.
pages.title: Startup funding in logistics is the next big investment opportunity

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_87.jpg
pages.abstract: This page introduces a discussion on the growing trend of private equity firms acquiring life and annuity in-force books. It serves as a guide for market entrants, existing players, and insurers on how to navigate this evolving landscape.
pages.title: Why private equity sees life and annuities as an enticing form of permanent capital

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_88.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the concept of permanent capital in private equity investments, focusing on life insurance and annuities. It highlights the growing trend of private investors acquiring life and annuity assets, the benefits for both investors and insurance carriers, and the strategies employed by general partners to maximize returns. The core attraction lies in the attractive margin between the cost of servicing liabilities and potential investment returns.
pages.title: Permanent capital and PE investments in life insurance

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_89.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the advantages of private equity firms investing in life insurance and annuities, highlighting higher investment yields, efficient operations, and strategic growth opportunities. It explains the potential for scale, the OCIO model, and the willingness of sellers to divest these assets, emphasizing the attractiveness of life insurance to PE buyers.
pages.title: Why private equity sees life and annuities as an enticing form of permanent capital

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_90.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses strategies for market entrants in the insurance sector, particularly for private equity firms. It highlights the challenges and opportunities in acquiring insurance assets, emphasizing the importance of defining a clear strategy, considering operational and IT issues, and exploring various entry methods like partnerships or closed-block acquisitions. The text also addresses the evolving dynamics of the insurance market and the need for firms to adapt their approaches to remain competitive.
pages.title: Market entrants: How to begin

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_91.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the risks and value-creation strategies for private equity firms acquiring life insurers. It highlights the importance of managing credit risk, regulatory uncertainty, and public opinion. The text outlines six levers for improving ROE, including investment performance, capital efficiency, and operational improvements. It emphasizes the need for PE firms to develop skills in engaging with regulators and stakeholders.
pages.title: Current owners: The value-creation playbook

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_92.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses how various levers, including operations/IT improvement, investments, capital efficiency, technical pricing adjustments, commercial uplift, and franchise growth, can increase return on equity by 4.0–7.0 percentage points. It highlights the importance of a digital-first approach and advanced analytics in reducing costs and enhancing value creation. The text also compares cost structures between US and European closed-book acquirers, emphasizing the need for process streamlining and scale benefits.
pages.title: The value-creation playbook can lift return on equity by four to seven percentage points.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_93.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how insurers can leverage AI techniques, technical excellence, commercial uplift, and franchise growth to enhance value creation. It highlights the role of advanced analytics in reducing complexity, improving customer understanding, and optimizing sales strategies. The text also explores partnerships and strategic asset allocation as means to navigate the challenging interest-rate environment and enhance investment performance.
pages.title: Insurers: Fight or flight?

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_94.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses strategies for insurers to unlock value through sales, reinsurance, or pooling assets. It emphasizes the need for insurers to adapt their value-creation approaches as competition increases and credit spreads remain low, urging them to deploy broader strategies to fully capitalize on current opportunities.
pages.title: Insurers' Value-Creation Strategies

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_95.jpg
pages.title: Digitally native brands: Born digital, but ready to take on the world

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_96.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the growing interest in digitally native brands (DNBs) among investors, highlighting their disruptive role in the market and their competitive advantages. It outlines four critical factors for assessing DNB investment potential, emphasizing the importance of customer file health and key metrics such as net customer growth, lifetime value, and acquisition costs.
pages.title: Digitally native brands (DNBs) are attracting significant investor attention these days

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_97.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses key metrics for digital native brands (DNBs), including the LTV:CAC ratio and the total addressable market (TAM) size. It highlights the importance of these metrics for business success and growth. Additionally, it explains how successful DNBs differentiate themselves in the market by focusing on unique propositions and playing in categories with favorable dynamics.
pages.title: Categories with the most potential

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_98.jpg
pages.abstract: This page provides a glossary of terms for DNB investors, including key metrics and strategies for optimizing customer acquisition, retention, and growth. It also discusses the importance of cross-channel campaign management and the strategic expansion of DNBs into new markets and customer segments.
pages.title: A glossary of terms for DNB investors

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_99.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the attractiveness of digitally native brands (DNBs) in categories with distinct dynamics, highlighting key drivers of consumer demand and economic success. It outlines essential capabilities for successful DNB teams, including building customer relationships, offering compelling reasons to shop, reducing acquisition costs, and leveraging technology for loyalty. The page also emphasizes community engagement and performance marketing as crucial strategies for DNBs.
pages.title: The most attractive digitally native brands typically play in categories with distinct dynamics.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_100.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the growth milestones for digitally native brands, emphasizing the importance of leveraging core infrastructure and an active customer base. It highlights the role of strong conversion-rate optimization, predictive analytics, and technology solutions in driving success. The page also warns of potential pitfalls that can hinder growth and profitability.
pages.title: Brands over time must move from start-up to grown-up and find sufficient scale to leverage core infrastructure and an active customer base.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_101.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the challenges and success factors for DNBs, including constrained market size, undifferentiated value propositions, poor unit economics, and lack of focus. It emphasizes the importance of a compelling value proposition, strong brand identity, and a clear path to profitability. Investors should be wary of the 'halo effect' and focus on core authenticity and problem-solving capabilities of DNBs.
pages.title: Challenges and Success Factors for DNBs

pages.title: Climate risk and the opportunity for real estate

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_103.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the critical role of real estate in the climate transition, highlighting the urgency for real-estate leaders to address climate change. It outlines the risks and opportunities associated with climate change, emphasizing the need for decarbonization and the potential for creating new value. The page suggests three actions for real-estate players to thrive: incorporating climate risks into valuations, decarbonizing assets, and creating new revenue streams.
pages.title: Climate risk and the opportunity for real estate

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_104.jpg
pages.abstract: Climate change poses significant physical and transition risks to real-estate assets, affecting valuation and portfolio performance. Companies are conducting stress tests, revealing potential losses and portfolio variations. Some assets may benefit from climate transitions, while others face value drops. Investors can identify mispriced assets, and the industry is recognizing climate-related value shifts, with real estate potentially being one of the hardest-hit sectors due to stranded assets.
pages.title: Incorporate climate change risks into asset and portfolio valuations

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_105.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the impact of climate change on real estate, including physical risks like flooding and wildfires, and transition risks such as regulatory requirements for decarbonization. It highlights the need for real-estate players to understand these risks and develop capabilities to assess their effects on asset performance and values.
pages.title: Climate risk and the opportunity for real estate

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_106.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the direct and indirect implications of physical and transition risks on revenue, operating and capital costs, and capitalization rate. It outlines the effects on revenue, operating costs, capital costs, and capitalization rate, emphasizing the need for prioritizing risks and mapping building exposures.
pages.title: Physical and transition risks have direct and indirect implications for revenue, operating and capital costs, and capitalization rate.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_107.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of quantifying portfolio impact by assessing economic risks on individual buildings and combining them into an impact map. It emphasizes taking action by integrating climate-related insights into core business processes. The page also highlights the need to decarbonize buildings and portfolios, estimating a $9.2 trillion annual investment for the net-zero transition. An illustrative chart shows the effects of physical and transition risks on the equity value of assets in a diversified real-estate portfolio.
pages.title: Climate risk and the opportunity for real estate

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_108.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the necessity of decarbonizing real estate to mitigate climate change risks. It outlines steps for real-estate players, including understanding baseline emissions, setting targets, identifying decarbonization levers, executing plans, and tracking progress. It also highlights opportunities for creating new value and revenue streams through local energy generation and green buildings.
pages.title: Decarbonizing real estate requires considering a building’s ecosystem

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_109.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses strategies for real estate firms to adapt to climate change, including green-building materials, extra on-site services, emission tracking services, and differentiated capital attraction. It emphasizes the importance of decarbonization in attracting capital and the role of real estate in supporting the transition to a sustainable future.
pages.title: Climate risk and the opportunity for real estate

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_110.jpg
pages.abstract: This page introduces an executive's guide to climate technology, emphasizing the importance of advanced technologies in combating climate change. It highlights five key themes expected to attract significant investment by 2025, aiming to accelerate the development and scaling of these technologies.
pages.title: Innovating to net zero: An executive’s guide to climate technology

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_111.jpg
pages.abstract: New technologies are crucial for global decarbonization. McKinsey research indicates mature climate technologies can deliver 60% of needed emissions abatement by 2050, but further innovation is required. The pace of decarbonization is unpredictable due to cost uncertainties. However, historical data shows significant cost reductions in renewable energy projects, driven by research, investment, and government incentives. Sustained demand can lead to production efficiencies and cost reductions for climate technologies.
pages.title: New technologies represent a critical part of the world's decarbonization tool kit

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_112.jpg
pages.abstract: This page illustrates the significant cost reductions in renewable energy technologies over time, showing learning rates for solar panels, electrolyzers, wind power, and electric-vehicle lithium-ion batteries, highlighting the impact of scaled production on cost efficiency.
pages.title: Charting cost reductions for climate technologies (continued)

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_113.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the vast potential markets and investment opportunities in climate technology, focusing on five key areas: electrifying transportation, buildings, and industry; launching the next green revolution in agriculture; remaking the power grid for clean electricity; delivering on hydrogen's promise; and expanding carbon capture, use, and storage. It highlights the need for innovation in EV batteries and battery-control software to reduce costs and improve performance, aiming for significant investment and emissions abatement by 2050.
pages.title: Climate risk and the opportunity for real estate

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_114.jpg
pages.abstract: This page highlights five key technology groups—Electrification, Agriculture, Power grid, Hydrogen, and Carbon capture—that could attract significant capital investment by 2025 and substantially reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. Each technology group includes specific innovations and applications, with projected annual investments and CO2 abatement impacts.
pages.title: Five groups of technologies could attract $2 trillion of capital per year by 2025 and abate 40 percent of greenhouse-gas emissions by 2050.

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_115.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses efficient building systems and the next green revolution in agriculture. It highlights the importance of electrifying buildings and industries to reduce CO2 emissions and the need for innovation in industrial electrification. It also addresses the significant role of agriculture in global GHG emissions and the potential of climate technologies to decarbonize agriculture, including the shift to zero-emissions farm equipment.
pages.title: Efficient building systems and launching the next green revolution in agriculture

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_116.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses various sustainable solutions for reducing emissions, including zero-emissions equipment, meat alternatives, methane inhibitors, anaerobic manure processing, bioengineering, and modernizing the power grid. It highlights the potential cost savings, technological advancements, and necessary investments to achieve significant emission reductions by 2050.
pages.title: Sustainable Solutions for Emissions Reduction

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_117.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses technologies for creating a zero-carbon grid, including long-duration storage, advanced controls, software and communications, vehicle-to-grid integration, and building-to-grid integration. It highlights the importance of long-duration storage for renewable energy, advanced control systems for grid efficiency, and the role of software and communication in managing grid balance. Vehicle-to-grid and building-to-grid integration are also explored as ways to enhance grid flexibility and reduce costs.
pages.title: Technologies for a Zero-Carbon Grid

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_118.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses advancements in nuclear energy, high-efficiency materials, and hydrogen technologies for decarbonization. It highlights emerging nuclear reactors, the potential of perovskites and graphene in clean energy, and the role of hydrogen in addressing GHG emissions. The page also covers the need for infrastructure development, low-cost hydrogen production, and the potential of hydrogen fuel-cell electric vehicles.
pages.title: Next-generation nuclear and hydrogen technologies

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_119.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the potential of low-carbon hydrogen in ammonia production, steel production, and aviation fuel. It highlights the need for expanding carbon capture, use, and storage (CCUS) technologies to decarbonize hard-to-abate sectors. The page also mentions the challenges and emerging technologies in CCUS, including pre- and postcombustion capture and direct air capture, aiming to reduce costs and make CCUS economically viable.
pages.title: Expanding carbon capture, use, and storage

pages.page_path: library_pages\McKinsey on Investing Perspectives and research for the investing industry_McKinsey_2022_11_01\page_120.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses climate technologies like BECCS, biochar, and CO2-enriched concrete, highlighting their potential to reduce carbon emissions and contribute to net-zero goals. It emphasizes the need for collaboration among companies, financial institutions, and governments to scale these technologies for climate stabilization.
pages.title: Bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS), Biochar, CO2-enriched concrete

This introduction welcomes readers to the eighth volume of McKinsey on Investing, highlighting the current challenges in private markets and emphasizing the importance of value creation. It discusses the impact of market conditions on fundraising and transactions, and the need for strategic approaches in uncertain times. The issue aims to provide a long-term perspective on investment firms' evolution and thematic ways of investing, including new research on diversity in private equity.
This page highlights key financial figures and trends in private markets, including capital deployment, climate tech investments, venture capital in biotech, private funding in space, gender diversity in private equity, and global investment managers' commitment to responsible investment. It also projects future energy investment needs.
This page introduces an interview with Indhira Arrington, Ares Management's first global chief DEI officer, discussing her efforts in developing the company's DEI strategy.
This page discusses the importance of diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) in business, focusing on Ares Management's approach. It highlights the need for formal DEI structures, embedding DEI into various business aspects, and using data-driven KPIs to drive accountability and long-term performance. The page also emphasizes the role of leadership, procurement processes, and community impact in achieving DEI goals.
Indhira Arrington, born in 1977, holds an MBA and a bachelor’s degree in economics. She has held various leadership roles in diversity and inclusion at major corporations like Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and Ares Management Corporation. She is a Cornell Certified Diversity Professional and serves on several boards and councils. She emphasizes a pragmatic approach to her role as a Chief Diversity Officer, focusing on data gathering and assessment.
This page discusses the implementation of a DEI strategy within Ares, involving team member interviews, external surveys, and strategic planning with portfolio companies. It highlights challenges faced by the CDO, the creation of a three-year DEI plan, and initiatives to increase diversity in management and suppliers. The page also covers changes in recruitment processes to enhance diversity and the launch of the AltFinance Investing in Black Futures initiative.
This page discusses a $90 million initiative by Apollo Global Management, Oaktree Capital Management, and Ares Management to support HBCU students in joining the asset management industry. It includes partnerships with AltFinance Investing and the Wharton School, aiming to provide scholarships, internships, and career pathways. The page also introduces key figures from Ares Management, McKinsey, and McKinsey's Atlanta office, emphasizing their roles in the initiative.
Sandra Horbach, cohead of US buyout and growth at Carlyle, discusses the importance of diversity and inclusion in private equity and offers advice for building a successful career in the industry.
This page discusses the evolution of the private equity industry, focusing on diversity, specialization, and the changing recruitment landscape. It highlights the importance of diverse teams for better investment decisions and the shift towards hiring individuals with varied backgrounds and functional expertise. The conversation also touches on career advancement in private equity, emphasizing the role of industry growth and the increasing sophistication of investment skills.
The page discusses the evolving responsibilities of managing directors in complex investment environments, emphasizing the importance of taking on challenging assignments and advocating for oneself. It also highlights the significance of diversity initiatives, particularly at Carlyle, where at least 50% of incoming classes are women or minorities. The role of leadership commitment, policy enforcement, and flexible work arrangements in promoting diversity and work-life balance is also addressed.
This page discusses the importance of flexibility, work-life balance, and inclusive culture in the private equity industry. It highlights the challenges of compressed deal timelines and the need for effective communication and relationship-building. The text emphasizes the role of leaders in fostering an inclusive environment and the benefits of networking for career advancement.
This page provides career advice for women in private equity, emphasizing persistence, hard work, and adaptability. It highlights the importance of not taking oneself too seriously and learning from setbacks. The conversation features insights from Sandra Horbach, Alexandra Nee, and Rodney Zemmel, discussing the diverse experiences and opportunities in the industry.
Jenny Johnson, CEO of Franklin Templeton, discusses how the acquisition of Legg Mason strengthens the firm's position for future growth.
Jenny Johnson discusses the challenges and successes of acquiring Legg Mason, emphasizing clear communication, talent integration, and client-focused strategies during the pandemic.
This page discusses the integration challenges and benefits of acquisitions in asset management, focusing on client relationships, cross-selling opportunities, and the importance of cultural alignment for successful mergers. It highlights the strategic decisions made to maintain the independence of acquired investment teams while fostering collaboration.
This page discusses the impact of blockchain and digital assets on the investment industry, highlighting tokenization, NFTs, and decentralized finance. It explores how these innovations can democratize asset ownership and bring alternative investments to retail investors, while also addressing potential risks and challenges for asset managers and smaller investors.
This page discusses the evolving focus on stakeholder capitalism and ESG in the asset management industry. It highlights the importance of data in active management, the role of M&A in driving industry shifts, and the necessity of having the right people in leadership roles. The conversation also touches on the challenges and opportunities presented by ESG data and the expectations of clients regarding returns and impact.
This page introduces a research article on the state of diversity in global private markets in 2022. It highlights regional differences in diversity within private equity and explores the role of institutional investors in driving change. The collaborative effort involves experts from McKinsey's Private Equity and Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Service lines.
This report explores diversity in global private markets, focusing on PE firms and institutional investors. It highlights key findings on gender and ethnic/racial diversity, including allocation preferences, representation at various levels, and geographic differences. The report also discusses the role of institutional investors as catalysts for change in promoting diversity, equity, and inclusion within the industry.
This page discusses the role of institutional investors (IIs) in private equity, their challenges with standardized metrics, and the need for diversity improvement in PE firms. It highlights the importance of aligning IIs' priorities with PE firms' actions and the difficulties in data comparison due to lack of standardization.
Institutional investors are increasingly considering diversity in PE firms' investment teams when allocating capital. More diverse teams receive higher allocations, even if they have lower historical performance. Surveyed investors show a preference for gender, ethnic, and racial diversity in investment teams and portfolio companies.
The document highlights that women are more represented in non-investing roles at every level in private equity firms. Despite achieving near gender parity in entry-level roles, women's representation in investing roles is significantly lower compared to non-investing roles. This disparity is evident across various seniority levels, with women holding only 34% of entry-level investing roles compared to 57% in non-investing roles. The data suggests a cultural dynamic affecting women's career advancement in private equity.
This page details the job levels in private equity, classifying them into six levels from C-level executives to entry level. It highlights the gender distribution in higher-level roles, showing that women comprise only 9% of investment committees globally, with regional variations. The data is based on responses from 31 private equity firms covering over 11,000 employees.
This page discusses the gender diversity in private equity firms, highlighting that leading firms in diversity at the managing director level have a higher representation of women in investing roles compared to the industry average. It also notes regional differences in gender diversity within the PE industry and the impact of women's representation at the top on overall gender diversity in the organization.
This page presents data on gender diversity in private equity roles across different regions. It shows the percentage of women and men in various investment roles, changes in women's representation between levels, and differences in representation from the beginning to the end of 2021. The data highlights regional variations in gender diversity within the private equity sector.
This page discusses the gender representation of women in private equity offices across different regions, highlighting the highest shares of women in various roles in the Americas, APAC, and Europe. It also explains the role of investment committees in private equity firms and their significance in decision-making processes.
The document highlights the underrepresentation of ethnic and racial minorities in top private equity roles. Despite making up 17% of investing employees, they only constitute 9% of investment committee members. White professionals dominate investing roles, especially at higher levels. Asians, while the largest minority group at the associate level, see a significant decline in representation at the MD level. Black and Hispanic professionals have consistently low representation across all levels, with minimal presence in leadership roles.
This page discusses the underrepresentation of Black and Hispanic professionals in private equity (PE) firms, highlighting disparities in leadership roles and gender imbalances. It suggests evaluating investment committee diversity and addressing region-specific challenges to promote inclusivity.
The page discusses ethnic and racial diversity in private equity firms in Canada and the United States, showing that leading firms with higher diversity in L2 roles outperform industry benchmarks. It includes data on managing director roles and entry-level to managing director roles, highlighting disparities between leading, average, and lagging firms. The page also suggests strategies for APAC and European offices to improve diversity and retention of women.
This page discusses strategies for increasing diversity in private equity (PE) investing teams, emphasizing the need for intersectional diversity data and standardized diversity metrics. It highlights the importance of creating an inclusive culture and the role of institutional investors (IIs) in promoting diversity.
