pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_12.jpg

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_14.jpg

pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of R&D and product development excellence in the medtech industry, highlighting four key areas for focus: systematic portfolio management, empowered product managers, agile principles, and outward orientation. pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_18.jpg
pages.abstract: Medtech companies excel in R&D by adopting a holistic transformation approach, focusing on systematic portfolio management, strong decision-making culture, continuous performance monitoring, and excelling in three key capabilities for world-class products.
pages.title: Reimagining medtech R&D for growth

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_19.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of product management, design thinking, systems engineering, and agile practices in medtech R&D. It emphasizes the need for skilled product managers, the application of design thinking for user-centric solutions, the role of systems engineering in translating user needs into product specifications, and the benefits of agile development for speeding up product development while maintaining quality and regulatory compliance.
pages.title: Product management, design thinking, systems engineering, and agility in medtech R&D

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_20.jpg
pages.abstract: Medtech companies benefit most from agile practices when combined with core agile principles. Digital tools streamline design controls, reduce development time, and enhance product quality. Agile methods, such as cross-functional teams and daily rituals, improve R&D efficiency and productivity.
pages.title: Medtech companies draw the most benefit from agile practices when used in concert with other core agile principles.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_21.jpg
pages.abstract: Medtech companies can benefit from external development strategies, including joint ventures, corporate venture funds, and spinning off ventures. These approaches can accelerate innovation, access capital, and maintain strategic focus, ultimately driving commercial growth.
pages.title: External development

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_22.jpg

It suggests that medtech companies can learn from leading software firms. The content is authored by Venky Anant, Shih-Yung Huang, Sreeharsha Konga, and Delphine Nain Zurkiya.

It highlights the need for medtech companies to adapt their R&D models by building a robust tech stack, adopting software development best practices, and strategically sourcing intellectual property. The text also outlines the three layers of a tech stack: engagement, intelligence, and the importance of continuous user interaction for software development.
pages.title: Adapting software R&D operating models for success

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_25.jpg
pages.abstract: Medtech companies face constraints in software development, including R&D team capacity, skills needed, and profitability. Effective algorithms and cloud-based infrastructure are crucial. Adopting software development best practices and rethinking product management can improve outcomes and reduce costs.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_26.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the role of product managers in medtech companies, emphasizing their importance in tracking usage data, shaping product roadmaps, and promoting engineering excellence. The text also addresses the challenges of increasing development velocity, leading in cybersecurity, and tailoring development processes to regulatory needs.

pages.abstract: Medtech companies face challenges in returning to pre-pandemic normal due to labor shortages, inflation, and changing customer expectations. Medtech leaders are adapting by augmenting traditional models with omnichannel strategies, including self-service portals and webinars, to meet these expectations. Despite the shift towards digital, in-person interactions remain crucial for certain activities. Omnichannel engagement is becoming a necessity for improved business performance.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_41.jpg

It highlights revenue growth differences between surveyed companies and the industry average across three maturity levels. Additionally, it emphasizes the shift towards subscription-based offerings in the medtech sector, driven by customer demand for modern engagement models and financial pressures on health systems.
pages.title: Omnichannel maturity is associated with stronger business performance and faster postpandemic recovery.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_42.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses building a new commercial model for medtech companies, emphasizing the importance of omnichannel capabilities and personalized engagement. The content provides insights into strategies for improving customer satisfaction, revenue growth, and selling efficiency.

pages.abstract: This page discusses foundational capabilities for medtech companies, emphasizing CRM systems, pricing discipline, and performance measurement. It also highlights the importance of personalizing omnichannel engagement and leadership in driving transformation.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_44.jpg

pages.title: Omnichannel engagement orchestrates touchpoints and assets to create a seamless experience in line with customers' needs.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_45.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses evolving commercial models in the medical industry for a digital-first future. It emphasizes the use of AI, machine learning, and digital twins for customer engagement, ecosystem selling, and pricing strategies. Examples of companies successfully implementing these strategies are provided.
pages.title: Creating and capturing value beyond core medical products allows executives to further evolve their commercial models for a digital-first future.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_46.jpg

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_47.jpg

It highlights the importance of foundational practices, omnichannel strategies, and ecosystem selling for a resilient and customer-centric future.

pages.abstract: This chapter discusses the importance of operations in the medtech industry, highlighting the need for resilient supply chains and the value of digitalization and Industry 4.0. It emphasizes the role of operations in translating innovations into patient impact and the challenges faced during disruptions like the COVID-19 pandemic. The text also outlines strategies for building supply chain resilience and leveraging digital technologies to enhance operational efficiency.
pages.title: Reimagining medtech operations: Bridging medical innovation to better patient care

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_51.jpg

It emphasizes the importance of improving forecast accuracy, product visibility, and inventory management. The page also introduces the design-to-value (DtV) approach as a strategy for medtech companies to enhance innovation and manage product life cycles effectively.
pages.title: Over a ten-year period, supply shocks could cost the average medtech company 38 percent of one year’s earnings.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_52.jpg

pages.title: Adopting a value-based approach to procurement excellence

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_53.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how medtech companies can achieve significant cost reductions through procurement excellence and manufacturing network transformation. It highlights the complexity of modern manufacturing networks and the need for a holistic approach involving cross-functional teams and senior leadership. The page also emphasizes the importance of embedding quality into business processes through advanced technologies and modern design techniques.
pages.title: Given the scale of the complexity, a manufacturing network transformation can be the ‘bold move’ that drives a step change in gross-profit performance.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_54.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how smart quality drives measurable impact across various building blocks in organizations. It highlights direct sources of value such as increased productivity, efficiency, and cost savings. Enablers like smart quality ways of working and compliance foundations are also emphasized. The importance of a medtech company's talent strategy in achieving operational excellence is underscored.
pages.title: Smart quality drives measurable impact across all building blocks.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_55.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the skills gap in the medtech workforce, highlighting the need for a well-designed talent strategy. It also emphasizes the pivotal moment for medtech companies to reimagine their operations through supply chain visibility and investment in people and digital tools to improve healthcare access and affordability.
pages.title: Medtech Pulse: Thriving in the next decade

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_56.jpg
pages.abstract: This section discusses how ESG strategies offer medtech companies a unique opportunity to differentiate their devices beyond mere compliance, emphasizing the potential for innovation and competitive advantage.
pages.title: Committing to ESG as a differentiator

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_57.jpg
pages.title: Blue Spiral Texture

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_58.jpg
pages.abstract: The medtech industry is increasingly influenced by ESG considerations, affecting investors, customers, regulators, and employees. While ESG has expanded its influence on financial performance, its scope remains limited. Companies should monitor ESG targets and consider it as a new vector for differentiation in commoditized device categories.
pages.title: The medtech industry and ESG considerations

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_59.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of setting clear ESG objectives for medtech companies, focusing on achieving net-zero greenhouse gas emissions, reducing waste, and designing sustainable products. It highlights the need for a marginal abatement cost curve (MACC) to prioritize decarbonization efforts and explores opportunities for differentiation in environmental, social, and governance areas.
pages.title: ESG performance starts with clear objectives

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_60.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses strategies for medtech companies to reduce Scope 3 emissions through supplier collaboration, circular business models, and marketing capabilities. It highlights the increasing number of companies setting science-based emissions targets and the importance of engaging upstream suppliers.
pages.title: Decarbonize Scope 3 emissions through supplier collaboration and development of new materials

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_61.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the importance of marginal abatement cost curves (MACC) in achieving net-zero emissions and highlights health inequities in device access. It mentions the mismatch between available devices and disease burden in low- and middle-income countries, racial bias in pulse oximetry, and the need to address noncommunicable diseases.
pages.title: Marginal abatement cost curves are critical to establishing a pathway to net-zero emissions.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_62.jpg
pages.abstract: Medtech companies are implementing health equity strategies by democratizing access and affordability, embedding equity in product development, and promoting diversity, equity, and inclusion in the workplace. While improvements have been made, women and minorities remain underrepresented in senior leadership positions.
pages.title: Medtech companies' health equity strategies

pages.page_path: library_pages\Medtech Pulse_ Thriving in the next decade_20023_09_01\page_63.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of a business-led approach to diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) in the medtech industry, emphasizing the need for systematic strategies and bold actions. It outlines a four-step approach for companies to guide their ESG journey, including understanding the relevant ESG context, defining the company's contribution, engaging broadly, and sustaining the ESG commitment. The page also highlights the challenges and opportunities associated with ESG ambitions and the role of medtech leaders in maximizing value creation.

This letter addresses medtech leaders, highlighting the industry's impact and challenges. It encourages bold action for future growth, resilience, and value creation, posing strategic questions for leaders to consider.
This section introduces the imperative for medtech leaders to create value in response to patient needs and uncertain shareholders, outlining strategies for a new wave of value creation.
The medtech industry significantly impacts global healthcare, extending life expectancy, improving patient care, and driving economic growth. Despite past successes, challenges remain in unserved therapeutic areas and financial burdens. Companies must innovate and transform to meet future needs and create value for patients and shareholders.
The document discusses how medtech innovation pipelines align with patient needs, highlighting unmet needs and the focus of innovation. It suggests transformation strategies for medtech leaders, emphasizing the creation of the next frontier of innovation through miniaturization, new materials, and digitalization. The text also mentions the rising cost of care, the importance of premium innovation, and the impact of new technologies on patient outcomes and cost-efficiency.
The document discusses the performance of medtech companies compared to the S&P 500, highlighting that while medtech outperformed in the 2010s, value creation has slowed. It emphasizes the need for companies to reassess incremental innovation, participate in premium areas of innovation, and enable shifts to new care sites to thrive in the next decade.
The document discusses the challenges faced by medtech companies in adapting to shifting healthcare profit pools and the need to rethink global growth strategies. It highlights the importance of refining value propositions and commercial operations to compete in new care settings. The text also addresses the regulatory and competitive challenges in global markets, emphasizing the need for innovation and strategic adjustments.
This page discusses strategies for medtech companies to thrive in the next decade, emphasizing the importance of tailored global strategies, intelligent competition in digital ecosystems, commitment to execution excellence, and attention to investors' focus on profit margins. It highlights the need for companies to reassess investments, embrace digital solutions, and align organizational priorities for long-term success.
The page discusses the growing importance of profit margins in company valuations, showing a stronger correlation between margin and enterprise-value-to-revenue ratio compared to growth. It emphasizes the need for companies to focus on profitability programs alongside growth investments to create long-term value and meet future healthcare needs.
This page discusses the need for medtech companies to significantly improve R&D and product development to achieve sustainable long-term growth. It highlights the collaborative effort by experts from McKinsey's Life Sciences Practice.
This page discusses the importance of R&D and product development excellence in the medtech industry, highlighting four key areas for focus: systematic portfolio management, empowered product managers, agile principles, and outward orientation. It also addresses challenges such as gaps in R&D execution, unrealistic timelines, and the need for new solutions to diagnose and treat diseases.
The average medtech company has seen a decline in FDA approvals per billion of R&D spending from 2005 to 2022, with a -9% annual decrease. Timely innovation delivery is crucial due to intense competition and the significant impact of product launch order on market shares.
Medtech companies excel in R&D by adopting a holistic transformation approach, focusing on systematic portfolio management, strong decision-making culture, continuous performance monitoring, and excelling in three key capabilities for world-class products.
This page discusses the importance of product management, design thinking, systems engineering, and agile practices in medtech R&D. It emphasizes the need for skilled product managers, the application of design thinking for user-centric solutions, the role of systems engineering in translating user needs into product specifications, and the benefits of agile development for speeding up product development while maintaining quality and regulatory compliance.
Medtech companies benefit most from agile practices when combined with core agile principles. Digital tools streamline design controls, reduce development time, and enhance product quality. Agile methods, such as cross-functional teams and daily rituals, improve R&D efficiency and productivity.
Medtech companies can benefit from external development strategies, including joint ventures, corporate venture funds, and spinning off ventures. These approaches can accelerate innovation, access capital, and maintain strategic focus, ultimately driving commercial growth.
This page discusses the need for a different approach in software development compared to traditional product development methods. It suggests that medtech companies can learn from leading software firms. The content is authored by Venky Anant, Shih-Yung Huang, Sreeharsha Konga, and Delphine Nain Zurkiya.
This page discusses the evolving role of software in medtech, emphasizing its value as a differentiator. It highlights the need for medtech companies to adapt their R&D models by building a robust tech stack, adopting software development best practices, and strategically sourcing intellectual property. The text also outlines the three layers of a tech stack: engagement, intelligence, and the importance of continuous user interaction for software development.
Medtech companies face constraints in software development, including R&D team capacity, skills needed, and profitability. Effective algorithms and cloud-based infrastructure are crucial. Adopting software development best practices and rethinking product management can improve outcomes and reduce costs.
This page discusses the role of product managers in medtech companies, emphasizing their importance in tracking usage data, shaping product roadmaps, and promoting engineering excellence. It highlights the need for product managers to have a strong product sense and collaborate with designers, engineers, and data scientists. The text also addresses the challenges of increasing development velocity, leading in cybersecurity, and tailoring development processes to regulatory needs.
The page highlights four key software development drivers—Culture, Tools, Talent management, and Product management—that significantly impact overall business performance. Culture and Tools are the most influential, followed by Talent management and Product management. Detailed sub-factors for each driver are provided, emphasizing psychological safety, planning tools, incentives, and project management capabilities as critical components.
This page discusses strategies for medtech companies to optimize software development through branching and strategic talent acquisition. It highlights the benefits of categorizing software features and the challenges of relying on contingent labor. The text also emphasizes the importance of restructuring organizations to prioritize in-house talent for long-term success.
This page discusses the correlation between the percentage of digital and analytics employees in medtech companies and their growth potential. Companies with a higher percentage of such employees exhibit higher median sales growth projections. The page also highlights the importance of engaging with the younger generation and adapting to their preferences. Additionally, it mentions the need for medtech companies to overhaul their R&D processes to support software development at scale, which could lead to expanded patient access to higher-quality healthcare services.
This page discusses how medtech companies can enhance their role in digital healthcare by integrating hardware and software, aiming to improve patient care outcomes through combined devices and data.
This chapter discusses the evolution of medical devices into smarter ecosystems, emphasizing the integration of devices and data in digital health. It outlines the three technology layers—engagement, intelligence, and infrastructure—crucial for ecosystem functionality. The roles of builders and orchestrators in shaping these ecosystems are also explored, highlighting the potential market opportunities for medtech companies.
This page describes an ecosystem built around a medical device, comprising three layers: engagement, intelligence, and infrastructure. It explains the roles of participants in the ecosystem and provides examples, such as ResMed's AirSense machine, which connects to an app and a provider-facing platform to enhance patient care and therapy adherence.
This page discusses the considerations for open and closed ecosystems in the medtech industry, highlighting the benefits and challenges of each type. It provides examples of devices suitable for open and closed ecosystems based on their complexity, data reliance, and integration needs.
This page discusses the considerations for open and closed ecosystems in medical technology, emphasizing the variability in decision-making across technical layers. It provides examples from sleep apnea and radiotherapy ecosystems, illustrating how different layers can be open or closed based on specific needs, such as data integration, analytics, and patient value. The page also includes diagrams summarizing the open and closed decisions in sleep care and radiotherapy ecosystems.
This page discusses how medtech companies can create value through closed ecosystems and multiple business models. It explains the two primary revenue streams: stand-alone revenue and pull-through device value. The page also includes Exhibit 2, which details the ecosystem use cases, target customers, and revenue streams, highlighting the total addressable market for 2025.
This page discusses strategies for medtech companies to launch or advance ecosystem initiatives, emphasizing the importance of defining value, clarifying roles, and creating network effects. It highlights the potential for monetization through high-quality data and the benefits of aligning ecosystem economics with user needs. The page also acknowledges the contributions of various authors and contributors.
This page discusses the need for evolving commercial models in the medtech industry to support new offerings, adapt to customer expectations, and ensure success in the coming decade. It highlights a collaborative effort by experts from McKinsey's Life Sciences Practice.
Medtech companies face challenges in returning to pre-pandemic normal due to labor shortages, inflation, and changing customer expectations. Customers, including HCPs, procurement departments, and administrators, expect new forms of digital engagement. Medtech leaders are adapting by augmenting traditional models with omnichannel strategies, including self-service portals and webinars, to meet these expectations. Despite the shift towards digital, in-person interactions remain crucial for certain activities. Omnichannel engagement is becoming a necessity for improved business performance.
The page discusses how omnichannel maturity correlates with stronger business performance and faster postpandemic recovery. It highlights revenue growth differences between surveyed companies and the industry average across three maturity levels. Additionally, it emphasizes the shift towards subscription-based offerings in the medtech sector, driven by customer demand for modern engagement models and financial pressures on health systems.
This page discusses building a new commercial model for medtech companies, emphasizing the importance of omnichannel capabilities and personalized engagement. It outlines three layers of capabilities: mastering the basics, personalizing omnichannel engagement, and harnessing the power of ecosystem selling. The content provides insights into strategies for improving customer satisfaction, revenue growth, and selling efficiency.
This page discusses foundational capabilities for medtech companies, emphasizing CRM systems, pricing discipline, and performance measurement. It also highlights the importance of personalizing omnichannel engagement and leadership in driving transformation.
This page discusses omnichannel engagement strategies, emphasizing the integration of diverse touchpoints and digital assets to create a seamless customer experience. It highlights the importance of strategically choosing starting points, assembling dedicated customer experience groups, shifting ways of working, and building data science capabilities for effective customer engagement.
This page discusses evolving commercial models in the medical industry for a digital-first future. It emphasizes the use of AI, machine learning, and digital twins for customer engagement, ecosystem selling, and pricing strategies. The text highlights the importance of advanced commercial capabilities, including pricing XaaS models, evolving commercial organizations, and customer success functions. Examples of companies successfully implementing these strategies are provided.
This page outlines a checklist for building a next-generation commercial model in medtech, emphasizing the importance of people, process, and technology. It provides specific considerations for ecosystem, omnichannel, and basics, and concludes that building these capabilities requires time and organizational commitment.
This page concludes the discussion on building commercial capabilities in the medtech industry, emphasizing the need for a compelling vision, employee engagement, and celebrating successes. It highlights the importance of foundational practices, omnichannel strategies, and ecosystem selling for a resilient and customer-centric future.
This section discusses how medtech companies are reevaluating their operations post-COVID-19 to enhance patient service and competitiveness. It highlights the need for innovation and strategic changes in the industry.
This chapter discusses the importance of operations in the medtech industry, highlighting the need for resilient supply chains and the value of digitalization and Industry 4.0. It emphasizes the role of operations in translating innovations into patient impact and the challenges faced during disruptions like the COVID-19 pandemic. The text also outlines strategies for building supply chain resilience and leveraging digital technologies to enhance operational efficiency.
This page discusses the potential financial impact of supply shocks on various industries over a ten-year period, highlighting that medtech companies could lose 38% of one year's earnings. It emphasizes the importance of improving forecast accuracy, product visibility, and inventory management. The page also introduces the design-to-value (DtV) approach as a strategy for medtech companies to enhance innovation and manage product life cycles effectively.
The page discusses the importance of adopting a value-based approach to procurement excellence, highlighting that medtech companies lag behind other industries in procurement maturity. It presents data showing that medtech has lower average purchasing practice scores compared to industries like consumer products and automotive, indicating a need for investment in procurement processes.
This page discusses how medtech companies can achieve significant cost reductions through procurement excellence and manufacturing network transformation. It highlights the complexity of modern manufacturing networks and the need for a holistic approach involving cross-functional teams and senior leadership. The page also emphasizes the importance of embedding quality into business processes through advanced technologies and modern design techniques.
This page discusses how smart quality drives measurable impact across various building blocks in organizations. It highlights direct sources of value such as increased productivity, efficiency, and cost savings. Enablers like smart quality ways of working and compliance foundations are also emphasized. The importance of a medtech company's talent strategy in achieving operational excellence is underscored.
This page discusses the skills gap in the medtech workforce, highlighting the need for a well-designed talent strategy. It also emphasizes the pivotal moment for medtech companies to reimagine their operations through supply chain visibility and investment in people and digital tools to improve healthcare access and affordability.
This section discusses how ESG strategies offer medtech companies a unique opportunity to differentiate their devices beyond mere compliance, emphasizing the potential for innovation and competitive advantage.
The medtech industry is increasingly influenced by ESG considerations, affecting investors, customers, regulators, and employees. While ESG has expanded its influence on financial performance, its scope remains limited. Companies should monitor ESG targets and consider it as a new vector for differentiation in commoditized device categories.
This page discusses the importance of setting clear ESG objectives for medtech companies, focusing on achieving net-zero greenhouse gas emissions, reducing waste, and designing sustainable products. It highlights the need for a marginal abatement cost curve (MACC) to prioritize decarbonization efforts and explores opportunities for differentiation in environmental, social, and governance areas.
This page discusses strategies for medtech companies to reduce Scope 3 emissions through supplier collaboration, circular business models, and marketing capabilities. It highlights the increasing number of companies setting science-based emissions targets and the importance of engaging upstream suppliers.
The page discusses the importance of marginal abatement cost curves (MACC) in achieving net-zero emissions and highlights health inequities in device access. It mentions the mismatch between available devices and disease burden in low- and middle-income countries, racial bias in pulse oximetry, and the need to address noncommunicable diseases.
Medtech companies are implementing health equity strategies by democratizing access and affordability, embedding equity in product development, and promoting diversity, equity, and inclusion in the workplace. While improvements have been made, women and minorities remain underrepresented in senior leadership positions.
This page discusses the importance of a business-led approach to diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) in the medtech industry, emphasizing the need for systematic strategies and bold actions. It outlines a four-step approach for companies to guide their ESG journey, including understanding the relevant ESG context, defining the company's contribution, engaging broadly, and sustaining the ESG commitment. The page also highlights the challenges and opportunities associated with ESG ambitions and the role of medtech leaders in maximizing value creation.

pages.abstract: This report introduces a quantitative risk assessment framework for financial institutions in Africa, focusing on nature-related opportunities and risks. It extends previous assessments by estimating asset value changes under future climate and nature scenarios. The findings highlight the materiality of nature-related risks and opportunities in Africa, offering a practical example of the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures' approach. The report also discusses the potential for Africa to breach environmental tipping points, leading to severe physical risks for financial assets, and acknowledges limitations in current modelling frameworks.

pages.abstract: This page discusses the mounting physical risks related to nature loss, leading to increased consumer and policy actions. It highlights the impact of these actions on financial institution portfolios, with significant changes in equity and loan book values by 2030. The agriculture and extractives sectors face substantial value shifts, requiring immediate attention. The page also emphasizes the need for careful risk management in lending to these sectors to maintain profitability.
pages.title: Mounting physical risks make global consumer and policy action to address the nature crisis more likely

pages.abstract: This page discusses the risks and opportunities driving asset value in Africa, focusing on water stress, land use changes, and shifts in food demand. It highlights the potential impacts on agriculture, extractives, and ecotourism, emphasizing the need for supply-side adjustments and nature-positive transitions to mitigate physical risks and preserve space for nature.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_14.jpg
pages.abstract: This report introduces risk assessment frameworks for financial institutions regarding nature-related opportunities and risks in Africa. It demonstrates the feasibility of nature-related risk assessment, highlights materiality in high-growth regions, and provides a world-first example for Africa. The report applies the TNFD framework, estimates exposure of key sectors, and conducts stress tests for financial institutions. It also outlines the structure of the report, covering materiality, connections between nature and lending portfolios, links to corporate performance, potential obstacles, and options for financial risk management.
pages.title: Nature and financial institutions in Africa: A first assessment of opportunities and risks

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_15.jpg
pages.abstract: This page introduces the background section, setting the stage for the content that follows. It likely provides context and foundational information necessary for understanding the subsequent topics.
pages.title: Background

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_16.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the critical dependence of Africa's economy on natural systems, highlighting the rapid degradation of nature and its severe impacts on the continent. It outlines global and private sector actions towards a 'net-zero and nature-positive' transition, emphasizing the urgency of addressing nature loss to avoid environmental tipping points and ensure sustainable development.
pages.title: The state of nature in Africa

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_17.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the TNFD beta framework's application in Africa, focusing on its LEAP approach to quantify nature-related risks in financial portfolios. It outlines the framework's alignment with TCFD pillars and its integration into sustainability reporting standards. The page also maps the LEAP approach to specific actions: locating nature interfaces, evaluating dependencies and impacts, assessing material risks and opportunities, and preparing to respond and report.
pages.title: Link to TNFD beta framework

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_18.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses existing assessments of nature-related risks and opportunities, highlighting studies in France, the Netherlands, Brazil, Malaysia, and global DFIs. It introduces a new study estimating the impact of nature-related risks on financial institutions, extending previous approaches to quantify changes in financial asset values under future climate and nature scenarios.
pages.title: Comparison to existing assessments of nature-related risks and opportunities

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_19.jpg
pages.title: Case studies

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_20.jpg
pages.abstract: This page introduces five scenarios of future action on climate and nature, ranging from baseline to ambitious coordinated action. It discusses the transition and physical risks associated with each scenario and their potential natural outcomes. The scenarios progressively layer additional actions over time, with the most ambitious scenario aiming to halt and reverse nature loss by 2030.
pages.title: Introduction to nature scenarios

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_21.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the application of the TNFD framework to various financial portfolios in Africa, highlighting geographical diversity, exposure to agriculture and extractives, and sectoral composition. It emphasizes the varying levels of exposure across different sectors and countries, with a focus on the synthetic equity portfolio and national lending portfolios.
pages.title: Portfolio composition

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_22.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the significant predicted changes in equity portfolio value under the Climate + Nature Now scenario, driven by direct exposure to agriculture and extractives sectors and geographical exposure. It highlights the variance in financial impacts and the sensitivity of equity values to crop mix, water availability, and deforestation. By 2030, total equity value could fall by up to 5 percent.
pages.title: Aggregate impact on equity portfolio

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_23.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the aggregate impact of nature-related risks and opportunities on lending portfolios, showing significant variation in cumulative gains and losses by 2030 under the Climate + Nature Now scenario. It highlights that impacts are generally lower for lending compared to equity due to the non-linear relationship between profits and expected losses. The variation in impacts is driven by geographical and sectoral composition, with cumulative gains and losses potentially reaching +1.1% and -2.8% by 2050. The document also explains the threshold at which companies may default on loans and provides an example of a bank's loan portfolio under these conditions.
pages.title: Aggregate impact on lending portfolios

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_24.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the negative financial impacts on lending portfolios under less nature-ambitious scenarios, comparing the Climate + Protection and Climate + Nature Now scenarios. It highlights the differences in expected losses and the factors driving these impacts, including changes in food demand and costs associated with deforestation. The page also includes an exhibit showing the projected fall in loan book values by 2030 under the Climate + Protection scenario.
pages.title: Negative financial impacts on lending portfolios under less nature-ambitious scenarios

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_25.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the material but relatively small impacts on whole lending portfolios due to limited exposure to sectors like agriculture and extractives. It highlights that nature-related risks could roughly double expected losses from agriculture by 2030 for some portfolios. The impacts on exposed sectors are proportionately larger, with expected losses reaching a maximum of 3.2% and 2.6% of total loan book value for agriculture and extractives, respectively, under the Climate + Nature Now scenario.
pages.title: Impacts on equity and lending portfolios by sector

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_26.jpg
pages.abstract: Nature-related risks in agriculture and extractives are comparable to climate-related risks in manufacturing, chemicals, and extractives. By 2050, profits in agriculture could decrease by 20% and deforestation-linked extractives by 15% under nature-related risks. Climate-related risks could lead to even higher losses, with oil and gas profits dropping by 70%. These risks significantly impact lending portfolios and company profits.
pages.title: Nature-related risks in agriculture and extractives

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_27.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the financial impacts of the agriculture sector on equity investments by 2030, highlighting gains and losses ranging from +55% to -22%. It categorizes agricultural commodities into high growth, minor impacts, and slow growth based on financial performance. Examples include sugar cane in Mauritius and corn producers in South Africa. The equity value of agriculture producers could vary significantly under Climate + Nature Now.
pages.title: Agriculture sector deep dive

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_28.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the impact of lending to agriculture across different countries, highlighting the variation in impacts due to the national mix of crops. It presents a scenario where cumulative changes in losses on agricultural loans by 2030 range from +5.4% to -3.2%, influenced by the exposure to high-growth, mixed, and slow-growth commodities. The Zambian financial system faces the highest risk, while Private Bank 2 and the Mauritian financial system see substantial gains. The exhibit provides a detailed breakdown of expected losses and loan shares for various financial institutions.
pages.title: Cumulative changes in losses by 2030 on agricultural loans

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_29.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the impact of the extractives sector on equity value and loan losses under the Climate + Nature Now scenario by 2030. It highlights the significant risks associated with deforestation driven by gold and copper production in Africa. The analysis shows that equity values could vary from +1.0% to -3.7% and loan losses could reach up to 2.6%, with substantial impacts on portfolios heavily exposed to key gold and copper producers like Ghana.
pages.title: Extractives sector deep dive

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_30.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the muted impacts of price increases on downstream sectors, estimating equity value declines and loan portfolio losses. It highlights the importance of input price changes versus demand shifts and the varying significance of commodities in downstream production costs. The text also addresses nature-related risks in agriculture and extractives, emphasizing the need for integrated risk management considering both nature loss and climate change. A micro-level model is introduced to assess nature-related impacts on lending and equity portfolios.
pages.title: Downstream sectors deep dive

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_31.jpg
pages.abstract: This page illustrates how changes in loan book and equity value are estimated based on firm-level profit changes, considering various demand, cost, and price drivers. It highlights the impact of factors like deforestation cost, production costs, and demand elasticity on company-level profits and equity value. The diagram also shows the relationship between these factors and the probability of default, affecting loan book value and shareholder earnings.
pages.title: Changes in loan book and equity value are estimated based on firm-level profit changes.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_32.jpg
pages.abstract: Nature loss impacts company profits and loan performance, with equity values reflecting future profit changes and lending risks altering credit ratings. The analysis covers a subset of material risk channels, underestimating risks for downstream sectors. Africa faces potential environmental tipping points, such as Amazon rainforest loss, leading to severe business costs. Current modelling underestimates nature-related physical risks, particularly large-scale tail risks and sub-national impacts. Underestimating physical risks may result in higher negative financial impacts in less ambitious nature scenarios.
pages.title: The effects of nature loss on company-level profits and loans

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_33.jpg
pages.title: Risks and opportunities driving asset value

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_34.jpg
pages.abstract: Nature-intensive sectors significantly contribute to Africa's GDP, with agriculture, extractives, and tourism varying in importance across countries. Water stress is a critical issue, affecting agriculture and potentially increasing production costs. Habitat loss and declining natural capital pose severe risks to businesses, particularly in tourism and agriculture.
pages.title: Nature-intensive sectors are central to the African economy

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_35.jpg
pages.abstract: Water stress significantly raises production costs in Morocco, Egypt, and South Africa by 2050. Tourism in Africa is vulnerable to habitat and species loss, with flagship species attracting visitors. Countries with high water stress and deforestation face economic and ecological challenges.
pages.title: Water stress significantly raises production costs. Tourists are attracted by species richness, making tourism vulnerable to habitat and species loss.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_36.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the benefits and vulnerabilities of ecotourism in Africa, focusing on the impact of flagship species on tourism revenue and the potential risks posed by deforestation and agricultural expansion. It highlights the importance of protecting natural habitats and expanding protected areas to mitigate climate and nature crises, while also addressing the economic implications for agriculture and commodity production.
pages.title: Ecotourism in Africa benefits from the abundance of animal species in tourist locations

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_37.jpg
pages.abstract: Limited land availability will lead to agricultural intensification, increasing production costs by 4-13% in 2030. Intensification involves higher initial investments but generates long-term efficiencies. For example, a 6% yield improvement in Kenyan pulses could reduce unit production costs by 1%. Intensification actions in Kenya might lower costs by 6-9% in 2050. This trend stimulates demand for agricultural inputs like fertilizers and machinery.
pages.title: Limited land availability could significantly increase agricultural production costs by 2030.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_38.jpg
pages.abstract: Gold and copper significantly impact African deforestation, with associated regulations potentially increasing production costs by 2030 and 2050. Future policies may require restoration and restrict exploration in protected areas, affecting market access and profitability.
pages.title: Gold and copper impacts on African extractive sector through deforestation

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_39.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the risk of deforestation on market access for gold and copper exports from Africa. It highlights the share of mines in forest areas by mineral in 2020, showing that 20% of gold mines, 10% of iron mines, 7% of copper mines, 2% of manganese mines, and 1% of chromium mines are located in forest areas. It also presents the share of metals and minerals export revenue for Sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America & Caribbean in 2020. The predicted production cost and profit changes relative to baseline in key sub-Saharan mining countries are provided for 2030 and 2050.
pages.title: Deforestation could quickly become a market access risk for gold and copper exported from Africa.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_40.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how agricultural producers pass a high proportion of production cost increases onto consumers, with cost pass-through rates of 80 to 95 percent. It highlights the impact on Ghana's fruit, nut, and vegetable producers in 2030 under a Climate Only scenario. The minerals sector, however, would absorb more cost increases due to its concentrated market structure, leading to lower cost pass-through rates and larger profit margin hits.
pages.title: Agricultural producers pass a high proportion of costs onto consumers.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_41.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how shifts in consumer demand, particularly reducing meat and dairy consumption and cutting food waste, could alleviate pressure on land and reduce demand for certain crops. It highlights potential scenarios where demand for crops like corn and tropical roots could decrease by 50% by 2050 under ambitious climate and nature protection actions. The page also includes a graphical representation of changes in demand for various agricultural commodities over time.
pages.title: Shifts in consumer demand might create space for nature

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_42.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the projected increase in agricultural profits in Africa across various scenarios, driven by rising food demand due to population and income growth. Despite different climate and nature action scenarios, profits are expected to rise significantly, with the baseline scenario showing a 470% increase by 2050. Even under the most ambitious demand reduction scenario, profits still grow by 365%. The analysis includes specific crops and is supported by data from NatuRisk and Vivid Economics.
pages.title: Under all scenarios, agriculture profits increase substantially over time.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_43.jpg
pages.abstract: Slower demand growth limits cost increases in Africa's food system. Climate + Nature Now scenario reduces production costs compared to Climate Only, especially for cereals and sugar cane. Lower costs stabilize food prices and reduce price volatility, benefiting consumers and food security.
pages.title: Costs associated with limited land availability are higher under Climate Only relative to Climate + Nature Now.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_44.jpg
pages.abstract: The shift to plant-based and alternative proteins will drive significant investment opportunities and increase demand for crops like sugar cane, especially in Africa. By 2030, sugar cane demand could rise by 15 to 36 percent in climate and nature-action scenarios, with total profits doubling by 2050 compared to the baseline.
pages.title: A big shift to alternative proteins would bring big growth opportunities for agribusiness.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_45.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how businesses in nature-intensive sectors in Africa can adapt to climate change and nature loss, creating opportunities for agribusinesses, alternative protein producers, and extractive companies. It highlights the potential for slower growth relative to the baseline and the benefits of minimizing nature impacts. A graph illustrates projected profit changes in crops, gold, and copper by 2050.
pages.title: Producers could capture competitive advantages or capture new markets

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_46.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses significant variations in profit impacts across agriculture and extractives subsectors under the Climate + Nature Now scenario in 2030. It highlights the impact on different commodities and the deforestation intensity associated with gold and copper extraction. A heatmap illustrates profit changes and subsector sizes across various countries.
pages.title: Profit impacts across agriculture and extractives subsectors

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_47.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the financial impacts of climate and nature changes on various subsectors and countries, highlighting that impacts are generally consistent within subsectors but vary across countries due to factors like water stress, deforestation, and policy actions. It emphasizes that extractive commodities face more severe impacts due to differences in deforestation intensity, leading to competitive disadvantages and profit losses in more deforestation-intensive countries.
pages.title: Profit impacts in 2050 follow a similar pattern across subsectors and countries but are more severe.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_48.jpg
pages.title: Nature and financial institutions in Africa: A first assessment of opportunities and risks

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_49.jpg
pages.title: Practical management of nature-related opportunities and risks

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_50.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the TNFD framework's adaptation of TCFD pillars for nature-related risks and opportunities, emphasizing long-term risk, data sources, capacity building, data acceptability, and integrated climate-nature scenarios. It outlines recommended disclosures for governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets.
pages.title: The TNFD disclosure pillars align with the TCFD.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_51.jpg
pages.abstract: The LEAP-FI Framework guides financial institutions through assessing nature-related risks and opportunities by locating their interface with nature, evaluating dependencies and impacts, assessing material risks and opportunities, and preparing to respond and report. It includes four stages and considers the type of financial institution, product or asset class, level of aggregation, and sectors for capital allocation.
pages.title: The LEAP-FI Framework intends to guide financial institutions through an assessment of nature-related risks and opportunities.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_52.jpg
pages.abstract: Financial institutions in Africa face challenges in managing nature-related risks due to regulatory, time horizon, and sector-specific factors. They prefer an integrated approach to climate and nature, extending existing climate risk frameworks. Guidance is needed for sectors with indirect exposure, and data availability for nature-related risk assessments is limited.
pages.title: Engagement with the banking, asset management, and insurance industries across multiple African countries

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_53.jpg
pages.abstract: Financial institutions need clear regulatory signals and skilled talent to adopt TNFD, requiring proficiency in spatial data, scientific processes, and reporting standards. Regulatory guidance and cross-departmental coordination are crucial for building risk management capacity.
pages.title: Nature and financial institutions in Africa: A first assessment of opportunities and risks

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_54.jpg
pages.abstract: The image illustrates a person on a cliff, symbolizing the intersection of human activity and natural landscapes in Africa. It highlights the potential for financial institutions to engage with nature conservation and sustainable development opportunities.
pages.title: Nature and financial institutions in Africa: A first assessment of opportunities and risks

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_55.jpg
pages.abstract: This page introduces the section titled 'Options for action,' likely discussing potential strategies or measures related to nature and financial institutions in Africa. It sets the stage for exploring opportunities and risks in this context.
pages.title: Options for action

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_56.jpg
pages.abstract: This section outlines roles of financial institutions in addressing nature-related risks and opportunities, highlighting existing frameworks and initiatives. It suggests ways financial institutions can prepare for nature-related disclosures, including assessing portfolios, supporting customers, investing in capabilities, and upgrading support systems.
pages.title: Financial institutions

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_57.jpg
pages.abstract: Financial regulators in Africa can support the integration of nature-related risks into financial regulations by providing clear guidance, engaging with the TNFD, and adopting micro-prudential supervision tools. This includes regular stress tests and adapting Basel III frameworks to include nature-related risks.
pages.title: Financial regulators

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_58.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the broader ecosystem for nature-related financial frameworks, emphasizing the role of framework issuers, policymakers, data providers, and African financial institutions in shaping global standards and practices. It highlights the importance of consultative processes, flexible approaches, and collaboration to address data availability and policy uncertainty.
pages.title: The broader ecosystem

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_59.jpg
pages.abstract: This appendix outlines a five-step approach for assessing nature-related risk exposure of financial institutions, covering scenario development, commodity-level risk assessment, company-level cost shocks, and portfolio-level impacts using the NatuRisk Toolkit.
pages.title: Appendix 1: Approach to opportunity and risk assessment

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_60.jpg
pages.abstract: This page outlines five nature scenarios developed by NatuRisk, varying in ambition and coordination between climate and nature action. It describes the baseline scenario, current policies, climate-only action, climate plus protection, climate plus nature future, and climate plus nature now. Each scenario's description includes transition risk, physical risk, and natural outcome, providing a comprehensive overview of plausible biodiversity and ecosystem pathways.
pages.title: Scenarios

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_61.jpg
pages.abstract: This page outlines key levers defining policy scenarios for nature-related risks, categorized into policy, demand-driven, and technology levers. It explains how these levers are parameterized based on existing literature and adjusted for African countries. The levers support narratives on policy, demand change, and technology, with examples like stricter nature regulations and shifts in dietary patterns.
pages.title: Risk levers defining the policy scenarios support the policy, demand change, and technology narratives.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_62.jpg
pages.abstract: This page outlines various risk levers defined through a literature review, focusing on bioenergy demand, protected areas, diet shifts, and food waste. It categorizes these levers under different policy scenarios, ranging from current policies to ambitious climate actions, and provides literature benchmarks for each.
pages.title: Exhibit 30: Risk levers defined after literature review of current scenario projections and peer-reviewed studies

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_63.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses sector-level risk assessment, focusing on nature-related risks and opportunities. It outlines a model that assesses dependencies and impacts on nature, translating them into financial impacts on companies. The assessment considers eight risk channels, including physical risks like pollination and water availability, and transition risks like air pollution and demand shifts, mapping them onto specific industries and financial risks.
pages.title: Sector-level risk assessment

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_64.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the estimation of future nature risks and opportunities by predicting demand and land-use changes. It outlines cost shocks from deforestation, protected areas, pollinator loss, pollution, water availability, and soil quality. Company-level impacts are assessed using supply chain footprints and competitive models, with adjustments for private companies.
pages.title: Nature risks and opportunities assessment

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_65.jpg
pages.abstract: This page explains how portfolio-level impacts are derived from profit impacts, using an asset valuation model for securities and a five-step approach for estimating loan book value changes. It also discusses the aggregation of security value changes and the use of synthetic portfolios for sector-level data.
pages.title: Portfolio-level impacts

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_66.jpg
pages.abstract: This appendix provides context on the agricultural sector and policy stringency for five African countries, detailing crop mix coverage and national data points used in risk assessment. It highlights the diverse crop compositions and policy indicators for each country.
pages.title: Appendix 2: Context and coverage for top-priority countries

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_67.jpg
pages.abstract: This page presents two exhibits. Exhibit 33 illustrates the variety of terrestrial eco-regions in Africa in 2019, highlighting diverse ecosystems like deserts, forests, and savannas. Exhibit 34 shows the diverse crop composition in African countries, detailing the distribution of agriculture production value by crop in 2018, with significant contributions from crops like sugarcane, mixed fruit and vegetables, and cereals.
pages.title: Africa hosts a variety of terrestrial eco-regions (2019) and African countries have a diverse crop composition.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_68.jpg
pages.abstract: This page provides country fact sheets for Ghana, South Africa, Mauritius, Kenya, and Egypt, detailing key observed indicators such as biodiversity intactness, forest cover, governance, and pollution levels. Each country's data is presented with rankings and qualitative assessments, offering insights into their environmental pressures and policy ambitions.
pages.title: Country fact sheets include key observed indicators underlying our methodology.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_69.jpg
pages.abstract: This appendix elaborates on nature-related risks and opportunities, defining nature and ecosystem services, presenting a taxonomy aligned with the TNFD framework, and discussing the translation of real economy risks to financial institutions. It highlights the economic value of nature, the challenges in quantifying its decline, and the interplay between climate and nature-related risks.
pages.title: Appendix 3: Risk definitions and taxonomy

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_70.jpg
pages.abstract: This page defines nature, natural capital, and natural services, emphasizing biodiversity, ecosystem processes, and the benefits humans derive from ecosystems. It highlights the roles of market strategies, business management, and quantifiable metrics in understanding and managing natural resources.
pages.title: Definition of nature, natural resources, and nature services

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_71.jpg
pages.abstract: Nature provides essential ecosystem services like direct inputs, production enablement, and disaster protection, crucial for economic sectors. Even businesses not directly dependent on nature can be indirectly affected through their supply chains, highlighting nature's pervasive role in the economy.
pages.title: Nature's role in economic activities and services

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_72.jpg
pages.abstract: Nature-related risks and opportunities stem from business activities' dependency on and impact on nature. Physical risks include chronic loss of natural inputs and acute material damages from natural disasters. Transition risks involve new policies, innovation, and consumer shifts towards a nature-positive economy, potentially increasing production costs and reducing profitability. However, these shifts also create opportunities for businesses supporting nature.
pages.title: Nature-related risks and opportunities

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_73.jpg
pages.abstract: Financial institutions can create value by managing nature-related risks and opportunities through improving portfolio management, preparing for new policies, managing reputation, and adapting strategy. Businesses' impacts and dependencies on nature translate into financial risks and opportunities for financial institutions via a transmission mechanism.
pages.title: Value of nature-related risk management for financial institutions and systems

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_74.jpg
pages.abstract: Nature-related risk management enables financial institutions to de-risk portfolios, prepare for regulatory requirements, mitigate reputational risks, and seize commercial opportunities. It supports financial system stability by addressing systemic nature-related risks.
pages.title: Nature-related risk management for financial institutions

pages.page_path: library_pages\Nature and financial institutions in Africa_ A first assessment of opportunities and risks_McKinsey_2022_06_01\page_75.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the interconnection between climate change and nature loss, emphasizing the need for an integrated approach to address both issues. It highlights the compounding risks and uncertainties in climate and nature pathways, advocating for scenario analysis and integrated frameworks for financial institutions to manage these risks effectively.
pages.title: The climate-nature nexus
