pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_1.jpg
pages.title: Reimagining economic growth in Africa

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_2.jpg
pages.title: McKinsey Global Institute

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_3.jpg
pages.title: Contents

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_4.jpg
pages.abstract: Africa's economic growth has been slow despite its young and growing population. Productivity is lower than in comparable regions, but there are opportunities for growth through industrialization, trade, and agricultural productivity. Urbanization is rapid, requiring better infrastructure and jobs. Large companies have mixed performance, but there is potential for growth. Africa can reignite growth through improved productivity and collaboration.
pages.title: At a glance

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_5.jpg
pages.abstract: This introduction highlights Africa's potential for economic growth and prosperity, driven by its young population, urbanization, and innovation. Despite challenges like poverty and economic deceleration, certain countries and cities have shown success, offering models for productivity-led growth. The report analyzes Africa's diverse economic landscape from 2000 to 2019, emphasizing the importance of leveraging individual strengths to achieve sustainable development.
pages.title: Introduction

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_6.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses Africa's economic growth trends, highlighting a significant shift since 2010. It references MGI's 2007 report 'Lions on the move' and compares the economic performance between 1990 and 2019, emphasizing the continent's potential and challenges.
pages.title: Africa's growth has downshifted since 2010, after a promising opening to the millennium

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_7.jpg
pages.abstract: The document highlights Africa's slow GDP per capita growth of 1.1% annually from 1990 to 2019, contrasting with India's 5% and China's 8%. It includes a graph showing GDP per capita trends and compound annual growth rates (CAGR) for Africa, India, and China, emphasizing Africa's lagging economic performance despite population growth.
pages.title: Africa's real GDP per capita has grown only 1.1% annually since 1990.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_8.jpg
library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_9.jpg
pages.abstract: Africa's economic growth increased from 2000 to 2010 but has since declined to near 1990s levels. The region's debt-to-GDP ratio rose, and productivity growth fell sharply, particularly in extractive and service sectors, due to weak public finance management and high inflation. The real GDP growth decomposition shows a shift in growth drivers over time.
pages.title: Economic growth increased in Africa from 2000 to 2010 but has since fallen to near 1990s levels.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_10.jpg
pages.abstract: Climate change poses significant risks to Africa's growth, including increased weather-related events and threats to productivity. Rising physical risks and global decarbonization efforts could affect the continent's economy, particularly its dependence on fossil fuels and minerals. Adaptation measures and renewable energy adoption are crucial for Africa's future economic resilience.
pages.title: Climate change holds risks for Africa and creates opportunities to reinvigorate its economies

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_11.jpg
pages.abstract: The net-zero transition offers Africa significant economic opportunities in green manufacturing, including jobs and revenue from renewable energy systems and critical minerals. However, uncertainties remain, and leveraging these opportunities requires strategic efforts in business growth, capital acquisition, and technical expertise.
pages.title: Africa's green manufacturing opportunities

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_12.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the economic diversity within Africa, highlighting that the continent's recent slowdown masks significant divergence among countries. Some have sustained growth while others have declined. Nearly half of Africa's population lives in countries with GDP growth exceeding the continent's average, driven by increased investment, exports, and urbanization. These countries are typically in earlier stages of development and less reliant on commodities.
pages.title: There is no ‘one Africa’—the continent’s recent slowdown masks divergence across countries

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_13.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the economic growth patterns in Africa, categorizing countries into clusters based on their growth rates from 2000 to 2019. It highlights the performance of consistent growers and recent accelerators, emphasizing their contributions to GDP, urbanization, investment, and poverty reduction. The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on economic growth is also noted.
pages.title: Economic Growth in Africa: Patterns and Clusters

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_14.jpg
pages.abstract: This page illustrates the diverse economic performance across African countries, highlighting consistent growers, recent accelerators, recent slowdowns, and slow growers. The data shows significant variation in GDP growth rates between 2000-10 and 2010-19, emphasizing that there is no single economic narrative for Africa.
pages.title: Wide variation in economic performance across the continent makes it clear that there is no 'one Africa.'

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_15.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the economic performance of African countries, categorizing them into recent slowdowns and slow growers. Recent slowdowns, despite initial outperformance, slowed from 2010 to 2019, accounting for 46% of Africa's GDP and 37% of its population. Slow growers underperformed over 20 years, with 26% of GDP and 13% of the population, experiencing below-average investment, exports, and urbanization.
pages.title: Countries' share of Africa's 2019 GDP and population

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_16.jpg
pages.abstract: This page highlights the economic growth trends in East and West Africa, showing that these regions have experienced faster growth due to increased investment, exports, and urbanization. The map and accompanying charts illustrate the varying growth patterns across countries, with some showing consistent growth, recent acceleration, or slowdowns. The data underscores the importance of investment per capita, export growth, and urban population growth as key drivers of economic development.
pages.title: Economies are growing faster in East and West Africa, where investment, exports, and urbanization have increased more rapidly.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_17.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the varying productivity levels and growth rates among African economic clusters, highlighting the impact of recent slowdowns and slow growers on the continent's economic growth. It emphasizes the significant difference in GDP growth between 2000-2010 and 2010-2019, with Nigeria and Egypt playing crucial roles in the deceleration.
pages.title: Had Africa’s GDP continued to grow at the pace it achieved from 2000 to 2010, its GDP in 2019 would have been $3 trillion instead of $2.6 trillion.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_18.jpg
pages.abstract: The chart illustrates that countries categorized as recent accelerators and consistent growers have lower real productivity but faster-growing productivity compared to other groups. It highlights the productivity levels and growth rates of various African countries, showing that some countries have achieved higher productivity growth despite lower absolute productivity levels.
pages.title: Recent accelerators and consistent growers have lower but faster-growing productivity.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_19.jpg
pages.abstract: The chart illustrates the decline in GDP from 2010 projections to 2019, highlighting that Egypt, Nigeria, and South Africa account for 65% of Africa's GDP slowdown. It compares the extrapolated 2019 GDP based on 2000–10 growth rates with the actual 2019 GDP, showing significant differences across various countries and sectors.
pages.title: Downward trends in Egypt, Nigeria, and South Africa explain 65% of Africa’s GDP slowdown.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_20.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses Africa's economic shift from agriculture and extraction to services, highlighting the lag in productivity compared to emerging markets. It explains the importance of labor productivity for long-term economic growth and notes a structural shift towards services, with employment in services increasing from 30% to 39% over 20 years.
pages.title: Africa's economies are shifting rapidly from agriculture and extraction to services, but productivity still lags behind

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_21.jpg
pages.abstract: Africa's economy is shifting towards services, which now contribute 56% of its economic output. This transition mirrors India's path and boosts productivity. However, African service-sector productivity remains low compared to other regions and has declined since 2010.
pages.title: Africa is undergoing a fundamental structural shift to services.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_22.jpg
pages.abstract: The services sector in Africa has seen significant shifts in employment and productivity from 2010 to 2019. While the sector has potential to create millions of jobs and boost the continent's economy, productivity varies across subsectors, with trade being a major employer but low in productivity.
pages.title: The shift to services between 2010 and 2019 occurred across all clusters.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_23.jpg
pages.abstract: Financial and business services are highly productive in Africa, contributing significantly to GVA. Targeted interventions like digitization and skill development can boost other service sectors. Africa's growing working-age population can address global talent shortages through outsourcing. However, digital infrastructure and internet access remain major challenges.
pages.title: Africa will soon have the world’s largest working-age population, which could meet the growing global talent shortage via services outsourcing.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_24.jpg
pages.abstract: The financial and business services sector in Africa is the most productive but employs the fewest people. It shows high productivity growth, value added, and employment growth compared to other sectors like government, transport, trade, and other services. The data spans from 2000 to 2019, highlighting significant CAGR percentages and employment figures.
pages.title: Africa's financial and business-services subsector is the most productive, but it employs the fewest people.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_25.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses Africa's projected addition of 796 million people to the global workforce by 2050, making it the largest and youngest population. It highlights the distribution of imports and exports by sector, emphasizing the decline in the value added by extractive industries and the shift in commodity export revenues. pages.abstract: This page discusses Africa's resource sector, emphasizing the need to reverse declining hydrocarbon production and decarbonize the sector. It highlights the importance of investing in gas infrastructure and transitioning to low-carbon energy. The text also explores opportunities in the metals value chain and the need for agricultural development to support the continent's economy and food security.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_30.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the challenges and potential improvements in agricultural productivity in Africa. It highlights the need for increased productivity and strategic initiatives to enhance food security and economic growth. Key strategies include aligning production with comparative advantage, improving logistics, empowering midsize change agents, and developing financial solutions for farmers.
pages.title: Agricultural Productivity in Africa

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_31.jpg
pages.abstract: Africa is rapidly urbanizing, with its urban population growing faster than the global average. By 2040, the continent will have the largest urban population in the world. Urbanization drives economic growth, with cities contributing significantly to GDP and providing employment opportunities. However, Africa relies heavily on its primary cities, which account for a large share of the continent's GDP and have lower poverty rates compared to the rest of Africa.
pages.title: Africa is the world’s fastest-urbanizing region but depends too heavily on its primary cities

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_32.jpg
pages.abstract: By 2040, Africa will have 12 cities with over ten million people. GDP growth varies across cities, with some thriving despite national economic challenges. Primary cities attract significant urban migration and contribute to GDP growth, but slower-growing cities need accelerated economic growth to offset population increase.
pages.title: By 2040, Africa will be home to 12 cities of more than ten million people each as ten more cities join Cairo and Lagos.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_33.jpg
pages.abstract: This page illustrates the projected population growth of African cities by 2040, highlighting 31 cities expected to exceed five million inhabitants. It categorizes countries based on GDP growth trends and visualizes the distribution of these cities across the continent.
pages.title: By 2040, Africa will have 31 cities—19 more than today—with more than five million people.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_34.jpg
pages.abstract: This page shows the real GDP CAGR over 2010-19 for Africa's largest cities and their countries, highlighting that cities with the fastest-growing GDP are generally located in countries that are consistent growers or recent accelerators. The data is categorized into consistent growers, recent slowdowns, recent accelerators, and slow growers, with specific GDP growth percentages for each city and country.
pages.title: Cities with fastest growing GDP are generally located in countries that are consistent growers or recent accelerators.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_35.jpg
pages.abstract: The exhibit illustrates the GDP per capita CAGR of African cities from 2010 to 2019, showing that cities with faster population growth have higher GDP per capita growth. It categorizes cities into consistent growers, recent accelerators, recent slowdowns, and slow growers, highlighting their respective growth rates and population sizes.
pages.title: Per capita GDP is increasing more rapidly in African cities that are growing faster.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_36.jpg
pages.abstract: Africa's second cities face growth challenges but offer opportunities for expansion. They can focus on urbanization basics, competitive advantages, and infrastructure development. Critical needs include affordable housing and essential services. Significant infrastructure gaps exist, especially in electricity, water, and roads. Urbanization supports economic development, but challenges remain in accommodating the rising population.
pages.title: Africa's second cities: Growth and opportunities

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_37.jpg
pages.abstract: This exhibit compares the population sizes of secondary cities to their primary cities in African and non-African countries, showing that African secondary cities are generally smaller in proportion to their primary cities. The data highlights disparities in urban development and population distribution.
pages.title: African second cities are undersized compared with primary cities.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_38.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the need for significant infrastructure investment in African cities, estimated at 8.6% of GDP annually, to support urbanization and economic growth. It highlights the importance of private partnerships, investment accountability, and technology in improving project viability and attracting private financing. Coordinated infrastructure plans can enhance individual welfare and deliver socioeconomic returns, with each dollar invested adding 20 cents to GDP.
pages.title: The scale of infrastructure investment required on the continent is estimated to be roughly 8.6 percent of GDP annually.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_39.jpg
pages.title: St. James beach, Cape Town; Kejetia market, Kumasi

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_40.jpg
pages.abstract: Cape Town and Kumasi demonstrate how Africa's second cities can leverage investments, policies, and local resources to foster economic growth and productivity, despite divergent growth paths and challenges in infrastructure and urban planning.
pages.title: Two thriving second cities

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_41.jpg
pages.abstract: Africa's large private companies are crucial for economic progress, contributing significantly to growth, innovation, and employment. Despite challenges like the COVID-19 pandemic, these companies have shown resilience and potential for growth, positively impacting smaller enterprises and job creation.
pages.title: Africa’s large companies have proven resilient—and most have considerable unmet potential for growth

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_42.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the significant growth of large companies in Africa, highlighting their revenues and diverse sectors. It emphasizes the concentration of large companies in South Africa and the disparity in the number of large companies across different African economies, suggesting opportunities for expansion in other countries.
pages.title: Africa is home to many large companies

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_43.jpg
pages.abstract: This map illustrates the distribution of African companies with revenues of $1 billion or more, highlighting South Africa's dominance with 147 companies. It categorizes countries based on economic trends, showing consistent growers, recent accelerators, and slowdowns. The map excludes 54 foreign companies without specific bases in Africa.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_44.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the ownership structure of large companies in Africa, highlighting the distribution of public, private, and state-owned enterprises. It emphasizes the significant role of foreign-owned companies and their potential to integrate more deeply into the African business economy. The page also notes sectoral variations in ownership, with services dominated by homegrown and foreign companies, and extractive industries by state-owned enterprises.
pages.title: Across Africa, the distribution of sectors varies by ownership.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_45.jpg
pages.abstract: The performance of large African companies varied significantly from 2015 to 2021, with a net decrease in large firms. Despite this, aggregate revenues grew by 4.9% annually. South and North African companies performed better than the rest of the continent. Sectoral performance varied, with power, utilities, agriculture, and mining leading, while oil and gas declined. Within sectors, some companies outperformed the average growth rate.
pages.title: Performance of Africa's large companies varies

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_46.jpg
pages.abstract: The exhibit illustrates the change in companies' CAGR by sector from 2015 to 2021, showing diverse growth paces within each sector but similar average growth rates across sectors. Data includes 190 companies with revenue data, highlighting variations in growth rates for sectors like retail, consumer goods, and manufacturing.
pages.title: Companies are growing at diverse paces within each sector, but average growth rates remain close across sectors.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_47.jpg
pages.abstract: The data shows that companies with above-average revenue growth were more likely to be private and located in North Africa. Public companies were more prevalent among those with below-average growth. Regionally, North Africa had the highest proportion of above-average growth companies, while the South had the highest proportion of below-average growth companies. In terms of country-level growth trends, recent slowdowns and slow growers had a higher proportion of below-average growth companies.
pages.title: The companies with revenue growth faster than the average were disproportionately private and located in north Africa.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_48.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses significant value creation opportunities for large African companies by 2030, estimating a collective revenue increase of over $550 billion. It highlights growth potential in various sectors, the importance of partnerships, and five key levers for growth, including becoming African champions, integrating into the global market, addressing local community needs, collaborating with governments, and prioritizing the energy transition.
pages.title: Significant value creation opportunities exist

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_49.jpg
pages.abstract: Africa's consumer market is growing rapidly, with the potential to exceed $3 trillion by 2030. This growth is driven by urbanization and rising incomes, though challenges like inflation and varying consumer patterns across countries must be addressed. Businesses can capitalize on this by targeting growth hotspots and innovating within local value chains.
pages.title: Africa has the potential to unlock more than $3 trillion in consumer spending—but this will take more than a growing population

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_50.jpg
pages.abstract: The exhibit compares the distribution of population by consumer segments in Africa, China, India, Southeast Asia, and Latin America from 2000 to 2020, highlighting that Africa's consumption lags behind other regions due to a larger portion of its population living in poverty.
pages.title: Consumption in Africa lags behind other developing regions, in part because more people on the continent live in poverty.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_51.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of productivity as the foundation for economic growth in Africa, emphasizing the need to shift from growth for growth's sake to productivity-driven growth. It highlights the continent's diverse assets and suggests ten practical ways for businesses and governments to improve productivity and economic vitality.
pages.title: Fostering productive growth in Africa: Opportunities for African businesses and governments

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_52.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses embracing digital technologies, developing African talent, reimagining manufacturing for domestic and export purposes, and increasing regional connectedness to enhance economic growth and productivity in Africa.
pages.title: Fully embrace digital technologies and systems in all areas of the economy

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_53.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses strategies for Africa to enhance resource productivity, benefit from the global net-zero agenda, and improve agricultural productivity. It emphasizes the need for investment in digital technologies, sustainable resource management, and climate-resilient agriculture to foster economic growth and development.
pages.title: Invest to enhance resource productivity and tap into new opportunities, Explore opportunities to benefit from the global net-zero agenda, Spur the agricultural transition by improving farming productivity

pages.page_path: library_pages\Reimagining economic growth in Africa_ Turning diversity into opportunity_McKinsey_2023_06_01\page_54.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses strategies to enhance urban infrastructure and cultivate African business champions, emphasizing the need for coherent planning, digital technology adoption, and public-private collaboration. It highlights the importance of thriving corporations for economic growth and the role of governments in fostering conducive environments. The urgency for decisive action to achieve sustainable and inclusive development is also stressed.
pages.title: Increase and improve urban infrastructure in Africa's primary and second cities. Grow and cultivate African business champions.

Africa's economic growth has been slow despite its young and growing population. Productivity is lower than in comparable regions, but there are opportunities for growth through industrialization, trade, and agricultural productivity. Urbanization is rapid, requiring better infrastructure and jobs. Large companies have mixed performance, but there is potential for growth. Africa can reignite growth through improved productivity and collaboration.
This introduction highlights Africa's potential for economic growth and prosperity, driven by its young population, urbanization, and innovation. Despite challenges like poverty and economic deceleration, certain countries and cities have shown success, offering models for productivity-led growth. The report analyzes Africa's diverse economic landscape from 2000 to 2019, emphasizing the importance of leveraging individual strengths to achieve sustainable development.

The document highlights Africa's slow GDP per capita growth of 1.1% annually from 1990 to 2019, contrasting with India's 5% and China's 8%. It includes a graph showing GDP per capita trends and compound annual growth rates (CAGR) for Africa, India, and China, emphasizing Africa's lagging economic performance despite population growth.
Africa's economic growth increased from 2000 to 2010 but has since declined to near 1990s levels. The region's debt-to-GDP ratio rose, and productivity growth fell sharply, particularly in extractive and service sectors, due to weak public finance management and high inflation. The real GDP growth decomposition shows a shift in growth drivers over time.
Climate change poses significant risks to Africa's growth, including increased weather-related events and threats to productivity. Rising physical risks and global decarbonization efforts could affect the continent's economy, particularly its dependence on fossil fuels and minerals. Adaptation measures and renewable energy adoption are crucial for Africa's future economic resilience.
The net-zero transition offers Africa significant economic opportunities in green manufacturing, including jobs and revenue from renewable energy systems and critical minerals. However, uncertainties remain, and leveraging these opportunities requires strategic efforts in business growth, capital acquisition, and technical expertise.
The document discusses the economic diversity within Africa, highlighting that the continent's recent slowdown masks significant divergence among countries. Some have sustained growth while others have declined. Nearly half of Africa's population lives in countries with GDP growth exceeding the continent's average, driven by increased investment, exports, and urbanization. These countries are typically in earlier stages of development and less reliant on commodities.

The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on economic growth is also noted.

pages.abstract: Retailers face significant challenges in decarbonizing Scope 3 emissions due to complex, fragmented value chains. These emissions, generated by upstream and downstream activities, span various industries and systems. Effective strategies are needed to navigate this complexity and achieve decarbonization goals.
pages.title: Executive summary

pages.page_path: library_pages\Retailers’ climate road map_ Charting paths to decarbonized value chains_McKinsey_2024_07_01\page_5.jpg
pages.abstract: Retailers face complex challenges in reducing Scope 3 emissions, which require collaboration across value chains. By engaging suppliers and implementing sustainable practices, retailers can achieve significant reductions. Innovations and existing technologies can enable further emission cuts. Reporting standards like the Greenhouse Gas Protocol and ISO 14064 guide retailers in quantifying and reporting these emissions. The majority of Scope 3 emissions stem from upstream activities, emphasizing the need for strategic decarbonization efforts.
pages.title: Retailers' Scope 3: A complex array of value-chain emissions

pages.page_path: library_pages\Retailers’ climate road map_ Charting paths to decarbonized value chains_McKinsey_2024_07_01\page_6.jpg
pages.abstract: This page details the breakdown of greenhouse gas emissions across 13 retail channels, highlighting significant differences in Scope 3 emissions. Automotive retail has the highest emissions, primarily from downstream activities, while food and consumer staples retail show substantial upstream emissions. The data underscores the need for targeted decarbonization strategies within specific retail sectors.
pages.title: Retailers' Scope 3 emissions reflect wide-ranging differences in production and consumption within product channels.

pages.abstract: Retailers face challenges in delineating Scope 3 emissions across complex value chains. pages.title: More than 80 percent of emissions in the electronic equipment value chain are generated upstream, primarily by tier-two suppliers and above.

The page emphasizes the importance of sustainable practices and incentives in reducing emissions and improving agricultural resilience.
pages.title: Retailers' climate road map: Charting paths to decarbonized value chains

Toilet tissue production can similarly benefit from technology upgrades.

82.file_desc:
This page acknowledges the contributors and organizations involved in the research and insights for the report, highlighting their invaluable support and expertise.
Retailers face significant challenges in decarbonizing Scope 3 emissions due to complex, fragmented value chains. These emissions, generated by upstream and downstream activities, span various industries and systems. Effective strategies are needed to navigate this complexity and achieve decarbonization goals.
Retailers face complex challenges in reducing Scope 3 emissions, which require collaboration across value chains. By engaging suppliers and implementing sustainable practices, retailers can achieve significant reductions. Innovations and existing technologies can enable further emission cuts. Reporting standards like the Greenhouse Gas Protocol and ISO 14064 guide retailers in quantifying and reporting these emissions. The majority of Scope 3 emissions stem from upstream activities, emphasizing the need for strategic decarbonization efforts.
This page details the breakdown of greenhouse gas emissions across 13 retail channels, highlighting significant differences in Scope 3 emissions. Automotive retail has the highest emissions, primarily from downstream activities, while food and consumer staples retail show substantial upstream emissions. The data underscores the need for targeted decarbonization strategies within specific retail sectors.
Retailers face challenges in delineating Scope 3 emissions across complex value chains. For beef, 86% of emissions are upstream, driven by feed production, fertilizer, and cattle ranching. Reducing emissions requires addressing methane, efficient agricultural practices, and consumer behavior changes.
This page discusses the significant upstream emissions in the electronics product value chain, primarily from tier-two suppliers and above. It highlights the importance of decarbonizing power use in retail and the role of renewable energy availability in fragmented markets. The PCBA is identified as a key emission hotspot due to energy-intensive semiconductor production.
The page discusses the significant upstream emissions in the apparel value chain, highlighting the role of tier-two and tier-three suppliers. It emphasizes the need for systemic transformations in energy and land use to reduce Scope 3 emissions, involving various stakeholders in the value chain.
This page outlines near-term decarbonization opportunities for retailers, focusing on transitioning to clean energy, reducing livestock emissions, and adopting regenerative agriculture practices. These actions could significantly reduce Scope 3 emissions by 2030, with potential cost savings.
This page discusses various decarbonization themes and their corresponding levers for emissions reduction, including clean energy, farming practices, regenerative agriculture, circularity, waste reduction, transportation, and plant-based proteins, emphasizing the role of technology and data transparency in achieving these goals.
This page outlines strategies for retailers to prioritize decarbonization efforts by categorizing levers into four groups, emphasizing the potential for significant emissions reduction and the importance of multistakeholder collaboration.
This page presents data on retailers' potential to reduce Scope 3 emissions using cost-saving or neutral strategies. It categorizes reduction themes and their potential, highlighting cost-effective and prohibitive measures. Notable themes include transitioning to renewable energy, reducing farming emissions, and increasing circularity. The total reduction potential ranges from 55-65%, with varying cost implications across different tiers.
This page outlines various levers retailers can use to reduce Scope 3 emissions, categorized into cost-effective near-tier, cost-effective far-tier, costlier near-tier, and cost-prohibitive far-tier levers. It details specific actions and collaborations needed for each group, emphasizing the importance of innovation, partnerships, and systemic changes. Challenges in measuring and reporting emissions are also discussed.
Retailers face challenges in decarbonizing value chains due to data inconsistencies, accounting complexities, and public sector initiatives. They address these by improving data quality, simplifying methodologies, providing supplemental information, and engaging with stakeholders. System-level change involving multiple sectors is essential for successful decarbonization.
This page introduces the complexity of retailers' Scope 3 emissions, focusing on the value chain emissions. It highlights the challenges and intricacies associated with addressing emissions beyond direct operations, emphasizing the need for a comprehensive approach to decarbonization.
This page discusses the Scope 3 emissions metric for retailers, capturing emissions from sourcing, making, transporting, and using products. It highlights that value chain emissions account for 98% of total retail sector emissions, emphasizing the significant contribution of Scope 3 emissions to global GHG emissions.
The exhibit details Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions across 13 retail channels, showing significant differences in upstream and downstream emissions. Automotive retail has the highest emissions, mainly from downstream fossil fuel use, while food retail and consumer staples have high upstream emissions due to manufacturing and farming. The data highlights the need for targeted decarbonization strategies in different retail sectors.
Retailers' Scope 3 emissions dominate the retail sector's total emissions, with 98 percent originating from upstream and downstream activities across various industries. Decarbonization efforts must address these extensive value chains.
This page details the distribution of retailers' Scope 3 emissions across various product categories, highlighting the significant contribution of upstream suppliers in sectors like agriculture and industry. It provides a comprehensive breakdown of emissions by product type, showing the percentage contribution of each value chain step and the total emissions per product. The data underscores the importance of addressing upstream emissions to achieve decarbonization goals.
This page highlights retailer challenges in addressing Scope 3 emissions across three value chains, emphasizing the importance of delineating emissions for decarbonization efforts.
This page discusses the challenges retailers face in addressing Scope 3 emissions due to fragmented value chains and lack of reliable data. It highlights that 86% of beef value-chain emissions are generated upstream, emphasizing the complexity and difficulty in influencing supplier emissions. The page includes a detailed graphic illustrating the share of emissions by scope for different tiers in the beef value chain.
This page discusses the challenges faced by smaller suppliers in the beef value chain regarding emissions tracking and decarbonization efforts. It highlights the variability in fragmentation, production capacity, data disclosure, and emissions data disclosure among different tiers of suppliers. The page also includes an exhibit summarizing the characteristics of key supplier archetypes in the beef value chain.
This page discusses potential decarbonization measures for cattle ranching and plant-based animal feed production, highlighting their benefits in increasing efficiency, reducing costs, and lowering emissions. It also addresses the challenges and investments required for transitioning to more sustainable practices.
The electronic equipment value chain faces significant upstream emissions, primarily from tier-two suppliers. Decarbonizing power use is crucial, with PCBA and other materials contributing heavily to Scope 3 emissions. Retailers must address energy-intensive production and consumer electricity use to reduce their carbon footprint.
This page discusses the challenges of decarbonizing the electronic-equipment value chain, emphasizing the importance of renewable energy availability. It highlights the wide variation in supplier characteristics across tiers, including fragmentation, production capacity, and data disclosure levels. The page also notes that a significant portion of emissions in this value chain occurs at the PCB and PCBA component levels due to energy-intensive manufacturing processes.
This page discusses the decarbonization efforts in the PCB and PCBA value chain, focusing on reducing Scope 3 emissions through renewable energy use, green procurement, and consumer behavior changes. It highlights the potential impact of these measures on emissions reduction and the challenges in transitioning to clean energy grids.
This page discusses the apparel value chain, highlighting that 73% of retailers' Scope 3 emissions are generated upstream, primarily by tier-two suppliers. It includes a detailed chart showing the share of emissions by scope for various suppliers and retailers, emphasizing the significant role of upstream activities in the apparel industry's carbon footprint.
This page discusses the challenges in decarbonizing the apparel value chain, focusing on upstream suppliers in Southeast Asia. It highlights the need for reducing downstream Scope 3 emissions by influencing consumer behavior and promoting sustainable practices. The page also provides a detailed table showing the characteristics of key supplier archetypes across different tiers, including their market size, number of contractors, degree of fragmentation, capacity, direct emissions, and level of data disclosure.
This page discusses fiber raw material production and garment manufacturing, focusing on decarbonization measures for small farmers and wet processors in India. It highlights potential obstacles and benefits, such as yield gains and cost savings, while emphasizing the need for training and renewable energy access.
The 1.5°C pathway necessitates a significant reduction in retailers' Scope 3 emissions, requiring a 60% decrease by 2030. This involves transformations in energy and land-use systems, engaging value chain stakeholders. The chart illustrates the projected emissions under different scenarios, highlighting the need for accelerated decarbonization efforts to achieve the 1.5°C target.
This section discusses near-term opportunities for retailers to reduce emissions across their value chains, emphasizing practical strategies and immediate actions that can be implemented.
McKinsey identified seven themes for Scope 3 emissions reduction for retailers, based on analysis of change levers in product categories and value chains. Implementation could reduce emissions by 55-65% by 2030, with some levers reducing costs and others potentially increasing them.
This page discusses key examples of levers by enablers of emissions reduction across seven decarbonization themes. It covers economic resources, natural and physical resources, and human resources required for each theme, including transitioning to clean energy, reducing farming emissions, adopting regenerative practices, increasing circularity, reducing waste, reducing transportation emissions, and transitioning from animal to plant protein products. The page provides specific cost estimates, resource requirements, and workforce needs for each theme.
This page outlines key examples of levers for emissions reduction across seven decarbonization themes, including transitioning to clean energy, reducing farming emissions, adopting regenerative practices, increasing product circularity, reducing waste, cutting transportation emissions, and shifting to plant-based proteins. It highlights the role of low-carbon technology and data transparency in achieving these goals.
This page introduces strategies and considerations for retailers to catalyze broader decarbonization efforts. It highlights the importance of retailers in driving sustainable practices and outlines key approaches to achieve decarbonized value chains.
This page discusses strategies for retailers to reduce Scope 3 emissions through collaboration with suppliers and stakeholders. It categorizes these strategies into four groups based on cost-effectiveness and tier level, highlighting potential emission reductions and the importance of multistakeholder collaboration for significant impact.
This page discusses the potential for retailers to reduce Scope 3 emissions by up to 17 percent through cost-saving or neutral measures. It highlights various reduction themes such as transitioning to clean energy, reducing farming emissions, adopting regenerative practices, increasing circularity, reducing waste, cutting transportation emissions, and switching to plant-based proteins. The table provides detailed data on the reduction potential and cost implications for each theme, categorized into cost-saving, cost-neutral, cost-prohibitive, and advocacy efforts.
Retailers can lead cost-effective sustainability measures with value chain partners, potentially reducing Scope 3 emissions by up to 2%. Transitioning to renewable energy and implementing energy efficiency practices could lower emissions further. Examples include adopting geothermal energy in apparel and using sugarcane bagasse in packaged goods, with significant cost savings and emission reductions.
The page outlines strategies for retailers to reduce Scope 3 emissions in t-shirt production by prioritizing decarbonization actions based on their potential impact and position in the value chain. It includes a detailed bubble chart and a list of abatement levers across various stages of production, emphasizing cost-effectiveness and carbon neutrality.
This page discusses retailer-led actions to reduce emissions in suppliers' value chains, including switching to clean energy, supporting net-zero implementations, promoting sustainable consumption, and reducing waste. Examples include Walmart's Gigaton PPA program, Nike's partnership with CEBI, and Tide's Turn to Cold campaign. The page also highlights the potential cost savings and emissions reductions in tissue and apparel categories.
Retailers are implementing cost-effective strategies to reduce Scope 3 emissions by encouraging value chain partners to adopt regenerative practices in agriculture and EV infrastructure. Efforts in plant-based inputs and livestock farming can significantly lower emissions, with potential reductions of 5-15% in Scope 3 emissions for retailers.
This page discusses various strategies retailers can adopt to decarbonize their value chains, including setting supplier standards, providing training for farmers, engaging feed aggregators, collaborating with suppliers using incentives, and forming alliances. Examples include Walmart's DCF policies, Tyson Foods' training programs, PepsiCo's long-term contracts, and Kering's grant support for regenerative agriculture. The page emphasizes the importance of sustainable practices and incentives in reducing emissions and improving agricultural resilience.
Retailers can reduce waste and optimize processes among tier-three suppliers, lowering Scope 3 emissions and costs. Public-private collaborations like SmartWay enhance fuel efficiency. Lean manufacturing adoption by suppliers, such as Nike's program, significantly improves efficiency. Systemwide collaborations with value chain partners also reduce waste. Chemicals and pharmaceuticals can save costs and reduce emissions through continuous manufacturing. Toilet tissue production can similarly benefit from technology upgrades.
This page discusses costlier near-tier levers for decarbonization, focusing on collaborative efforts to reduce Scope 3 emissions. It highlights opportunities for retailers to collaborate with suppliers in tiers one to three, particularly in reducing livestock farming emissions. The page provides specific examples in dairy and beef categories, detailing the cost and impact of implementing sustainable practices such as management-intensive grazing and anaerobic manure digestion.
This page outlines strategies for retailers to reduce Scope 3 emissions in beef production by prioritizing actions based on decarbonization potential and value chain proximity. It includes a visual representation of abatement levers across the value chain, categorized by cost relative to carbon price and placement in the value chain. The content covers various abatement levers such as controlled-release fertilizers, renewable electricity, and regenerative silvopastures, emphasizing cost-neutral and cost-effective solutions.
Retailers can boost demand for sustainable beef, collaborate on research, support emission-reducing innovations, and encourage renewable energy adoption through supplier engagement and financing incentives, while also promoting plant-based proteins to reduce animal protein emissions.
This page discusses the reduction potential for Scope 3 emissions in electronics production, highlighting retailer-led transitions to renewables. It outlines various abatement levers across the value chain, including renewable energy, material sourcing, and packaging changes, and categorizes them based on their cost relative to carbon price and placement in the value chain.
This page discusses cost-prohibitive far-tier levers for reducing Scope 3 emissions, focusing on systemic changes involving multistakeholder actions. It highlights the potential of transitioning to clean and renewable energy, engaging local communities for feedstock, and supporting grid greening initiatives. A snapshot shows the cost and impact of replacing beef with plant protein, aiming for an 82% reduction in Scope 3 emissions.
This page discusses the potential reductions in Scope 3 emissions through transitions to renewables in chemicals, chicken, and beef sectors, highlighting costs and impacts. It also covers private sector initiatives, such as Walmart's community solar projects, and efforts to increase circularity and recycling in value chains.
This page discusses the cost and impact of increasing circularity and recycling in chemicals and pharmaceuticals and apparel categories, highlighting potential Scope 3 emission reductions. It also covers initiatives like refurbishment programs, recycling options, joint ventures for rare earth element recycling, and private sector alliances for circular initiatives.
The page discusses the impact of private sector initiatives and coalitions in adopting regenerative agriculture practices and circular economy strategies. It highlights the World Bank's $100 million bond for plastic recycling projects and the potential cost savings and CO₂ reduction from using controlled-release fertilizers, variable-rate fertilization, and low-tillage soil in beef production. The page also emphasizes the role of recycling in reducing plastic pollution and the importance of public sector-led incentives for implementing regenerative practices.
This page discusses the Transition Incentives Program (TIP) for sustainable agriculture, precision agriculture innovations, and decarbonizing transportation. It highlights the cost and impact of electrifying transportation in packaged goods and electronics sectors, modeled using McKinsey analysis. The page also covers incentives for electric vehicle production and the challenges retailers face in measuring and reporting Scope 3 emissions.
This page discusses the challenges retailers face in measuring, accounting, and reporting Scope 3 emissions, including variability in data, inconsistent standards, and the impact of external initiatives on carbon footprints. It highlights the need for transparency and accurate methodologies to address these challenges.
This page discusses the challenges retailers face in accounting and reporting Scope 3 emissions, including disconnects between industry averages and project impacts, changes in baselines and methodologies, lagging emissions factors, and limited influence over certain emissions. It highlights the difficulty in accurately incorporating decarbonization efforts and maintaining data quality.
Retailers face challenges in reporting product-level emissions data due to business growth and lack of standardized accounting. They are improving data quality, using estimation methods for Scope 3 emissions, and providing supplemental information to demonstrate decarbonization efforts. Engaging with carbon accounting standards and public sector initiatives is crucial for practical measurement and reporting, and coordinated multistakeholder action is essential for achieving a net-zero planet.
This appendix provides a detailed methodology for assessing global retailers' greenhouse gas emissions, including data collection, assumptions, and calculations. It also offers examples of emissions reduction opportunities, focusing on transitioning to clean and renewable energy, with specific economic and natural resource examples.
This page discusses examples of human, low-carbon, and economic resources, highlighting potential job gains in renewable energy, the need for technology adoption to meet climate goals, and cost savings from regenerative agricultural practices.
This page discusses various strategies for reducing CO2 emissions through efficient crop land management, low-carbon technologies like sprinkler irrigation and silvopasture, increasing product and packaging circularity, and enhancing recycling technology. It also highlights the need for skilled workforces, consumer behavior changes, streamlined logistics, and large-scale adoption of low-carbon materials and circular business models. The page emphasizes the importance of these measures in achieving net-zero targets by 2030 and 2050.
This page discusses various examples of reducing emissions and waste in different industries, including apparel, transportation, and agriculture. It covers the use of low-liquor dyeing machines, compostable packaging, consumer behavior changes, advanced technologies like IoT, and data transparency. The page also highlights the need for electrifying transport, increasing EV sales, and upskilling workers to support large-scale EV deployment.
This page discusses various examples of data transparency, economic resources, natural and physical resources, human resources, low-carbon technology, and data transparency in the context of transitioning from animal protein to plant protein products. It highlights the use of digital technologies, economic benefits of plant-based proteins, environmental impacts, consumer awareness, and technological advancements in supporting the shift towards plant-based protein production.

pages.title: Securing competitiveness in India's chemical industry

pages.page_path: library_pages\Securing competitiveness in India’s chemical industry_McKinsey_2024_02_01\page_11.jpg
pages.abstract: India's chemical industry has outperformed the global market with robust revenue growth and optimized operations, but margin pressure in recent years has impacted returns and raised concerns about future performance.
pages.title: India’s chemical industry: Interrupted momentum

pages.page_path: library_pages\Securing competitiveness in India’s chemical industry_McKinsey_2024_02_01\page_12.jpg
pages.abstract: The Indian chemical industry's TSR has recently declined compared to global peers. While it outperformed the market from 2014 to 2023, its CAGR dropped from 20% to 9% between 2020 and 2023, necessitating further analysis.
pages.title: The Indian chemical industry's relatively higher returns to shareholders have recently been muted.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Securing competitiveness in India’s chemical industry_McKinsey_2024_02_01\page_13.jpg
pages.abstract: The document illustrates that over the past three years, upstream and downstream industries have outperformed the chemical industry in terms of total shareholder returns. The data shows significant growth in various sectors, including metals and mining, oil and gas, chemicals, automobiles, construction materials, consumer products, and pharmaceuticals, compared to the Indian market index.
pages.title: Over the last three years, the associated upstream and downstream industries have also started outperforming the chemical industry.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Securing competitiveness in India’s chemical industry_McKinsey_2024_02_01\page_14.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the decline in total shareholder returns (TSR) for top Indian chemical companies, attributed to falling margins despite revenue growth. It highlights the impact of operating and nonoperating factors on TSR, with a focus on revenue growth, margin changes, and investment. The data shows a revenue CAGR increase but also notes price escalation in the chemical industry.
pages.title: The impact on total shareholder returns

pages.page_path: library_pages\Securing competitiveness in India’s chemical industry_McKinsey_2024_02_01\page_15.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the impact of revenue growth on TSR in the Indian chemical industry, highlighting a decline in NOPAT margins despite revenue growth. It includes a visual representation of margin and revenue growth trends for 38 companies between 2017-2020 and 2020-2023, emphasizing the need to address falling margins.
pages.title: A recent high-revenue phase has come at the expense of falling margins, which need to be addressed.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Securing competitiveness in India’s chemical industry_McKinsey_2024_02_01\page_16.jpg
pages.title: Securing competitiveness in India's chemical industry

pages.page_path: library_pages\Securing competitiveness in India’s chemical industry_McKinsey_2024_02_01\page_17.jpg
pages.abstract: The chemical industry faces global headwinds due to sluggish consumption, stalling demand in India's export markets, overcapacity, and commodity price fluctuations. These factors hurt competitiveness and reduce margins. While global per capita consumption is stagnating, India's is expected to rise. Three intertwined factors affecting competitiveness include declining exports, falling demand from importers, and geopolitical instability disrupting supply chains.
pages.title: 02 The effect of global headwinds

pages.page_path: library_pages\Securing competitiveness in India’s chemical industry_McKinsey_2024_02_01\page_18.jpg
library_pages\Securing competitiveness in India’s chemical industry_McKinsey_2024_02_01\page_19.jpg
library_pages\Securing competitiveness in India’s chemical industry_McKinsey_2024_02_01\page_20.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the decline in India's chemical exports to major markets like Europe and APAC, with a 37% drop in total imports and reduced trade deficits. It highlights the sluggish consumption in Europe and APAC from 2021 to 2023, with Europe's growth slowing from 11% to 1% and APAC's from 10% to 4%. The provided graphs illustrate the total chemical consumption in Europe and Central Asia and Asia-Pacific, showing trends in sales, imports, and exports.
pages.title: Europe and APAC markets, both major importers (greater than 50 percent), have been sluggish over the past two years.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Securing competitiveness in India’s chemical industry_McKinsey_2024_02_01\page_21.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the overcapacity in Europe's chemical industry due to falling export demand, leading to potential utilization rates under 70% by 2030. It highlights challenges in APAC, particularly in China, where local capacity growth and demand slowdowns are creating oversupply issues. The analysis projects market balances and disruptions, emphasizing China's growing role as a potential exporter.
pages.title: Overcapacity in Europe

pages.page_path: library_pages\Securing competitiveness in India’s chemical industry_McKinsey_2024_02_01\page_22.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the impact of overcapacity from China on global chemical markets, leading to steep competition for Indian exports. It highlights the challenges of commodity price fluctuations and the need for resilience in the chemical industry. The text emphasizes the importance of cost leadership and market diversification for Indian chemical companies to remain competitive.
pages.title: Overcapacity is resulting in excess supply from China in global markets, creating steep competition for Indian exports.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Securing competitiveness in India’s chemical industry_McKinsey_2024_02_01\page_23.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the margin pressure faced by petrochemicals due to increasing feedstock prices and demand-supply imbalance. It includes a graph showing EBITDA margin changes for different materials and questions about customer focus, sustainability, and growth strategies.
pages.title: Petrochemicals have faced a dual challenge of increasing feedstock prices and demand-supply imbalance, resulting in margin pressure.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Securing competitiveness in India’s chemical industry_McKinsey_2024_02_01\page_24.jpg

pages.page_path: library_pages\Securing competitiveness in India’s chemical industry_McKinsey_2024_02_01\page_25.jpg
pages.abstract: This page outlines five key focus areas for India's chemical leaders to enhance competitiveness and resilience. These include building functional excellence through digital tools, becoming truly global, accelerating innovation, focusing on sustainability, and deepening the talent pool. Specific strategies and benefits for each area are discussed.
pages.title: 03 Focus areas for India’s chemical leaders

pages.page_path: library_pages\Securing competitiveness in India’s chemical industry_McKinsey_2024_02_01\page_26.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses how companies can leverage the World Economic Forum's 4th Industrial Revolution Lighthouse initiative to guide their digital and analytics transformation. It highlights the potential benefits, such as improved productivity, agility, sustainability, and customization, with observed impact ranges provided in Exhibit 10.
pages.title: Companies embarking on a digital and analytics enablement journey could be guided by focused improvement areas such as the World Economic Forum (WEF)'s accredited 4th Industrial Revolution (4IR) Lighthouse

pages.page_path: library_pages\Securing competitiveness in India’s chemical industry_McKinsey_2024_02_01\page_27.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the potential of digital and analytics in the chemical industry, highlighting the limited number of WEF-identified Lighthouses from India. It emphasizes the importance of overcoming misconceptions about digital adoption and the relevance of dynamic pricing for improving profitability. A case study of a global specialties player demonstrates the benefits of advanced analytics-based pricing. The text also addresses the significance of data-driven value-based pricing and procurement excellence for company profitability.
pages.title: Securing competitiveness in India's chemical industry

pages.page_path: library_pages\Securing competitiveness in India’s chemical industry_McKinsey_2024_02_01\page_28.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses how digital tools and AI can enhance procurement resilience in the chemical industry by predicting price movements, managing risk, and improving efficiency. It highlights the importance of data-driven models, generative AI, and supply chain optimization for competitive advantage.
pages.title: Securing competitiveness in India’s chemical industry

pages.page_path: library_pages\Securing competitiveness in India’s chemical industry_McKinsey_2024_02_01\page_29.jpg
pages.abstract: Companies can tap into strategic international markets and end-use segments for growth, using data-driven approaches and digital channels. Investing in infrastructure, talent, and digital tools can enhance export market capture and customer experience. M&A can also drive growth by accessing new markets and capabilities.
pages.title: 2. Becoming truly global

pages.page_path: library_pages\Securing competitiveness in India’s chemical industry_McKinsey_2024_02_01\page_30.jpg
pages.abstract: Indian chemical companies can enhance competitiveness through application-based innovation and new product development, focusing on import substitution. Prioritizing the product development pipeline, implementing a stage-gate process, and leveraging digital tools can lead to significant revenue uplifts. Smart R&D and AI-driven analytics can help identify market opportunities and improve research productivity.
pages.title: 3. Accelerating innovation

pages.page_path: library_pages\Securing competitiveness in India’s chemical industry_McKinsey_2024_02_01\page_31.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the applications of Gen AI in R&D, highlighting molecule selection, development, and application development. It also presents the impact of Gen AI on various business functions, estimating the total impact in billions of dollars and as a percentage of industry revenue. The data is sourced from MGI Data and excludes implementation costs.
pages.title: Gen AI in R&D can help build opportunities.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Securing competitiveness in India’s chemical industry_McKinsey_2024_02_01\page_32.jpg
pages.abstract: Indian chemical companies face the dual challenge of meeting ESG expectations and addressing talent shortages. They can enhance sustainability by tracking ESG impact, managing climate exposure, and implementing net-zero plans. Green growth opportunities include introducing sustainable products and exploring bio-based investments. Addressing talent shortages requires overcoming educational and training gaps to secure competitiveness.
pages.title: 4. Sustainability as a dual play (defense and offense)

It also discusses strategies to address talent gaps in the industry through training, partnerships, and investments in R&D.

It emphasizes the importance of building a strong middle-management layer and global leadership team to navigate challenges and regain global prominence.
pages.title: Securing competitiveness in India's chemical industry

pages.title: February 2024

83.file_desc:
The Indian chemical industry, once a global outperformer, faces challenges due to global headwinds like declining demand, overcapacity, and commodity price volatility. Despite these issues, some companies are building resilience and competitiveness.
The document outlines five key priorities for India's chemical leaders to enhance competitiveness: building functional excellence, internationalization, accelerating innovation, sustainability, and deepening talent pools. These strategies aim to boost EBITDA, revenue, and relevance in the global market.
This page depicts an industrial chemical facility with key components like storage tanks, control panels, and piping systems. Two workers in safety attire are engaged in inspection, emphasizing operational safety and maintenance in the chemical industry.
India's chemical industry has outperformed the global market with robust revenue growth and optimized operations, but margin pressure in recent years has impacted returns and raised concerns about future performance.
The Indian chemical industry's TSR has recently declined compared to global peers. While it outperformed the market from 2014 to 2023, its CAGR dropped from 20% to 9% between 2020 and 2023, necessitating further analysis.
The document illustrates that over the past three years, upstream and downstream industries have outperformed the chemical industry in terms of total shareholder returns. The data shows significant growth in various sectors, including metals and mining, oil and gas, chemicals, automobiles, construction materials, consumer products, and pharmaceuticals, compared to the Indian market index.
The page discusses the decline in total shareholder returns (TSR) for top Indian chemical companies, attributed to falling margins despite revenue growth. It highlights the impact of operating and nonoperating factors on TSR, with a focus on revenue growth, margin changes, and investment. The data shows a revenue CAGR increase but also notes price escalation in the chemical industry.
The page discusses the impact of revenue growth on TSR in the Indian chemical industry, highlighting a decline in NOPAT margins despite revenue growth. It includes a visual representation of margin and revenue growth trends for 38 companies between 2017-2020 and 2020-2023, emphasizing the need to address falling margins.
The chemical industry faces global headwinds due to sluggish consumption, stalling demand in India's export markets, overcapacity, and commodity price fluctuations. These factors hurt competitiveness and reduce margins. While global per capita consumption is stagnating, India's is expected to rise. Three intertwined factors affecting competitiveness include declining exports, falling demand from importers, and geopolitical instability disrupting supply chains.
The document discusses the decline in India's chemical exports to major markets like Europe and APAC, with a 37% drop in total imports and reduced trade deficits. It highlights the sluggish consumption in Europe and APAC from 2021 to 2023, with Europe's growth slowing from 11% to 1% and APAC's from 10% to 4%. The provided graphs illustrate the total chemical consumption in Europe and Central Asia and Asia-Pacific, showing trends in sales, imports, and exports.
The document discusses the overcapacity in Europe's chemical industry due to falling export demand, leading to potential utilization rates under 70% by 2030. It highlights challenges in APAC, particularly in China, where local capacity growth and demand slowdowns are creating oversupply issues. The analysis projects market balances and disruptions, emphasizing China's growing role as a potential exporter.
The page discusses the impact of overcapacity from China on global chemical markets, leading to steep competition for Indian exports. It highlights the challenges of commodity price fluctuations and the need for resilience in the chemical industry. The text emphasizes the importance of cost leadership and market diversification for Indian chemical companies to remain competitive.
This page discusses the margin pressure faced by petrochemicals due to increasing feedstock prices and demand-supply imbalance. It includes a graph showing EBITDA margin changes for different materials and questions about customer focus, sustainability, and growth strategies.
This page outlines five key focus areas for India's chemical leaders to enhance competitiveness and resilience. These include building functional excellence through digital tools, becoming truly global, accelerating innovation, focusing on sustainability, and deepening the talent pool. Specific strategies and benefits for each area are discussed.
This page discusses how companies can leverage the World Economic Forum's 4th Industrial Revolution Lighthouse initiative to guide their digital and analytics transformation. It highlights the potential benefits, such as improved productivity, agility, sustainability, and customization, with observed impact ranges provided in Exhibit 10.
The document discusses the potential of digital and analytics in the chemical industry, highlighting the limited number of WEF-identified Lighthouses from India. It emphasizes the importance of overcoming misconceptions about digital adoption and the relevance of dynamic pricing for improving profitability. A case study of a global specialties player demonstrates the benefits of advanced analytics-based pricing. The text also addresses the significance of data-driven value-based pricing and procurement excellence for company profitability.
The document discusses how digital tools and AI can enhance procurement resilience in the chemical industry by predicting price movements, managing risk, and improving efficiency. It highlights the importance of data-driven models, generative AI, and supply chain optimization for competitive advantage.
Companies can tap into strategic international markets and end-use segments for growth, using data-driven approaches and digital channels. Investing in infrastructure, talent, and digital tools can enhance export market capture and customer experience. M&A can also drive growth by accessing new markets and capabilities.
Indian chemical companies can enhance competitiveness through application-based innovation and new product development, focusing on import substitution. Prioritizing the product development pipeline, implementing a stage-gate process, and leveraging digital tools can lead to significant revenue uplifts. Smart R&D and AI-driven analytics can help identify market opportunities and improve research productivity.
This page discusses the applications of Gen AI in R&D, highlighting molecule selection, development, and application development. It also presents the impact of Gen AI on various business functions, estimating the total impact in billions of dollars and as a percentage of industry revenue. The data is sourced from MGI Data and excludes implementation costs.
Indian chemical companies face the dual challenge of meeting ESG expectations and addressing talent shortages. They can enhance sustainability by tracking ESG impact, managing climate exposure, and implementing net-zero plans. Green growth opportunities include introducing sustainable products and exploring bio-based investments. Addressing talent shortages requires overcoming educational and training gaps to secure competitiveness.
This page outlines green business initiatives in various categories for the chemical industry, including decarbonization, low-carbon mobility, circular products, water management, agriculture, hydrogen fuels, high-efficiency buildings, industrial decarbonization, carbon capture, and carbon markets. It also discusses strategies to address talent gaps in the industry through training, partnerships, and investments in R&D.
The document discusses strategies for chemical companies in India to enhance competitiveness by addressing leadership gaps, fostering talent, and focusing on growth, innovation, and sustainability. It emphasizes the importance of building a strong middle-management layer and global leadership team to navigate challenges and regain global prominence.
