It highlights the increasing interest in marketplaces, personalization, and supply chain digitization, with examples from companies like H&M and Shein. The text also mentions the role of venture capital in supporting new business models and technologies in the fashion industry.
pages.title: Fashion Tech Investments and Innovations

pages.abstract: The page discusses investments in fashion and retail, focusing on sustainability, resale, and emerging technologies like Web3 and the metaverse. It highlights H&M's investments in secondhand fashion and technology, as well as the growing interest in resale logistics and virtual fashion collections. Investors are exploring opportunities in these areas, aiming to address industry challenges and prepare for future consumer trends.
pages.title: Web3 and the metaverse are inescapable topics, and while capital is pouring into metaverse-related companies, investment on the fashion and retail side is just getting started.
Person using a smartphone

pages.abstract: Brands can now use advanced personalisation tools and technologies, including Big Data and AI, to create tailored customer experiences that foster long-term loyalty.
pages.title: HYPER PERSONALISATION

pages.abstract: This page discusses key insights on advanced personalisation techniques, tech enablers like AI and Big Data, and an executive playbook for implementing personalisation strategies. It highlights the importance of first-party data, cross-channel data integration, AI model development, scalable solutions, and establishing personalisation as a core capability.
pages.title: KEY INSIGHTS, TECH ENABLERS, EXECUTIVE PLAYBOOK

pages.abstract: Fashion brands must provide highly personalised customer experiences due to consumer expectations shaped by Netflix, Spotify, and Amazon. 71% of global consumers want tailored communications and products, while 76% are unhappy without them. Personalisation was once exclusive to luxury shoppers but is now a priority due to declining brand loyalty, increased competition, and data regulation changes. Data privacy regulations have increased advertising costs and decreased efficiency.
pages.title: 02. HYPER PERSONALISATION

pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of personalisation in the fashion industry, highlighting how brands can leverage data analytics and AI to offer hyper-personalised experiences. It explores the shift from search-based shopping to individualised discovery, using examples like Zalando and The Yes to illustrate how personalisation can enhance customer engagement and loyalty.
pages.title: Personalisation in Fashion E-commerce

pages.abstract: Hyper personalisation in fashion e-commerce requires companies to reimagine operations across platforms. Challenges include managing first-party data collection, creating a 360-degree customer view, and aligning human touch with AI. Solutions involve leveraging loyalty programs, customer data platforms, and adhering to data privacy regulations.
pages.title: 02. HYPER PERSONALISATION

pages.abstract: This page discusses the challenges and solutions for scaling personalisation in e-commerce, emphasizing the need for advanced AI models, behavioural data incorporation, and a comprehensive portfolio of design and distribution tools. It highlights the importance of establishing hyper-personalisation as a core competency and investing in data and analytics activations.
pages.title: Companies need a full range of analytics capabilities for a new era of personalisation

pages.abstract: This page introduces an executive interview with Robert Gentz, Co-Founder & Co-Chief Executive of Zalando, discussing the integration of data science into the fashion retail industry.
pages.title: Zalando: Bringing Data Science to the Art of Fashion Retail

pages.abstract: Zalando, Europe's largest online fashion retailer, leverages AI and data to personalize customer experiences, aiming to match millions of customers with the right products. By 2025, it targets €30 billion in merchandise sales, using algorithms to optimize customer interactions and long-term value.
pages.title: AI and other technologies are critical to how the fashion giant matches millions of customers with the right product in the right fit

pages.abstract: This page discusses Zalando's approach to personalization, size and fit challenges, logistics management, organizational structure for technology integration, data cleanliness, and emerging technologies like AR and VR. It highlights the importance of human curation, cross-functional teams, and data-driven solutions in addressing customer needs and operational efficiency.
pages.title: EXECUTIVE INTERVIEW

pages.abstract: The page discusses the virtual try-on experience and Zalando's Connected Retail platform, emphasizing the role of technology in solving size-and-fit and sustainability issues. It highlights the importance of data, collaboration, and resource optimization in the fashion industry.
pages.title: The Virtual Try-On Experience and Connected Retail

pages.abstract: The rise of e-commerce is reshaping physical stores. Fashion executives can improve consumer experience using in-store mobile apps and micro-fulfilment technologies to enhance retail networks for quick-commerce.
pages.title: 03. CONNECTED STORES

pages.abstract: This page discusses key insights on customer shopping preferences, the role of technology in enhancing the shopping experience, and tech enablers like cloud computing, mobile apps, and micro-fulfilment. It also outlines an executive playbook for assessing customer needs, understanding pain points, and bridging online and offline shopping.
pages.title: KEY INSIGHTS, TECH ENABLERS, EXECUTIVE PLAYBOOK

pages.abstract: Physical retail is adapting to changing consumer behaviors, with a focus on integrating technology to enhance the in-store experience. Mobile apps and interactive technologies are being used to address operational challenges and provide personalized experiences, catering to both convenience-driven and experience-seeking shoppers. Brands like Zara, Nike, and Burberry are leading the way with innovative solutions that blend digital and physical shopping.
pages.title: 03. CONNECTED STORES

pages.abstract: Technology can enhance shoppers' reasons for visiting physical stores and address pain points. Brands can use mobile apps for better in-store experiences and workflow management. Leading players are adopting technologies to turn stores into micro-fulfilment centers, improving stock levels and enabling fast delivery. Stock optimization technologies like RFID tags help integrate in-store and online stock for efficient order fulfillment.
pages.title: Technology can contribute to shoppers' reasons for visiting physical stores and address in-store pain points

pages.abstract: This page discusses the concept of connected stores, highlighting the role of cloud computing in enabling micro-fulfilment centres. It identifies three types of fulfilment models: back-office delivery centres, dedicated in-store sections for e-commerce, and dark stores. The page also emphasizes the cost savings and efficiency improvements these models can bring, supported by real-world examples.
pages.title: 03. CONNECTED STORES

pages.abstract: This page describes the behaviors of convenience shoppers and experience shoppers in a retail environment, highlighting their interactions with technology and store associates. It also discusses the role of automation in fulfilling orders, emphasizing the importance of stock optimization, last mile optimization, and robotic systems. The text advises executives on choosing the right fulfillment model based on brand size, store density, and e-commerce activity.
pages.title: Convenience Shopper and Experience Shopper

pages.abstract: Luxury brands are leveraging technology to enhance customer experience, complementing traditional face-to-face service with engaging digital channels and new technologies.
pages.title: How Luxury Brands Are Using Technology to Enhance the Customer Experience

pages.abstract: This page discusses the integration of digital tools and touchpoints in luxury retail, emphasizing the importance of personal, face-to-face service in physical stores. It highlights how luxury brands are leveraging technology to enhance the customer experience, with examples from Gucci, Burberry, and Chanel. The page also introduces the concept of 'Clienteling 2.0' through Farfetch's technology, which connects customers directly with sales associates and provides a 'connected retail layer' for better product storytelling and customer engagement.
pages.title: Luxury Retail in the Digital Age

pages.abstract: Luxury brands are increasingly integrating technology and digital channels into their customer experience, using clienteling apps, virtual reality, and personalized data insights. This shift is altering the relationship between brands and retailers, with a growing emphasis on direct-to-consumer models and e-commerce. The industry's past skepticism towards online sales is being replaced by a recognition of digital channels' importance in enhancing customer journeys.
pages.title: E-commerce and social media are increasingly where shoppers now encounter products

pages.abstract: This page discusses the collaboration between Farfetch and Neiman Marcus Group to integrate Bergdorf Goodman's digital presence with Farfetch's technology platform. It highlights the growing role of technology in luxury retail, including virtual worlds, NFTs, and customized production, to enhance customer experience and brand extension.
pages.title: Luxury Retail and Technology Integration

pages.abstract: Digital tools and analytics have transformed the fashion value chain, but siloed optimisations limit cross-functional improvements. Brands need end-to-end value chain integration for efficiency and profitability.
pages.title: 04. END-TO-END UPGRADE

pages.abstract: This page highlights key insights and tech enablers for fashion industry digitisation, including the need for integrated digital processes, custom solutions, and the benefits of adopting digitally enabled value chain solutions. It also outlines an executive playbook for calibrating analytics, prioritising critical journeys, investing in key enablers, and focusing on change management.
pages.title: Key Insights and Tech Enablers for Fashion Industry Digitisation

pages.abstract: This page discusses the need for a digitised value chain model in the fashion industry to address complex challenges like consumer demand and supply chain disruptions. It highlights the importance of end-to-end process management and the lack of comprehensive off-the-shelf solutions. The page also presents an exhibit showing executives' top digital investment priorities, with capacity planning and end-to-end process management leading the way.
pages.title: 04. END-TO-END UPGRADE

pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of integrating digital applications across the value chain to enhance efficiency and decision-making. It highlights how end-to-end integration can accelerate market speed, improve sell-through, and reduce costs. Examples from Levi’s and Shein illustrate the use of AI and machine learning in optimizing pricing, inventory management, and supply chain logistics.
pages.title: Digital applications need to be connected along the value chain

pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of end-to-end upgrades in the fashion industry, emphasizing the need for seamless data and knowledge flow across processes. It highlights the role of technology in achieving value chain integration and the challenges of change management, upskilling teams, and adopting user-centric tools. The page also introduces Exhibit 11, which outlines the layers of technology needed for value chain integration, including connected applications, AI & ML models, a data backbone, and cloud-based servers.
pages.title: 04. END-TO-END UPGRADE
Container Terminal Aerial View

pages.abstract: Traceability systems using tracking software and Big Data enable fashion brands to delve deep into their supply chains, enhancing sustainability by understanding the full lifecycle of their products.
pages.title: 05. TRACEABILITY FIRST

pages.abstract: This page highlights key insights on supply chain traceability in the fashion industry, emphasizing the need for centralised systems and emerging technologies. It outlines tech enablers like Big Data, Blockchain, product passports, and RFID. The executive playbook suggests laying foundations, prioritizing impact areas, and scaling solutions for effective traceability.
pages.title: Key Insights and Tech Enablers for Supply Chain Traceability

pages.abstract: The page discusses the importance of traceability in the fashion industry to address environmental and social impacts. It highlights challenges such as manual processes, unreliable data, and lack of industry-wide standards. The text also covers regulatory compliance, investor expectations, and customer demands for transparency and sustainability.
pages.title: 05. TRACEABILITY FIRST

pages.abstract: The document discusses the importance of traceability in the fashion industry for sustainability. It highlights the need for brands to collaborate on data sharing and standardization, mentioning initiatives like the Taskforce on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures and certification tools. Concerns about fragmented schemes are noted, but the emergence of industry-wide standards is expected to enhance traceability efforts. The role of technology in developing a common data language is emphasized.
pages.title: Traceability is a key to unlocking the sustainability challenge

pages.abstract: This page discusses the necessity of a standardised data format for scaling traceability in supply chains. It highlights the use of digital tools and decentralised ledgers for efficient data collection and distribution. Examples include TextileGenesis's blockchain technology and TrusTrace's centralised database. The complex nature of value chains necessitates technological solutions for traceability.
pages.title: A standardised data format is necessary to scale traceability

pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of knowledge sharing in supply chain traceability, highlighting initiatives like the Aura Blockchain Consortium and H&M's Treadler service. It emphasizes the need for collaboration among brands and the role of technology in achieving traceability.
pages.title: Knowledge Sharing

pages.page_path: library_pages\State of grocery Europe 2023_ Living with and responding to uncertainty_McKinsey\page_4.jpg
pages.abstract: The foreword discusses the challenges faced by the European grocery sector in 2022 due to inflation and consumer price sensitivity, leading to decreased margins. It highlights key trends shaping the industry, including consumer behavior, cost pressures, and sustainability efforts. The report, a collaboration between McKinsey & Company and EuroCommerce, provides insights from surveys and interviews to help grocers navigate uncertainty and drive future growth.
pages.title: Foreword

pages.page_path: library_pages\State of grocery Europe 2023_ Living with and responding to uncertainty_McKinsey\page_5.jpg
pages.title: Editors

pages.page_path: library_pages\State of grocery Europe 2023_ Living with and responding to uncertainty_McKinsey\page_6.jpg
pages.title: Living with and responding to uncertainty – State of Grocery Retail 2023 Europe

pages.page_path: library_pages\State of grocery Europe 2023_ Living with and responding to uncertainty_McKinsey\page_7.jpg
pages.title: Living with and responding to uncertainty

pages.page_path: library_pages\State of grocery Europe 2023_ Living with and responding to uncertainty_McKinsey\page_8.jpg
pages.abstract: The European grocery retail market in 2022 was marked by high inflation, volume decline, and consumer downtrading. Despite a 2.9% growth in overall sales, this was driven by a 10.7% increase in prices, offset by a 3.6% drop in volume. Private labels saw substantial growth, influenced by consumer behavior and price dynamics. The market dynamics varied significantly across countries, with some experiencing food inflation twice as high as general inflation.
pages.title: Did anyone say inflation?

pages.page_path: library_pages\State of grocery Europe 2023_ Living with and responding to uncertainty_McKinsey\page_9.jpg
pages.abstract: Discounters gained market share in Europe due to aggressive growth, recovery from the pandemic, and price sensitivity. Margins of European grocery retailers declined due to cost inflation and price-sensitive customers. Consumer confidence is rising but remains below pre-pandemic levels. Grocery CEOs are cautious about 2023, expecting challenges and focusing on cost management and private labels.
pages.title: 2023: Are we out of the woods?

pages.page_path: library_pages\State of grocery Europe 2023_ Living with and responding to uncertainty_McKinsey\page_10.jpg
pages.abstract: The survey shows that European CEOs are less pessimistic about 2023 market conditions compared to 2022. While 44% expect conditions to worsen, this is a 16 percentage point decrease from 2022. Conversely, 23% anticipate improvement, up 6 percentage points. The industry is described with terms like 'Price/Competitive,' 'Challenging/Difficult,' and 'Changing/Uncertain,' reflecting a complex and evolving landscape.
pages.title: European CEOs are less pessimistic about market conditions in 2023 compared with last year.

pages.page_path: library_pages\State of grocery Europe 2023_ Living with and responding to uncertainty_McKinsey\page_11.jpg
pages.abstract: The page details consumer trends in grocery shopping across European countries, highlighting increased prioritization of price-saving measures, reduced focus on premium and healthy products, and stable online shopping attitudes. Data shows significant shifts in consumer behavior, with notable differences across regions.
pages.title: Consumers actively look for more ways to save money across all surveyed countries.

pages.page_path: library_pages\State of grocery Europe 2023_ Living with and responding to uncertainty_McKinsey\page_12.jpg
pages.abstract: European CEOs anticipate margin pressure, downtrading of customers, and private label differentiation as top trends for the grocery industry in 2023. Product sustainability and entry price tier also rank high, while supply chain disruption and scaling online grocery face challenges. Decarbonization targets and modernizing IT are emerging priorities.
pages.title: European CEOs expect inflation, downtrading, and an increased focus on private labels to be the predominant trends in 2023.

pages.page_path: library_pages\State of grocery Europe 2023_ Living with and responding to uncertainty_McKinsey\page_13.jpg
pages.abstract: The European grocery retail market in 2023 will be characterized by eight key trends, including gradual price normalization, focus on cheaper private labels, margin pressure, economies of scale, online growth, retail media, automation, and sustainability efforts.
pages.title: Key trends

pages.page_path: library_pages\State of grocery Europe 2023_ Living with and responding to uncertainty_McKinsey\page_14.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses the gradual normalization of retail volume and inflation in Europe, predicting stable or slightly declining volumes in 2023 compared to 2022, with a significant slowdown in food inflation expected in the second half of 2023 due to decreasing commodity prices and energy costs.
pages.title: Gradual normalization of price and volume

pages.page_path: library_pages\State of grocery Europe 2023_ Living with and responding to uncertainty_McKinsey\page_15.jpg
pages.abstract: Consumers across income groups are prioritizing cheaper food options in 2023, with increased use of private labels and discounters. Despite potential market improvements, many consumers remain satisfied with private labels and discounters, showing a strong correlation between market share and private label attractiveness. Supermarkets may need to enhance their value propositions to attract customers back. Healthy eating remains a concern, but spending on premium products is decreasing.
pages.title: A focus on cheaper food through private labels and discounters

pages.page_path: library_pages\State of grocery Europe 2023_ Living with and responding to uncertainty_McKinsey\page_16.jpg
pages.abstract: The profitability of grocers declined in 2022 due to margin and cost pressures, with EBITDA margins decreasing for both retailers and food processors. Cost pressures are expected to continue in 2023, exacerbated by rising salaries and delayed cost increases. Grocery retailers face additional challenges from increasing investment requirements and higher costs of capital, making financing more difficult. The foreword discusses the challenges faced by the European grocery sector in 2022 due to inflation and consumer price sensitivity, leading to decreased margins. It highlights key trends shaping the industry, including consumer behavior, cost pressures, and sustainability efforts. The report, a collaboration between McKinsey & Company and EuroCommerce, provides insights from surveys and interviews to help grocers navigate uncertainty and drive future growth.
The European grocery retail market in 2022 was marked by high inflation, volume decline, and consumer downtrading. Despite a 2.9% growth in overall sales, this was driven by a 10.7% increase in prices, offset by a 3.6% drop in volume. Private labels saw substantial growth, influenced by consumer behavior and price dynamics. The market dynamics varied significantly across countries, with some experiencing food inflation twice as high as general inflation.
Discounters gained market share in Europe due to aggressive growth, recovery from the pandemic, and price sensitivity. Grocery CEOs are cautious about 2023, expecting challenges and focusing on cost management and private labels.
The survey shows that European CEOs are less pessimistic about 2023 market conditions compared to 2022. While 44% expect conditions to worsen, this is a 16 percentage point decrease from 2022. pages.abstract: The European grocery industry faced challenges in 2023 due to inflation, leading to decreased volume and downtrading. Industry growth lagged behind food price inflation. Discounters and private labels thrived. In 2024, despite macroeconomic uncertainty, there are early signs of recovery with improved consumer confidence and wage increases, though consumer behavior remains polarized.
pages.title: Signs of Hope

pages.page_path: library_pages\State of Grocery Europe 2024_ Signs of Hope_McKinsey\page_8.jpg
pages.abstract: Grocery sales in Europe grew by 8.6% in 2023 due to inflation and downtrading, with real terms declining. Inflation eased but remained dominant. Real wages were compressed, impacting consumer purchasing power. Consumers traded down, benefiting private labels and discounters. Supermarkets in some countries found strategies to succeed despite price pressure.
pages.title: 2023: Again all about price

pages.page_path: library_pages\State of Grocery Europe 2024_ Signs of Hope_McKinsey\page_9.jpg
pages.abstract: The European grocery retail market saw improvements in 2023 as inflation slowed. Online sales remained stable at 6% of total grocery sales, with varying trends across countries. Inflation and volume changes influenced retail sales, with food inflation peaking in Q2 and declining by Q4. Volume declines slowed, and downtrading decreased, leading to a near-zero decline in the fourth quarter of 2023.
pages.title: Europe's grocery retail market improved during 2023 as inflation slowed.

pages.page_path: library_pages\State of Grocery Europe 2024_ Signs of Hope_McKinsey\page_10.jpg
pages.abstract: The document discusses positive signs for the European grocery retail industry in 2024, despite initial challenges. It highlights improving economic fundamentals, stabilizing inflation, and growing real wages. Consumer behavior is shifting, with some groups planning to trade up. However, market performance is expected to vary significantly across countries and consumer segments. Grocery CEOs remain concerned but less so than in previous years, with a focus on prices, inflation, and market conditions. The 2024 agenda includes margin pressure, downtrading, and emerging priorities like talent and food to go.
pages.title: 2024: Signs of hope?

pages.page_path: library_pages\State of Grocery Europe 2024_ Signs of Hope_McKinsey\page_11.jpg
pages.abstract: The document highlights that in most European countries, consumers are less focused on saving money in 2024 compared to 2023. It presents data on net intent for various shopping behaviors, showing a decline in price consciousness but an increase in interest in healthy, sustainable, and premium products. Online shopping behavior also shows a positive trend.
pages.title: In most European countries, shoppers are less focused on saving money in 2024 than they were in 2023.

pages.page_path: library_pages\State of Grocery Europe 2024_ Signs of Hope_McKinsey\page_12.jpg
pages.abstract: European CEOs are less pessimistic about 2024 market conditions, with 24% expecting improvement and 40% expecting stability. The grocery industry is described as challenging, competitive, and price-focused, with concerns about inflation and public scrutiny.
pages.title: European CEOs are less pessimistic about market conditions in 2024 compared with last year.

The survey provides insights into the strategic focus areas shaping the industry's future.

pages.abstract: The profitability of grocers declined further in 2023, with margin pressure remaining a top priority for CEOs. Grocery retailers and CPG companies experienced margin decreases between 2019 and 2022, but 2023 saw a different trend. Retailers lost more margin due to cost increases, while CPG companies gained back some margin by passing costs to retailers. In 2024, rising rent and labor costs will continue to pressure margins. Retailers are expected to intensify supplier negotiations, form buying alliances, and pursue M&A activities to improve margins.
pages.title: Cost and margin pressure

pages.page_path: library_pages\State of Grocery Europe 2024_ Signs of Hope_McKinsey\page_17.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses consumer behavior trends in Europe, highlighting that most groups plan to trade down in 2024, while high-income households show signs of uptrading. It notes a decline in the intent to save money but an increased interest in quality and health. Private labels and discounters are growing, and consumers prioritize health and longevity, with functional food claims gaining traction.
pages.title: The return of polarization

pages.abstract: The food-to-go market is surging as consumers spend more time on the move. It encompasses various channels like prepackaged meals, ready-to-heat convenience meals, and meal delivery. The growth is driven by busy lifestyles and the return of workers to offices. Foodservice providers are gaining share from grocery retailers. Grocery retailers are expanding their food-to-go offerings to capture this growth.
pages.title: Food to go: A wrestling match for share of stomach

pages.abstract: The page discusses the progress and challenges in achieving sustainability goals in the European grocery retail sector. It highlights the decreasing consumer interest in sustainable products, the difficulty in measuring and reducing Scope 3 emissions, and the potential of regenerative agriculture. The top ten European grocers are making efforts to meet their 2025 sustainability targets, with varying levels of progress reported across different dimensions.
pages.title: Sustainability: Progress made, still a long way to go

A woman and her baby enjoy a pleasant grocery shopping experience, interacting with fresh produce in a well-stocked store.
The European grocery industry faced challenges in 2023 due to inflation, leading to decreased volume and downtrading. Industry growth lagged behind food price inflation. Discounters and private labels thrived. In 2024, despite macroeconomic uncertainty, there are early signs of recovery with improved consumer confidence and wage increases, though consumer behavior remains polarized.
Grocery sales in Europe grew by 8.6% in 2023 due to inflation and downtrading, with real terms declining. Inflation eased but remained dominant. Real wages were compressed, impacting consumer purchasing power. Consumers traded down, benefiting private labels and discounters. Supermarkets in some countries found strategies to succeed despite price pressure.
The European grocery retail market saw improvements in 2023 as inflation slowed. Online sales remained stable at 6% of total grocery sales, with varying trends across countries. Inflation and volume changes influenced retail sales, with food inflation peaking in Q2 and declining by Q4. Volume declines slowed, and downtrading decreased, leading to a near-zero decline in the fourth quarter of 2023.
The document discusses positive signs for the European grocery retail industry in 2024, despite initial challenges. It highlights improving economic fundamentals, stabilizing inflation, and growing real wages. Consumer behavior is shifting, with some groups planning to trade up. However, market performance is expected to vary significantly across countries and consumer segments. Grocery CEOs remain concerned but less so than in previous years, with a focus on prices, inflation, and market conditions. The 2024 agenda includes margin pressure, downtrading, and emerging priorities like talent and food to go.
The document highlights that in most European countries, consumers are less focused on saving money in 2024 compared to 2023. It presents data on net intent for various shopping behaviors, showing a decline in price consciousness but an increase in interest in healthy, sustainable, and premium products. Online shopping behavior also shows a positive trend.
European CEOs are less pessimistic about 2024 market conditions, with 24% expecting improvement and 40% expecting stability. The grocery industry is described as challenging, competitive, and price-focused, with concerns about inflation and public scrutiny.
The document highlights the top 15 trends in the grocery industry for 2024, as identified by CEOs. Key concerns include cost and margin pressure, downtrading of consumers, and talent hiring and development. The data shows shifts in priorities compared to the previous year, with some areas gaining importance while others decline. The survey provides insights into the strategic focus areas shaping the industry's future.
The European grocery retail market in 2024 will be characterized by eight key trends, including cost and margin pressure, polarization in consumer behavior, growth in food to go, sustainability challenges, online shopping shifts, retail media expansion, conversational commerce advancements, and talent acquisition efforts.
This page depicts a shopping basket with fresh vegetables in a grocery store, symbolizing the state of grocery retail in Europe for 2024. The image highlights consumer behavior and the retail environment.
The profitability of grocers declined further in 2023, with margin pressure remaining a top priority for CEOs. Grocery retailers and CPG companies experienced margin decreases between 2019 and 2022, but 2023 saw a different trend. Retailers lost more margin due to cost increases, while CPG companies gained back some margin by passing costs to retailers. In 2024, rising rent and labor costs will continue to pressure margins. Retailers are expected to intensify supplier negotiations, form buying alliances, and pursue M&A activities to improve margins.
The page discusses consumer behavior trends in Europe, highlighting that most groups plan to trade down in 2024, while high-income households show signs of uptrading. It notes a decline in the intent to save money but an increased interest in quality and health. Private labels and discounters are growing, and consumers prioritize health and longevity, with functional food claims gaining traction.
The food-to-go market is surging as consumers spend more time on the move. It encompasses various channels like prepackaged meals, ready-to-heat convenience meals, and meal delivery. The growth is driven by busy lifestyles and the return of workers to offices. Foodservice providers are gaining share from grocery retailers. Grocery retailers are expanding their food-to-go offerings to capture this growth.
The page discusses the progress and challenges in achieving sustainability goals in the European grocery retail sector. It highlights the decreasing consumer interest in sustainable products, the difficulty in measuring and reducing Scope 3 emissions, and the potential of regenerative agriculture. The top ten European grocers are making efforts to meet their 2025 sustainability targets, with varying levels of progress reported across different dimensions.
The page discusses the resurgence and profitability of online grocery and meal delivery services, highlighting their growth potential and differentiation from offline channels. It includes a chart showing market size projections for EU-5 countries, emphasizing the expected outpacing of offline growth by online channels.
Retail media is a significant profit driver for grocery retailers in Europe, with a market value of €11 billion in 2023 and expected 15% annual growth. Large retailers dominate, with Amazon leading. Standardization, impact measurement, and ad diversification are crucial for engaging CPGs. Retailers are expanding offerings to include video and connected TV to stay relevant.
Conversational commerce, enabled by generative AI, is poised to transform shopping experiences. While advanced analytics and traditional AI dominate current value creation, generative AI contributes 10-20% of potential value in grocery retail. Key use cases include hyper-personalization, smart search, and conversational commerce, enhancing both revenue and efficiency. Retailers like Walmart are already leveraging these technologies to improve customer engagement and operational efficiency.
This page discusses the challenges faced by European grocery retailers, including high job vacancy and turnover rates, a shortage of skilled talent, and the impact of an aging population. It highlights the need for developing talent and adapting to automation and digitalization, emphasizing the importance of social, emotional, and technological skills. The page also addresses the need for attractive career opportunities and work-life balance in the retail sector.
Grocery retailers face challenges but have opportunities to build competitive advantages. Priorities include future-proofing assortments, driving efficiency savings, and monetizing retail media. Success requires balancing affordability with value, optimizing costs, and enhancing advertising offerings.

pages.abstract: The introduction discusses the current state of AI investment in companies, highlighting the gap between investment and maturity. It emphasizes the transformative potential of AI, similar to the steam engine in the Industrial Revolution, and the challenges leaders face in steering their organizations towards AI maturity. The report, inspired by Reid Hoffman’s book, explores how companies can harness AI to drive positive change and avoid becoming uncompetitive.
pages.title: Introduction

pages.page_path: library_pages\Superagency in the workplace_ Empowering people to unlock AIs full potential_McKinsey_2025_01_01\page_4.jpg
pages.abstract: This page highlights key statistics on employee readiness for AI adoption, company investment in AI, and leadership challenges. Employees are more prepared for AI changes than leaders think, with millennials showing higher familiarity. Companies are investing but moving slowly, and employees trust their leaders to balance speed and safety. Despite plans for future investment, maturity is low. Leadership needs to address employee readiness and training support.
pages.title: Superagency: By the numbers

pages.page_path: library_pages\Superagency in the workplace_ Empowering people to unlock AIs full potential_McKinsey_2025_01_01\page_5.jpg
pages.abstract: This report examines AI adoption readiness in companies, highlighting employees' positive attitudes towards AI and the need for leadership to address challenges. It covers technology advancements, employee perceptions, deployment safety, strategic goals, and leadership requirements for AI success.
pages.title: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI's full potential

pages.title: An innovation as powerful as the steam engine

pages.abstract: This page discusses the transformative potential of AI, emphasizing its ability to enhance human productivity, creativity, and decision-making. It highlights AI's role in reshaping interactions with technology and society, detailing advancements in AI capabilities and their impact on business. The sidebar introduces the concept of 'AI superagency,' exploring how AI can empower individuals and enhance human potential.
pages.title: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI's full potential

pages.page_path: library_pages\Superagency in the workplace_ Empowering people to unlock AIs full potential_McKinsey_2025_01_01\page_8.jpg
pages.abstract: This page illustrates the rapid evolution of generative AI capabilities over two years, comparing various platforms from leading labs. It highlights advancements from text-only models with limited reasoning and contextual understanding to multimodal systems with advanced reasoning, real-time data integration, and enhanced contextual coherence. The exhibit underscores significant progress in AI capabilities, including experimental tool usage and comprehensive training.
pages.title: Gen AI capabilities have evolved rapidly over the past two years.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Superagency in the workplace_ Empowering people to unlock AIs full potential_McKinsey_2025_01_01\page_9.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses advancements in AI intelligence and reasoning, highlighting the performance of LLMs on standardized tests and their ability to reason and act autonomously. It mentions specific examples like GPT-4's performance and the potential of AI bots and agents in various applications.
pages.title: Intelligence and reasoning are improving

pages.page_path: library_pages\Superagency in the workplace_ Empowering people to unlock AIs full potential_McKinsey_2025_01_01\page_10.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the gradual yet sudden impact of AI, highlighting its integration into software products, multimodal capabilities, and hardware innovations that enhance AI performance. Examples include Salesforce's Agentforce, Google's Gemini Live, and OpenAI's Sora, showcasing advancements in AI-driven solutions for businesses.
pages.title: 'AI, like most transformative technologies, grows gradually, then arrives suddenly.'

pages.page_path: library_pages\Superagency in the workplace_ Empowering people to unlock AIs full potential_McKinsey_2025_01_01\page_11.jpg
pages.abstract: AI transparency and explainability are improving, reducing risks and biases. The Stanford CRFM Transparency Index shows significant progress, with Anthropic and Amazon increasing their scores. Explainability in AI and ML allows tracing model outputs to data inputs, aiding bias detection and compliance. Continuous evolution is needed to match growing model capabilities. Achieving AI superagency involves supporting people and managing governance.
pages.title: Transparency is increasing

pages.page_path: library_pages\Superagency in the workplace_ Empowering people to unlock AIs full potential_McKinsey_2025_01_01\page_12.jpg
pages.abstract: This page highlights the readiness of employees for AI and calls for leaders to step up. It includes a quote from Sam Altman, emphasizing the potential of AI to create astonishing achievements in the future.
pages.title: Employees are ready for AI; now leaders must step up

pages.page_path: library_pages\Superagency in the workplace_ Empowering people to unlock AIs full potential_McKinsey_2025_01_01\page_13.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the significant gap between employees' and leaders' perceptions of AI usage in the workplace. Employees are more familiar with AI tools and expect to use them more extensively than leaders anticipate. The survey highlights the need for leaders to step up and support AI adoption to unlock its full potential.
pages.title: Employees are three times more likely to be using gen AI today than their leaders expect.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Superagency in the workplace_ Empowering people to unlock AIs full potential_McKinsey_2025_01_01\page_14.jpg
pages.abstract: The page details employee attitudes toward AI, categorizing them into Doomers, Gloomers, Bloomers, and Zoomers. It highlights their varying levels of familiarity and comfort with AI, emphasizing that even skeptical groups have significant exposure to AI tools. The data reveals that Bloomers are the largest group, followed by Gloomers and Zoomers, with Doomers being the smallest. The page also includes a detailed breakdown of each group's sentiment, familiarity, and expectations regarding AI adoption and impact.
pages.title: Employee segments differ, but all indicate a high familiarity with gen AI.

pages.page_path: library_pages\Superagency in the workplace_ Empowering people to unlock AIs full potential_McKinsey_2025_01_01\page_15.jpg
pages.abstract: Employees desire more formal AI training and support from their companies to enhance AI adoption. Nearly half of US employees want formal training, seamless integration, and access to AI tools. However, many report minimal support. The perceived level of support for AI capability building is expected to increase in the next three years.
pages.title: Leaders can invest more in their employees

pages.page_path: library_pages\Superagency in the workplace_ Empowering people to unlock AIs full potential_McKinsey_2025_01_01\page_16.jpg
pages.abstract: International employees receive more support for AI skill development and have greater involvement in gen AI tool development compared to their US counterparts, with notable differences in feedback and beta testing activities.
pages.title: Global perspectives on training

pages.page_path: library_pages\Superagency in the workplace_ Empowering people to unlock AIs full potential_McKinsey_2025_01_01\page_17.jpg
pages.abstract: Millennials aged 35 to 44 are leading in AI expertise and enthusiasm. They are more familiar with AI, comfortable using it at work, and willing to provide feedback and participate in AI tool design compared to other age groups. Leaders can leverage this to enhance AI adoption.
pages.title: C-suite leaders can help millennials lead the way

pages.page_path: library_pages\Superagency in the workplace_ Empowering people to unlock AIs full potential_McKinsey_2025_01_01\page_18.jpg
pages.abstract: Managers frequently act as sounding boards for their teams on gen AI, with two-thirds receiving weekly inquiries and recommending AI tools. pages.title: The 2022 McKinsey Global Payments Report
The 2022 McKinsey Global Payments Report
Contents

pages.abstract: The foreword discusses the resilience of the global payments ecosystem amid macroeconomic and geopolitical challenges, highlighting revenue growth in 2021 and future outlook. It introduces key topics like embedded finance and sustainability in payments, emphasizing shifts in growth drivers and new opportunities for market participants.
pages.title: Foreword

pages.abstract: This chapter discusses the importance of banks creating a sustainable payments value proposition, explores the development of central-bank digital currencies (CBDCs), and examines the growth of digital payments in emerging markets. It highlights the role of public-private partnerships, competition among various sectors, and the potential for innovation in digital payments.
pages.title: The 2022 McKinsey Global Payments Report
The chessboard rearranged: Rethinking the next moves in global payments

pages.abstract: The global payments industry showed resilience in 2021, with revenues growing 11% to reach $2.1 trillion. Fee-based revenue surpassed net interest income, and growth was strong across regions. Factors like rising interest rates, geopolitical shifts, and technological advancements are reshaping the industry, creating opportunities for both incumbents and disruptors.
pages.title: The global payments industry demonstrated its resilience again in 2021

pages.abstract: The page discusses the resilience of the payments industry, highlighting the growth in electronic payment transactions and e-commerce, particularly in Asia-Pacific. It details the impact of COVID-19 on cash usage and the strong revenue growth across regions in 2021, with Asia-Pacific accounting for over half of global payments revenues. The exhibit provides a detailed breakdown of global payments revenues by region and type of transaction.
pages.title: Asia-Pacific accounts for over half of global payments revenues.

pages.abstract: The document discusses global payment trends, focusing on A2A transaction revenues, credit and debit card usage, and the impact of instant payments. It highlights regional variations, pricing dynamics, and the recovery of global trade flows post-pandemic, projecting future growth rates and revenue opportunities.
pages.title: Global Payments Trends and Revenue Growth

pages.abstract: This page presents a scatter plot comparing payments revenues per capita and per transaction across various countries. The United States leads in revenue per capita, while Indonesia has the lowest. China shows a high revenue per transaction but moderate revenue per capita. The data highlights significant variations in payment revenues among countries.
pages.title: Payments revenues per capita and per transaction vary markedly by country.

pages.abstract: The document discusses six forces reshaping the global payments landscape, focusing on macroeconomic and geopolitical environments. It highlights projected revenue growth, regional differences, and the impact of inflation and geopolitical disruptions on business models and strategies.
pages.title: Looking ahead: Six forces reshaping the landscape

pages.abstract: This page discusses six forces reshaping the global payments landscape: capital markets reset, commerce expectations, technology modernization, social responsibility, and macroeconomic factors like higher interest rates and inflation. It explores how these forces impact payments revenue and offers insights for players to adapt and thrive in the evolving ecosystem.
pages.title: The chessboard rearranged: Rethinking the next moves in global payments

pages.abstract: This page discusses the impact of inflation on payment models, highlighting the challenges and opportunities for traditional and emerging payment systems. It explores the geopolitical environment's influence on regional payment infrastructures and the need for localization. The text also addresses the complexity of regulations, compliance, and security in cross-border payments, as well as the effects of geopolitical events and sanctions on global supply chains and trade finance strategies.
pages.title: Geopolitical environment: Payments regionalization and localization

pages.abstract: The document discusses the decline in total shareholder returns for payments companies, particularly attacker firms, over the past year. It highlights the impact of changing investor expectations and macroeconomic conditions, with a focus on the stark moderation in growth expectations and the shift in performance between attacker and incumbent payments companies.
pages.title: Capital markets reset: Turning unicorns into workhorses

pages.abstract: The document discusses the decline in valuations of payments companies, the strategic shifts by attackers, and the potential for consolidation. It highlights the importance of commerce facilitation and embedded finance in capturing revenue pools, and the challenges of technology modernization in payments.
pages.title: Commerce expectations: From payments to commerce facilitation

pages.abstract: This page discusses the transformation of payment infrastructures, highlighting the shift from legacy systems to cloud-based solutions, the rise of instant payments, and the influence of social responsibility and ESG on payment systems. It also covers the role of payments in financial inclusion, data privacy, and governance.
pages.title: The chessboard rearranged: Rethinking the next moves in global payments

pages.abstract: The payments industry is expected to grow significantly over the next five years, driven by changing interest rates and inflation. ESG concerns will be central to strategies for payments providers. Players need to adapt their models and platforms to remain competitive, leveraging flexibility and innovation to navigate market complexities and capitalize on emerging opportunities.
pages.title: The chessboard rearranged: Rethinking the next moves in global payments
Embedded finance: Who will lead the next payments revolution?

pages.abstract: This page discusses the embedded finance revolution, explaining how small businesses can access financial services through e-commerce and accounting platforms. It highlights the role of software companies partnering with banks and technology providers, the growth of embedded finance in the US, and the factors driving its evolution, including changes in commerce, consumer behavior, and technology.
pages.title: Embedded finance: Who will lead the next payments revolution?

pages.abstract: Embedded finance is growing in deposits, payments, issuing, and lending, with various distributors like retailers, software firms, and telecom companies offering financial products to enhance customer experience and revenue. Novel use cases include prepaid cards for employees and instant payments for merchants. The product portfolio is expanding due to digitization and real-time risk analytics, but regulatory and case-specific constraints may limit growth.
pages.title: Demand for embedded finance is already growing in deposits, payments, issuing, and lending.

pages.abstract: This page discusses the enablers of embedded finance, including technology providers and balance sheet providers, and explains how they collaborate to offer embedded financial products. It also highlights the value capture dynamics, emphasizing that revenue primarily accrues to risk takers and customer relationship owners.
pages.title: Who are the enablers of embedded finance?

pages.abstract: The page discusses strategies for success in embedded finance, emphasizing product breadth, depth, and program management support as key differentiators. It highlights the importance of building customer relationships, capturing data, and managing regulatory risks for new entrants.
pages.title: What does it take to win in embedded finance?

pages.abstract: This page discusses strategies for financial institutions and fintechs to succeed in embedded finance, including choosing competitive areas, building developer experiences, adapting sales motions, and developing support and risk services. It highlights the importance of technology, partnerships, and risk management in this fast-growing market.
pages.title: Embedded finance: Who will lead the next payments revolution?
Sustainability in global transaction banking: A market imperative

pages.abstract: This page discusses the growing importance of sustainability in global transaction banking (GTB), highlighting the strong growth in sustainable debt instruments and the potential for sustainable GTB products. It emphasizes the need for banks to embed sustainability in their GTB offerings to meet customer demands and stay competitive. The page also addresses the challenges faced by banks in incorporating sustainability features and the benefits of embedding sustainability-tracking capabilities within core transaction banking services.
pages.title: Sustainability in GTB: Opportunity and imperative

pages.abstract: This page discusses the role of banks in assessing and reducing scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions in supply chains, enhancing sustainability efforts, and the projected growth in sustainable global transaction banking revenue pools. It highlights the benefits of adopting sustainability-rated GTB offerings, including reputation enhancement, favorable conditions from buyers, and access to credit. The page also projects the revenue opportunity in sustainable GTB to grow to $28-$35 billion by 2025, representing 8% of global transaction banking revenue.
pages.title: Sustainability in global transaction banking: A market imperative

pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of sustainable GTB in achieving financial performance and sustainability goals. It outlines the three waves of value proposition for banks in this space and defines sustainability for GTB products, emphasizing their role in supporting the UN SDGs. It also highlights the differences between internal sustainability frameworks and the UN SDGs and introduces the Greenhouse Gas Protocol.
pages.title: A best-in-class sustainable GTB ecosystem

pages.title: Next steps: How to build a sustainability value proposition

pages.abstract: Digital payment transactions have surged in emerging markets due to pandemic-driven shifts to contactless payments and e-commerce. Growth is particularly strong in Africa and Southeast Asia, driven by low banking penetration. While banks remain dominant in most countries, nonbanks lead in some markets. Four major trends—pandemic acceleration, e-commerce growth, government pushes for cashless payments, and investor interest—have fueled this growth. Despite this, cash remains widely used in some markets, especially in Africa and Southeast Asia, through extensive retail agent networks.
pages.title: Digital payment transactions

pages.abstract: This page discusses the competition between banks and third-party wallets in emerging markets, highlighting the role of solid payments infrastructure and captive customer bases. It also mentions government interventions in markets like Brazil and India, and strategies adopted by banks in developed markets.
pages.title: The emerging markets where banks are the strongest, such as Brazil and Nigeria, tend to have a solid payments infrastructure and a captive customer base stemming from historical first-mover advantage or regulatory restrictions on alternative rails.

pages.abstract: This page discusses how market structure influences the success of nonbank wallets. It highlights the roles of banks, tech giants, and nonbanks in various countries, showing that regulatory openness and payment infrastructure openness are key factors. Examples include partnerships between banks and tech companies and the success of nonbank wallets in markets with less developed payment systems.
pages.title: Market structure largely determines whether nonbank wallets can gain an edge.

pages.abstract: The evolving landscape of digital wallets and payments is shaped by regulatory changes, partnerships, and ecosystem integration. While wallets have high adoption, their usage frequency remains low. Successful wallets are embedded in broader ecosystems, expanding into various categories. Profitability remains a challenge due to thin margins and competitive pressures.
pages.title: An evolving landscape

pages.abstract: Digital payment platforms face challenges like squeezed margins and high acquisition costs. Providers like M-Pesa are under pressure to reduce fees. Wallets are exploring monetization paths by entering other payment arenas and offering comprehensive financial and lifestyle services to become a one-stop shop for consumers.
pages.title: Social-media, e-commerce, and ride-hailing platforms are well placed to scale up into digital payments ecosystems.

pages.abstract: This page details the services offered by digital wallets across Asia, Latin America, and Africa, categorized by their distance from core services. The text explains extended payments, emphasizing merchant services and business digitization.
pages.title: Successful wallets are extending into a range of payment types, financial services, and consumer lifestyle services.

pages.abstract: This page discusses the diverse financial services offered by digital wallets, including investment, lending, and insurance. It highlights partnerships and regulatory adaptations in various markets, such as the Philippines, Indonesia, and Brazil. pages.abstract: This page discusses innovative features in digital wallets, including green initiatives, loyalty programs, and social features. pages.abstract: Financial services companies are prioritizing emerging technologies like cloud computing, AI, and digital identity, but must also address associated cyber risks. They need to strengthen cybersecurity capabilities, align technology priorities with security, and ensure proper metrics and talent to manage risks effectively.
pages.title: Executive summary

pages.page_path: library_pages\The cyber clock is ticking_ Derisking emerging technologies in financial servers_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_6.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses ten emerging technologies, including next-generation software development, trust architectures, industrialized machine learning, Web3, advanced connectivity, quantum technologies, future of mobility, and immersive-reality technologies. It highlights their potential impacts on various industries and presents a survey result showing that cloud and edge computing are the most applicable trends in financial services, followed by applied AI.
pages.title: Ten emerging technologies (continued)

pages.page_path: library_pages\The cyber clock is ticking_ Derisking emerging technologies in financial servers_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_7.jpg
pages.abstract: Financial institutions are focusing on emerging technologies like cloud and edge computing to enhance automation, scalability, and cost savings. They are prioritizing investments in DevOps and AI while considering the maturity and applicability of each technology. Cloud computing is the most mature technology, with 84% of respondents recognizing its relevance and 60% having more than 25% of their workload in the cloud.
pages.title: Financial institutions have emerging technologies in their sights

pages.page_path: library_pages\The cyber clock is ticking_ Derisking emerging technologies in financial servers_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_8.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the growing adoption of applied AI in financial services, highlighting its potential value and the evolving maturity of AI technologies. It emphasizes the promise and risks of generative AI, estimating its economic impact and the need for responsible implementation. The text also touches on the benefits of next-gen software development and the importance of trust architecture in the industry.
pages.title: The promises—and risks—of generative AI

pages.page_path: library_pages\The cyber clock is ticking_ Derisking emerging technologies in financial servers_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_9.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the adoption of digital identity and trust architecture in financial services, highlighting benefits like faster innovation and stronger asset protection. It also explores emerging technologies like quantum computing and their potential impact on the industry, emphasizing the need for secure digital footprints and identity-related capabilities.
pages.title: Emerging Technologies in Financial Services

pages.page_path: library_pages\The cyber clock is ticking_ Derisking emerging technologies in financial servers_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_10.jpg
pages.abstract: Financial services organizations recognize the need to increase spending on key technologies like industrialized machine learning, next-gen software development, and applied AI. More than half of respondents believe they should invest more in these areas, with cloud and edge computing also receiving significant attention. This trend is expected to accelerate as technologies mature and proliferate.
pages.title: Financial-services organizations are spending the most on cloud and edge computing technologies.

pages.page_path: library_pages\The cyber clock is ticking_ Derisking emerging technologies in financial servers_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_11.jpg
pages.abstract: Emerging technologies bring significant benefits but also amplify existing cyber risks. Financial institutions face increasing cyberattacks from well-funded criminals using advanced technologies like AI. Cyber incidents are rising in frequency and severity, necessitating robust risk management strategies. The 2024 CrowdStrike report highlights eCrime as the most pervasive threat, with data-theft extortion on the rise. Companies must stay vigilant and consider various cyber risks, including AI, talent management, and supply chain security.
pages.title: Emerging technologies amplify existing risks and add new ones

pages.page_path: library_pages\The cyber clock is ticking_ Derisking emerging technologies in financial servers_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_12.jpg
pages.abstract: The page discusses the increasing frequency and severity of cyberattacks on financial services organizations from 2007 to 2023, highlighting major incidents and their impacts. It emphasizes the need for robust cybersecurity strategies and skilled talent to mitigate risks as companies adopt new technologies.
pages.title: Exhibit 3. As financial-services organizations continue to transform and modernize, the frequency and severity of cyberattacks are increasing.

pages.page_path: library_pages\The cyber clock is ticking_ Derisking emerging technologies in financial servers_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_13.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the top cyber risks for financial services organizations over the next 3–5 years, highlighting cyber attacks, emerging technology misuse, and talent management as key concerns. It emphasizes the regulatory risks associated with AI and the importance of building strong cybersecurity capabilities to secure technologies and protect environments. The text also addresses the risks of next-gen software development and trust architecture, zero-trust architecture implementation, and the need for organizations to understand both the benefits and risks of new technologies.
pages.title: Exhibit 4. Cyberattacks, AI misuse, and talent management are key risks for financial-services organizations.

pages.page_path: library_pages\The cyber clock is ticking_ Derisking emerging technologies in financial servers_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_14.jpg
pages.abstract: This page highlights the strategic importance of digital transformation, emphasizing investment in emerging technologies like cloud and AI. It underscores the critical need for managing cyber and technology risks to ensure service resilience, build customer trust, and protect the bank's safety and soundness.
pages.title: Digital Transformation and Cyber Risk Management

pages.page_path: library_pages\The cyber clock is ticking_ Derisking emerging technologies in financial servers_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_15.jpg
pages.abstract: Financial institutions face pressure to keep pace with emerging technologies and worry about inadequate cybersecurity investments. Surveyed companies identified weaknesses in third-party management and metrics/reporting, critical for deploying new technologies. Enhancing these capabilities is essential to mitigate cyber risks and align with risk appetites.
pages.title: Companies need strong foundational cybersecurity capabilities to counter cyber risks

pages.page_path: library_pages\The cyber clock is ticking_ Derisking emerging technologies in financial servers_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_16.jpg
pages.abstract: This page outlines McKinsey's cybersecurity capability model, detailing eight domains and their sub-domains, including strategy, governance, architecture, operations, identity management, resilience, data privacy, and physical security.
pages.title: McKinsey cybersecurity capability model

pages.page_path: library_pages\The cyber clock is ticking_ Derisking emerging technologies in financial servers_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_17.jpg
pages.abstract: Financial services organizations recognize the need to improve technical capabilities, particularly in third-party security, metrics and reporting, and privileged access management. New regulations emphasize the importance of better reporting and governance of cybersecurity risks. Companies must develop robust processes for measuring and managing risks associated with emerging technologies and vulnerabilities.
pages.title: Financial-services organizations are often strong in overarching security governance and strategy but feel they could improve technical capabilities.

pages.page_path: library_pages\The cyber clock is ticking_ Derisking emerging technologies in financial servers_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_18.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of proper PAM, secure cloud infrastructure, and data life cycle management in financial services. It highlights the risks associated with emerging technologies like AI and next-gen software development, emphasizing the need for robust security measures to prevent data exposure and optimize technology benefits.
pages.title: The cyber clock is ticking: Derisking emerging technologies in financial services

pages.page_path: library_pages\The cyber clock is ticking_ Derisking emerging technologies in financial servers_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_19.jpg
pages.abstract: Financial services organizations are struggling to keep up with the rapid pace of cybersecurity adoption. Increased compliance with regulations and defense against threats are key factors driving maturity. Companies recognize critical underinvestment in cybersecurity, with 70% of respondents acknowledging underspending. Proactive compliance and future-proofing technologies are essential for addressing emerging regulations.
pages.title: How are companies prioritizing and investing in cybersecurity?

pages.page_path: library_pages\The cyber clock is ticking_ Derisking emerging technologies in financial servers_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_20.jpg
pages.abstract: Financial services organizations prioritize compliance and security against threats as key drivers for maturing cybersecurity capabilities. Increased compliance and security protection are the top factors, with 70% of respondents citing these. Business drivers and competitive differentiation follow. Cybersecurity spending is expected to rise, with regional banks seeing the largest growth. Special initiatives are needed to address emerging technology risks.
pages.title: Financial-services organizations value compliance and security against threats as top drivers for cybersecurity capabilities.

pages.page_path: library_pages\The cyber clock is ticking_ Derisking emerging technologies in financial servers_McKinsey_2024_01_01\page_21.jpg
pages.abstract: This page discusses the importance of developing standards for integrating cybersecurity measures into emerging technologies. It emphasizes the need for tighter integration with existing frameworks like ISO and NIST CSF to ensure uniform implementation across financial institutions.

Despite heavy reliance on cloud technology, many firms plan to maintain or reduce security spending, underestimating the need for robust cloud security practices. Third-party security risks and supply chain management are major concerns, highlighting the need for firms to prioritize and upskill in cloud security.

93.file_desc:
Financial services companies are prioritizing emerging technologies like cloud computing, AI, and digital identity, but must also address associated cyber risks. They need to strengthen cybersecurity capabilities, align technology priorities with security, and ensure proper metrics and talent to manage risks effectively.
This page discusses ten emerging technologies, including next-generation software development, trust architectures, industrialized machine learning, Web3, advanced connectivity, quantum technologies, future of mobility, and immersive-reality technologies. It highlights their potential impacts on various industries and presents a survey result showing that cloud and edge computing are the most applicable trends in financial services, followed by applied AI.
Financial institutions are focusing on emerging technologies like cloud and edge computing to enhance automation, scalability, and cost savings. They are prioritizing investments in DevOps and AI while considering the maturity and applicability of each technology. Cloud computing is the most mature technology, with 84% of respondents recognizing its relevance and 60% having more than 25% of their workload in the cloud.
This page discusses the growing adoption of applied AI in financial services, highlighting its potential value and the evolving maturity of AI technologies. It emphasizes the promise and risks of generative AI, estimating its economic impact and the need for responsible implementation. The text also touches on the benefits of next-gen software development and the importance of trust architecture in the industry.
The page discusses the adoption of digital identity and trust architecture in financial services, highlighting benefits like faster innovation and stronger asset protection. It also explores emerging technologies like quantum computing and their potential impact on the industry, emphasizing the need for secure digital footprints and identity-related capabilities.
Financial services organizations recognize the need to increase spending on key technologies like industrialized machine learning, next-gen software development, and applied AI. More than half of respondents believe they should invest more in these areas, with cloud and edge computing also receiving significant attention. This trend is expected to accelerate as technologies mature and proliferate.
Emerging technologies bring significant benefits but also amplify existing cyber risks. Financial institutions face increasing cyberattacks from well-funded criminals using advanced technologies like AI. Cyber incidents are rising in frequency and severity, necessitating robust risk management strategies. The 2024 CrowdStrike report highlights eCrime as the most pervasive threat, with data-theft extortion on the rise. Companies must stay vigilant and consider various cyber risks, including AI, talent management, and supply chain security.
The page discusses the increasing frequency and severity of cyberattacks on financial services organizations from 2007 to 2023, highlighting major incidents and their impacts. It emphasizes the need for robust cybersecurity strategies and skilled talent to mitigate risks as companies adopt new technologies.
This page discusses the top cyber risks for financial services organizations over the next 3–5 years, highlighting cyber attacks, emerging technology misuse, and talent management as key concerns. It emphasizes the regulatory risks associated with AI and the importance of building strong cybersecurity capabilities to secure technologies and protect environments. The text also addresses the risks of next-gen software development and trust architecture, zero-trust architecture implementation, and the need for organizations to understand both the benefits and risks of new technologies.
This page highlights the strategic importance of digital transformation, emphasizing investment in emerging technologies like cloud and AI. It underscores the critical need for managing cyber and technology risks to ensure service resilience, build customer trust, and protect the bank's safety and soundness.
Financial institutions face pressure to keep pace with emerging technologies and worry about inadequate cybersecurity investments. Surveyed companies identified weaknesses in third-party management and metrics/reporting, critical for deploying new technologies. Enhancing these capabilities is essential to mitigate cyber risks and align with risk appetites.
This page outlines McKinsey's cybersecurity capability model, detailing eight domains and their sub-domains, including strategy, governance, architecture, operations, identity management, resilience, data privacy, and physical security.
Financial services organizations recognize the need to improve technical capabilities, particularly in third-party security, metrics and reporting, and privileged access management. New regulations emphasize the importance of better reporting and governance of cybersecurity risks. Companies must develop robust processes for measuring and managing risks associated with emerging technologies and vulnerabilities.
This page discusses the importance of proper PAM, secure cloud infrastructure, and data life cycle management in financial services. It highlights the risks associated with emerging technologies like AI and next-gen software development, emphasizing the need for robust security measures to prevent data exposure and optimize technology benefits.
Financial services organizations are struggling to keep up with the rapid pace of cybersecurity adoption. Increased compliance with regulations and defense against threats are key factors driving maturity. Companies recognize critical underinvestment in cybersecurity, with 70% of respondents acknowledging underspending. Proactive compliance and future-proofing technologies are essential for addressing emerging regulations.
Financial services organizations prioritize compliance and security against threats as key drivers for maturing cybersecurity capabilities. Increased compliance and security protection are the top factors, with 70% of respondents citing these. Business drivers and competitive differentiation follow. Cybersecurity spending is expected to rise, with regional banks seeing the largest growth. Special initiatives are needed to address emerging technology risks.
This page discusses the importance of developing standards for integrating cybersecurity measures into emerging technologies. It emphasizes the need for tighter integration with existing frameworks like ISO and NIST CSF to ensure uniform implementation across financial institutions.
Financial institutions are increasingly adopting cloud and edge computing but are not adequately investing in cloud security. Despite heavy reliance on cloud technology, many firms plan to maintain or reduce security spending, underestimating the need for robust cloud security practices. Third-party security risks and supply chain management are major concerns, highlighting the need for firms to prioritize and upskill in cloud security.
The page discusses the increasing cybersecurity spend relative to IT budgets among US regional banks, particularly Tier 2 banks. It highlights the challenges financial services companies face in attracting and retaining skilled cybersecurity talent, emphasizing the need for upskilling existing talent and exploring technology solutions like AI to address capability gaps.
The page discusses cybersecurity measures and strategies for addressing security gaps in top tech trends, showing that a significant percentage of respondents plan to use special initiatives and internal resources to secure emerging technologies.
Financial institutions must future-proof their environment by aligning technology priorities with security capabilities, establishing transparent metrics, investing in the right technologies, and addressing talent gaps. This involves assessing third-party risks, monitoring performance, and building cybersecurity capabilities to handle emerging risks.
The appendix details the methodology of a 2023 survey involving 37 global financial services firms, categorized by geography, market focus, revenue size, and supervisory classification. Insights are derived from diverse institutions, including asset managers, banks, and insurers, with revenue ranges from under $30 billion to over $90 billion. The survey structure is informed by cybersecurity frameworks and industry trends.
